name: Computer Science
tagline: Every BSc and MSc CSE course, explained like a friend would.
description: One lesson per university course, from your first C program to your MSc thesis. Each one tells you what it is, why it matters, how it works and where you see it in real life.

messages.welcome: Hey! Forget the heavy textbooks for a bit. We'll go through the whole CSE degree one course at a time, with simple words and real examples.
messages.comeback: Your next course is waiting. Just read the first paragraph, that's all. You'll want to keep going.
messages.pass: Nice! You actually get this course now, not just the name.
messages.fail: No worries, even toppers miss questions. Read the explanations, look at the lesson again and try once more.
messages.finished: You just walked through the whole BSc and MSc in CSE: programming, math, hardware, systems, networks, AI and the future tech. Pick the course you liked most and build one small project with it.

lessons.title: Introduction to Computer Systems
lessons.content:
What is it? This is the "hello, computer" course. It shows you what a computer really is: a machine that takes input, processes it, stores it and gives you output. Think of a kitchen. The ingredients are the input, the cook is the processor, the fridge is storage, and the plate of food is the output. A computer does the same thing, just with data and millions of times faster.

Why learn it? Every other CSE course stands on this one. When you later study programming, operating systems or networks, you will keep coming back to words like CPU, RAM, bit and byte. If these feel clear and friendly from day one, the rest of the degree feels much less scary. It also helps in normal life: you will know why your phone gets slow, what "8 GB RAM" means and which laptop is worth buying.

What's inside the course? Usually: the parts of a computer (hardware), the programs that run on it (software), number systems like binary, how data is stored in bits and bytes, a quick history of computers, the basics of operating systems, networks and the internet, and a first look at problem solving with flowcharts and algorithms.

Hardware: These are the parts you can touch. The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the brain that does the thinking. RAM is the desk where work happens right now: fast, but it forgets everything when the power goes off. Storage like a hard disk or SSD is the cupboard: slower, but it keeps your files for years. Input devices (keyboard, mouse, camera, mic) bring data in, and output devices (screen, speaker, printer) send results out. All these parts sit on a big board called the motherboard, which works like the roads of a city, carrying data between them. There is also a small, very fast memory inside the CPU called cache, which keeps the things the CPU needs most often right next to it, like keeping your pen in your hand instead of in your bag.

Software: These are the instructions that tell hardware what to do. System software like Windows, Android or Linux manages the machine. Application software like Facebook, MS Word or a game does a job for you. Without software, hardware is just an expensive box. Without hardware, software has nowhere to run. They need each other, like a body and a mind.

Binary and number systems: Computers only understand two states: current on or off, written as 1 and 0. One 0-or-1 is called a bit. Eight bits make one byte, enough to store one English letter. Then 1024 bytes make a kilobyte, 1024 KB a megabyte, 1024 MB a gigabyte. In binary, 5 is written 101 (that is 4 + 0 + 1). You also meet octal (base 8) and hexadecimal (base 16), which are just shorter ways to write long binary numbers. Converting is easy once you see the trick. To turn 13 into binary, keep dividing by 2 and write down the remainders: 13 gives 1, 6 gives 0, 3 gives 1, 1 gives 1. Read them from bottom to top and you get 1101. To check, add the place values: 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13.

How data is stored: Everything becomes numbers. A letter gets a code number (in ASCII, capital A is 65). A photo is millions of tiny dots called pixels, each stored as red, green and blue numbers. A song is a long list of numbers measuring the sound wave many thousands of times a second. So when you say "a 3 MB photo", you mean about 3 million bytes of numbers.

The fetch-execute cycle: The CPU works in a simple loop. It fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it to understand what it says, executes it, then moves to the next one. A CPU running at 3 GHz can do this kind of tick about 3 billion times every second. That is why computers feel instant even though each single step is tiny.

Operating system and networks: The operating system is the manager. It decides which app gets the CPU, gives memory to each program and keeps files organised in folders. Networks connect computers so they can share data. The internet is simply a giant network of networks, and every device on it has an address, called an IP address, so data knows where to go. When you type a website name like google.com, a system called DNS works like a phone book and finds its IP address for you. The data then travels in small pieces called packets, which may take different roads and get put back together in the right order when they arrive.

Real life example 1: Sending money on bKash. You type the number and amount (input). The app checks your balance and the CPU does the calculation (processing). Your transaction is saved in the phone and on bKash's servers (storage). You see "Send Money Successful" on the screen (output). Every single step of the input-process-storage-output model is right there in a 10-second action.

Real life example 2: Why your phone hangs with too many apps open. Each open app sits in RAM, the desk. If the desk is full, the phone has to move things back and forth between RAM and storage, which is much slower. Closing a few apps, or buying a phone with more RAM, gives you a bigger desk, and everything feels smooth again.

Where everyone gets confused / exam questions: Students often mix up RAM and storage. RAM is temporary and fast, storage is permanent and slower. Another mix-up: a bit and a byte are not the same, 8 bits make 1 byte. Common exam questions are: draw the block diagram of a computer, convert a number between decimal and binary, explain the difference between hardware and software, and list the types of memory.

After this course you will understand what is inside any computer, read a laptop spec sheet without confusion, and speak the basic language of CSE. Next you move to Structured Programming, where you finally start telling the computer what to do yourself.
key_points: A computer takes input, processes it, stores it and gives output.
The CPU is the brain; RAM is fast but temporary; storage keeps data after power off.
Computers use binary: a bit is 0 or 1, and 8 bits make one byte.
Everything (letters, photos, songs) is stored as numbers.
Software tells hardware what to do; the operating system manages everything.
The CPU runs a fetch-decode-execute loop billions of times per second.
lessons.tip: Open your phone or laptop settings and find the 'About' page. Match every word you see there (RAM, storage, processor) with what you learned. Real things stick better than definitions.
lessons.task: Pick any app you use daily, like bKash or YouTube. Write down one example each of input, processing, storage and output in that app.

quiz.q: Which part of a computer is often called its brain?
quiz.explain: The CPU does the actual processing and follows instructions, so it is called the brain of the computer.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between RAM and storage?
options: RAM is fast and temporary, storage keeps data even after power off
Storage is where the CPU does its math
quiz.explain: RAM is the fast work desk that is cleared when power goes off. Storage like an SSD keeps your files for later.

quiz.q: How many bits make one byte?
quiz.explain: One byte is 8 bits. Each bit is a single 0 or 1.

lessons.title: Structured Programming (C)
lessons.content:
What is it? This is usually your first real programming course, and the language is C. Structured programming means writing a program in a clean, top-to-bottom way using three simple building blocks: steps in order (sequence), choices (if-else) and repeats (loops). No random jumping around. It is like writing a recipe so clearly that even a robot who knows nothing could cook the dish.

Why learn it? C is the grandfather of many languages. C++, Java, C# and even parts of Python borrow its style. Operating systems like Linux, the firmware inside your microwave and many game engines are written in C. Learning C teaches you how the computer actually handles memory, which makes you a much stronger programmer later in any language. Almost every later course, from Data Structures to Operating Systems, assumes you are comfortable with it.

What's inside the course? Variables and data types, input and output, operators, if-else and switch, loops (for, while, do-while), functions, arrays, strings, pointers, structures, and reading and writing files. You also learn how to compile a program and how to find and fix bugs.

Variables and data types: A variable is a labelled box that holds a value. In C you must say what kind of value goes in the box. int holds whole numbers like 25, float holds decimals like 3.5, char holds one character like 'A'. Example: int age = 20; means "make a box called age and put 20 in it". Choosing the right type matters, because an int cannot hold 3.5 properly. Each type also takes a fixed amount of memory. On most computers an int uses 4 bytes and can hold numbers up to about 2 billion, while a char uses only 1 byte. If you store a number that is too big, it overflows and wraps around to a strange value, which is a very real bug in real programs.

Sequence, selection and loops: Sequence means steps run one after another, top to bottom. Selection means choosing: if (marks >= 80) print "A+"; else print "Keep trying". Loops mean repeating: for (i = 1; i <= 10; i++) print i; prints 1 to 10 without writing ten lines. With just these three blocks you can, in theory, write any program in the world. That is the big idea of structured programming.

Functions: A function is a small named machine that does one job. You write it once and call it whenever you need it. For example, a function square(x) returns x * x, so square(4) gives 16. Functions keep code short, readable and reusable. A big program is just many small functions working together, like players in a cricket team each doing their own role. Every C program starts from a special function called main(). C also gives you ready-made library functions: printf() shows output, scanf() reads input and sqrt() finds a square root. A function can even call itself; this is called recursion, and factorial(n) = n × factorial(n - 1) is the classic first example.

Arrays and strings: An array is a row of boxes with the same type, numbered from 0. int marks[5]; makes five boxes, marks[0] to marks[4]. It is perfect for storing the marks of 5 students. A string in C is just an array of characters ending with a special '\0' character, so "Dhaka" is stored as D, h, a, k, a and then '\0'.

Pointers: This is the topic everyone fears, but the idea is simple. Every variable lives at an address in memory, like every house has a house number. A pointer is a variable that stores that address instead of a normal value. If p points to age, then *p means "go to that address and look at the value", which gives 20. Pointers let functions change your original variables and let you build flexible structures later.

Structures and files: A struct groups different types together, like a student record with name (string), roll (int) and CGPA (float). Files let your program save data on the disk so it is still there tomorrow, using functions like fopen, fprintf and fclose. Without files, everything disappears when the program ends.

Real life example 1: A result calculator for your class. The program reads marks for 40 students using a loop, stores them in an array, uses a function to turn each mark into a grade with if-else (80+ is A+, 70+ is A, and so on), then counts how many got A+. Every main topic of the course appears in this one small program.

Real life example 2: A shop's billing machine. The cashier types each item's price, a loop keeps adding until they press 0, the total is calculated, VAT is added with a simple formula and the receipt is printed. Many simple shop machines and older systems run code written in exactly this C style.

Where everyone gets confused / exam questions: Arrays start at index 0, not 1, so the last element of a 5-element array is index 4. Writing = (assignment) instead of == (comparison) inside an if is a classic bug. Forgetting the & in scanf("%d", &x) crashes programs. Exam questions often ask you to trace output of a loop, write a program for factorial, prime check, Fibonacci or reverse a string, and explain call by value versus call by reference using pointers.

After this course you can write real working programs, think in clear steps and read error messages without panic. Next comes Object Oriented Programming, where you organise bigger code, and Data Structures, where you store data smartly.
key_points: Structured programming uses three blocks: sequence, selection (if-else) and loops.
Variables are typed boxes: int, float, char and more.
Functions are reusable mini-machines that do one job.
Arrays store many values of one type, starting from index 0.
A pointer stores a memory address, not a normal value.
Structs group related data; files keep data after the program ends.
lessons.tip: Type every example yourself instead of copy-pasting. Your fingers learn the syntax, and the errors you make teach you more than the book.
lessons.task: On paper, write the steps for a program that reads a student's marks and prints A, B, C or F. Use if-else for the grades and a loop to do it for 5 students.

quiz.q: What are the three building blocks of structured programming?
quiz.explain: Structured programs are built only from steps in order, choices and repeats, which keeps them easy to read.

quiz.q: What does a pointer in C store?
quiz.explain: A pointer holds the address of where some data lives in memory, like a house address.

quiz.q: Why is a function useful?
options: You can reuse the same code again and again by calling it
It makes the program run without a CPU
quiz.explain: A function packs a task into one named block, so you call it whenever needed instead of rewriting the code.

lessons.title: Discrete Mathematics
lessons.content:
What is it? Discrete maths is the maths of separate, countable things: people, phones, cities, true or false. Not smooth curves, but steps and pieces. It is the maths computers love, because computers also work with separate things: 0 or 1, yes or no. Think of counting stairs instead of measuring a smooth slide.

Why learn it? This is the language of computer science. Logic helps you write correct if-conditions. Sets help you understand databases. Counting helps you estimate how many passwords exist. Graphs are behind Google Maps and Facebook friend suggestions. Proofs help you be sure an algorithm really works. Algorithms, Theory of Computation, Databases and Networks all lean on this course.

What's inside the course? Propositional logic, sets, relations and functions, counting (permutations and combinations), proof techniques including induction, recurrence relations, graphs and trees, and sometimes a little number theory and Boolean algebra.

Logic: A proposition is a sentence that is either true or false, like "It is raining". We combine them with AND, OR and NOT. "It is raining AND I have an umbrella" is true only if both are true. A truth table lists every combination. The tricky one is IF-THEN: "If it rains, the road gets wet" is only false when it rains and the road stays dry. This exact logic runs inside every if-statement you write. Two sentences can look different but mean the same thing. De Morgan's law says NOT (A AND B) is the same as (NOT A) OR (NOT B). So "it is not true that I have both a pen and a pencil" means "I am missing a pen, or I am missing a pencil". Programmers use this trick all the time to simplify conditions.

Sets: A set is a collection of distinct things, like {red, green, blue}. Union (A ∪ B) means everything in either set. Intersection (A ∩ B) means things in both. If A is students who play cricket and B is students who play football, A ∩ B is students who play both. Databases use these same ideas when you search or join tables.

Relations and functions: A relation connects items from one set to another, like "student takes course". A function is a special relation where every input has exactly one output, like "student to roll number". Each student has one roll, so that is a function. These ideas show up later in programming functions and database keys.

Counting: How many ways can things happen? Permutation means order matters: arranging 3 friends in a row gives 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 ways. Combination means order does not matter: picking 11 players from 15 for a team is C(15, 11) = 1365 ways. Counting tells you, for example, that a 4-digit PIN has 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 10,000 possibilities, which is why banks lock you out after a few wrong tries. Another simple but powerful idea is the pigeonhole principle. If 13 people are in a room, at least two of them must share a birth month, because there are only 12 months. It sounds obvious, but it helps prove surprising things, like why any compression program cannot make every possible file smaller.

Proofs and induction: A proof is a step-by-step argument that something is always true. Mathematical induction is like falling dominoes. Show the first domino falls (base case). Show that if any domino falls, the next one falls too (inductive step). Then all of them fall. This is how you prove things like "1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2" for every n.

Recurrences: A recurrence defines something using smaller versions of itself. Fibonacci is the famous one: F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2), starting 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. Recurrences describe how recursive programs behave and how much time divide-and-conquer algorithms take.

Graphs and trees: A graph is dots (nodes) joined by lines (edges). Cities joined by roads, people joined by friendships, web pages joined by links. A tree is a graph with no loops, like a family tree or folders on your computer. Questions like "shortest path from Dhaka to Sylhet" or "who is the most connected person" are graph questions. Each dot has a degree, the number of lines touching it. An Euler path walks over every edge exactly once; the famous Königsberg bridge puzzle asked whether you could cross all seven bridges of a city once each, and Euler proved you could not. That puzzle is where graph theory was born.

Real life example 1: Facebook's "People You May Know". Facebook stores friendships as a graph. If you and Rahim are not friends but you share 25 mutual friends, the graph shows a short path between you, so Facebook suggests him. That is graph theory plus counting, working every day on your phone.

Real life example 2: Picking a cricket team. The selectors have 15 players and need 11. Since order does not matter, that is a combination: 1365 possible teams. If they also need to choose a captain and vice-captain from those 11, that part is a permutation, because who is captain and who is vice-captain matters.

Where everyone gets confused / exam questions: Students mix up permutation and combination. Ask yourself, "does order matter?" If yes, permutation. If no, combination. Many also get IF-THEN truth tables wrong. Common exam questions: build a truth table, prove a statement by induction, count arrangements, solve a recurrence, find paths or degrees in a graph, and check whether a relation is reflexive, symmetric or transitive.

After this course you will think more precisely, spot logical mistakes and model real problems as sets, graphs and counting questions. Next, use these tools in Data Structures, Algorithms and Theory of Computation.
key_points: Discrete maths studies separate, countable things, just like computers do.
Logic (AND, OR, NOT, IF-THEN) is the base of every program condition.
Permutation: order matters. Combination: order does not.
Proof by induction works like falling dominoes.
Graphs model networks of friends, roads and web pages.
Recurrences describe things defined by smaller versions of themselves.
lessons.tip: Draw everything. Sets as circles, graphs as dots and lines, logic as truth tables. A drawing makes a scary formula look friendly.
lessons.task: Draw a graph of 6 of your friends or family: dots for people, lines if they know each other. Who has the most lines? That person is the most 'connected' node.

quiz.q: Why is discrete maths important for computer science?
options: It is used for drawing pictures
Computers work with separate values like 0 and 1, just like discrete maths
quiz.explain: Computers deal with separate, countable values, and discrete maths is exactly the maths of such things.

quiz.q: Picking 11 players from 15, where order does not matter, is a...
quiz.explain: When order does not matter, it is a combination. If order mattered, it would be a permutation.

quiz.q: Proof by induction is often compared to...
quiz.explain: Show the first case is true and that each case leads to the next, and like dominoes, all cases fall into place.

lessons.title: Calculus & Differential Equations
lessons.content:
What is it? Calculus is the maths of change. It answers two big questions: how fast is something changing right now (derivatives), and how much has piled up over time (integrals). Differential equations are rules that describe how something changes, like "a population grows faster when it is bigger". If arithmetic is a photo, calculus is a video.

Why learn it? Things in the real world keep changing: speed, temperature, money, battery level. Calculus gives you tools to describe and predict that change. In CSE it is the engine behind machine learning, computer graphics, physics in games, signal processing and simulations. When an AI "learns", it is literally using derivatives to improve itself step by step.

What's inside the course? Functions and limits, derivatives and their rules, applications like finding maximum and minimum, integrals and area, sometimes series, partial derivatives for functions of many variables, and first-order and second-order ordinary differential equations.

Limits: A limit asks, "what value does this get closer and closer to?" If you keep walking half the remaining distance to a wall, you get closer and closer to it, and the limit is the wall. Limits are the foundation that makes derivatives and integrals exact rather than rough guesses. For example, as x gets bigger and bigger, 1/x gets closer and closer to 0 but never actually reaches it, so we say the limit of 1/x as x goes to infinity is 0. A function is called continuous when you can draw it without lifting your pen, and limits are exactly how mathematicians check that.

Derivatives: The derivative is the rate of change at one moment. Your speedometer shows a derivative: how fast your position is changing right now. For f(x) = x², the derivative is 2x, so at x = 3 the curve is rising at a rate of 6. Rules like the power rule, product rule and chain rule let you find derivatives quickly without drawing anything. The chain rule handles functions inside functions. If y = (3x + 1)², think of the outside part (something squared) and the inside part (3x + 1). Take the derivative of the outside, 2(3x + 1), then multiply by the derivative of the inside, 3. The answer is 6(3x + 1). Like peeling an onion, layer by layer.

Maximum and minimum: Where a curve reaches its highest or lowest point, the derivative becomes 0, because the curve is flat there for a moment. This is how you solve real problems like "what price gives the most profit?" or "what box size uses the least material?". Set the derivative to 0, solve, and check.

Integrals: An integral adds up tiny pieces to find a total. If you know your speed every second, integrating gives the total distance travelled. Geometrically, it is the area under a curve. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says integration and differentiation are opposites, like zipping and unzipping a bag. A simple example: the integral of 2x from 0 to 3 is x² from 0 to 3, which is 9 - 0 = 9. That is exactly the area of the triangle under the line y = 2x between 0 and 3, because half of base 3 times height 6 is also 9. Two different methods, the same answer.

Partial derivatives: Real things depend on many inputs. A house price depends on size, location and age. A partial derivative asks, "how does the output change if I change just one input and freeze the rest?" Machine learning models with millions of inputs use exactly this idea to know which knob to turn.

Differential equations: A differential equation connects a quantity with its own rate of change. dy/dt = ky means "the bigger y is, the faster it grows", which describes population growth, compound interest and viruses spreading. A cooling cup of tea follows Newton's law of cooling, another differential equation. Solving it tells you what happens over time. The solution of dy/dt = ky is y = y₀ e^(kt), the famous exponential growth curve. If k is negative, it becomes exponential decay instead, which describes a medicine leaving your blood or a phone battery slowly losing its health. Second-order equations describe things that swing back and forth, like a pendulum or a spring.

Real life example 1: Google Maps estimating arrival time. Your phone knows your position at each moment. The change in position over time is your speed, a derivative. Adding up expected speeds along the route is like integrating, which gives total travel time. When traffic jams in Farmgate slow you down, the estimate updates.

Real life example 2: How an AI learns, called gradient descent. Imagine standing on a foggy hill and wanting to reach the lowest valley. You feel the slope under your feet (the derivative) and take a small step downhill. Repeat many times and you reach the bottom. An AI model does the same: the "hill" is its error, and derivatives tell it which way to adjust to make fewer mistakes.

Where everyone gets confused / exam questions: Many students memorise rules but forget the meaning: derivative is rate of change, integral is total or area. People also forget the "+ C" in indefinite integrals and mess up the chain rule. Exam questions usually include: find derivatives, find maximum or minimum, evaluate integrals, find area under a curve and solve simple differential equations.

After this course you can describe and predict change mathematically, which you will use in Numerical Methods, Machine Learning, Graphics and Signal Processing. Next, pair it with Linear Algebra, the other big maths tool of CSE.
key_points: Calculus is the maths of change.
A derivative is the rate of change right now, like a speedometer.
An integral adds tiny pieces to get a total, like area or distance.
Max and min happen where the derivative is zero.
Differential equations describe how things change over time.
Machine learning uses derivatives in gradient descent to improve.
lessons.tip: Always ask 'what is changing, and with respect to what?' Once you say it in words, the formula becomes much easier to set up.
lessons.task: Note your phone battery percentage every 10 minutes for an hour while using it. How much does it drop per minute? You just calculated a rate of change, a derivative in real life.

quiz.q: A speedometer showing your speed right now is an example of a...
quiz.explain: A derivative tells how fast something changes at one moment, exactly what a speedometer shows.

quiz.q: What does an integral do?
options: Adds up tiny pieces to find a total
quiz.explain: An integral collects many small pieces to give a total, like total distance travelled.

quiz.q: Where is calculus used in machine learning?
options: Gradient descent uses derivatives to improve the model
It is not used at all
quiz.explain: Gradient descent uses derivatives to find which way to adjust a model so its error goes down.

lessons.title: Electrical Circuits
lessons.content:
What is it? This course is about how electricity flows through wires and parts like resistors, capacitors and inductors. Every computer is, deep down, a giant electric circuit, so CSE students learn the basics of how current moves. Think of electricity like water in pipes: voltage is the pressure, current is how much water flows, and resistance is how narrow the pipe is.

Why learn it? If you want to understand hardware, build robots, work with Arduino or IoT, or simply know why your charger gets hot, you need these basics. Later courses like Electronic Devices, Digital Logic Design, Microprocessors and Embedded Systems all build on this one. Even software engineers benefit from knowing what really happens inside the machine.

What's inside the course? Voltage, current, resistance and power, Ohm's law, series and parallel circuits, Kirchhoff's laws, methods to analyse circuits (nodal and mesh analysis, Thevenin's theorem), capacitors and inductors, and the basics of AC versus DC.

Voltage, current and resistance: Voltage (V, measured in volts) is the push. Current (I, in amperes) is the flow of charge. Resistance (R, in ohms) is how much a part resists the flow. A thin pipe lets less water through, and a high resistance lets less current through. Power (P = V × I, in watts) tells how much energy is used per second. You measure these with a multimeter. Voltage is measured across a part, by touching both of its ends, and current is measured through a part, by putting the meter in the path of the flow. Mixing these up is a classic lab mistake, and putting a meter set to current directly across a battery can blow its fuse.

Ohm's law: The most famous formula of the course is V = I × R. If a 10 ohm resistor has 5 volts across it, current = 5 / 10 = 0.5 A. With just this one formula you can solve a huge number of simple circuit problems. Remember it like a triangle: cover the one you want, and the other two tell you how to find it.

Series and parallel: In series, parts are in one line, so the same current goes through all of them and resistances add: 2 Ω + 3 Ω = 5 Ω. If one breaks, everything stops, like old fairy lights. In parallel, each part gets its own path and the same voltage. If one breaks, the others keep working. That is why your house is wired in parallel.

Kirchhoff's laws: KCL (current law) says the current going into a junction equals the current coming out, just like water at a pipe joint: nothing disappears. KVL (voltage law) says if you go around any closed loop, all the voltage rises and drops add up to zero. These two laws let you solve complicated circuits where Ohm's law alone is not enough. Here is a tiny KCL example: if 5 A flows into a junction and 2 A leaves through one wire, then 3 A must leave through the other wire. For KVL: a 12 V battery with two resistors in a loop, one dropping 8 V, means the other must drop exactly 4 V, because the rises and drops must balance.

Circuit analysis tricks: Nodal analysis uses KCL at each junction. Mesh analysis uses KVL around each loop. Thevenin's theorem says any messy circuit, seen from two points, can be replaced by one voltage source and one resistor. It is like replacing a whole complicated water system with one tank and one pipe that behaves the same from the outside.

Capacitors, inductors and AC/DC: A capacitor stores energy in an electric field, like a tiny bucket that fills and empties fast. Your camera flash uses one. An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field and resists sudden changes in current. DC (direct current) flows in one direction, like a battery. AC (alternating current) keeps switching direction, 50 times a second in Bangladesh, and that is what comes from the wall socket. A capacitor in a circuit with a resistor does not charge instantly; it fills up along a curve, and the product R × C, called the time constant, tells you how fast. That is why a camera flash needs a few seconds before it is ready again. Inductors are used in transformers and chargers to step voltage up or down.

Real life example 1: Your room's wiring. The fan, the light and the phone charger are connected in parallel. Each gets the full 220 V from the line. When one bulb fuses, the fan keeps running, because its own path is still complete. If they were in series, one dead bulb would switch off everything in the room.

Real life example 2: Your phone charger. It takes 220 V AC from the wall and converts it to about 5 V DC for the phone. Read the label: 5V 2A means it gives 5 × 2 = 10 watts of power. A "fast charger" labelled 9V 2A gives 18 watts, which is why it fills the battery faster.

Where everyone gets confused / exam questions: Students mix up series and parallel formulas. In series, resistances add. In parallel, 1/R total = 1/R1 + 1/R2, so the total is smaller than the smallest one. Signs in KVL also cause mistakes, so pick a direction and stick to it. Common exam questions: find current or voltage with Ohm's law, find total resistance, solve a circuit with KCL/KVL or mesh analysis, and find a Thevenin equivalent.

After this course you can read and solve basic circuits, understand chargers and wiring, and you are ready for Electronic Devices and Digital Logic Design, where these circuits start to "think".
key_points: Voltage is the push, current is the flow, resistance slows the flow.
Ohm's law: V = I × R. Power: P = V × I.
Series: same current, resistances add. Parallel: same voltage, separate paths.
KCL: current in = current out. KVL: voltages around a loop add to zero.
Capacitors store energy in electric fields; inductors in magnetic fields.
Wall sockets give AC; batteries and phones use DC.
lessons.tip: Use the water pipe picture for everything. When a formula confuses you, ask what the pressure, the flow and the narrow part are.
lessons.task: Look at a phone charger. Find the printed output, like 5V 2A. Use P = V x I to calculate its power in watts.

quiz.q: What is Ohm's law?
quiz.explain: Ohm's law says voltage equals current times resistance.

quiz.q: Why does the fan keep running when one bulb in your room fuses?
options: Because the fan has its own battery
Because house wiring is in parallel
quiz.explain: In parallel, each device has its own path, so one broken path does not stop the others.

quiz.q: Which one is AC?
options: The electricity from a wall socket
quiz.explain: Wall sockets give alternating current that switches direction many times a second. Batteries give DC.

lessons.title: Object Oriented Programming
lessons.content:
What is it? Object Oriented Programming, or OOP, is a way of organising code around "objects", just like the real world is full of objects. A car, a student, a bank account: each has data (what it has) and behaviour (what it can do). OOP courses usually use Java, C++ or Python. Instead of a long list of steps, you build a little world of objects that talk to each other.

Why learn it? Big programs with thousands of lines become a mess if everything is mixed together. OOP keeps related things together and hides details that others do not need. Android apps, games, banking software and most large company projects are built in an object oriented way. Job interviews almost always ask about the four pillars of OOP.

What's inside the course? Classes and objects, constructors, the four pillars (encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and abstraction), interfaces and abstract classes, method overloading and overriding, exception handling, and sometimes basic design patterns and file handling, usually in Java or C++.

Classes and objects: A class is a blueprint, and an object is a real thing made from it. "Student" is a class. You, with your name and roll, are an object of that class. One blueprint can make many objects: Rahim, Karim and Fatima are three Student objects, each with their own data. In code: Student s = new Student("Rahim", 101); Inside a class, data is stored in fields (also called attributes), like name and roll, and actions are written as methods, like study() or giveExam(). When you write s.study(), you are asking the object s to do its action. Each object keeps its own copy of the fields, so changing Rahim's CGPA does not touch Karim's.

Constructors: A constructor is a special method that runs automatically when an object is born. It sets the starting values. When you create new Student("Rahim", 101), the constructor puts "Rahim" in the name and 101 in the roll. It is like filling in a new admission form the moment a student joins.

Encapsulation: Encapsulation means keeping data private and only allowing changes through safe methods. A bank account's balance should not be changed directly by anyone. Instead you call deposit(500) or withdraw(200), and those methods check the rules, like "you cannot withdraw more than you have". It is like a medicine capsule: the inside is protected. In code we use access modifiers to control this. private means only the class itself can touch the data, public means anyone can use it, and protected means the class and its children can. A common pattern is a private field with public getter and setter methods, like getBalance(), where the setter can refuse bad values such as a negative balance.

Inheritance: Inheritance lets a new class reuse an existing one. A CSEStudent class can inherit from Student and automatically get name, roll and study(), then add its own extra things like writeCode(). This saves you from copying code. It is like a child inheriting the family surname and then building their own skills on top. Inheritance makes an "is-a" relationship: a CSEStudent is a Student, a Dog is an Animal. But be careful not to overuse it. When something just has another thing, like a Car has an Engine, it is better to put an Engine object inside the Car class. This is called composition, and good designers often prefer it.

Polymorphism: Polymorphism means "many forms": the same command, different behaviour. Call makeSound() on a Cat object and it says meow, on a Dog object it says woof. Overloading is another form: the same method name with different inputs, like add(2, 3) and add(2.5, 3.5). Your code stays simple because it can just say makeSound() without caring which animal it is. The magic behind this is that a parent type variable can hold a child object: Animal a = new Dog(); then a.makeSound() still says woof. The program decides at runtime which version to run, which is called dynamic binding. That is how a game can keep one list of enemies and call attack() on each, even though every enemy attacks differently.

Abstraction and interfaces: Abstraction means showing only what is needed and hiding the complicated parts. When you drive a car, you use the steering and brake without knowing how the engine burns fuel. In code, an abstract class or interface says "every Shape must have an area() method" without saying how. Circle and Rectangle each fill in their own formula.

Real life example 1: A ride app like Pathao. There is a Rider class and a Driver class, both inheriting from a User class (name, phone, rating). A Ride object holds the pickup, drop and fare. The fare is private and only changes through a calculateFare() method (encapsulation). Bike rides and car rides calculate fare differently but both answer calculateFare() (polymorphism).

Real life example 2: A school management system. A Person class has name and address. Teacher and Student inherit from it. Each has a getInfo() method, but a teacher shows their subject and a student shows their class. The principal's screen can loop through everyone and just call getInfo(), without caring who is who.

Where everyone gets confused / exam questions: Students mix up class and object (blueprint versus real thing), and overloading versus overriding. Overloading is the same name with different parameters in one class. Overriding is a child class replacing its parent's method. Also, encapsulation and abstraction sound similar: encapsulation protects data, abstraction hides complexity. Exam questions often ask you to explain the four pillars with examples, write a class with a constructor, and show inheritance and overriding in code.

After this course you can design programs like a real software engineer, splitting big problems into neat objects. Next, Data Structures teaches you how to store data efficiently inside those objects, and Software Engineering shows how teams design big object oriented systems.
key_points: A class is a blueprint; an object is a real thing made from it.
Constructors set up an object's starting values.
Encapsulation hides data and allows changes only through safe methods.
Inheritance lets a child class reuse and extend a parent class.
Polymorphism: the same command behaves differently for different objects.
Abstraction shows what is needed and hides the complicated details.
lessons.tip: Before coding, look around your room and turn things into classes on paper: what data does a fan have, and what can it do? This trains the OOP eye.
lessons.task: Design a 'Student' class on paper: list 4 pieces of data (like name, roll) and 3 actions (like study, giveExam). Then make a 'CSEStudent' class that inherits it and adds one new action.

quiz.q: What is the relationship between a class and an object?
options: A class is a blueprint, an object is made from it
A class is a type of loop
quiz.explain: A class describes what something should be like. An object is one real copy built from that description.

quiz.q: Hiding a bank balance and only allowing changes through safe methods is called...
quiz.explain: Encapsulation keeps data private and exposes only safe ways to use it.

quiz.q: A cat says meow and a dog says woof to the same 'makeSound' command. This is...
quiz.explain: Polymorphism means one command can behave differently depending on the object.

lessons.title: Data Structures
lessons.content:
What is it? A data structure is a way to arrange data so you can use it quickly. Just like you keep clothes in a wardrobe, books on a shelf and spices in a rack, programs keep data in different shapes depending on what they need to do with it. The same data arranged badly can make a program crawl; arranged well, it flies.

Why learn it? The right structure can make a program thousands of times faster. Facebook, Google and Daraz handle millions of things every second, and they manage it because they pick smart data structures. It is also the number one topic in programming job interviews and contests. Algorithms, Databases, Operating Systems and Compilers all assume you know it well.

What's inside the course? Arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees (especially binary search trees), heaps, hash tables and graphs, plus searching and sorting and Big O notation to measure how fast operations are.

Big O notation: Big O describes how running time grows as the data grows. O(1) means constant time: instant, no matter the size. O(n) means time grows with the size, like checking every item in a list. O(log n) means very slow growth, like halving a phone book again and again. O(n²) means it gets slow fast: double the data and it takes four times longer. It helps you compare solutions before writing them.

Arrays: An array is a row of boxes side by side in memory. If you know the position, you get the item instantly, in O(1). But inserting in the middle is slow, because everything after it has to shift, like squeezing someone into the middle of a packed bench.

Linked lists: In a linked list each item holds its data and a pointer to the next item, like a treasure hunt where each clue tells you where the next one is. Inserting in the middle is easy, just change two pointers. But finding the 50th item means walking through 49 others first, which takes O(n). There are a few types. In a singly linked list each node only knows the next one. In a doubly linked list each node knows both the next and the previous, so you can walk backwards too, like your music player's previous and next buttons. In a circular linked list the last node points back to the first, which is handy for things that repeat in turns.

Stack: A stack is last in, first out (LIFO), like a pile of plates: you put on top and take from the top. Push adds, pop removes. The undo button in a text editor is a stack: your last action is undone first. Your browser's back button and function calls inside a program also use stacks.

Queue: A queue is first in, first out (FIFO), like the line at a bank counter: whoever came first is served first. Enqueue adds at the back, dequeue removes from the front. Printers, ticket booking systems and messaging apps use queues to handle requests fairly in order.

Trees and heaps: A tree has a root at the top and branches below, like a family tree or folders on your computer. In a binary search tree (BST), smaller values go left and bigger go right, so searching is like a guessing game: about O(log n). A heap is a special tree that always keeps the biggest (or smallest) value at the top, perfect for priority queues, like a hospital treating the most serious patient first. You can visit every node of a tree in different orders, called traversals. Inorder (left, root, right) visits the values of a BST in sorted order, which is a neat trick. Preorder (root first) is useful for copying a tree, and postorder (root last) is useful for deleting one, because you clean up the children before the parent.

Hash tables and graphs: A hash table uses a key to jump straight to the value, like finding a word in a dictionary using its first letter, but even faster: usually O(1). Your phone's contact search and Python dictionaries use it. Graphs are nodes connected by edges, used for maps, social networks and routes. Searching them uses BFS (level by level) and DFS (go deep first).

Real life example 1: Google Maps finding a route. Every junction is a node, every road is an edge with a travel time. The app stores the city as a graph and uses a priority queue (a heap) inside Dijkstra's algorithm to find the fastest route from Mohakhali to Motijheel in a fraction of a second.

Real life example 2: Daraz's shopping cart and order processing. Your cart is like a list you can add to and remove from. When thousands of orders arrive during an 11.11 sale, they wait in a queue so they are processed in order. Product lookup by ID uses a hash table so the page loads instantly even with millions of products.

Where everyone gets confused / exam questions: Students mix up stack (LIFO) and queue (FIFO). Remember plates versus a bank line. Many forget that a BST can become slow, O(n), if data arrives already sorted, which is why balanced trees like AVL exist. Exam questions often ask you to trace push/pop operations, insert values into a BST, perform tree traversals (inorder, preorder, postorder), find time complexity, and run BFS or DFS on a graph.

After this course you can choose the right structure for any problem and explain why it is fast. Next comes Algorithms, where you use these structures to solve problems in the smartest possible way.
key_points: A data structure arranges data so it can be used efficiently.
Big O shows how running time grows as data grows.
Stack is LIFO (plates); queue is FIFO (bank line).
Arrays give instant access by index; linked lists make insertion easy.
Binary search trees and heaps speed up searching and priorities.
Hash tables give near-instant lookup; graphs model maps and networks.
lessons.tip: Draw boxes and arrows for every operation: push, pop, insert, delete. If you can draw it, you can code it.
lessons.task: Find three examples at home or outside of a stack, a queue and a tree. Write them down with one line each on why they fit.

quiz.q: The undo button in a text editor works like a...
quiz.explain: Undo removes the last action first, which is last in, first out, exactly a stack.

quiz.q: A line of people at a bank counter is a...
quiz.explain: Whoever comes first gets served first, which is first in, first out, a queue.

quiz.q: What does Big O notation describe?
options: How running time grows as the data grows
quiz.explain: Big O describes how the time or memory a program needs grows when the input gets bigger.

lessons.title: Digital Logic Design
lessons.content:
What is it? Digital Logic Design is the course about how a computer thinks using only two answers: yes or no, 1 or 0, ON or OFF. Think of a light switch in your room. It is either on or off, never "a little bit on". A computer is made of billions of tiny switches like that, and this course shows how you connect them to do maths, make decisions and even remember things.

Why learn it? Every single chip, from your phone's processor to the chip inside a washing machine, is built from logic circuits. If you want to understand how a computer really works under all the software, this is where it starts. It is also the base for Computer Architecture, Microprocessors, Embedded Systems and VLSI Design, so you will use it again and again.

What's in the course? The usual syllabus covers number systems (binary, octal, hexadecimal), Boolean algebra, logic gates, simplifying expressions with Karnaugh maps (K-maps), combinational circuits like adders and multiplexers, and sequential circuits like flip-flops, registers and counters.

Number systems: We count in base 10 because we have ten fingers. Computers count in base 2, using only 0 and 1. So 5 in binary is 101, because 1x4 + 0x2 + 1x1 = 5. Hexadecimal (base 16) is a short way to write long binary numbers: 1111 1111 in binary is just FF in hex, which is 255. You will convert between these a lot. To convert 13 to binary, keep dividing by 2 and write the remainders from bottom to top: 13 gives 1101. To go back, add the place values: 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13. Computers also use two's complement to store negative numbers, so -1 in 8 bits is 1111 1111.

Boolean algebra and logic gates: Boolean algebra is maths with only 0 and 1. The basic gates are AND, OR and NOT. An AND gate gives 1 only when both inputs are 1, like "I get ice cream only if I finish homework AND clean my room". An OR gate gives 1 if at least one input is 1. A NOT gate just flips the value: 1 becomes 0, 0 becomes 1. Other gates are NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR. XOR gives 1 only when the inputs are different.

Truth tables: A truth table lists every possible input and the output for each. With 2 inputs there are 4 rows (00, 01, 10, 11), with 3 inputs there are 8. For AND, only the 11 row gives 1. This is the most honest way to check a circuit: if the table is right, the circuit is right.

K-maps (Karnaugh maps): A K-map is a grid that helps you simplify Boolean expressions. You put the 1s from your truth table into the grid, then circle groups of 1s next to each other (groups of 1, 2, 4 or 8). Each group becomes one short term. A messy expression like AB + AB' becomes just A. Simpler expression means fewer gates, a cheaper chip and less power. The rows and columns are written in Gray code order (00, 01, 11, 10), so neighbouring cells differ by only one bit. That is the secret that lets a group cancel out a variable. Cells you don't care about, called don't-cares, can be counted as 1 if it makes a group bigger.

Combinational circuits: These circuits give an output that depends only on the current inputs, with no memory. A half adder adds two bits: sum = A XOR B, carry = A AND B. Chain full adders together and you can add big numbers. A multiplexer (MUX) is like a TV remote choosing one channel out of many inputs. A decoder turns a binary code into one active line, like lighting up the right segment on a digital clock.

Sequential circuits: These have memory. Their output depends on the inputs and on what happened before. The basic memory unit is a flip-flop, which can hold one bit. Types include SR, D, JK and T flip-flops. Put several flip-flops together and you get a register (stores a number) or a counter (counts clock pulses). A clock signal ticks like a heartbeat to keep everything in step. A D flip-flop is the easiest: on each clock tick, whatever is at D gets copied to the output and stays there until the next tick. A JK flip-flop can also toggle, flipping its value when both J and K are 1. Designers draw state diagrams to plan sequential circuits like traffic light controllers.

Real life example 1: think about a lift in a building in Dhaka. The door should close only if no one is blocking the sensor AND someone pressed a floor button. That is an AND gate with a NOT: close = (NOT blocked) AND button. The floor display that shows 1, 2, 3 uses a decoder, and the lift's memory of which floor it is on is stored in flip-flops. A whole lift controller is just a bigger version of what you learn here.

Real life example 2: a digital clock on a microwave. A crystal makes a steady clock signal. Counters made of flip-flops count seconds, then minutes, then hours. When the seconds counter reaches 59, logic gates detect it and reset it to 00 while adding 1 to the minutes. A decoder then drives the 7-segment display so you see the numbers.

Where people get stuck and what comes in exams: students often mix up combinational and sequential circuits. Remember: no memory means combinational, memory means sequential. Another common mistake is grouping K-map cells wrongly; groups must be rectangles of 1, 2, 4 or 8 and can wrap around the edges. Typical exam questions: convert numbers between bases, draw a truth table, simplify an expression with a K-map, design a half or full adder, and explain how a D or JK flip-flop works with its table.

After this course you can design small circuits on paper, simplify them, and understand how a computer adds numbers and stores bits. Next, Computer Architecture shows how these pieces join into a full CPU, and Microprocessors shows how to talk to one directly.
key_points: Computers work with only 0 and 1, like ON/OFF switches.
AND gives 1 only when both inputs are 1; OR gives 1 if any input is 1; NOT flips.
A truth table lists every input combination and its output.
K-maps simplify Boolean expressions so circuits need fewer gates.
Combinational circuits have no memory; sequential circuits remember using flip-flops.
A flip-flop stores one bit; registers and counters are built from flip-flops.
lessons.tip: Make a truth table for every circuit before you trust it. Write all input combinations and check each output. It catches mistakes fast.
lessons.task: Write the truth table for 'I go out if it is NOT raining AND my homework is done'. Two inputs, four rows.

quiz.q: An AND gate gives 1 when...
quiz.explain: AND outputs 1 only when all its inputs are 1.

quiz.q: Which circuit can remember a value?
quiz.explain: A flip-flop is a sequential circuit that stores one bit, the basic unit of memory.

quiz.q: What is a K-map used for?
quiz.explain: Karnaugh maps are a visual way to simplify Boolean expressions so the circuit needs fewer gates.

lessons.title: Electronic Devices & Circuits
lessons.content:
What is it? Electronic Devices & Circuits is the course about the tiny parts that make electronics work: diodes, transistors and the materials they are made of. If Digital Logic is about 1s and 0s, this course is about the real physical parts that create those 1s and 0s. Think of it as learning about bricks before you build a house.

Why learn it? Every phone, laptop, charger and LED bulb is full of these devices. A modern processor has billions of transistors. Knowing how they work helps you understand why chips get hot, why batteries drain, and how computers became so small. It is the base for Digital Logic hardware, Microprocessors, Embedded Systems, VLSI Design and IoT.

What's in the course? A typical syllabus covers semiconductors (silicon, doping, P-type and N-type), the PN junction diode, diode circuits like rectifiers, the bipolar junction transistor (BJT), the MOSFET, amplifiers, and basic operational amplifier (op-amp) circuits.

Semiconductors: Some materials let electricity flow easily (conductors like copper). Some block it (insulators like plastic). A semiconductor, like silicon, is in between: we can control how much current it lets through. We do that with doping, which means adding a tiny bit of another element. Adding extra electrons makes N-type silicon; creating "holes" (missing electrons) makes P-type silicon. Pure silicon has four outer electrons per atom. Adding phosphorus, which has five, gives one spare electron, so we get N-type. Adding boron, which has three, leaves a hole, so we get P-type. Only about one atom in a million needs to change to make a big difference.

The diode: Put P-type and N-type silicon together and you get a PN junction, which is a diode. A diode lets current flow in only one direction, like a one-way gate at a metro station. Forward bias (positive to P side) lets current pass after about 0.7 volts for silicon. Reverse bias blocks it. An LED is a special diode that gives off light when current flows.

Rectifiers: The electricity in your wall socket is AC: it keeps changing direction, 50 times a second in Bangladesh. Phones need DC, which flows in one direction. A rectifier uses diodes to flip or cut the backward half of the wave. A half-wave rectifier uses one diode; a full-wave bridge rectifier uses four. Then a capacitor smooths the bumps. That is exactly what your phone charger does inside.

Transistors (BJT): A transistor is a device with three legs that can work as a switch or an amplifier. In a BJT, a small current at the base controls a much bigger current between collector and emitter. Like a small tap controlling a big water pipe. Current gain (beta) tells how much bigger: if beta is 100, 1 mA at the base can control 100 mA. BJTs come in two types, NPN and PNP. A BJT has three working regions: cut-off (fully OFF), saturation (fully ON) and active (in between, where it amplifies). Used as a switch, it jumps between cut-off and saturation; used as an amplifier, it stays in the active region.

MOSFET: The MOSFET is the transistor used inside almost every modern chip. A voltage at its gate turns it ON or OFF, using almost no current. That is why billions fit in a processor without melting it. In a chip, the transistor's main job is to act as a tiny switch: ON means 1, OFF means 0. CMOS logic pairs two kinds of MOSFETs so that power is used mainly when switching. A MOSFET has a gate, a source and a drain. In an N-channel MOSFET, putting enough positive voltage on the gate (above the threshold voltage) opens a channel so current flows from drain to source. Because the gate is insulated, almost no current enters it, which saves a lot of power.

Amplifiers and op-amps: An amplifier makes a weak signal stronger, like a microphone signal made loud enough for a speaker. An op-amp is a ready-made amplifier chip. With a few resistors you can make it multiply a signal by a fixed number, add signals, or compare two voltages. In an inverting amplifier, the gain is -Rf / Rin. So with Rf = 10k and Rin = 1k, a 0.1V input becomes -1V. A comparator op-amp simply says which of two voltages is bigger, which is how a battery-low warning knows when to turn on.

Real life example 1: your mobile charger. The wall gives 220V AC. A transformer or switching circuit brings it down, diodes in a bridge rectifier turn it into one-way current, capacitors smooth it, and a regulator keeps it at a steady 5V. A small LED tells you it is plugged in. Every part you learn in this course is in that little box.

Real life example 2: a road light that turns on by itself at night. A light sensor gives a small signal. A transistor acts as a switch: when it gets dark, the sensor's signal changes, the transistor turns on and lets a bigger current flow to the lamp. Same idea as the automatic lights in many apartment stairs.

Where people get stuck and what comes in exams: students mix up forward and reverse bias, or think a diode never conducts in reverse (it can break down at high reverse voltage, and Zener diodes use this on purpose). Many also forget that a transistor is both a switch and an amplifier depending on how you use it. Typical exam questions: explain P-type and N-type doping, draw diode I-V curves, design a bridge rectifier, find currents in a BJT circuit using beta, and explain how a MOSFET switch works.

After this course you will look at any gadget and know roughly what is happening inside. Next, Digital Logic and Computer Architecture show how millions of these switches become a working computer, and VLSI Design shows how they are packed onto a chip.
key_points: Silicon is a semiconductor; doping makes P-type and N-type material.
A diode lets current flow in only one direction; an LED is a diode that glows.
Rectifiers use diodes to turn AC from the wall into DC for gadgets.
A transistor can work as a switch or an amplifier.
Inside chips, MOSFET transistors act as tiny switches for 1s and 0s.
lessons.tip: Learn each device by its job first (one-way gate, switch, booster), then the formulas. Job first, maths second.
lessons.task: Find three LEDs in your home (charger light, TV standby light, router). Write what each one is telling you.

quiz.q: What does a diode do?
options: Lets current flow in only one direction
quiz.explain: A diode is a one-way gate for current, which is why it is used to turn AC into DC.

quiz.q: What is the transistor's main job inside a chip?
options: To act as a tiny switch
quiz.explain: Inside chips, transistors act as on/off switches, which make 0s and 1s.

quiz.q: What is silicon?
quiz.explain: Silicon is a semiconductor, so we can control whether it conducts, which is perfect for switches.

lessons.title: Linear Algebra
lessons.content:
What is it? Linear Algebra is the maths of lists and grids of numbers. A list of numbers is called a vector, and a grid of numbers in rows and columns is called a matrix. Think of a class marks sheet: each row is a student, each column is a subject. That whole sheet is a matrix.

Why learn it? Computers love grids of numbers. A photo is a matrix of brightness numbers. A 3D game moves objects using matrices. Google's early search ranking was built on linear algebra, and machine learning and AI do huge amounts of matrix multiplication every second. If you want to go into graphics, AI, data science or image processing, this course is a must.

What's in the course? A typical syllabus covers vectors, matrices and their operations, systems of linear equations, Gaussian elimination, determinants and inverses, vector spaces and basis, linear transformations, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

Vectors: A vector is a list of numbers, like (3, 4). You can think of it as an arrow: go 3 steps right and 4 steps up. Its length is the square root of 3x3 + 4x4, which is 5. You can add vectors (put arrows head to tail) and multiply them by a number to stretch them. The dot product of two vectors tells how much they point in the same direction.

Matrices and multiplication: A matrix is a grid of numbers in rows and columns. A 2x3 matrix has 2 rows and 3 columns. You can add matrices of the same size cell by cell. Multiplying matrices is special: each answer cell is a row times a column, multiplied pair by pair and added. To multiply A by B, the columns of A must equal the rows of B. Also, A times B is usually not the same as B times A. Example: [1 2; 3 4] times [5; 6] gives [1x5 + 2x6; 3x5 + 4x6] = [17; 39]. The identity matrix, with 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere, is like the number 1: multiplying by it changes nothing. The transpose flips rows into columns.

Systems of linear equations: Problems like "2x + y = 40 and x + 2y = 50" are linear equations. You can write them as a matrix times an unknown vector equals an answer vector: Ax = b. Gaussian elimination solves them step by step by turning the matrix into a staircase shape, then solving from the bottom up. Here x = 10 and y = 20. Step by step: subtract twice the second equation from the first and you get -3y = -60, so y = 20. Put it back and x = 10. A system can have exactly one answer, no answer (parallel lines that never meet) or infinitely many answers (the same line written twice).

Determinants and inverses: The determinant is one number calculated from a square matrix. For a 2x2 matrix [a b; c d] it is ad - bc. If it is 0, the matrix squashes space flat and has no inverse, and the equations have no unique answer. If it is not 0, the inverse exists and "undoes" the matrix, like dividing undoes multiplying. For [2 1; 1 2] the determinant is 2x2 - 1x1 = 3, so an inverse exists. Geometrically, the determinant tells how much the matrix stretches area: a determinant of 3 means every shape becomes 3 times bigger. A negative determinant means the shape also gets flipped.

Linear transformations: Multiplying a vector by a matrix moves it: rotates, stretches, flips or shears it. A matrix is basically a machine that transforms space. This is exactly how a game rotates a character or how a photo editor resizes an image.

Eigenvalues and eigenvectors: Most vectors change direction when a matrix acts on them. Some special vectors only get stretched or shrunk, keeping their direction. These are eigenvectors, and the stretch amount is the eigenvalue. They help find the most important patterns in data (used in PCA for machine learning) and were part of how Google ranked web pages. The rule is Av = λv: the matrix A acting on vector v gives the same vector just scaled by λ. You find λ by solving det(A - λI) = 0. For [2 0; 0 3] the eigenvalues are simply 2 and 3, with the x and y directions as eigenvectors.

Real life example 1: a black-and-white photo on your phone. It is a matrix where each cell is a pixel brightness from 0 (black) to 255 (white). Making the photo brighter means adding a number to every cell. Flipping it means rearranging the matrix. A colour photo is three matrices stacked: red, green and blue.

Real life example 2: a shop near your school sells shingara and tea. 2 shingaras + 1 tea = 40 taka, 1 shingara + 2 teas = 50 taka. Write it as a matrix equation and solve: shingara is 10 taka, tea is 20 taka. Businesses solve the same kind of system with thousands of unknowns to plan delivery routes and stock.

Where people get stuck and what comes in exams: the biggest mistake is assuming AB = BA. It usually isn't. Another is multiplying matrices with sizes that don't match. Many students also memorise formulas without picturing them. Typical exam questions: multiply two matrices, solve equations with Gaussian elimination, find a determinant and inverse, check if vectors are independent, and find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a 2x2 or 3x3 matrix.

After this course you can work with data as vectors and matrices, solve systems of equations, and understand the maths behind graphics and AI. Next, Numerical Methods shows how computers solve these fast, and Machine Learning and Computer Graphics put them to work.
key_points: A vector is a list of numbers; a matrix is a grid of numbers in rows and columns.
Matrix multiplication is row times column, and AB is usually not equal to BA.
Systems of equations can be written as Ax = b and solved with Gaussian elimination.
A determinant of 0 means the matrix has no inverse.
Photos are stored as matrices of brightness numbers.
Machine learning and AI use huge amounts of matrix multiplication.
lessons.tip: Picture every operation. Draw arrows for vectors and see what the matrix does to them. Geometry makes linear algebra click.
lessons.task: Solve: 2 shingaras + 1 tea = 40 taka, 1 shingara + 2 teas = 50 taka. Find each price, then check your answer.

quiz.q: What is a matrix?
options: A grid of numbers in rows and columns
quiz.explain: A matrix is a rectangular table of numbers arranged in rows and columns.

quiz.q: How is a black-and-white photo stored for linear algebra?
options: As a matrix of brightness numbers
quiz.explain: Each pixel's brightness is a number, so the whole image is a matrix.

quiz.q: Which area uses huge amounts of matrix multiplication?
quiz.explain: Neural networks do layer after layer of matrix multiplication, which is why GPUs are so useful for AI.

lessons.title: Probability & Statistics
lessons.content:
What is it? Probability & Statistics is the maths of chance and data. Probability tells you how likely something is, like the chance of rain tomorrow. Statistics helps you make sense of lots of data, like finding the average marks of a class or which team wins more often.

Why learn it? The real world is full of uncertainty and data. Spam filters guess if an email is spam. Weather apps predict rain. Netflix and YouTube guess what you'll like. Machine learning, data science, networking, AI and even game design all rely on probability and statistics. If you can read data well, you can make smarter decisions than people who guess.

What's in the course? A typical syllabus covers basic probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem, random variables, probability distributions (binomial, Poisson, normal), mean, median, mode, variance and standard deviation, sampling, correlation and regression, and hypothesis testing.

Basic probability: Probability is a number from 0 to 1. 0 means it can never happen, 1 means it surely happens. It equals favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes. A fair dice has 6 faces, so the chance of a 6 is 1/6. The chance of an even number is 3/6 = 1/2. If you ever get a probability above 1 or below 0, something went wrong.

Conditional probability and Bayes' theorem: Conditional probability is the chance of A given that B already happened, written P(A|B). Bayes' theorem lets you update a guess when you get new evidence: P(A|B) = P(B|A) x P(A) / P(B). A spam filter uses it: if an email contains "free money", the chance it is spam goes way up, because spam emails often contain those words. Try a number example: 1% of people have a disease, and a test is 90% accurate. If you test positive, the chance you really have it is only about 8%, because healthy people far outnumber sick ones, so the false alarms add up. Bayes keeps you from panicking too early.

Random variables and distributions: A random variable is a number that comes from a random event, like the number of heads in 10 coin tosses. A distribution tells how likely each value is. Binomial counts successes in a fixed number of tries. Poisson counts events in a time period, like customers arriving per minute. The normal distribution is the famous bell curve: most values near the middle, few at the extremes, like people's heights.

Describing data: The mean is the average (add all, divide by count). The median is the middle value when sorted, and it is not fooled by one crazy value. The mode is the most common value. Variance and standard deviation tell how spread out the data is. For scores 10, 20, 30, the mean is 20 and the spread is small; for 0, 20, 40 the mean is also 20 but the spread is bigger. Quick example: for 2, 4, 4, 6, 9 the mean is 25/5 = 5, the median is 4 and the mode is 4. To get the variance, find each value's distance from the mean, square it, then average: (9+1+1+1+16)/5 = 5.6. The standard deviation is its square root, about 2.4.

Sampling: You cannot ask all 17 crore people in Bangladesh a question. Instead you ask a sample, say 2,000 people chosen fairly. Statistics lets a good random sample represent the whole population, with a known margin of error. A bad sample, like only asking your friends, gives a biased answer.

Correlation and regression: Correlation tells if two things move together, like study hours and marks. It ranges from -1 to +1. But correlation is not causation: ice cream sales and drowning both go up in summer, but ice cream does not cause drowning. Regression draws the best straight line through data so you can predict, like marks = 30 + 5 x hours.

Hypothesis testing: This is how scientists check if a result is real or just luck. You assume nothing special is happening (the null hypothesis), then see how unlikely your data would be under that assumption. If it's very unlikely (a small p-value, often below 0.05), you reject the null hypothesis. Example: a coin lands heads 9 times out of 10. If the coin were fair, getting 9 or more heads is very unlikely, about 1%. So you'd say the coin is probably not fair. Two mistakes are possible: calling a fair coin unfair (Type I) or missing an unfair one (Type II).

Real life example 1: a cricket batsman's last 10 innings. Find the mean to see his usual score, the median to ignore one huge century, and the standard deviation to see if he is consistent or up and down. Team selectors do exactly this kind of thinking, just with more data.

Real life example 2: an election opinion poll. A survey company asks about 2,000 randomly picked voters and predicts the result for the whole country within plus or minus 2 percent. That works only because the sample is random and big enough.

Where people get stuck and what comes in exams: students often mix up P(A|B) and P(B|A), they are not the same. Others use the mean when one extreme value ruins it and the median would be better. And many confuse correlation with causation. Typical exam questions: dice and card probabilities, Bayes' theorem word problems, binomial or Poisson calculations, finding mean, median, variance and standard deviation, and fitting a regression line.

After this course you can measure chance, summarise data and spot misleading numbers. Next, Machine Learning, Data Mining and Simulation & Modeling build directly on this.
key_points: Probability is a number between 0 and 1: favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
Bayes' theorem updates a guess with new evidence; spam filters use it.
Mean, median and mode describe the centre of data; standard deviation shows the spread.
A good random sample can represent the whole population.
Correlation does not mean causation.
The normal distribution is the bell curve seen in many natural measurements.
lessons.tip: Always check your answer with common sense: a probability can never be below 0 or above 1. If it is, something went wrong.
lessons.task: Write down the runs of your favourite batsman's last 10 innings (or any 10 numbers). Find the mean, median and the highest and lowest score.

quiz.q: What is the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair dice?
quiz.explain: There is 1 favourable outcome out of 6 possible ones, so the chance is 1/6.

quiz.q: Which idea does a spam filter use to update its guess based on words in an email?
quiz.explain: Bayes' theorem updates the chance an email is spam based on the evidence, like the words it contains.

quiz.q: Why do surveys ask only a sample of people?
options: Because statistics lets a good sample represent the whole population
quiz.explain: A well-chosen sample can tell us about the whole population without asking everyone.

lessons.title: Complex Variables, Fourier & Laplace Transforms (Math III)
lessons.content:
What is it? This is the math course that gives engineers superpowers. It has three big parts: complex variables, Fourier analysis and the Laplace transform. Complex numbers are numbers like 3 + 4i, where i is the square root of -1. Fourier and Laplace transforms are like special glasses. Put them on, and a messy wave or a scary equation suddenly looks simple. Think of it like looking at a crowd from a rooftop instead of standing inside it: same crowd, but now you can see the pattern.

Why learn it? Sound, radio, Wi-Fi, images, electric circuits and control systems all deal with waves and things that change over time. This course gives you the tools to handle all of them without crying. Signals & Systems, Digital Signal Processing, Image Processing, Data Communication, Control Systems and even parts of Machine Learning lean on it again and again. Audio engineers, telecom engineers, chip designers and robotics people use these ideas every single day.

What's in the course? A typical syllabus covers: complex numbers and the complex plane, functions of a complex variable (analytic functions and the Cauchy-Riemann equations), complex integration (Cauchy's theorem and residues), Fourier series, the Fourier transform, the Laplace transform and using Laplace to solve differential equations. It sounds like a lot, but each part is one simple idea dressed up in fancy symbols.

Complex numbers: A complex number has a real part and an imaginary part, like z = 3 + 4i. You can draw it as a point on a flat plane: 3 steps right, 4 steps up. Its size (modulus) is the distance from the centre, here sqrt(3² + 4²) = 5. Multiplying by i turns the point 90 degrees, so i × i = -1 means turning twice, which points backwards. Euler's formula, e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ, connects complex numbers to circles and waves. That one line is why engineers love them.

Analytic functions: A function of a complex variable, like f(z) = z², takes a point on the plane and moves it somewhere else. Some functions are extra smooth and well behaved; these are called analytic. The test is the Cauchy-Riemann equations: if f = u + iv, then ∂u/∂x = ∂v/∂y and ∂u/∂y = -∂v/∂x. For example, z² passes the test, but the function that flips z to its conjugate does not. Analytic functions show up in fluid flow, electric fields and map making.

Complex integration and residues: You can integrate along a path in the complex plane, like walking around a loop. Cauchy's theorem says that if the function is analytic everywhere inside the loop, the total comes out to zero. If there are a few 'bad points' (poles) inside, only those points matter, and each one leaves a little leftover called a residue. The residue theorem says: loop integral = 2πi × (sum of residues inside). This trick solves some real integrals that are almost impossible the normal way.

Fourier series: Any repeating signal, even a square wave, can be built by adding simple sine and cosine waves. For example, a square wave ≈ sin x + (1/3) sin 3x + (1/5) sin 5x + ... The more terms you add, the closer you get. Each term has a frequency (how fast it wiggles) and an amplitude (how big it is). It's like making a song from many single musical notes played together.

Fourier transform: Real signals don't always repeat, so we use the Fourier transform instead. It takes a signal in time, like a voice recording, and shows how much of each frequency is inside it. A clean whistle shows one tall spike. A drum hit shows a wide spread. Going back with the inverse transform rebuilds the original signal. This 'time view vs frequency view' idea is the heart of audio, radio and image processing.

Laplace transform: The Laplace transform turns a function of time f(t) into a function of s, F(s). Its magic power: derivatives become multiplication by s. So a differential equation like y' + 2y = 0 becomes simple algebra: sY - y(0) + 2Y = 0, which gives Y = y(0)/(s + 2). Look it up in the table and you get y = y(0)e^(-2t). Transform, solve with algebra, transform back. That's the whole game.

Solving circuits and systems with Laplace: Engineers model circuits and machines with differential equations. With Laplace, a resistor, capacitor and inductor each become a simple expression in s, and the whole circuit becomes algebra. The result, called a transfer function, tells you whether a system is stable (settles down) or unstable (shoots off to infinity). That's how you check if a fan regulator or a motor controller will behave nicely.
