Real life example 1: You open a music app and play a song. The song is one messy wave. Step 1: the app grabs a small piece of the wave. Step 2: it uses the Fourier idea to split it into bass (low frequencies), mids and treble (high frequencies). Step 3: you push the bass slider up, so the app makes the low frequencies bigger. Step 4: it puts everything back together and plays it. That equalizer is Fourier analysis running live in your hand. Shazam uses the same trick to match a song from a few seconds of sound.

Real life example 2: Think of a car's cruise control on the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway, or a ceiling fan's speed control. Engineers write the physics as a differential equation, take the Laplace transform, and get a transfer function. From it they can see if the speed will settle smoothly at the target or keep jumping up and down. If it jumps, they tweak the design on paper before building anything. Cheap, fast and safe.

Where people get confused and what comes in exams: Many students mix up the Fourier series (for repeating signals) and the Fourier transform (for any signal). Others forget the initial value when taking the Laplace transform of a derivative. In the residue theorem, people often count poles that are outside the loop. Common exam questions: find the modulus and argument of a complex number, check if a function is analytic, find the Fourier series of a square or triangle wave, compute a Laplace transform from the table, and solve a differential equation using Laplace.

After this course you can switch between the time view and the frequency view of a signal, use complex numbers to handle waves and rotations, and solve circuit and control equations quickly. Next stop: Signals & Systems and Digital Signal Processing, where all of this turns into real gadgets.
key_points: Complex numbers (like 3 + 4i) are points on a plane; multiplying by i rotates 90 degrees.
Analytic functions pass the Cauchy-Riemann test.
The residue theorem turns hard loop integrals into adding up residues.
Fourier series build repeating signals from sine waves; the Fourier transform shows frequencies in any signal.
The Laplace transform turns differential equations into algebra.
Transfer functions from Laplace tell you if a system is stable.
lessons.tip: Don't just memorise transform tables. Each time, ask: what is this doing to the signal? Drawing a quick sketch of the wave helps a lot.
lessons.task: Open any music app with an equalizer and push the bass slider all the way up, then all the way down. Write one line on what changed. You just played with frequencies, which is the Fourier idea.

quiz.q: What does the Fourier transform show you?
options: Which frequencies are inside a signal
The file size of a signal
quiz.explain: The Fourier transform moves a signal from the time view to the frequency view, showing which wiggle speeds it contains.

quiz.q: Why do engineers use the Laplace transform?
options: To turn hard differential equations into simple algebra
quiz.explain: Laplace turns calculus-heavy equations into algebra, so you can solve them step by step and transform back.

quiz.q: In complex numbers, what does multiplying by i do on the complex plane?
quiz.explain: Multiplying by i turns the point by 90 degrees. That's why complex numbers are perfect for rotations and waves.

lessons.title: Algorithms (Design & Analysis)
lessons.content:
What is it? Algorithms (Design & Analysis) is the course about finding smart step-by-step methods to solve problems, and measuring how fast they are. An algorithm is like a recipe. Two recipes might give the same biryani, but one takes 1 hour and another takes 5. This course teaches you to pick and design the fast one.

Why learn it? When data is small, any method works. When data is huge, like Facebook's billions of users or Google Maps finding a route through a whole city, a slow algorithm can take years while a smart one takes a second. Algorithms are the number one topic in programming job interviews and contests, and they are the base for AI, networks, databases and everything else.

What's in the course? A typical syllabus covers complexity analysis and Big-O notation, sorting and searching, divide and conquer, greedy algorithms, dynamic programming, graph algorithms (BFS, DFS, shortest paths, minimum spanning trees), backtracking, and an introduction to NP-completeness.

Big-O notation: Big-O describes how the work grows as the input grows. O(1) means constant: same time no matter the size, like picking the first item. O(n) means the work grows with the input, like checking every name in a list. O(n^2) means it grows much faster, like comparing every pair. O(log n) grows very slowly. For 1 million items, O(n^2) is a trillion steps while O(n log n) is about 20 million.

Searching: Linear search checks items one by one, O(n). Binary search works on a sorted list: look at the middle, then throw away half each time. For 1,000 sorted items you need only about 10 checks, because 2^10 = 1024. That is O(log n). It is the "guess the number, higher or lower" trick.

Sorting: Bubble sort and insertion sort are easy but O(n^2). Merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half, then merges them: O(n log n). Quick sort picks a pivot and puts smaller items on one side and bigger on the other; it is usually very fast in practice. Sorting matters because sorted data makes searching and many other tasks much easier. Trace merge sort on 5, 2, 4, 1: split into [5, 2] and [4, 1], sort each to [2, 5] and [1, 4], then merge by always taking the smaller front item: 1, 2, 4, 5. Quick sort's worst case is O(n^2) when the pivot is always the smallest or biggest item.

Divide and conquer: Break a big problem into smaller copies of itself, solve them, then combine the answers. Merge sort and binary search are classic examples. It is like dividing a big pile of exam scripts among teachers, each checks a part, then results are combined.

Greedy algorithms: At each step, pick the choice that looks best right now. Giving change with the fewest notes (take the biggest note that fits each time) is greedy. It works for Bangladeshi notes, but greedy does not always give the best answer for every problem, so you must prove it works. Here's where greedy fails: imagine coins of 1, 3 and 4 taka and you need 6. Greedy takes 4, then 1, then 1, which is three coins. But 3 + 3 is only two coins. Greedy works well for activity selection and Huffman coding, where it has been proven correct.

Dynamic programming: Some problems solve the same small subproblems again and again. Dynamic programming remembers the answers to small subproblems so you never solve them twice. Fibonacci numbers are the simple example: without memory, finding the 50th number takes billions of steps; with memory it takes 50. Knapsack and longest common subsequence are classic DP problems. The DP recipe has three steps: define what a subproblem means, write a recurrence like fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2), then fill a table from small to big. In 0/1 knapsack, each item is either taken or left, and the table tells the best value for each bag size.

Graph algorithms: A graph is dots (nodes) joined by lines (edges), like cities joined by roads. BFS explores level by level, good for the fewest steps. DFS goes deep first, good for exploring mazes. Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path with weighted roads. Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms find a minimum spanning tree: the cheapest way to connect all cities.

NP-completeness: Some problems, like the Travelling Salesman Problem (shortest tour visiting every city once), have no known fast algorithm. Nobody has proved whether a fast one exists; that's the famous P vs NP question. For such problems, we use clever approximations.

Real life example 1: Pathao or Uber finding a route. The city is a graph: junctions are nodes, roads are edges with travel time as weight. A shortest path algorithm like Dijkstra (or a faster version called A*) finds the quickest route in a moment, even with thousands of roads, and recalculates when traffic changes.

Real life example 2: searching a contact on your phone. Your contacts are kept sorted, so typing a name uses a binary-search style lookup instead of checking all 2,000 contacts one by one. That is why it feels instant.

Where people get stuck and what comes in exams: students often think greedy always works; it doesn't. Others mix up the best, average and worst case. Many find dynamic programming hard until they practise writing the recurrence first. Typical exam questions: find the Big-O of a loop, trace merge sort or quick sort on a small array, solve a 0/1 knapsack with DP, run Dijkstra or BFS on a small graph, and find a minimum spanning tree.

After this course you can judge whether a solution will be fast enough before writing code, and you'll have a toolbox of classic techniques. Practise on sites like Codeforces or LeetCode, and later take Advanced Algorithms for even harder problems.
key_points: An algorithm is a step-by-step method; this course is about designing fast ones.
Big-O describes how the work grows as the input grows.
Binary search on sorted data needs only about log2(n) checks: ~10 for 1,000 items.
Merge sort and quick sort sort in about O(n log n).
Dynamic programming remembers subproblem answers so they are never solved twice.
Graph algorithms like BFS, DFS and Dijkstra solve routes and networks.
lessons.tip: Always trace your algorithm by hand on a tiny example first, like 5 numbers. If you can't do it on paper, the code will not save you.
lessons.task: Pick a random number between 1 and 100 and ask a friend to guess it, answering only higher or lower. Count the guesses. Then show them the binary search trick: always guess the middle. Can they always win in 7 guesses?

quiz.q: What does Big-O notation describe?
options: How the work grows as the input grows
quiz.explain: Big-O measures growth. It tells you how the time or memory needed grows when the input gets bigger.

quiz.q: Binary search on 1,000 sorted items needs roughly how many checks?
quiz.explain: Binary search halves the range every step. 1,000 halves down to 1 in about 10 steps.

quiz.q: Remembering answers to small subproblems so you never solve them twice is called...
quiz.explain: Dynamic programming stores answers to subproblems and reuses them, which saves a huge amount of repeated work.

lessons.title: Computer Architecture & Organization
lessons.content:
What is it? Computer Architecture & Organization is the course about how a computer is built inside: the CPU, memory, and how they talk to each other. Architecture is the design (what instructions the CPU understands), and organization is how that design is actually built with parts. Think of a restaurant: architecture is the menu and rules, organization is the kitchen layout, chefs and storage.

Why learn it? If you know how the hardware works, you write faster programs, you understand why some code runs slow, and you can choose the right computer for a job. It is essential for operating systems, compilers, embedded systems and high performance computing. It also explains why your phone has "8 cores" and "8 GB RAM" and what those numbers really mean.

What's in the course? A typical syllabus covers the von Neumann model, the CPU and its parts (ALU, control unit, registers), the instruction cycle, instruction sets and addressing modes, the memory hierarchy and cache, pipelining, input/output and buses, and multicore processors.

The von Neumann model: Most computers follow this design: a CPU, a memory that holds both programs and data, and input/output, all connected by buses. The program is just data in memory, which the CPU reads one instruction at a time. This simple idea is why one computer can run any software.

Inside the CPU: The ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) does the maths and comparisons. The control unit is the manager: it reads instructions and tells everyone what to do. Registers are tiny super-fast storage boxes inside the CPU. The program counter (PC) register always holds the address of the next instruction.

The instruction cycle: The CPU repeats one basic cycle billions of times a second: fetch, decode, execute. Fetch: get the next instruction from memory. Decode: figure out what it means. Execute: do it, like add two numbers. Then move to the next one. A 3 GHz CPU ticks 3 billion times per second. Example: the instruction ADD R1, R2 is fetched from the address in the PC, the PC moves to the next instruction, the control unit decodes it as 'add', the ALU adds R2 into R1, and the result is written back. Some instructions take several clock cycles; CPI (cycles per instruction) measures this.

Instruction set and addressing modes: The instruction set (ISA) is the list of commands a CPU understands, like ADD, LOAD, STORE and JUMP. x86 (Intel, AMD laptops) and ARM (most phones) are two famous ISAs. Addressing modes are the ways an instruction can find its data: directly in the instruction, in a register, or at a memory address.

Memory hierarchy and cache: Fast memory is expensive and small; big memory is cheap and slow. So computers use layers: registers (fastest, tiny), cache (very fast, small), RAM (medium), and SSD or hard disk (huge but slow). Cache keeps often-used data close to the CPU so it doesn't have to wait for slow RAM. It works because programs tend to reuse the same data and nearby data (this is called locality). When the CPU finds data in cache it's a hit, otherwise a miss. Average access time = hit time + miss rate x miss penalty. With a 1 ns cache, a 5% miss rate and 100 ns RAM, the average is 1 + 0.05 x 100 = 6 ns, far better than 100 ns every time.

Pipelining: Instead of finishing one instruction completely before starting the next, the CPU overlaps them, like a washing line: while one load is drying, the next is washing. With a 5-stage pipeline, up to 5 instructions are in progress at once. Problems called hazards happen when one instruction needs the result of another that isn't finished yet. The classic 5 stages are fetch, decode, execute, memory access and write back. Without a pipeline, 5 instructions take 25 cycles; with it, about 9. Hazards are fixed by stalling (waiting a cycle), forwarding (passing a result directly to the next instruction) or branch prediction (guessing which way a jump goes).

I/O, buses and multicore: Buses are the roads that carry data between CPU, memory and devices. I/O can be handled by the CPU checking devices (polling), by devices raising interrupts, or by DMA, where data moves to memory without bothering the CPU. Multicore processors put several CPUs on one chip so multiple tasks run truly at the same time.

Real life example 1: a busy restaurant in Old Dhaka. The chef (ALU) cooks, the manager (control unit) reads orders (instructions) and directs everyone. The chef keeps salt and oil right beside the stove (registers), common spices on a nearby shelf (cache), more stock in the kitchen store (RAM), and bulk rice sacks in the godown (disk). Walking to the godown every time would be painfully slow, which is exactly why cache exists.

Real life example 2: buying a new laptop. A seller says "Core i5, 4 cores, 3.2 GHz, 8 MB cache, 16 GB RAM, 512 GB SSD". Now you know: 4 cores means 4 tasks truly in parallel, 3.2 GHz is how fast each ticks, cache is the fast shelf, RAM is working space for open apps, and SSD is long-term storage.

Where people get stuck and what comes in exams: students often confuse RAM and storage, or think more GHz is always faster (cache, cores and design matter too). Pipelining hazards also confuse many. Typical exam questions: explain fetch-decode-execute, compare memory types by speed and size, calculate cache hit ratio or average access time, draw a pipeline diagram and find hazards, and explain addressing modes with examples.

After this course you understand what happens inside the machine when your code runs. Next, Microprocessors & Assembly lets you program the CPU directly, and Operating Systems shows how software manages all this hardware.
key_points: Architecture is the design (instruction set); organization is how it's built.
The CPU has an ALU, a control unit and registers.
The CPU repeats fetch, decode, execute billions of times per second.
Memory hierarchy: registers are fastest, then cache, RAM, then disk.
Cache keeps often-used data near the CPU so programs run faster.
Pipelining overlaps instructions; multicore runs tasks in parallel.
lessons.tip: Draw the diagrams yourself. CPU, buses and memory make much more sense when you sketch the boxes and arrows with your own hand.
lessons.task: Open your phone or computer settings and find the processor name, number of cores, RAM size and storage size. Write them down and label which one is the fastest and which one is the biggest.

quiz.q: What is the basic cycle the CPU repeats?
quiz.explain: The CPU fetches an instruction from memory, decodes what it means, then executes it, again and again.

quiz.q: Which memory is the fastest?
quiz.explain: Registers sit inside the CPU itself, so they are the fastest, but also the smallest.

quiz.q: Why do computers have cache memory?
options: To keep often-used data close to the CPU so it runs faster
quiz.explain: Cache keeps frequently used data close to the CPU, so it doesn't have to wait for slower RAM every time.

lessons.title: Microprocessors & Assembly Language
lessons.content:
What is it? Microprocessors & Assembly Language is the course where you talk to the CPU almost in its own language. A microprocessor is a CPU built on a single chip. Assembly language is a set of short commands, like ADD or MOV, that map almost directly to what the chip actually does. If high-level languages like Python are full sentences, assembly is giving orders one tiny word at a time.

Why learn it? It shows you exactly how a program runs on hardware: where values live, how loops really happen, and why some code is faster. It is needed for embedded systems, device drivers, security work (like reverse engineering and malware analysis), compilers and operating systems. Many universities teach it using the Intel 8086, a classic chip that is simple enough to understand fully.

What's in the course? A typical syllabus covers microprocessor history and architecture (often the 8086), registers, memory segmentation, assembly instructions (data movement, arithmetic, logic, jumps), addressing modes, loops and procedures, the stack, interrupts, and interfacing with memory and I/O devices.

Microprocessor basics: The microprocessor contains the ALU, control unit and registers on one chip. It connects to memory and devices through the address bus (which location), the data bus (the actual data) and the control bus (read or write signals). The 8086 has a 16-bit data bus and a 20-bit address bus, so it can reach 2^20 = 1 MB of memory.

Registers: Registers are the CPU's own tiny storage boxes. The 8086 has general registers AX, BX, CX and DX. AX is the main worker for maths, CX is often used as a loop counter. There are also segment registers (CS, DS, SS, ES), the instruction pointer IP, the stack pointer SP, and a flags register that records results like zero or carry.

Assembly instructions: Each line is one small command. MOV AX, 5 puts 5 in AX. ADD AX, BX adds BX into AX. SUB, MUL and DIV do maths. AND, OR and XOR do logic. CMP compares two values and sets flags. JMP jumps to another line. Conditional jumps like JZ (jump if zero) or JNZ (jump if not zero) make decisions. Example: MOV AX, 7 then CMP AX, 5 then JG BIG. Since 7 is greater than 5, the CPU jumps to the line labelled BIG. Each instruction is turned into machine code bytes by an assembler, so MOV AX, 5 becomes bytes like B8 05 00.

Loops and procedures: There are no for-loops in assembly. You build them: put a count in CX, do the work, decrease CX, and jump back if it's not zero. The LOOP instruction does "decrease CX and jump if not zero" in one go. Procedures are like functions: CALL jumps to them and RET comes back.

The stack: The stack is an area of memory that works like a pile of plates: last in, first out. PUSH puts a value on top, POP takes the top one off. When you CALL a procedure, the return address is pushed on the stack so RET knows where to go back. Messing up push and pop is a classic bug. In the 8086, the stack grows downward: PUSH AX makes SP go down by 2 and stores AX there, POP AX copies the value back and moves SP up by 2. Saving registers with PUSH at the start of a procedure and restoring them with POP at the end keeps the caller's values safe.

Interrupts: An interrupt makes the CPU pause what it's doing and handle an urgent event, then continue. A key press, a timer tick or a network packet can cause one. In 8086 programs, INT 21h is used to ask DOS to do things like print text or read a key. Without interrupts, the CPU would waste time checking every device again and again.

Interfacing: Microprocessors connect to memory chips and I/O devices like keyboards, displays and motors. Chips like the 8255 (parallel I/O) and 8259 (interrupt controller) help. You learn how address decoding picks which chip responds. Example: to light 8 LEDs, the 8086 sends a byte like 1010 1010 to an 8255 output port with an OUT instruction, and every 1 bit turns an LED on. Reading switches works the other way with an IN instruction. Memory-mapped I/O treats devices like memory addresses instead.

Real life example 1: adding numbers 1 to 5 in assembly. Put 0 in AX and 5 in CX. Loop: ADD AX, CX, then LOOP back. CX goes 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 and AX becomes 5, 9, 12, 14, 15. When CX hits 0 the loop ends and AX holds 15. A single line in Python, but here you see every step the CPU really takes.

Real life example 2: an ATM machine or a digital weighing scale in a shop. Inside is a small processor running low-level code. When you press a key, an interrupt wakes the processor, it reads the key, updates the display through an I/O port, and goes back to waiting. That's the same flow you write in this course.

Where people get stuck and what comes in exams: students forget that MOV copies (doesn't move away), mix up which register is the destination, and break the stack by pushing more than they pop. Segment:offset addressing also confuses many: physical address = segment x 16 + offset. Typical exam questions: explain 8086 registers and pin functions, calculate a physical address, write a small program (add numbers, find the largest, reverse a string), trace register values, and explain interrupt handling.

After this course you can read and write simple assembly and understand what the CPU is really doing with your code. Use an emulator like emu8086 to practise. Next, Embedded Systems takes this to real devices, and Compiler Design shows how high-level code becomes assembly.
key_points: A microprocessor is a CPU built on a single chip.
Assembly uses short instructions like MOV, ADD and JMP that map to machine actions.
Registers (AX, BX, CX, DX...) are the CPU's tiny fast storage boxes.
The stack is last-in-first-out; CALL and RET use it for return addresses.
An interrupt makes the CPU pause and handle an urgent event.
8086 physical address = segment x 16 + offset.
lessons.tip: Use an emulator like emu8086 or an online assembly simulator. Watching registers change after every single instruction is the fastest way to learn.
lessons.task: Write the steps to add the numbers 1 to 5 using only these commands: put a value in a box, add a box to another box, subtract 1, and jump back if not zero. Use 2 boxes named A and B.

quiz.q: What is a microprocessor?
options: A CPU built on a single chip
quiz.explain: A microprocessor puts the whole CPU on one integrated circuit chip.

quiz.q: Which is an assembly-style instruction?
quiz.explain: ADD AX, BX adds two registers. It is a typical low level assembly instruction.

quiz.q: What does an interrupt do?
options: Makes the CPU pause and handle an urgent event
quiz.explain: An interrupt signals the CPU to pause its current work and run special code for an event like a key press.

lessons.title: Numerical Methods
lessons.content:
What is it? Numerical Methods is the course about finding answers that are very, very close to the right answer, using lots of small, simple calculations. Some math problems have no neat formula, or the formula is too messy to use. So instead of solving them exactly, we make a good guess, check it, improve it, and repeat until the answer is close enough. It's like guessing how many sweets are in a jar: guess, count a few, adjust, and soon you're nearly spot on.

Why learn it? Computers don't really do algebra the way you do on paper. They are great at adding and multiplying millions of times per second. Numerical methods turn hard math into exactly that kind of repeated simple work. Weather forecasts, bridge design, game physics, rocket paths, machine learning training and even your calculator's square root button all use these methods. You'll need this course again in Simulation, Graphics, Machine Learning and Image Processing.

What's in the course: errors and how they grow, finding roots of equations (bisection, false position, Newton-Raphson), solving many equations together (Gaussian elimination), interpolation (filling in values between known points), numerical integration (trapezoidal and Simpson's rules), and solving differential equations step by step (Euler and Runge-Kutta methods).

Errors: every approximate answer is a little bit wrong, and that's okay as long as we know how wrong. If the true value is 10 and we get 9.98, the absolute error is 0.02 and the relative error is 0.02 / 10 = 0.2%. Computers also store decimals with limited digits, so 0.1 + 0.2 might come out as 0.30000000000000004. That's round-off error. Truncation error happens when we stop a long process early. A good engineer always asks: how big can my error be?

Bisection method: say you want x where f(x) = x² - 2 = 0, which is √2. f(1) = -1 (negative) and f(2) = 2 (positive), so the answer is somewhere between 1 and 2. Check the middle, 1.5: f(1.5) = 0.25, positive. So the answer is between 1 and 1.5. Check 1.25: negative, so it's between 1.25 and 1.5. Each step cuts the range in half. It's slow but it never fails, just like the guess-the-number game where someone says "bigger" or "smaller".

Newton-Raphson method: this one is much faster. You start with a guess, look at the slope of the curve at that point, and slide down the slope to where it hits zero. The formula is x_new = x - f(x) / f'(x). For √2, start at x = 1: next is 1.5, then 1.4167, then 1.41421, already correct to 5 decimal places in 3 steps! The catch: you need the derivative, and a bad starting guess can make it jump around and fail.

Solving many equations together: real problems often have many unknowns at once, like 3 equations with x, y and z. Gaussian elimination is a step-by-step recipe: use one equation to remove x from the others, then remove y, until the last equation has just one unknown. Solve it, then go back up and fill in the rest. This is the same idea you saw in Linear Algebra, now done carefully by a computer, sometimes with thousands of equations.

Interpolation: suppose you know the temperature at 6 am was 20°C and at 9 am it was 26°C. What was it at 7:30? A simple straight-line guess says 23°C. That's linear interpolation. Newton's and Lagrange's interpolation use more known points and draw a smooth curve through them, giving better guesses in between. Phones use this to smooth your finger's path when you draw.

Numerical integration: integration means finding area under a curve. When we can't do it with a formula, we cut the area into thin slices and add them up. The trapezoidal rule treats each slice as a trapezoid (a straight top). Simpson's rule uses little curves on top instead, so it's usually more accurate with the same number of slices. More slices means more accuracy, but more work.

Differential equations step by step: many things in nature are described by how fast they change, like a cooling cup of tea. Euler's method says: new value = old value + (rate of change × small time step). Repeat this for each small step and you trace the whole curve. It's simple but drifts away over time. Runge-Kutta (especially RK4) checks the slope at a few points inside each step and averages them, so it stays accurate for much longer.

Real life example 1: Google Maps estimates your arrival time on a Dhaka road. It doesn't have a formula for traffic. It has speed readings from phones at certain points and times. It interpolates between those readings to guess speeds on each piece of road, then adds up tiny slices of travel time along the route, which is basically numerical integration. Every few minutes it updates with new data and corrects the guess.

Real life example 2: a cricket video game needs the ball to fly realistically. Gravity and air push on the ball every moment. The game can't solve the full equation in one go, so 60 times every second it uses a step method like Euler's: new position = old position + speed × time step, and new speed = old speed + pull of gravity × time step. Each tiny step is easy, and together they make a smooth, believable six over long-on.

Where everyone gets confused / what comes in exams: people mix up bisection (always works, slow, needs a sign change) with Newton-Raphson (fast, needs the derivative, can fail). Many forget that the trapezoidal rule and Simpson's rule need equal-width slices, and that Simpson's 1/3 rule needs an even number of slices. Typical exam questions: find a root to 3 decimal places with bisection or Newton-Raphson, compute an integral with Simpson's rule, solve 3 equations with Gaussian elimination, or do 2-3 steps of Euler or RK4. Practice the steps in a table, neatly; most marks are lost in calculation slips.

After this course you can turn almost any hard math problem into a simple repeated calculation a computer can do, and you'll know how much to trust the answer. This is the base of scientific computing. Next, try writing bisection and Newton-Raphson in a few lines of code, then see how these ideas power Simulation & Modeling, Computer Graphics and Machine Learning.
key_points: Numerical methods find close-enough answers when exact formulas are hard or impossible.
Every approximation has an error, so always measure how far off you might be.
Root finding: bisection keeps halving a range, Newton-Raphson follows the slope and is faster.
Interpolation guesses values between known points.
Integration by adding small slices: trapezoidal and Simpson's rules.
Euler and Runge-Kutta solve differential equations step by step.
lessons.tip: Code every method in a few lines of Python or C. Watching the answer get closer with every loop makes the math click.
lessons.task: Find the square root of 20 by guessing: start with 4, then improve your guess step by step until your guess times itself is within 0.1 of 20. Count how many tries it took.

quiz.q: What do numerical methods usually give us?
quiz.explain: Numerical methods produce approximations that can be made as accurate as we need.

quiz.q: Which method keeps cutting the range in half to find a root?
quiz.explain: The bisection method halves the interval each time, keeping the half where the curve crosses zero.

quiz.q: Trapezoidal and Simpson's rules are used for...
quiz.explain: Both rules estimate the area under a curve by adding up small slices.

lessons.title: Theory of Computation
lessons.content:
What is it? Theory of Computation is the course that asks big questions: what can a computer solve, what can it never solve, and how much memory does a machine need for a job? To answer these, we don't use real laptops. We use tiny pretend machines made of circles and arrows that you can draw on paper. Think of it like the rules of football drawn on a whiteboard before you play a real match.

Why learn it? Every programming language, search box, compiler and spell checker is built on these ideas. Regex in your code, the part of a compiler that reads your program, and even the way your phone checks a password pattern all come from automata. It also saves you from wasting months trying to write a program that is mathematically impossible. You'll use it directly in Compiler Design and Advanced Algorithms.

What's in the course: alphabets, strings and languages; finite automata (DFA and NFA); regular expressions; context-free grammars and pushdown automata; Turing machines; decidability and the halting problem; and a first look at complexity classes P and NP.

Strings and languages: in this course an alphabet is just a set of symbols, like {0, 1} or {a, b}. A string is any sequence of them, like 0110. A language is a set of strings that follow some rule, for example "all binary strings that end with 0". Each machine we study is simply a judge: give it a string and it says accept (yes, it's in the language) or reject (no).

Finite automata (DFA and NFA): a finite automaton is a machine with a few states and arrows between them. It reads one symbol at a time and follows an arrow. If it ends in a special "accept" state, the string is accepted. A vending machine is a perfect example: state "0 taka", insert 10 → state "10 taka", insert 10 again → state "20 taka, give chips". A DFA has exactly one arrow for each symbol from each state. An NFA can have choices or none, but surprisingly any NFA can be turned into a DFA, so they are equally powerful. Its weakness: it has no memory except which state it's in.

Regular expressions: a regex is a short way to write a pattern, like a*b (any number of a's, then a b) or [0-9]{11} for an 11-digit phone number. The big result: anything a regex can describe, a finite automaton can recognize, and the other way round. That's exactly how your code editor's search or a form's email checker works under the hood. Some patterns are impossible for regex, like "same number of a's followed by b's" (aⁿbⁿ). The pumping lemma is the tool used to prove that.

Context-free grammars and pushdown automata: a grammar is a set of rules for building strings, like S → (S) | SS | empty, which builds all properly matched brackets. A pushdown automaton is a finite automaton plus a stack, a pile of plates where you can only touch the top one. When you see "(", push a plate; when you see ")", pop one. If the pile is empty at the end, the brackets match. This extra memory lets it handle aⁿbⁿ, nested brackets and the structure of programming languages.

Turing machines: Alan Turing imagined a machine with an endless tape of cells, a head that reads and writes one cell at a time, and a small rule table. That's it. Yet this simple machine can compute anything your laptop, a supercomputer or any program can compute. This idea is called the Church-Turing thesis. So whenever we say "computable", we mean "a Turing machine can do it".

Decidability and the halting problem: some problems can't be solved by any program, ever, no matter how fast the computer. The famous one is the halting problem: write a program that looks at any other program and says for sure whether it will stop or run forever. Turing proved this is impossible, using a clever self-contradiction trick, a bit like the sentence "this sentence is false". That's why no tool can perfectly detect every infinite loop or every virus.

P and NP: among problems that are solvable, some are fast (class P, like sorting) and some seem to need ages, even though checking an answer is quick (class NP, like solving a big Sudoku or finding the best delivery route). NP-complete problems are the hardest of these. Nobody knows if P = NP; it's one of the biggest unsolved questions in the world, with a million-dollar prize waiting.

Real life example 1: when you sign up on Daraz, the form checks if your email looks valid. Behind the scenes there's a regex like something@something.something. That regex becomes a finite automaton: it starts in a state "reading name", moves to "seen @" when it reads @, then to "seen dot", and only accepts if it ends in the right state. Tiny machine, millions of checks per day.

Real life example 2: you type a long formula in Excel with lots of brackets, and forget one. Excel says the formula has an error. It's doing what a pushdown automaton does: pushing for every "(" and popping for every ")". If something is left over, or it tries to pop from an empty stack, the brackets don't match. A compiler does the same for the { } blocks in your C code.

Where everyone gets confused / what comes in exams: students mix up DFA and NFA (both recognize the same languages; NFA is just easier to draw), and think a finite automaton can count without limit (it can't, it only has fixed states). Many confuse undecidable (impossible forever) with NP-complete (possible, just very slow). Typical exam questions: draw a DFA for strings ending in 01, convert an NFA to a DFA, write a regex for a given language, prove a language is not regular with the pumping lemma, write a CFG for balanced brackets, and explain the halting problem.

After this course you'll understand why some problems are easy, some are slow and some are simply impossible, and you'll be able to design small state machines for real software. Next, see these machines come alive in Compiler Design, where finite automata read your tokens and grammars check your syntax.
key_points: Theory of Computation asks what computers can and cannot do, using simple model machines.
Finite automata are tiny state machines behind regex, vending machines and lexers.
Regular expressions and finite automata describe the same kind of patterns.
Pushdown automata add a stack, useful for matching brackets and parsing.
Turing machines model everything a real computer can compute.
Some problems are undecidable, like the halting problem; NP-complete ones are just very slow.
lessons.tip: Draw state diagrams with circles and arrows for every problem. Theory becomes a fun puzzle when you can see the machine.
lessons.task: Draw a state machine for a turnstile gate: states Locked and Unlocked, inputs Coin and Push. Show what happens for every input in every state.

quiz.q: A vending machine that changes state with each coin is an example of...
quiz.explain: It has a fixed set of states and moves between them based on input, which is exactly a finite automaton.

quiz.q: What does the halting problem show?
options: No program can always decide if another program will stop
quiz.explain: Turing proved no general program can decide for every program and input whether it will halt.

quiz.q: Which machine adds a stack to a finite automaton?
quiz.explain: A pushdown automaton is a finite automaton plus a stack, which lets it handle things like nested brackets.

lessons.title: Data Communication
lessons.content:
What is it? Data Communication is the course about how bits actually travel from one device to another: through a wire, through glass, or through the air. Before we talk about the internet or apps, we need to know how a simple 0 and 1 jumps from your phone to a tower. It's like learning how a letter is physically carried by the post office before learning about addresses and post codes.

Why learn it? Every call, message, bKash transaction and YouTube video depends on signals moving correctly. If you want to understand networks, mobile communication, IoT or even why your Wi-Fi gets slow in the next room, this is the foundation. It comes right before Computer Networks, and that course assumes you know these basics.

What's in the course: analog and digital signals, bandwidth and data rate, noise and signal problems, encoding and modulation, transmission media (wires, fiber optic, wireless), multiplexing, switching, and error detection and correction.

Analog and digital signals: an analog signal is a smooth wave that can take any value, like the sound of your voice or the old landline phone. A digital signal has only a few fixed levels, usually two: high and low, meaning 1 and 0. Digital is easier to clean up: if a 1 gets a bit weak, the receiver still knows it's a 1. That's why almost everything today is digital.

Bandwidth, data rate and signal problems: bandwidth is how wide the 'pipe' is, the range of frequencies a channel can carry. Bigger bandwidth means more bits per second. But signals get weaker over distance (attenuation), get mixed with random disturbance (noise), and change shape (distortion). Shannon's formula, C = B log₂(1 + S/N), tells the maximum speed a channel can ever reach for a given bandwidth B and signal-to-noise ratio S/N.

Encoding and modulation: encoding is how we represent bits on a wire. For example, Manchester encoding sends a 1 as low-to-high and a 0 as high-to-low, so the clock stays in sync. Modulation is how we put bits onto a carrier wave: change its height (ASK, amplitude), its speed of wiggling (FSK, frequency) or where the wave starts (PSK, phase). QAM changes height and phase together to pack many bits into each symbol, which is how 4G and Wi-Fi go fast.

Transmission media: guided media are physical paths. Twisted pair is the copper cable in your LAN wire (twisted to cut noise). Coaxial is the thick dish/cable TV wire. Fiber optic sends light pulses through thin glass, which is super fast, travels very far and is not disturbed by electrical noise. The submarine cable that brings internet to Bangladesh through Cox's Bazar and Kuakata is fiber. Unguided media means wireless: radio, microwave and satellite signals through the air.

Multiplexing: one cable or one radio channel is expensive, so many users share it. In FDM (frequency division), each user gets a different frequency, like FM radio stations 88.0, 91.2, 104.0 all in the same air. In TDM (time division), users take turns very quickly, each getting a tiny time slot. WDM is FDM for light, using different colors in one fiber. CDMA lets everyone talk at once using different codes.

Switching: when data has to cross many points, how is the path set up? Circuit switching reserves a full path for the whole call, like the old phone network. Packet switching chops data into small packets that may take different roads and get reassembled at the end, like the internet. Packet switching shares lines better, which is why the internet uses it.

Error detection and correction: noise can flip a 0 into a 1. A parity bit is one extra bit that makes the count of 1s even (or odd). If the receiver counts an odd number, something broke. Checksum adds up the data and sends the total. CRC (cyclic redundancy check) does a smart division and sends the remainder; it catches most errors and is used in Ethernet and Wi-Fi. Hamming code goes further: it can find exactly which bit flipped and fix it.

Real life example 1: you send 500 taka by bKash. Your phone turns the request into bits, encodes them, and modulates them onto a 4G radio wave (using QAM). The tower receives it, checks it with CRC, and if the check fails it asks your phone to resend. The tower then sends it through fiber, as light, to bKash's servers. All of this happens in under a second, and not one digit of your 500 taka is allowed to change.

Real life example 2: at an Eid gathering, 30 relatives' phones connect to one Wi-Fi router. The router can't give each one a separate cable, so it shares the channel: it splits frequencies into many small sub-channels and gives users time slots, which is multiplexing. When someone stands behind a concrete wall, the signal weakens (attenuation) and the speed drops, because the router has to use simpler modulation that carries fewer bits but survives the noise.

Where everyone gets confused / what comes in exams: students mix up bandwidth (range of frequencies, in Hz) with data rate (bits per second), and bit rate with baud rate (signal changes per second; one change can carry several bits). Many forget that parity detects only an odd number of flipped bits. Typical exam questions: draw NRZ, Manchester and AMI encoding for a bit pattern, calculate capacity with Shannon or Nyquist formulas, compare FDM and TDM, compute a CRC remainder, and compare circuit vs packet switching.

After this course you'll understand what is really happening when data 'goes online': waves, light, noise, sharing and error checks. You'll be able to read Wi-Fi and 4G specs and know what they mean. Next, Computer Networks will build on top of this, showing how those packets find their way across the whole world.
key_points: Data travels as signals, analog (smooth waves) or digital (on/off).
Bandwidth, noise and attenuation decide how fast and clean data can travel.
Modulation turns bits into waves, light or voltage; encoding shapes the bits.
Media can be guided (twisted pair, coaxial, fiber optic) or wireless.
Multiplexing (FDM, TDM) lets many users share one line.
Parity, checksum and CRC detect errors in received data.
lessons.tip: Connect every topic to a device you use: WiFi, mobile data, fiber broadband, FM radio. Real gadgets make the theory stick.
lessons.task: Write your name in binary using ASCII codes (search an ASCII table), then add a parity bit to each letter so the number of 1s is even.

quiz.q: What is multiplexing?
options: Sharing one channel among many signals
quiz.explain: Multiplexing combines many signals over a single medium, like many radio stations sharing the air.

quiz.q: Which medium carries data as light pulses?
quiz.explain: Fiber optic cables send data as pulses of light, which is why they are so fast.

quiz.q: What is a parity bit used for?
quiz.explain: A parity bit lets the receiver check whether a bit got flipped during transmission.

lessons.title: Signals & Systems
lessons.content:
What is it? A signal is anything that changes and carries information: your voice, a heartbeat on an ECG, the temperature through the day, a photo, a cricket score updating live. A system is anything that takes a signal in and gives a new signal out, like a microphone, a speaker, a noise filter or your phone's camera software. Think of a juice machine: fruit goes in (input signal), juice comes out (output signal), and the machine is the system. This course teaches you to describe both with math.

Why learn it? Almost every gadget is a system working on signals. Phones, radios, TV, medical machines, cameras, smart speakers and car sensors all do it. If you want to work with sound, images, communication, sensors or control, this is the foundation. Digital Signal Processing, Data Communication, Image Processing, Control Systems and Machine Learning on audio all build on it. Telecom companies like Grameenphone and Robi need engineers who understand it.

What's in the course? The usual syllabus covers: types of signals (continuous and discrete), basic signal operations, system properties (linearity, time-invariance, causality, stability), LTI systems and the impulse response, convolution, Fourier analysis of signals and systems, sampling, and an introduction to the Laplace and Z transforms for systems.

Types of signals: A continuous-time signal has a value at every instant, like a real sound wave, written x(t). A discrete-time signal only has values at certain moments, like numbers stored in a computer, written x[n]. Signals can also be periodic (repeat forever, like a sine wave) or not, and even (mirror image around zero) or odd. Two special signals show up everywhere: the unit step (off, then switches on and stays on) and the unit impulse (one tiny tap at time zero, nothing else).

Signal operations: You can shift a signal in time (x(t - 2) is the same signal, 2 seconds late), flip it (x(-t) plays it backwards), and stretch or squeeze it (x(2t) plays it twice as fast). You can also add signals and multiply them by numbers. These simple moves are like editing a video clip: delay, reverse, fast-forward. Exam questions love asking you to draw the result.

System properties: A system is linear if doubling the input doubles the output, and adding two inputs adds the outputs. It is time-invariant if a delayed input gives the same output, just delayed. It is causal if the output only depends on now and the past, never the future (real-time systems must be causal). It is stable if a bounded input never gives an output that blows up to infinity. Example: y(t) = 3x(t) is linear and time-invariant; y(t) = x(t)² is not linear.

LTI systems and impulse response: Systems that are both linear and time-invariant are called LTI, and they are the stars of this course. Every LTI system is completely described by its impulse response h(t): how it reacts to one quick tap. Once you know h, you can predict the output for any input at all. It's like knowing exactly how a bell rings when hit once, then predicting any tune played on it.

Convolution: Convolution is the recipe that combines an input x with the impulse response h to get the output y. For discrete signals: y[n] = sum over k of x[k] × h[n - k]. In plain words: flip h, slide it across x, multiply the overlapping values and add them up, one position at a time. Example: x = [1, 2] and h = [1, 1] give y = [1, 3, 2]. It's the single most important calculation in the course.

Fourier analysis and sampling: Using Fourier, you look at signals in frequency: which wiggle speeds are inside. For LTI systems this is amazing, because convolution in time becomes simple multiplication in frequency: Y(f) = X(f) × H(f). H(f), the frequency response, shows which frequencies the system passes or blocks. Sampling turns a continuous signal into numbers. The sampling theorem says you must sample at least twice the highest frequency. Music is sampled at 44,100 times a second because humans hear up to about 20,000 Hz.

Laplace and Z transforms for systems: For continuous systems, the Laplace transform turns the impulse response into a transfer function H(s); for discrete systems, the Z-transform gives H(z). Poles of these functions tell you about stability. For a continuous system, if all poles are on the left half of the s-plane, the system is stable. These tools make designing filters and controllers much easier.

Real life example 1: Clap once in an empty classroom and listen to the echo. Step 1: your clap is almost an impulse. Step 2: the echo you hear is the room's impulse response. Step 3: record that echo. Step 4: convolve any song with it, and the song sounds as if it was played in that room. Music apps and movie sound designers do exactly this to create 'concert hall' or 'cathedral' effects.

Real life example 2: When you record a WhatsApp voice note, your phone samples your voice thousands of times every second, turning it into numbers. Then a system removes background hum (a filter blocking certain frequencies) and compresses the data. On the other side, the phone turns the numbers back into a smooth sound. An ECG machine at a hospital does a similar thing with heartbeat signals, filtering out noise from muscle movement.

Where people get confused and what comes in exams: Students often mix up time-shifting and time-scaling order (x(2t - 4) is shift by 4 then squeeze, or squeeze then shift by 2). Convolution by hand trips people when they forget to flip h. Many confuse 'linear' with 'straight line graph'. Common exam questions: check if a system is linear, time-invariant, causal and stable; compute a convolution; find the Fourier transform of a simple signal; and find the minimum sampling rate.

After this course you can describe any signal, predict how a system will change it, compute outputs with convolution and understand why phones, radios and sensors work the way they do. Next: Digital Signal Processing, where you write the code that does all of this.
key_points: A signal carries information; a system turns an input signal into an output signal.
Signals can be shifted, flipped and scaled in time.
Key system properties: linear, time-invariant, causal, stable.
An LTI system is fully described by its impulse response.
Convolution gives the output; in frequency it becomes multiplication.
Sample at least twice the highest frequency to keep all the information.
lessons.tip: Connect every formula to a sound you can imagine. If you can hear it in your head, the math becomes much less scary.
lessons.task: Clap once in a small room and once in a big empty room or stairwell. Write down how the sound was different. That difference is two different impulse responses.

quiz.q: What does a system do?
options: Takes an input signal and produces an output signal
quiz.explain: A system takes a signal in and gives a changed signal out, like a filter or a speaker.

quiz.q: A system is linear if...
options: Doubling the input doubles the output
quiz.explain: Linear means scaling and adding inputs scales and adds the outputs the same way.

quiz.q: What fully describes an LTI system?
quiz.explain: Knowing how an LTI system reacts to one quick tap (the impulse) lets you find its output for any input using convolution.

lessons.title: Computer Peripherals & Interfacing
lessons.content:
What is it? Peripherals are all the devices that connect to a computer: keyboard, mouse, printer, monitor, scanner, speakers, sensors and motors. Interfacing is how the computer and these devices talk. Think of the processor as a brain with no eyes, ears or hands. Peripherals are its eyes, ears and hands, and interfacing is the nervous system that connects them. This course is about those wires, signals and rules.

Why learn it? A processor alone can't see, hear or move anything. It needs devices to get data in and send results out. If you want to build robots, IoT gadgets, ATM machines, medical devices, factory machines or any hardware project, you must know how to connect devices to a processor and control them. It's essential for embedded systems engineers, hardware engineers and anyone working with Arduino or Raspberry Pi.

What's in the course? A typical syllabus covers: I/O ports and addressing, data transfer methods (programmed I/O or polling, interrupts and DMA), programmable interface chips like the 8255 PPI, 8259 interrupt controller and 8253/8254 timer, serial and parallel communication, standard buses and protocols (USB, UART, SPI, I2C), ADC and DAC, and how common peripherals like keyboards, displays and printers work.

I/O ports and addressing: Every device sits at an address, like every house has a holding number. The processor reads from or writes to that address to talk to the device. There are two styles. In isolated I/O, devices have their own separate address space and special instructions like IN and OUT. In memory-mapped I/O, devices look like normal memory, so a simple MOV instruction works. Example: writing 1 to address 0x20 might turn on an LED.

Polling, interrupts and DMA: These are the three ways to move data. Polling: the processor keeps asking the device 'ready yet?' in a loop. Simple, but it wastes time. Interrupts: the device sends a signal when it's ready, the processor pauses what it's doing, runs a small handler (an ISR), then goes back. DMA (Direct Memory Access): a DMA controller copies a big block of data between the device and memory by itself, while the processor does other work. Disk and network transfers use DMA.

Programmable interface chips: The 8255 PPI gives a processor three 8-bit parallel ports (A, B and C) that you can set as input or output with a control word. The 8259 PIC handles up to 8 interrupt lines and decides which device gets served first by priority. The 8253/8254 timer counts clock pulses to make delays, generate square waves or measure time. Even though modern chips put these inside, the ideas are the same.

Serial and parallel communication: Parallel sends many bits at once on many wires, like 8 lanes on a road. Serial sends bits one after another on one wire, like a single lane. Parallel looks faster, but over long distances the wires get out of sync, so modern systems mostly use fast serial links. UART is a simple serial method using a start bit, 8 data bits and a stop bit. The baud rate, like 9600, tells how many bits per second are sent.

USB, SPI and I2C: USB connects almost everything to computers and supplies power too. SPI is fast and uses 4 wires (clock, data out, data in, chip select), great for SD cards and displays. I2C uses only 2 wires (data and clock) and lets many devices share them, each with its own address, which is great for sensors. Choosing the right one depends on speed, number of wires and number of devices.

ADC and DAC: The real world is analog: temperature, light, sound all change smoothly. An ADC (Analog to Digital Converter) measures a voltage and turns it into a number. A 10-bit ADC gives 1024 levels, so with 5 V input each step is about 4.9 mV. A DAC does the opposite: it turns numbers into voltages, for example to play sound on a speaker. Every sensor project needs at least one ADC.

Real life example 1: Think of a classroom. Step 1, polling: the teacher asks every student one by one, 'any question?', over and over. Most of the time the answer is no, so time is wasted. Step 2, interrupts: students raise their hand only when they have a question, and the teacher answers then. Step 3, DMA: the teacher lets the class captain hand out and collect a big stack of copies while the teacher keeps teaching. That's exactly how a computer handles a keyboard (interrupt) and a file copy (DMA).

Real life example 2: A digital thermometer at a pharmacy. Step 1: the temperature sensor gives a small voltage that changes with heat. Step 2: an ADC turns that voltage into a number. Step 3: the microcontroller converts the number into degrees. Step 4: it sends the result over I2C or SPI to a small display. Step 5: if the temperature is too high, it triggers an interrupt and beeps. A tiny gadget, but it uses half of this course.

Where people get confused and what comes in exams: Students often mix up memory-mapped and isolated I/O, and confuse which of polling, interrupts and DMA is best for which job. Many forget how to write the 8255 control word. Others mix up baud rate and bit rate. Common exam questions: compare polling, interrupts and DMA; write the 8255 control word for a given port setup; explain interrupt priority in the 8259; calculate ADC resolution; and compare SPI, I2C and UART.

After this course you can connect sensors, displays, motors and buttons to a microcontroller, choose the right protocol and make everything work together reliably. Next: Embedded Systems and IoT, where you build full gadgets.
key_points: Peripherals are devices connected to a computer; interfacing is how they communicate.
Devices sit at addresses, using isolated or memory-mapped I/O.
Polling keeps asking, interrupts wait to be told, DMA moves data without the CPU.
Chips like the 8255, 8259 and 8254 handle ports, interrupts and timing.
UART, SPI, I2C and USB are common ways to talk to devices.
ADC turns real-world signals into numbers, DAC does the opposite.
lessons.tip: Draw a picture for every protocol: which wire carries what, and in what order. Timing diagrams make much more sense when you sketch them yourself.
lessons.task: Look around your room and list 6 devices that connect to a phone or computer. For each, write whether it mostly sends data in (input) or gets data out (output).

quiz.q: What is the problem with polling?
options: The processor wastes time asking devices again and again
quiz.explain: With polling the CPU keeps checking even when nothing has happened, which wastes time.

quiz.q: What does DMA let a device do?
options: Move data straight to memory without the CPU doing the copying
quiz.explain: Direct Memory Access lets a device transfer data to memory while the CPU is free for other work.

quiz.q: Which converts a real-world signal like temperature into a number?
quiz.explain: An ADC (Analog to Digital Converter) turns smooth real signals into digital numbers.

lessons.title: Graph Theory
lessons.content:
What is it? In math, a graph is not a bar chart. It is a bunch of dots, called vertices or nodes, joined by lines, called edges. That's all! But this simple idea can model roads, friendships, computer networks, flight routes, electric wires and even the whole web. Think of a city map: places are dots and roads are lines. That's a graph.

Why learn it? A huge number of real problems are graph problems in disguise. Finding the shortest route, suggesting friends, routing internet traffic, scheduling exams so no student has two at once, designing cheap networks, all of them use graphs. Google Maps, Facebook, Pathao and every delivery app run on graph theory. It's also a must for Algorithms, Networks, AI and competitive programming, and it shows up in job interviews all the time.

What's in the course? The syllabus usually covers: basic definitions and types of graphs, degree and the handshake lemma, paths, cycles and connectivity, trees and spanning trees, Euler and Hamiltonian paths, shortest paths, graph colouring, planar graphs, and matching. Some courses also add network flow.

Types of graphs: In an undirected graph, edges go both ways, like friendships. In a directed graph, edges have arrows, like one-way roads or Twitter follows. A weighted graph puts a number on each edge, like distance or cost. A simple graph has no loops or double edges. A complete graph Kn joins every pair of n nodes; K4 has 6 edges. A graph can be stored in a computer as an adjacency matrix (a table of 0s and 1s) or an adjacency list (each node lists its neighbours).

Degree and the handshake lemma: The degree of a node is how many edges touch it. The handshake lemma says: the sum of all degrees = 2 × number of edges, because each edge has two ends. Example: in a party where 4 people each shake 3 hands, total degree is 12, so there were 6 handshakes. A fun result follows: the number of people who shook an odd number of hands is always even.

Paths, cycles and connectivity: A path is a route from one node to another along edges. A cycle is a path that comes back to where it started. A graph is connected if you can reach every node from every other node. If not, it splits into separate pieces called components. Algorithms like BFS and DFS explore a graph to find these paths and pieces.

Trees and spanning trees: A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. A tree with n nodes always has exactly n - 1 edges. A spanning tree of a graph is a tree that touches every node using some of the graph's edges. A minimum spanning tree (MST) is the one with the smallest total weight, found by Kruskal's or Prim's algorithm. It answers questions like: what's the cheapest way to connect 10 villages with electric wire?

Euler and Hamiltonian paths: An Euler path uses every edge exactly once. It exists in a connected graph only if 0 or 2 nodes have odd degree. This started graph theory: the famous Königsberg bridges puzzle had 4 odd nodes, so no such walk existed. A Hamiltonian path visits every node exactly once. It sounds similar, but it's much harder: no fast general method is known. The travelling salesman problem is its weighted cousin.

Shortest paths, colouring, planarity and matching: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path from one node to all others when weights are not negative. Graph colouring gives each node a colour so neighbours never match; the smallest number of colours needed is the chromatic number. A planar graph can be drawn without crossing edges, and the four colour theorem says any map needs at most 4 colours. Matching pairs nodes up, like matching students to project supervisors. Euler's formula for planar graphs: V - E + F = 2.

Real life example 1: Getting home with Pathao. Step 1: every intersection in Dhaka is a node. Step 2: every road is an edge, with weight = travel time right now (traffic included). Step 3: the app runs a shortest-path algorithm like Dijkstra from your pickup point. Step 4: it picks the path with the smallest total time. Step 5: when traffic changes, weights change, and the route updates. Graph theory is literally driving you home.

Real life example 2: Making an exam routine. Step 1: each course is a node. Step 2: if any student takes two courses, join them with an edge. Step 3: colour the graph so joined courses never share a colour. Step 4: each colour becomes one exam slot. If the graph needs 5 colours, you need at least 5 slots, and no student will ever have a clash. Your university's exam office may be doing exactly this.

Where people get confused and what comes in exams: Students often mix up Euler (every edge) with Hamiltonian (every node). Many forget that a tree with n nodes has n - 1 edges, or that Dijkstra fails with negative weights. Others confuse a spanning tree with a shortest-path tree. Common exam questions: prove the handshake lemma, check if an Euler path exists, find an MST with Kruskal or Prim, run Dijkstra on a small graph, find a chromatic number, and use V - E + F = 2.

After this course you can turn a messy real problem into dots and lines and use proven tools to solve it. It pairs perfectly with Algorithms, where you code BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, Kruskal and more, and with Computer Networks, where routing is all graphs.
key_points: A graph is nodes (dots) joined by edges (lines).
Sum of degrees = 2 × number of edges (handshake lemma).
A tree with n nodes has n - 1 edges and no cycles.
Euler paths use every edge once; Hamiltonian paths visit every node once.
Dijkstra finds shortest paths; Kruskal and Prim find minimum spanning trees.
Graph colouring solves scheduling problems like exam routines.
lessons.tip: Always draw the graph. Even a rough sketch with 5 dots on paper makes a scary theorem obvious.
lessons.task: Draw 6 of your friends as dots. Connect two dots if those two friends know each other. Who has the most connections? That person is the 'hub' of your little social network.

quiz.q: In graph theory, what is a graph made of?
quiz.explain: A graph is a set of nodes (vertices) connected by edges.

quiz.q: What is a tree in graph theory?
options: A graph with only one node
A connected graph with no cycles
A graph where every node connects to every other
quiz.explain: A tree connects all its nodes without forming any loop.

quiz.q: Scheduling exams so no student has two exams at the same time can be solved with...
quiz.explain: Make each course a node, join courses that share a student, then colour it. Each colour becomes a time slot.

lessons.title: Operating Systems
lessons.content:
What is it? An operating system (OS) is the big manager software that sits between your hardware and your apps. Windows, Linux, macOS, Android and iOS are all operating systems. When you open YouTube and WhatsApp together, both want the CPU, memory, screen and internet at the same time. The OS decides who gets what and when, like a teacher managing a class so everyone gets a turn and nobody fights.

Why learn it? Every program you write runs on top of an OS. Knowing how it works helps you write faster programs, find strange bugs (like a program freezing forever) and understand servers, cloud, Android development and security. Job interviews love OS questions, and courses like Distributed Systems, Embedded Systems and Cloud Computing build directly on it.

What's in the course: processes and threads, CPU scheduling, process synchronization, deadlocks, memory management (paging, segmentation, virtual memory), file systems, and I/O and device management. You'll often practise with Linux commands and small C programs.

Processes and threads: a program sitting on disk is just a file. When you run it, it becomes a process: it gets its own memory, a program counter and a state (new, ready, running, waiting, terminated). A thread is a smaller worker inside a process; threads of the same process share memory. A browser may use one thread to download a picture and another to keep the page scrolling smoothly. Switching the CPU from one process to another is called a context switch.

CPU scheduling: the CPU can run only one thing per core at a time, so the OS picks who goes next. FCFS (first come, first served) is like a bank queue. SJF (shortest job first) lets quick tasks go first, which lowers average waiting time. Round Robin gives everyone a small time slice, say 10 ms, and then moves to the next, like passing a ball around a circle. Priority scheduling serves important tasks first, but low-priority ones may starve, so 'aging' slowly raises their priority.

Synchronization: when two threads touch the same data at once, things go wrong. Imagine two people withdrawing from the same account at the same moment: both read 1000 taka, both subtract 500, both write 500, and the bank lost 500. This is a race condition. The fix is to protect the 'critical section' so only one enters at a time, using a lock (mutex) or a semaphore, which is a counter of free passes. Classic puzzles: producer-consumer and dining philosophers.

Deadlock: picture two cars on a narrow bridge from opposite sides, neither backing up. Both wait forever. In an OS, process A holds the printer and wants the scanner, while process B holds the scanner and wants the printer. Deadlock needs four conditions together: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Break any one and deadlock can't happen. The Banker's algorithm checks requests in advance to stay in a 'safe state'.

Memory management: RAM is limited, and many programs want it. Paging splits memory into equal-size blocks called frames, and each program into pages of the same size, so a program can be placed in scattered frames without wasted gaps. A page table maps each page to its frame. Virtual memory lets a program act like it has huge memory: pages not in use stay on disk and are brought in when needed (a page fault). When RAM is full, page replacement algorithms like FIFO, LRU (least recently used) or Optimal decide which page to throw out.

File systems: the OS organises your storage into files and folders, keeps track of which disk blocks belong to which file, and checks permissions (who can read, write or run). Different file systems exist: NTFS on Windows, ext4 on Linux, FAT32 on pen drives. Allocation methods include contiguous (all blocks together), linked (each block points to the next) and indexed (one block lists all the others).

I/O and devices: keyboards, disks and printers are much slower than the CPU. The OS uses device drivers to talk to each one, interrupts so devices can say 'I'm done!' instead of the CPU waiting, and buffering and spooling, like the print queue, so the CPU can move on while the printer slowly works. Disk scheduling algorithms (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN) decide the order in which to read disk locations to reduce arm movement.

Real life example 1: on your Android phone you're listening to music, downloading a file in Chrome and chatting on Messenger. The OS gives each app a time slice of the CPU so fast that it feels like all run together. When you open a heavy game, RAM fills up, so Android quietly kills or pages out apps you haven't used in a while (like LRU). That's why an old app sometimes reloads when you switch back to it.

Real life example 2: during an online exam, 200 students in a university lab submit answers to the same server at the last minute. The server's OS runs a thread for each request. Without locks, two submissions could overwrite each other in the database file. With proper synchronization, each one waits for its turn for a few microseconds, and every answer is saved safely.

Where everyone gets confused / what comes in exams: students mix up process and program, and process and thread. Many think deadlock and starvation are the same; they aren't: deadlock means nobody moves, starvation means one keeps being skipped. Belady's anomaly (FIFO getting more page faults with more frames) also surprises people. Typical exam questions: Gantt charts and average waiting time for FCFS/SJF/RR, Banker's algorithm safe sequence, counting page faults with FIFO/LRU/Optimal, semaphore solution for producer-consumer, and the four deadlock conditions.

After this course you'll understand what really happens when you double-click an app, why systems hang and how to avoid it in your own code. You'll be comfortable with Linux, threads and memory. Next, try writing a small multithreaded C or Java program with a lock, and then move on to Distributed Systems and Cloud Computing.
key_points: The OS is the manager that shares CPU, memory, files and devices among all programs.
A process is a running program; threads are smaller workers inside it.
Scheduling (FCFS, SJF, Round Robin, Priority) decides which process runs next.
Locks and semaphores stop programs from messing up shared data.
Deadlock happens when processes wait on each other forever.
Virtual memory and paging give each program its own space; file systems organise storage.
lessons.tip: Install Linux in a virtual machine or use WSL and play with commands like ps, top and kill. Seeing processes live makes the chapters real.
lessons.task: Open Task Manager on Windows or Activity Monitor on Mac (or running apps on your phone). List 5 processes and note how much memory and CPU each one is using.

quiz.q: Which of these is an operating system?
quiz.explain: Android is an OS. The others are apps that run on top of an OS.

quiz.q: Round robin is a type of...
quiz.explain: Round robin gives each process a small time slice in turn, a classic CPU scheduling method.

quiz.q: Two processes each holding something the other needs, and both waiting forever, is called...
quiz.explain: That circular waiting is a deadlock, and OS designers work hard to prevent or detect it.

lessons.title: Database Management Systems
lessons.content:
What is it? A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that stores data in an organised way and lets you add, find, change and delete it quickly and safely. MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQLite are examples. Think of a giant, super-smart register book in a shop: it never loses a page, many people can write in it at once, and it can find any customer in a blink.

Why learn it? Almost every app you use has a database behind it: Facebook stores posts, Daraz stores orders, your university stores results, bKash stores every transaction. Backend developers, data analysts and app developers all need SQL every single day. This course also leads to Advanced Databases, Big Data and Data Mining.

What's in the course: why a DBMS beats plain files, the ER model, the relational model and keys, SQL, relational algebra, normalization, indexing and storage, transactions and ACID, and concurrency control and recovery.

Why not just files? You could store students in a text file, but soon problems pile up: the same data is copied in many files and gets out of sync, searching is slow, two people editing at once can corrupt it, and a power cut can lose everything. A DBMS solves all of that with structure, rules, indexes, locking and crash recovery.

ER model: before building, we draw a plan called an Entity-Relationship diagram. Entities are the things we store, like Student and Course. Attributes are their details, like name, roll and credit. Relationships connect them: a Student 'enrolls in' a Course. We also mark how many: one-to-one, one-to-many (one teacher, many courses) or many-to-many (many students, many courses). This plan is then turned into tables.

Relational model and keys: data lives in tables (relations) with rows (records) and columns (attributes). A primary key uniquely identifies each row, like student ID. A foreign key in one table points to the primary key of another, like enrollment.student_id pointing to student.id, which links the tables. Constraints, like 'CGPA must be between 0 and 4', keep bad data out.

SQL: SQL is the language to talk to a relational database. SELECT name FROM student WHERE cgpa > 3.5; finds good students. INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes them, DELETE removes them. JOIN combines tables: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM student s JOIN enrollment e ON s.id = e.student_id JOIN course c ON c.id = e.course_id; lists who takes what. GROUP BY with COUNT or AVG gives summaries like average marks per department. Relational algebra (select, project, join) is the math behind these queries.

Normalization: say a table stores student name, course and the teacher's phone number in every row. If the teacher changes their number, you must update 100 rows, and missing one makes data wrong. Normalization splits tables so each fact lives in one place. 1NF: no lists inside a cell. 2NF: no column depends on just part of a combined key. 3NF: no column depends on another non-key column. BCNF is a slightly stricter 3NF. Fewer copies means fewer mistakes.

Indexing and storage: data lives on disk in blocks. Searching a million rows one by one is slow. An index is like the index at the back of a textbook: it tells you exactly which page to open. Most databases use a B+ tree index, which keeps keys sorted so any search takes just a few steps. Hash indexes are great for exact matches. But indexes take space and slow down inserts a little, so we add them only where searches happen often.

Transactions and ACID: a transaction is a group of steps that must act as one. Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: rules stay true before and after. Isolation: two transactions running together don't mess each other up. Durability: once saved, it survives a crash. Concurrency control uses locks (like two-phase locking) or timestamps so parallel users stay safe, and recovery uses a log so the database can undo half-done work or redo finished work after a power cut.

Real life example 1: you send 1000 taka from your bKash to your friend's. Two things must happen: your balance goes down 1000 and theirs goes up 1000. If the server crashes in the middle, atomicity rolls back the first step, so money is never lost or created out of thin air. Durability means once you see 'Transaction successful', it stays saved even if the power goes.

Real life example 2: your university result portal. A student table, a course table and a marks table are linked with keys. When you click 'View Result', a SQL query JOINs your ID with your marks and courses, and GROUP BY semester calculates your GPA. On result day thousands log in at once; an index on student ID makes each lookup take milliseconds instead of seconds.

Where everyone gets confused / what comes in exams: students mix up primary key and foreign key, and think normalization always makes things faster (it reduces repetition but can need more joins). WHERE vs HAVING is a common trap: WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after. Typical exam questions: draw an ER diagram for a library or hospital, convert it to tables, write SQL queries with JOIN and GROUP BY, normalize a table up to 3NF or BCNF, find candidate keys from functional dependencies, and explain ACID with an example.

After this course you can design a database for a real app, write SQL to answer almost any question about your data, and keep that data correct even when many users hit it at once. Next, install SQLite or MySQL and build a small database for your hall's canteen, then explore Advanced Databases and Big Data.
key_points: A DBMS stores and manages data safely, quickly and for many users at once.
Design first with an ER diagram: entities, attributes and relationships.
Relational databases use tables with primary and foreign keys, and SQL to query them.
Normalization (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF) avoids storing the same data many times.
Indexes make searches fast, like the index at the back of a book.
Transactions follow ACID so data stays correct, even with many users or a crash.
