lessons.tip: Install SQLite or use an online SQL playground and practice queries daily. SQL is learned by typing, not by reading.
lessons.task: Design tables on paper for a small library: books, members and borrowings. Decide the columns for each and which column links them together.

quiz.q: What is SQL used for?
options: Asking and changing data in a database
quiz.explain: SQL is the standard language for querying and updating relational databases.

quiz.q: Why do we normalize tables?
options: To avoid repeating the same data in many places
quiz.explain: Normalization removes duplicate data, so updates happen in one place and data stays consistent.

quiz.q: A money transfer that must fully happen or not happen at all relies on...
quiz.explain: Transactions with ACID properties guarantee all-or-nothing behavior, even if something fails midway.

lessons.title: Computer Networks
lessons.content:
What is it? Computer Networks is the course about how computers talk to each other, from two laptops in a room to billions of devices on the internet. It's about the rules (protocols), the devices (switches, routers) and the addresses that make sure your message reaches the right place. Think of it like the whole postal system: addresses, post offices, sorting, delivery and receipts.

Why learn it? You use networks every second: Facebook, Google, online games, Zoom classes, bKash. Developers need networking to build web and mobile apps, fix slow apps and understand security. Jobs like network engineer, DevOps, cloud engineer and cyber security analyst start here. It builds on Data Communication and leads to Advanced Networks, Distributed Systems and Security.

What's in the course: network types and topologies, the layered models (OSI and TCP/IP), the data link layer and MAC addresses, the network layer with IP addressing, subnetting and routing, the transport layer with TCP and UDP, and the application layer with DNS, HTTP and email.

Network types and layers: a LAN covers a small area like a home or lab, a MAN covers a city, a WAN covers countries, and the internet is a network of networks. Sending data is a big job, so it's split into layers, each doing one thing. The OSI model has 7 layers: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application. The practical TCP/IP model has 4: link, internet, transport, application. Each layer wraps the data in its own 'envelope' (header), like packing a gift box inside another box.

Data link layer and MAC addresses: every network card has a fixed MAC address, like 3C:22:FB:9A:11:07, burned in at the factory. Inside one local network, a switch looks at the MAC address on each frame and sends it only to the right port, instead of shouting it to everyone. This layer also detects errors with CRC and controls who can talk when on a shared link, which is how Wi-Fi avoids collisions with CSMA/CA.

IP addressing and subnetting: to cross between networks we need IP addresses, like 192.168.1.10 (IPv4, 32 bits) or the much longer IPv6 (128 bits), made because IPv4 addresses ran out. An address has a network part and a host part. Subnetting splits a big network into smaller ones; for example 192.168.1.0/24 has 256 addresses, and /26 splits it into 4 subnets of 64 each. Your home router also uses NAT to let many devices share one public IP.

Routing: a router connects different networks and decides the next hop for each packet, like a traffic police at a junction pointing the way. It keeps a routing table. Routing algorithms fill that table: distance vector (RIP) tells neighbours 'I can reach X in 3 hops', and link state (OSPF) lets every router build a full map and run Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm. Between big internet companies, BGP decides routes.

Transport layer, TCP and UDP: IP gets packets to the right computer, but which app gets it? Port numbers decide: 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS. TCP is the careful courier: it starts with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), numbers every piece, waits for acknowledgements, resends lost pieces, and slows down when the network is crowded (congestion control). UDP is the fast courier: just sends, no checking. Video calls and online games use UDP because a lost frame is better than a late one.

Application layer, DNS and HTTP: humans remember names, computers need numbers. DNS is the internet's phonebook: you type facebook.com, DNS replies with its IP address. HTTP (and the secure HTTPS) is how browsers ask for web pages: GET to fetch, POST to send a form. Status codes tell you what happened: 200 OK, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error. Email uses SMTP to send and IMAP or POP3 to read, and DHCP automatically gives your phone an IP when it joins Wi-Fi.

Network security basics: since data passes through many hands, it can be peeked at or changed. HTTPS uses TLS encryption so only you and the website can read it. Firewalls block unwanted traffic. That small lock icon in your browser means the connection is encrypted.

Real life example 1: you type youtube.com on your phone in Dhaka. DHCP has already given your phone an IP. DNS turns youtube.com into an IP address. Your phone opens a TCP connection to port 443 with a handshake, then sends an HTTPS GET request. The packets go from your home Wi-Fi router to your ISP, through many routers, maybe through the submarine cable to Singapore, to a Google server, and the video comes back in small packets that TCP puts back in the right order.

Real life example 2: while playing an online game like PUBG with friends, your position updates are sent by UDP 20-30 times a second. If one update gets lost, the game doesn't wait, the next one is already coming. But when you buy an item in the game shop, that goes over TCP, because losing a payment message is not okay. Same game, two transport protocols, each chosen for its job.

Where everyone gets confused / what comes in exams: students mix up MAC address (local, fixed on the card) and IP address (global, can change), and switch (works with MAC inside a LAN) and router (works with IP between networks). Many forget that TCP is connection-oriented and UDP is connectionless. Typical exam questions: name and explain the OSI layers, subnetting calculations (number of subnets, hosts, broadcast address), Dijkstra's shortest path on a small graph, TCP three-way handshake and congestion control, and step-by-step what happens when you type a URL.

After this course you'll be able to explain exactly how a message travels across the world, set up and troubleshoot a small network, and build apps that talk over the internet. Next, open your terminal and try ping google.com, nslookup google.com and tracert (or traceroute) to see these ideas live, then move on to Distributed Systems and Network Security.
key_points: Networks are built in layers (OSI 7, TCP/IP 4), each with one job.
MAC addresses work inside a local network; switches use them to forward frames.
IP addresses identify devices across networks; routers find paths using routing algorithms.
TCP is reliable and ordered, UDP is fast but unchecked.
DNS turns names like google.com into IP addresses; HTTP carries web pages.
Subnetting splits a network into smaller ones.
lessons.tip: Use tools like ping, tracert/traceroute and Wireshark. Watching real packets fly makes protocols far easier to remember.
lessons.task: Open a command prompt or terminal and run: ping google.com. Note the IP address and the time in milliseconds. Then try a website from another country and compare.

quiz.q: What does DNS do?
options: Turns domain names into IP addresses
quiz.explain: DNS works like a phone book, translating names like google.com into IP addresses.

quiz.q: Which protocol makes sure no data is lost?
quiz.explain: TCP numbers the data, confirms delivery and resends missing pieces.

quiz.q: What device finds paths and forwards packets between networks?
quiz.explain: Routers read the destination address and forward packets toward it.

lessons.title: Software Engineering
lessons.content:
What is it? Software Engineering is the course about building big, useful software the right way, with a team, on time and without everything falling apart. Writing a 50-line program alone is coding. Building an app like Pathao with 100 developers, millions of users and constant updates is engineering. It's the difference between making a paper boat and building a real ship.

Why learn it? Most software projects that fail don't fail because of bad code; they fail because of unclear requirements, poor planning, no testing or bad teamwork. In any software company you'll work in sprints, use Git, write tests and attend stand-up meetings. This course teaches that whole world. It connects to System Analysis & Design, Software Testing, Project Management and your final year project.

What's in the course: the software development life cycle (SDLC), process models (Waterfall, Spiral, Agile, Scrum), requirements engineering, software design and UML, design principles and patterns, testing, version control with Git, project estimation and risk, and maintenance.

SDLC: every software goes through the same life stages. Requirements: find out what users actually need. Design: plan the structure. Coding: build it. Testing: find and fix bugs. Deployment: release it to users. Maintenance: fix problems and add features for years. Maintenance often takes more than half the total effort, so code that's easy to change matters a lot.

Process models: Waterfall does each stage once, in order, like a waterfall that can't go back up. It works when requirements are clear and fixed, like a government form system. The Spiral model adds risk checks in repeated loops. Agile builds in small pieces: every 1-4 weeks (a sprint) the team delivers something working, shows it to the user and adjusts. Scrum is a popular Agile style with a product backlog, a daily stand-up meeting, a Scrum Master and a review at the end of each sprint.

Requirements engineering: you talk with users and write down what the system must do. Functional requirements are features: 'a user can reset their password'. Non-functional requirements are qualities: 'the page loads in under 2 seconds', 'works on cheap Android phones'. A common Agile style is the user story: 'As a rider, I want to see the driver's location so that I know when they'll arrive.' A clear requirement saves weeks of rework.

Design and UML: before coding, we draw the plan. UML (Unified Modeling Language) is a set of standard diagrams: a use case diagram shows who does what, a class diagram shows the classes and how they connect, a sequence diagram shows the order of messages between objects. Good design follows principles like high cohesion (each part does one job) and low coupling (parts don't depend on each other too much), plus SOLID. Design patterns like Singleton, Observer and MVC are tried-and-tested solutions to common problems.

Testing: unit testing checks one small function. Integration testing checks that parts work together. System testing checks the whole app. Acceptance testing is the user saying 'yes, this is what I wanted'. Black-box testing checks inputs and outputs without looking at the code; white-box testing looks inside to cover every branch. Automated tests run every time code changes, so old features don't break silently.

Version control with Git: when 10 people edit the same code, chaos happens without Git. Git saves snapshots called commits, so you can always go back. Each person works on their own branch, then merges it into main through a pull request, where teammates review the code. If two people change the same line, Git shows a merge conflict for a human to fix. GitHub and GitLab host these repositories online.

Estimation, risk and maintenance: managers need to know 'how long and how much?'. Techniques like COCOMO or story points estimate effort. Risk management lists what could go wrong (a key developer leaves, a server is late) and plans for it. After release, maintenance fixes bugs (corrective), adapts to new phones or OS versions (adaptive), and adds improvements (perfective).

Real life example 1: think about how a team builds a food delivery app like Foodpanda. They gather requirements by talking to customers, riders and restaurants. In sprint 1 they build login and the restaurant list; in sprint 2, the cart and payment; in sprint 3, live rider tracking. After each sprint they show it to the client, get feedback ('add a cash-on-delivery option') and adjust. Every feature is on its own Git branch, reviewed, tested and merged.

Real life example 2: building a house in your village. First the family says what they need: 3 rooms, a kitchen, a veranda (requirements). An engineer draws the plan (design). Masons build it (coding). Someone checks for cracks and leaks (testing). The family moves in (deployment), and every year they repaint and fix the roof (maintenance). If they changed the plan after the roof was built, it would cost a lot, exactly like changing requirements late in software.

Where everyone gets confused / what comes in exams: students think Agile means 'no planning' (it means planning in small loops), and mix up verification ('are we building it right?') with validation ('are we building the right thing?'). Functional vs non-functional requirements is another common mix-up. Typical exam questions: compare Waterfall and Agile, draw a use case or class diagram for an ATM or library system, write user stories, explain the testing levels, and estimate effort using COCOMO.

After this course you'll know how real software teams plan, build, test and ship products, and you'll be ready to join one. Next, put your next class project on GitHub, use branches and pull requests with your friends, and try running it as a two-week sprint. Then look at Software Testing and Software Project Management.
key_points: Software engineering is building big, reliable software as a team, on time and on budget.
SDLC: requirements, design, coding, testing, deployment, maintenance.
Waterfall goes step by step; Agile and Scrum build in small sprints with feedback.
UML diagrams and design patterns help plan and share designs.
Testing (unit, integration, system, acceptance) catches bugs before users do.
Git lets a team work on the same code safely; estimation and risk keep projects on track.
lessons.tip: Treat every class project like a real product: write a short requirements list, use Git from day one and write at least a few tests.
lessons.task: Pick an app you use daily. Write 5 requirements for it in the form: As a user, I want to ... so that ... . This is called a user story.

quiz.q: Which step comes first in the software life cycle?
quiz.explain: You must first know what to build, so gathering requirements comes first.

quiz.q: Building software in short sprints and improving often is called...
quiz.explain: Agile methods like Scrum deliver small working pieces frequently and adapt to feedback.

quiz.q: What is Git mainly used for?
options: Version control and team collaboration on code
quiz.explain: Git tracks every change in code and lets many people work together without overwriting each other.

lessons.title: Compiler Design
lessons.content:
What is it? A compiler is a translator. You write code in a language people can read, like C or Java, and the compiler turns it into machine code, the 0s and 1s the CPU actually understands. Think of a friend who translates your Bangla letter into English for a pen pal. The friend has to read every word, understand the grammar, catch your mistakes, and then write a clean English letter. Compiler Design is the course where you learn how that translator is built.

Why learn it? Every program you have ever run went through a compiler or an interpreter. Learning how they work makes you a much better programmer: you finally understand error messages, why some code runs faster, and what "syntax error on line 12" really means. The same ideas are used in code editors that colour your code, in tools that check your code for bugs, in SQL databases that read your queries, and even in calculators that understand "2 + 3 * 4". If you like Theory of Computation, this is where that theory becomes a real tool.

What is in the course? A compiler works in phases, like a factory line. The usual syllabus goes through lexical analysis, syntax analysis (parsing), semantic analysis with the symbol table, intermediate code generation, code optimization and finally code generation. You also meet tools like Lex and Yacc that build parts of a compiler for you.

Lexical analysis: This is the first phase. The compiler reads your code character by character and groups them into small meaningful pieces called tokens, just like you group letters into words when you read. For the line "total = price + 5;" the lexer produces tokens: identifier(total), operator(=), identifier(price), operator(+), number(5), semicolon. Spaces and comments are thrown away here. Lexers are usually built using regular expressions and finite automata, the same machines you saw in Theory of Computation.

Syntax analysis (parsing): Now the compiler checks whether the tokens follow the grammar rules of the language, the way an English teacher checks whether a sentence is built correctly. The grammar is written as a context-free grammar, for example: expr -> expr + term | term. The parser builds a parse tree. For "2 + 3 * 4" the tree puts 3 * 4 deeper, so multiplication happens first. If you forget a semicolon or a bracket, this is the phase that shouts "syntax error". You learn top-down parsers (like LL(1) and recursive descent) and bottom-up parsers (like LR, SLR and LALR).

Semantic analysis and symbol table: A sentence can have perfect grammar and still be nonsense, like "The rice ate the cat". Semantic analysis catches this kind of meaning mistake in code. It checks types (you cannot add a number to a whole array in C), checks that every variable was declared before use, and that functions get the right number of arguments. It keeps a symbol table, a big notebook listing every name, its type and where it lives, for example: price -> float, declared at line 3.

Intermediate code generation: Before writing real machine code, the compiler writes a simple in-between version that is easy to work with. A popular form is three-address code, where each line does one small step. "a = b + c * d" becomes "t1 = c * d" then "a = b + t1". Because this middle form does not depend on any specific CPU, the same front part of a compiler can produce code for many different machines.

Code optimization: Here the compiler makes the program faster or smaller without changing what it does. If you wrote "x = 2 * 60 * 60", the compiler can calculate 7200 once while compiling (constant folding). If a calculation inside a loop never changes, it can move it outside the loop. It also removes dead code, lines whose result is never used. This is why the same code can run noticeably faster with optimization turned on.

Code generation: The last phase turns the optimized intermediate code into real machine instructions for a specific CPU. It decides which values live in fast registers and which go to slower memory (register allocation) and picks the best instructions. After this you get an executable file you can run, like a .exe on Windows.

Real life example 1: You write a small C program for your lab: "int marks = 85; if (marks >= 80) printf("A+");". You press compile. The lexer chops it into tokens. The parser checks that the if has its brackets. Semantic analysis confirms marks is an int and printf exists. The intermediate code says "if marks < 80 goto skip". The optimizer notices marks is always 85 and might simplify the check. Code generation produces machine code. You see "A+" on the screen in a blink, but six phases worked behind it.

Real life example 2: Think of Google Translate turning a Bangla sentence into English. It first splits the sentence into words (lexical analysis), figures out who is doing what (parsing), makes sure the meaning makes sense (semantic analysis), and then writes the English sentence with good word order (code generation). A compiler does the same job, only with much stricter rules and zero room for guessing.

Where students get confused and what exams ask: Many mix up compiler and interpreter. A compiler translates the whole program first and then you run it, while an interpreter (like Python's) reads and runs line by line. Students also mix up syntax errors (grammar broken, like a missing semicolon) and semantic errors (grammar fine but meaning wrong, like using an undeclared variable). Typical exam questions: list and explain the phases with a diagram, show the tokens for a given line, draw a parse tree, compute FIRST and FOLLOW sets, build an LL(1) or SLR parsing table, and write three-address code for an expression.

After this course you can explain exactly what happens when you press "Run", read compiler errors like a pro, and even build a small calculator language of your own. Good next steps are learning a parser generator like ANTLR, looking at how LLVM works, or reading about how JavaScript engines compile code while it runs.
key_points: A compiler translates human-written code into machine code.
Lexical analysis splits code into tokens.
Syntax analysis (parsing) checks the grammar and builds a parse tree.
Semantic analysis checks types and meaning, using a symbol table of all names.
Optimization makes code faster or smaller without changing what it does.
Code generation produces real machine code for a specific CPU.
lessons.tip: Build a tiny project: a calculator that reads text like 2 + 3 * 4 and gives the right answer. It teaches you lexing and parsing better than any book.
lessons.task: Take the line: total = price * 2 + 10; and split it into tokens on paper. Label each one as a name, number, operator or symbol.

quiz.q: Which phase splits code into tokens?
quiz.explain: Lexical analysis reads characters and groups them into tokens such as names, numbers and operators.

quiz.q: Checking that code follows grammar rules is called...
quiz.explain: The parser checks grammar and builds a parse tree from the tokens.

quiz.q: What does code optimization do?
options: Makes the output code faster or smaller
quiz.explain: Optimization improves the generated code so it runs faster or uses less memory, without changing what it does.

lessons.title: System Analysis & Design
lessons.content:
What is it? System Analysis and Design is about planning a computer system before building it. Think of building a house. You do not just start laying bricks. First you ask the family what they need: how many rooms, how big a kitchen, how much money they have. Then an architect draws a plan. Only then do the builders start. System analysts are the architects of software: they understand the problem, draw the plan, and then hand it to the programmers.

Why learn it? Most software projects that fail do not fail because of bad code. They fail because people built the wrong thing. A clinic wanted an appointment system and got a billing system, or the users found it too confusing to use. This course teaches you to ask the right questions, understand how a business really works and design a system people will actually use. Jobs like business analyst, system analyst, product manager and solution architect use these skills every day, and so does any senior developer.

What is in the course? The usual syllabus covers the System Development Life Cycle (SDLC), feasibility study, requirement gathering, modelling with diagrams like DFD, ER diagrams and use case diagrams, system design (input, output, database, interface), and finally implementation, testing, training and maintenance.

System Development Life Cycle (SDLC): This is the step-by-step journey of a system from idea to retirement. The classic phases are planning, analysis, design, implementation, testing, and maintenance. In the Waterfall approach you finish each phase before moving to the next, like going down steps. In iterative and Agile approaches you go round in small loops, showing users a working piece every few weeks and improving it.

Feasibility study: Before spending money, you check if the system is possible, affordable and worth building. There are a few types. Technical feasibility asks: do we have the technology and skills? Economic feasibility asks: will the benefits be bigger than the costs? Operational feasibility asks: will people actually use it? Schedule feasibility asks: can it be ready in time? For example, if building a system costs 10 lakh taka but saves only 1 lakh a year, it may not be worth it.

Requirement gathering: Here you find out what the users really need. You use interviews, questionnaires, observing people at work, and reading existing forms and reports. Requirements are split into functional ones (what the system must do, like "print a receipt") and non-functional ones (how well it must do it, like "respond within 2 seconds" or "work on slow internet"). A good analyst listens more than they talk, because users often ask for one thing but need another.

Data flow diagram (DFD): A DFD is a picture showing how information moves through a system. It uses four symbols: external entities (people or other systems outside, like Customer), processes (things that transform data, like "Take Order"), data stores (where data is kept, like the Orders table) and data flows (arrows showing data moving). You start with a context diagram, Level 0, which shows the whole system as one bubble, then break it into more detailed levels.

Other models and design: An ER diagram shows the data and how it is related, for example a Student enrolls in many Courses. Use case diagrams show who uses the system and what they can do. Decision tables and decision trees describe complicated rules, like discount rules. In the design phase you plan the screens, the forms, the reports, the database tables and how the system will be tested, installed and how users will be trained.

Real life example 1: A school in Rajshahi wants to stop keeping results on paper. The analyst first runs a feasibility study: there are computers in the office, the cost is reasonable and teachers are willing, so it is feasible. Then they interview teachers, the headmaster and a few parents. Requirements: teachers enter marks, the system calculates GPA, parents check results by SMS. A DFD shows marks flowing from Teacher into "Calculate GPA", into the Results store and out to Parent. Only after this plan is approved do programmers start coding.

Real life example 2: Think of how a ride app like Pathao might have been planned. Analysts first studied how people actually took rides: standing on the road, bargaining with drivers, not knowing the price. They wrote requirements like "show the fare before booking" and "show the driver's location live". They drew how data flows: rider location to the matching process, to the driver, back to the rider. Good analysis is the reason the app solved a real pain.

Where students get confused and what exams ask: Students often mix up analysis (understanding WHAT is needed) and design (deciding HOW to build it). Another common mistake in DFDs is drawing data flowing directly from one data store to another, or from an external entity straight into a data store, without a process in between, which is not allowed. Typical exam questions: explain SDLC phases, compare Waterfall and Agile, list types of feasibility, draw a context diagram and a Level 1 DFD for a library or hospital, draw an ER diagram, and make a decision table for a set of rules.

After this course you can take a messy real-world problem, talk to the people involved, and turn it into a clear plan that programmers can build. Next, go deeper with Software Engineering, Database Management Systems and Human Computer Interaction, which all build on these ideas.
key_points: System analysis means understanding the problem and real needs before building.
SDLC is a system's step-by-step journey from idea to maintenance.
A feasibility study checks if a system is possible, affordable and worth building.
Requirements are functional (what it does) and non-functional (how well it does it).
A DFD shows how information moves through a system.
Analysis says what is needed; design says how to build it.
lessons.tip: Practice on real places: a shop, a clinic, your department office. Talking to real users teaches more than any textbook example.
lessons.task: Pick a small shop near you. Write down 3 problems it faces with its current way of working, and for each, one feature a simple app could add to fix it.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of system analysis?
options: Understanding the problem and real needs
quiz.explain: Analysis focuses on understanding the current situation and what users truly need.

quiz.q: A diagram showing how information moves through a system is a...
quiz.explain: A DFD shows the flow of data between processes, data stores and outside entities.

quiz.q: A feasibility study checks whether a system is...
quiz.explain: Feasibility looks at technical, economic and practical sides before committing to a project.

lessons.title: Management Information Systems
lessons.content:
What is it? A Management Information System, or MIS, is a computer system that collects a company's data and turns it into reports that help managers make decisions. Think of it as the company's dashboard. Sales, stock, salaries, customers: it gathers all of it and shows the boss what is going on, the same way a car's dashboard shows speed and fuel so the driver can decide what to do.

Why learn it? Every big organisation runs on information. A shop owner with one store can remember everything in their head, but a company with 500 branches cannot. Without an MIS, managers guess. With one, they decide using real numbers. This course also teaches you to talk with business people, which is a big plus for any software engineer. Banks, hospitals, garment factories, telecom companies and government offices all hire people who understand both computers and business.

What is in the course? The usual syllabus covers data versus information, types of information systems (TPS, MIS, DSS, ESS), the levels of management, ERP and other enterprise systems, databases and data warehouses for business, how information systems give a competitive advantage, and the security, ethics and human side of running these systems.

Data versus information: Data is raw facts, like "rice, 2 kg, 140 taka, 10:05 am". Information is data that has been processed so it means something, like "rice sales went up 20% this week". Good information has a few qualities: it is accurate, on time, complete enough, relevant to the decision, and easy to understand. A perfect report that arrives a month late is almost useless.

Transaction Processing System (TPS): This is the base of everything. A TPS records the everyday work of the business, one transaction at a time: every sale at the counter, every bKash payment, every product received at the warehouse. It must be fast, accurate and reliable, because if it loses even one sale, the numbers above it are wrong. The point of sale machine at a supermarket is a classic TPS.

Management Information System (MIS): The MIS takes the data from the TPS and summarises it into regular reports for middle managers: daily sales per branch, weekly stock levels, monthly salary totals. There are scheduled reports (every Monday morning), on-demand reports (when the manager asks), and exception reports, which only show unusual things, like "these 5 products are almost out of stock".

Decision Support System (DSS) and Executive Support System (ESS): A DSS goes one step further and answers "what if" questions, like "what happens to profit if we drop the price by 10%?" It lets the manager play with numbers and models to compare options. An ESS is for the top bosses: it shows a few big-picture charts, like total profit and market trends, often on a simple dashboard. The idea of management levels is key here: workers at the bottom use the TPS, middle managers use the MIS, and top managers use the DSS and ESS.

ERP and enterprise systems: Big companies connect all their departments, like sales, purchase, stock, finance and HR, into one system called ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning). Then when a sale happens, stock goes down, the accounts update and the report changes, all automatically, with no one copying numbers between departments. SAP and Oracle are famous ERP products. You also learn about CRM (Customer Relationship Management) for handling customers and SCM (Supply Chain Management) for handling suppliers.

Real life example 1: Think of a big superstore chain like Shwapno. Every time a cashier scans a packet of rice, the TPS records it. At night the MIS adds up sales from every branch. Next morning the manager sees "Rice is selling fast in Mirpur but sitting unsold in Uttara" and moves stock around. An exception report warns that cooking oil will run out in two days. A DSS lets the head office test "what if we give 5% off on Friday?" No one counted by hand, the system did it.

Real life example 2: A hospital in Chattogram uses an information system. The TPS records each patient registration, each test and each bill. The MIS gives the manager a weekly report of how many patients came to each department. The director's dashboard (ESS) shows that the cardiology department is always full, so they decide to hire two more heart doctors. Good information led straight to a good decision.

Where students get confused and what exams ask: Students often mix up data and information, and mix up the types of systems. Remember: TPS records, MIS summarises, DSS answers "what if", ESS shows the big picture to top bosses. Another confusion is thinking an MIS is only software; in this course an information system means people, procedures, data, hardware and software together. Typical exam questions: define MIS and explain its parts, compare TPS, MIS, DSS and ESS, explain ERP with its benefits and problems, describe the qualities of good information, and discuss how an information system gives a company a competitive advantage.

After this course you will understand how software helps a business run, and you can design systems that give managers the right report at the right time. Next, look at Database Management Systems, System Analysis and Design and Data Mining to go deeper.
key_points: An MIS turns a company's raw data into reports for decision making.
Data is raw facts; information is processed, meaningful data.
TPS records daily work, MIS summarises it, DSS answers 'what if' questions, ESS shows top bosses the big picture.
ERP connects all departments of a company in one system.
Good information is accurate, on time and useful to the person reading it.
lessons.tip: For every topic, picture a real business you know, like a pharmacy or a superstore, and ask: what report would the owner want every morning?
lessons.task: Pick a small shop near you. Write down 3 things the owner records every day and 2 reports a monthly summary of those records could give them.

quiz.q: What is the main job of an MIS?
options: Turning business data into reports that help managers decide
quiz.explain: An MIS collects data and summarises it so managers can make decisions based on real numbers.

quiz.q: Which system records each sale at the counter?
quiz.explain: A Transaction Processing System records daily transactions like sales. The MIS then summarises them.

quiz.q: "What happens to profit if we cut the price by 10%?" Which system is built for this kind of question?
quiz.explain: A Decision Support System helps answer 'what if' questions by playing with the data.

lessons.title: Artificial Intelligence
lessons.content:
What is it? Artificial Intelligence, or AI, is about making computers do things that usually need human thinking: solving puzzles, playing games, understanding language, planning a route or making decisions. Think of teaching a very fast but very literal friend how to think step by step. AI does not mean a robot with feelings like in the movies. Most of it is clever methods for searching, reasoning and learning.

Why learn it? AI is everywhere now: Google Maps finds your shortest route, Facebook picks which posts you see, chess apps beat grandmasters, and chatbots answer customer questions for banks and mobile operators. This course is the foundation for Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Natural Language Processing, Computer Vision and Robotics. Even if you never become an AI engineer, you will understand how the smart parts of modern apps actually work.

What is in the course? A typical AI course covers intelligent agents, problem solving by search (uninformed and informed), heuristics and A*, game playing with minimax and alpha-beta pruning, constraint satisfaction problems, knowledge representation and logic, reasoning under uncertainty with probability, and an introduction to machine learning.

Intelligent agents: In AI, an agent is a program that senses its world and picks actions. It takes in percepts through sensors (like a camera or input data) and acts using actuators (like motors or screen output). A robot vacuum cleaner is an agent: it senses dirt and walls and decides where to move. A rational agent tries to choose the action that gives the best expected result. We describe an agent's task with PEAS: Performance measure, Environment, Actuators and Sensors.

Search: Many AI problems can be seen as searching for a path from a start state to a goal state. Think of finding a way out of a maze. Uninformed search methods do not know where the goal is. Breadth-first search (BFS) checks all places one step away, then two steps away and so on, so it always finds the shortest path when all steps cost the same. Depth-first search (DFS) goes as deep as possible down one path before backing up. Uniform cost search always expands the cheapest path so far.

Heuristics and A*: A heuristic is a smart guess that helps the search reach the goal faster. If you are in Dhaka going to Sylhet, a straight-line distance on the map is a good guess of how far you still have to go. A* search adds the cost so far g(n) to the heuristic guess h(n), so f(n) = g(n) + h(n), and always expands the node with the smallest f. If the heuristic never overestimates the real cost (we call this admissible), A* is guaranteed to find the best path. This is the idea behind route finding in maps and games.

Game playing with minimax: For two-player games like tic-tac-toe or chess, the computer uses minimax to choose moves. It imagines all possible future moves as a tree. On its own turns it picks the move with the maximum score, and it assumes the opponent will pick the move with the minimum score for it. Alpha-beta pruning is a trick that skips branches that cannot change the final decision, so the same search runs much faster and can look deeper.

Constraint satisfaction, logic and uncertainty: Some problems are about filling in values that obey rules, like Sudoku, exam timetables or map colouring, where no two neighbours get the same colour. These are constraint satisfaction problems, solved with backtracking. Knowledge representation uses logic, like "If it rains then the road is wet. It rains. So the road is wet", to let the computer reason. The real world is uncertain, so AI also uses probability and Bayesian networks to reason like "there is an 80% chance this email is spam".

Real life example 1: You open a map app to go from Mohammadpur to Motijheel. The roads are a graph. Each road has a cost: its distance or the travel time in current traffic. The app runs a search like A*, using straight-line distance as the heuristic, to find the fastest path without checking every single road in Dhaka. When traffic on one road gets worse, the costs change and the app searches again and suggests a new route.

Real life example 2: A chess or ludo app with a computer opponent is a game-playing agent. In chess, it uses minimax with alpha-beta pruning to look several moves ahead, giving each board position a score, like plus points for having more pieces. In ludo, there is dice luck, so it uses a version called expectiminimax that also averages over the possible dice rolls. That is how the computer seems to plan.

Where students get confused and what exams ask: Students mix up AI and machine learning. Machine learning is one part of AI; search, logic and planning are AI too, even without any learning. Another confusion is BFS versus DFS: BFS uses a queue and finds the shortest path, DFS uses a stack and saves memory but may go down a very long path. Typical exam questions: write PEAS for an agent, trace BFS, DFS and A* on a graph, show whether a heuristic is admissible, run minimax and alpha-beta on a game tree, solve a small constraint problem, and convert sentences into propositional or first-order logic.

After this course you can model real problems as search, build simple game AIs, and reason about how smart systems make decisions. Next, move on to Machine Learning to see how computers learn from data, and then Deep Learning, NLP and Computer Vision.
key_points: AI makes computers do tasks that usually need human thinking.
An agent is a program that senses its world and picks actions.
BFS and DFS search without knowing the goal; a heuristic is a smart guess that speeds search up.
A* uses f(n) = g(n) + h(n) and finds the best path if the heuristic never overestimates.
Minimax picks moves in two-player games; alpha-beta pruning makes it faster.
Machine learning is one part of AI, not all of it.
lessons.tip: Draw the search on paper. A tiny maze with 6 boxes and arrows will teach you BFS and DFS faster than any slide.
lessons.task: Draw a 4 by 4 grid maze on paper with a start and a goal. Find a path by always trying the box closest to the goal first. Count how many boxes you checked.

quiz.q: What does a heuristic do in search?
options: It gives a smart guess to reach the goal faster
quiz.explain: A heuristic is an estimate, like how far the goal is, so the search tries promising paths first.

quiz.q: Which method helps a computer choose moves in tic-tac-toe or chess?
quiz.explain: Minimax imagines the opponent's best reply and picks the move that is safest for the computer.

quiz.q: In AI, an agent is...
options: A program that senses its world and picks actions
quiz.explain: An agent looks at its environment and decides what action to take.

lessons.title: Computer Graphics
lessons.content:
What is it? Computer Graphics is about how computers draw pictures, shapes, animations and 3D worlds on the screen. Every game, cartoon, phone icon and even the letters you are reading right now were drawn using graphics methods. Think of the screen as a giant sheet of graph paper where each tiny square can be coloured, and the computer has to decide the right colour for every single square, many times per second.

Why learn it? Graphics is behind video games, animated movies, design apps like Photoshop and Canva, maps, medical scans, virtual reality, and every app interface you touch. Game developers, animators, UI engineers and AR/VR developers all need it. It also teaches you very practical math, like how coordinates, angles and matrices actually move things on a screen.

What is in the course? A typical syllabus covers pixels and display devices, line and circle drawing algorithms, filling shapes, 2D transformations (translation, rotation, scaling), clipping, 3D transformations and projection, building 3D objects from triangles, hidden surface removal, lighting and shading, colour models and an introduction to OpenGL.

Pixels and the screen: A pixel is a tiny dot on the screen, short for "picture element". A Full HD screen has 1920 x 1080, about 2 million pixels. Each pixel's colour is usually stored as three numbers, Red, Green and Blue (RGB), each from 0 to 255. So (255, 0, 0) is pure red and (255, 255, 255) is white. The part of memory that stores the colour of every pixel is called the frame buffer.

Drawing lines and circles: Even a straight line is tricky, because the screen is made of squares. If you draw a line from (0,0) to (5,2), you must decide which pixels to colour so it looks straight. The DDA algorithm steps along the line and rounds to the nearest pixel. Bresenham's line algorithm is smarter: it uses only whole-number addition and a running error value to decide whether to go straight or step up, so it is very fast. There is a similar midpoint algorithm for circles.

2D transformations: Transformations change where and how a shape is drawn. Moving a shape from one place to another without turning it is called translation: add tx to x and ty to y. Scaling makes it bigger or smaller by multiplying the coordinates. Rotation turns it around a point using sine and cosine. We write these as matrices, and using homogeneous coordinates (adding a third value, 1) lets us combine many transformations into one matrix by multiplying them, which is super efficient.

Clipping: When a shape is partly outside the window, we must cut off the part outside, otherwise the computer wastes time drawing what you cannot see. Cohen-Sutherland line clipping gives each end of a line a 4-bit code saying if it is left, right, above or below the window, and quickly decides if the line is fully in, fully out, or needs cutting. Polygon clipping does the same job for whole shapes.

3D, projection and triangles: 3D objects in games are usually built from triangles, called a mesh. A character might be made of thousands of tiny triangles. To show a 3D world on a flat screen, we use projection. Perspective projection makes far things look smaller, like real eyes. Orthographic (parallel) projection keeps sizes the same, which is useful for engineering drawings. Hidden surface removal, like the Z-buffer method, makes sure nearer objects cover farther ones.

Lighting, shading and colour: To look real, objects need light. The Phong lighting model adds three parts: ambient light (a little light everywhere), diffuse light (brighter on the side facing the light) and specular light (the shiny spot). Shading methods like Gouraud and Phong shading spread the lighting smoothly across triangles. You also learn colour models: RGB for screens and CMYK for printers.

Real life example 1: When you play a cricket game on your phone and the ball flies toward the boundary, the phone redraws the screen about 60 times every second. The ball is a 3D mesh of triangles. Each frame, a translation matrix moves it along its path and a rotation matrix spins it. Perspective projection makes it look smaller as it flies away. Lighting makes one side brighter. The Z-buffer makes sure the fielder in front hides the ball when needed.

Real life example 2: When you pinch to zoom a photo or a map on your phone, the app is applying scaling. When you rotate a photo in the gallery, it is applying rotation. When you drag it, that is translation. Parts that move off the screen are clipped so the phone does not waste effort drawing them. The same simple math from this course is running right under your finger.

Where students get confused and what exams ask: Students often forget that rotation and scaling happen around the origin. To rotate around another point, you translate the point to the origin, rotate, then translate back. The order of matrix multiplication matters too: rotate then translate is not the same as translate then rotate. Typical exam questions: draw a line using DDA or Bresenham step by step, apply a combined transformation using matrices, perform Cohen-Sutherland clipping, explain perspective versus parallel projection, and explain Z-buffer and the Phong lighting model.

After this course you understand how every image, game and animation reaches your screen, and you can write simple drawing and 3D programs with OpenGL. Next, try a game engine like Unity or Godot, or move on to Digital Image Processing and Computer Vision.
key_points: A pixel is a tiny dot on the screen, its colour stored as RGB numbers.
DDA and Bresenham algorithms draw straight lines with pixels.
Translation moves, scaling resizes and rotation turns shapes, all with matrices.
Clipping cuts off the parts outside the window.
3D game objects are built from triangles; projection puts them on a flat screen.
Lighting and shading make objects look real.
lessons.tip: Graphics is math you can see. Whenever a formula feels dry, draw it on graph paper and watch the shape move.
lessons.task: On graph paper draw a small square. Now move it 3 boxes right (translation), then double its size (scaling). Write the new corner points each time.

quiz.q: What is a pixel?
options: A tiny dot on the screen
quiz.explain: A screen is made of many tiny colored dots called pixels.

quiz.q: Moving a shape from one place to another without turning it is called...
quiz.explain: Translation just shifts a shape. Rotation turns it and scaling resizes it.

quiz.q: 3D objects in games are usually built from...
quiz.explain: Graphics cards are very fast at drawing triangles, so 3D models are made of many small triangles.

lessons.title: Web Engineering
lessons.content:
What is it? Web Engineering is about building websites and web apps properly, from the page you see in the browser to the server and database working behind it. Think of a restaurant. The frontend is the dining area where customers sit, look at the menu and order. The backend is the kitchen where the food is actually made. The waiter running between them carries the orders and the food, and on the web that waiter is HTTP.

Why learn it? Most of the software people use daily runs on the web: Facebook, Daraz, online banking, university result portals, government services and Google Docs. Web developers are among the most hired programmers in Bangladesh and abroad, and many freelancers earn by building websites. This course also teaches engineering habits: planning, security, performance and testing, so your site does not crash on a big sale day.

What is in the course? The usual syllabus covers how the web works (client, server, HTTP, URLs, DNS), HTML for structure, CSS for design and layout, JavaScript for interactivity, backend programming with a server language, connecting to databases, web architecture like MVC and REST APIs, sessions and cookies, web security, and performance and deployment.

How the web works: When you type a web address, your browser (the client) first asks DNS, the internet's phonebook, for the server's IP address. Then the browser uses HTTP to ask the server for a page. The server sends back a response with a status code: 200 means OK, 404 means the page was not found, 500 means the server itself had an error. HTTPS is the secure version that encrypts everything, which is why you see a little lock in the address bar.

HTML: HTML is the skeleton of a page. It describes what is on the page: headings, paragraphs, images, links, buttons and forms. For example, a tag like h1 makes a big heading and an img tag shows a picture. HTML alone looks plain, like a building with only bricks and no paint.

CSS: CSS mainly controls how a web page looks: colours, fonts, spacing and layout. With CSS you say things like "make all buttons green with rounded corners". Modern layout tools like Flexbox and Grid let you arrange things in rows and columns. Responsive design uses media queries so the same page looks good on a big laptop screen and a small phone.

JavaScript: JavaScript makes the page alive. It runs inside the browser and reacts to what you do: clicking a like button, showing a dropdown menu, checking that your phone number has 11 digits before submitting a form, or loading new posts without reloading the whole page. Frameworks like React, Vue and Angular help build big interactive apps.

Backend, databases and APIs: The backend runs on the server. It is written in languages like PHP, Python (Django), JavaScript (Node.js) or Java. It checks logins, does the business logic and talks to a database like MySQL or PostgreSQL. Many apps follow MVC: the Model handles data, the View shows the page and the Controller connects them. A REST API is a set of URLs the frontend or a mobile app can call to get or send data, usually in JSON format, like GET /products/25.

Security, sessions and performance: HTTP itself forgets you after each request, so websites use cookies and sessions to remember that you are logged in. Security is huge: SQL injection is when an attacker types database commands into a form, XSS is when they inject harmful JavaScript, and passwords must be stored as hashes, never as plain text. For speed, sites use caching, compress images and use CDNs that keep copies of files near users.

Real life example 1: You search for "headphones" on Daraz. The browser sends an HTTP request. The backend gets your search word, asks the database for matching products and sends back the results, often as JSON. JavaScript in your browser then puts those results on the page, and CSS makes the product cards look neat. When you add to cart, a cookie or session remembers your cart even if you go to another page. In the restaurant picture: you ordered from the dining area, the kitchen cooked, and the waiter brought it back.

Real life example 2: Think of your university result website on result day. Thousands of students open it at the same time. A well-engineered site uses caching so the same result page is not rebuilt for every student, a database with proper indexes so searching by student ID is fast, and maybe several servers behind a load balancer. A badly engineered site just shows "500 Internal Server Error" and everyone panics.

Where students get confused and what exams ask: Many students think HTML is a programming language; it is a markup language that describes structure, while JavaScript is the programming language. Students also mix up frontend (what runs in the browser) and backend (what runs on the server), and GET versus POST: GET asks for data and shows it in the URL, POST sends data in the body, which is used for forms like login. Typical exam questions: explain the client-server model and HTTP, write a simple HTML form with CSS, explain the DOM and events, explain MVC and REST, describe cookies versus sessions, and explain SQL injection and how to prevent it.

After this course you can build a complete website, from the page design to the server and database, and put it online. Next, learn a modern framework like React or Laravel, study Software Testing and Cloud Computing, or try building a small online shop as a project.
key_points: The frontend is the restaurant's dining area, the backend is the kitchen, and HTTP is the waiter.
HTML gives structure, CSS gives looks and layout, JavaScript gives interactivity.
The browser asks the server for pages with HTTP; the server answers with a status code.
The backend handles logins, logic and the database; REST APIs exchange JSON.
Guard against SQL injection and XSS, and store passwords as hashes.
lessons.tip: Build while you learn. After every class, add one small thing to your own personal website.
lessons.task: On any website, right-click and choose "View page source" (on a computer) or just look closely at a page. List 3 things you think are HTML, 3 that are CSS, and 1 that needs JavaScript.

quiz.q: Which language mainly controls how a web page looks, like colors and layout?
quiz.explain: CSS is for style. HTML is for structure and JavaScript is for behavior.

quiz.q: In the restaurant example, the backend is like the...
quiz.explain: The kitchen does the real work out of sight, just like the backend server.

quiz.q: What does the browser use to ask a server for a page?
quiz.explain: HTTP (or HTTPS) is the language browsers and servers use to talk.

lessons.title: Mobile Application Development
lessons.content:
What is it? Mobile Application Development is about building apps for phones and tablets, like the bKash, Pathao, Facebook or Daraz apps you use every day. A phone is a small computer, but a special one: it has a touch screen, a battery that runs out, a camera, GPS, sometimes weak internet, and users who switch apps every few seconds. This course teaches you how to build apps that work well under all those conditions.

Why learn it? In Bangladesh, most people go online through their phones, not laptops. Banks, shops, delivery services and even government services all want apps. Mobile developers are in high demand for jobs and for freelancing, and you can publish your own app to Google Play and reach millions. It also brings together many things you already learned: programming, OOP, databases, networking and user interface design.

What is in the course? A typical syllabus covers mobile platforms (Android and iOS), native versus cross-platform development, tools like Android Studio, Xcode and Flutter, user interface design with layouts and widgets, the app lifecycle, navigating between screens, storing data on the phone, calling web APIs, using sensors like camera and GPS, permissions and security, notifications, testing and publishing to app stores.

Platforms and tools: The two big platforms are Android, made by Google, and iOS for iPhones, made by Apple. Native Android apps are written in Kotlin or Java with Android Studio, and native iOS apps in Swift with Xcode. Cross-platform tools let you write one code for both. Flutter, made by Google and written in Dart, is very popular for this, and React Native uses JavaScript. Native gives the most control; cross-platform saves a lot of time and money.

User interface: Mobile screens are small, so design matters a lot. Screens are built from small pieces: in Flutter they are called widgets, in Android they are views and layouts. Buttons must be big enough for a thumb, text must be readable, and the layout must adjust to many different screen sizes. Following design guidelines like Google's Material Design and Apple's Human Interface Guidelines makes apps feel familiar to users.

App lifecycle: The app lifecycle is about what happens when an app opens, goes to the background or closes. On Android, an Activity moves through states like created, started, resumed, paused, stopped and destroyed. Why does this matter? If someone is filling in a long form and a phone call comes, the app goes to the background. A good app saves their work so nothing is lost when they come back. The phone may also kill background apps to save memory, so you must be ready for that.

Screens, data and networking: Most apps have several screens, and navigation moves between them, like going from a product list to product details. Apps store data on the phone using simple key-value storage (like shared preferences) for small settings, or a local database like SQLite for bigger data, so the app can work offline. To get fresh data, the app calls a REST API over the internet and receives JSON. Because mobile internet can be slow or disappear, good apps show a loading indicator and handle errors politely.

Sensors, permissions and notifications: Phones have a camera, GPS, microphone, accelerometer and fingerprint sensor. Before using the camera, location or contacts, a good app should ask the user for permission, and explain why it needs it. Push notifications let the app tell the user something even when it is closed, like "Your order is on the way". Use them carefully, because too many notifications make people uninstall your app.

Testing and publishing: You test apps on emulators and on real phones, especially cheap phones with little memory, because that is what many users actually have. Then you build a release version, sign it, and upload it to the Google Play Store or Apple App Store with screenshots and a description. After launch you watch crash reports and user reviews, and keep sending updates.

Real life example 1: Think of the Pathao app when you book a ride. It asks for location permission, then uses GPS to find where you are. It calls the server's API with your pickup and drop points and gets back the fare as JSON. The map widget shows nearby drivers. If you switch to WhatsApp for a moment, the lifecycle pauses the app, and when you return, your booking is still there. When the driver arrives, a push notification tells you, even if the app is closed.

Real life example 2: A simple expense tracker app for students. You add "lunch 80 taka" and it is saved in a local SQLite database, so it works without internet. A chart widget shows how much you spent this week. Once a day, when there is internet, it backs up your data to the cloud through an API. This small app uses almost every topic from the course.

Where students get confused and what exams ask: Students often think an app works the same on every phone. In reality, screen sizes, Android versions and phone power differ a lot, so you must test widely. Another confusion is native versus cross-platform: cross-platform does not mean slow or bad, it means one codebase for two platforms. Students also forget the lifecycle and lose user data when the app goes to the background. Typical exam questions: compare native and cross-platform development, explain the Android activity lifecycle with a diagram, explain how an app gets data from a REST API, explain permissions, and design screens for a given app.

After this course you can build a real app from idea to Play Store and handle real-world problems like slow internet and small screens. Next, build your own app, learn more about Human Computer Interaction for better design, and study Cloud Computing for the backend side.
key_points: Mobile apps must handle small screens, batteries and weak internet.
Native apps target one platform; cross-platform tools like Flutter use one code for Android and iPhone.
The app lifecycle is what happens when an app opens, goes to the background or closes.
Apps store data on the phone (SQLite) and fetch JSON from servers through REST APIs.
Ask the user for permission before using the camera or location.
Test on real, especially cheap, phones before release.
lessons.tip: Copy apps you love. Rebuild one screen of a famous app by yourself, and you will learn more than from ten tutorials.
lessons.task: Pick any app on your phone. Draw its main screen on paper and label each part: button, text, image, list. Then write what happens when you tap each button.

quiz.q: Which tool lets you write one code for both Android and iPhone?
quiz.explain: Flutter (and React Native) are cross-platform, so one codebase runs on both.

quiz.q: What is the app lifecycle about?
options: How long a phone battery lasts
What happens when an app opens, goes to background or closes
quiz.explain: The lifecycle is the set of stages an app goes through while running.

quiz.q: Before using the camera or location, a good app should...
quiz.explain: Phones protect privacy, so apps must ask the user before using sensitive features.

lessons.title: Human Computer Interaction
lessons.content:
What is it? Human Computer Interaction, or HCI, is the study of how people use computers, phones and apps, and how to design them so they feel easy. Think of a door. A good door has a handle that tells you "pull" and a flat plate that tells you "push". You never think about it. A bad door makes you push when you should pull, and you feel silly. HCI is about making every screen behave like the good door.

Why learn it? An app can have perfect code and still fail because people find it confusing. If users cannot find the button, for them the feature does not exist. Companies like Google, Apple, bKash and Pathao hire UX designers and researchers whose whole job is HCI. Even as a programmer, knowing HCI helps you build screens people actually like, and it connects to Software Engineering, Mobile App Development and Web Engineering.

What's in the course? The usual syllabus covers how humans see, remember and make mistakes, design principles, the user-centred design process, personas and scenarios, prototyping, usability testing and evaluation, accessibility, and newer kinds of interaction like voice, touch and gestures.

The human side: People have limits. Short-term memory holds only a few things at once, so a good app does not ask you to remember a 10-digit code from one screen and type it on another. People read screens in patterns, they notice colour and movement first, and they make slips like tapping the wrong small button. HCI says that when many users make the same mistake, the design should be improved, not the users blamed.

Design principles: Don Norman and others gave simple rules. Visibility: important actions should be easy to see. Feedback: when you tap, something should happen, like a button changing colour or a little loading circle. Consistency: the back button should be in the same place on every screen. Affordance: a thing should look like what it does, like a raised button that looks pressable. Error prevention: ask "Are you sure you want to delete?" before something you cannot undo.

User-centred design: You do not design for yourself. First you study real users: interview them, watch them work. Then you write down who they are using a persona, which is a realistic imaginary user, for example "Rahima, 45, uses a basic Android phone, reads Bangla better than English, sends money to her son every month". Scenarios describe what Rahima wants to do step by step. Now every design choice can be checked: would Rahima understand this?

Prototyping: Before writing real code, you make cheap versions. A paper prototype is just screens drawn on paper. A low-fidelity wireframe shows boxes and labels. A high-fidelity prototype in a tool like Figma looks almost real and you can tap through it. Cheap prototypes let you throw away bad ideas in minutes instead of weeks.

Usability testing: You give the prototype to 5 real users and a task, like "send 500 taka to this number". You watch quietly and note where they get stuck. You measure things like how long it took, how many errors they made and how satisfied they felt. Research shows even 5 users find most of the big problems. Other methods include heuristic evaluation, where experts check the design against a list of rules, and A/B testing, where half the users see version A and half see version B and you compare results.

Accessibility: Making apps usable for everyone, including people with weak eyesight, colour blindness, shaky hands or hearing problems. Examples: letting users make text bigger, good contrast between text and background, labels that screen readers can read out loud, buttons big enough to tap, and never using only colour to show meaning. In many countries this is even the law for government websites.

Real life example 1: Think of the bKash app sending money. Step 1, the main actions (Send Money, Cash Out, Mobile Recharge) are big icons on the home screen, that is visibility. Step 2, you type the number and it shows the name saved in your contacts, that is feedback, so you know you picked the right person. Step 3, before sending, it shows a summary and asks for your PIN, that is error prevention. Step 4, the tap-and-hold to confirm stops accidental sends. Each step is HCI in action.

Real life example 2: A lift (elevator) in a shopping mall. The buttons are arranged in floor order, they light up when pressed (feedback), the door-open button has a standard symbol, and there are Braille dots for blind people (accessibility). If the open and close buttons looked the same, people would press the wrong one, and that is a design failure, not a user failure.

Where people get confused / exam questions: Many think HCI just means making things pretty. It is about being easy and effective, not only beautiful. Students also mix up usability (how easy it is) and user experience (the whole feeling, including emotions). Common exam questions: list and explain Norman's design principles, draw the user-centred design cycle, write a persona for a given app, compare paper and high-fidelity prototypes, and describe how to run a usability test.

After this course you will look at every app and door differently. You will be able to plan a design around real users, build quick prototypes and test them. Next, practise with a tool like Figma and connect this with Mobile App Development and Web Engineering.
key_points: HCI is about designing computers and apps that feel easy for real people.
If many users make the same mistake, fix the design, not the users.
Key principles: visibility, feedback, consistency, affordance and error prevention.
A persona is a realistic imaginary user that guides design decisions.
Prototype cheaply, then do usability testing with real users.
Accessibility makes apps usable for people with weak eyesight and other needs.
lessons.tip: You are not your user. Always test with someone else, like a parent or a friend, and just watch quietly.
lessons.task: Give your phone to a family member and ask them to do one small task in an app, like set an alarm. Do not help. Write down every place they got stuck.

quiz.q: If users keep pressing the wrong button, what does HCI say?
quiz.explain: In HCI, repeated user mistakes point to a design problem, not a user problem.

quiz.q: A persona is...
options: A realistic imaginary user used in design
quiz.explain: Personas help designers remember who they are building for.

quiz.q: Making an app usable for people with weak eyesight is called...
quiz.explain: Accessibility means designing so people with different abilities can use the product.

lessons.title: Embedded Systems
lessons.content:
What is it? An embedded system is a small computer hidden inside another machine to do one special job. You do not see a keyboard or a screen like a laptop, but the computer is there. A microwave oven, a washing machine, a digital weighing scale, a car's airbag, a TV remote and a smart watch all have a tiny computer inside. Think of it like a cook who only makes tea all day. One job, done again and again, very reliably.

Why learn it? Most computers in the world are not laptops or phones, they are embedded systems. There are dozens in a modern car. Factories, hospitals, home appliances, drones and IoT devices all need people who can program them. This course joins what you learned in Digital Logic, Microprocessors and C programming, and it leads straight into IoT and Robotics.

What's in the course? The usual topics are microcontrollers, sensors and actuators, input/output and interfacing, interrupts and timers, embedded C programming, real-time systems and real-time operating systems, power saving, and the full design process from idea to a working board.

Microcontroller: The heart of an embedded system. A microcontroller is a whole small computer on one chip: CPU, a little RAM, flash memory for the program and input/output pins. Famous ones are the ATmega328 used in Arduino, the ESP32 with built-in WiFi, and ARM Cortex-M chips. Compared to a laptop processor it is slow and has very little memory, maybe a few kilobytes, but it is cheap, small and uses very little power.

Sensors and actuators: Sensors are the system's eyes and ears. They measure the world: temperature, light, distance, motion, gas. Actuators are the hands. They do something in the world: a motor spins, a buzzer beeps, an LED glows, a valve opens. So the loop is simple: the sensor reads, the microcontroller decides, the actuator acts. For example: if temperature sensor reads above 30, turn on the fan motor.

Inputs, outputs and interfacing: Pins can be digital (only on or off, 1 or 0) or analog (a range of values). An ADC (analog to digital converter) turns a sensor voltage like 2.1 volts into a number like 430 that the program can use. Chips talk to each other using simple protocols like UART, I2C and SPI, which are just agreed ways of sending bits over wires.

Interrupts and timers: Imagine you are studying and the doorbell rings. You stop, open the door, and then go back to studying. That is an interrupt. Instead of checking a button a million times a second, the microcontroller does its normal work and the button press interrupts it. Timers count clock ticks so the system can do things at exact times, like blinking an LED every 500 milliseconds or measuring how long a pulse lasted.

Real-time systems: A real-time system must respond within a fixed time, not just respond correctly. A car's airbag must open within a few milliseconds of a crash. Late is as bad as wrong. Hard real-time means missing the deadline is a disaster (airbag, pacemaker). Soft real-time means missing it occasionally is just annoying (a video call that stutters). Bigger embedded systems use a real-time operating system (RTOS) like FreeRTOS, which runs many small tasks and makes sure the urgent ones always get the CPU first.

Power and reliability: Many embedded devices run on batteries for months or years. So the chip sleeps most of the time and wakes up only when needed. A watchdog timer resets the system if the program gets stuck, so the device does not freeze forever. Embedded code must be careful, because you cannot ask a microwave user to restart Windows.

Real life example 1: A digital rice cooker. Step 1, you press Cook, and that is an input. Step 2, the microcontroller turns on the heater, an actuator. Step 3, a temperature sensor keeps reading the pot. Step 4, when all the water is gone, the temperature rises fast above 100 degrees, and the program sees it. Step 5, it switches the heater to Keep Warm mode and beeps the buzzer. One tiny chip, one clear job.

Real life example 2: An automatic gate at a parking lot. An infrared sensor detects a car, an interrupt wakes the microcontroller, it checks the RFID card, turns a motor to lift the barrier, starts a timer, and when the car passes and the timer ends it lowers the barrier again. Every step must happen on time, or cars crash into the gate.

Where people get confused / exam questions: Students mix up microprocessor and microcontroller. A microprocessor is just the CPU and needs separate memory chips. A microcontroller has everything on one chip. Many also think real-time means very fast; it really means predictable, always within the deadline. Typical exam questions: define embedded system with examples, compare microprocessor and microcontroller, explain sensors vs actuators, what is an interrupt, hard vs soft real-time, and draw a block diagram of a given system.

After this course you can design small smart devices: read sensors, control motors and make things react on time. Buy a cheap Arduino or ESP32 kit and blink your first LED. Next, move on to IoT, Robotics and Computer Peripherals & Interfacing.
key_points: An embedded system is a small computer inside a machine that does one special job.
A microcontroller has CPU, memory and input/output pins on one chip.
Sensors measure the world; actuators like motors and buzzers act on it.
Interrupts let the chip react to events without checking all the time.
A real-time system must respond within a fixed time, not just correctly.
Embedded devices must save power and never freeze, so they use sleep modes and watchdog timers.
lessons.tip: Buy a cheap Arduino kit. Blinking one LED with your own code feels like magic and keeps you motivated.
lessons.task: Walk around your home and list 5 machines that have a tiny computer inside. For each one, write one sensor (input) and one actuator (output) it might have.

quiz.q: Which of these is an embedded system?
quiz.explain: A microwave has a small computer inside that controls time and power.

quiz.q: In an embedded system, a motor or buzzer is an...
quiz.explain: Actuators produce action or output. Sensors read input from the world.

quiz.q: A real-time system must...
quiz.explain: For things like airbags or brakes, a late answer is a wrong answer.

lessons.title: Digital Signal Processing
lessons.content:
What is it? Digital Signal Processing, or DSP, means using a computer to clean, change or understand signals that have been turned into numbers. Sound, images, radio waves and sensor readings all become lists of numbers, and DSP is the math and code that works on those lists. Think of it like a kitchen: the raw signal is the vegetables, DSP is the cutting, washing and cooking, and the clean output is the finished curry.

Why learn it? Your phone does DSP every second: cancelling noise during calls, compressing songs into MP3, sharpening photos, decoding 4G and Wi-Fi signals. Hearing aids, ECG machines, voice assistants, radar, music studios and self-driving cars all need it. DSP engineers work in telecom, audio, medical devices, defence and chip companies, and it's the base for Image Processing, Computer Vision and speech AI.

What's in the course? A standard DSP syllabus covers: discrete-time signals and systems, sampling and aliasing, quantization, convolution and difference equations, the Z-transform, the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) and the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), and digital filter design (FIR and IIR filters).

Sampling and aliasing: To process a real signal, you first measure it many times per second; that's sampling. The Nyquist rule says the sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency in the signal. If a voice goes up to 4,000 Hz, sample at 8,000 times per second or more. If you sample too slowly, high frequencies pretend to be low ones; this is aliasing. You see it in videos when a spinning wheel looks like it's turning backwards.

Quantization: After sampling, each measured value is rounded to the nearest allowed level. With 8 bits you get 256 levels, with 16 bits 65,536 levels. Rounding causes a small error called quantization noise. More bits means less noise but bigger files. CD audio uses 16 bits, which is why it sounds clean.

Difference equations and convolution: A digital system is often written as a difference equation, like y[n] = 0.5x[n] + 0.5x[n - 1], which means: output = average of the current and previous sample. That's a tiny smoothing filter. Feed it [2, 4, 6] and you get [1, 3, 5] (assuming the value before the start is 0). The output can also be found by convolving the input with the system's impulse response.

Z-transform: The Z-transform is the digital cousin of the Laplace transform. It turns a sequence of numbers into a function of z, and turns difference equations into simple algebra. A delay of one sample becomes multiplication by z^(-1). From the result, H(z), you can see the poles and zeros of a system. If all poles are inside the unit circle, the system is stable.

DFT and FFT: The Discrete Fourier Transform takes N samples and tells you how much of each frequency is in them. Doing it directly needs about N² multiplications. The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) gets the same answer with about N log N. For N = 1024 that's around 10,000 instead of 1,000,000, about 100 times faster. FFT is one of the most important algorithms ever, and it runs inside every phone.

Digital filters, FIR and IIR: A filter keeps the frequencies you want and removes the rest. Low-pass keeps low frequencies (removes hiss), high-pass keeps high ones (removes hum), band-pass keeps a middle range. FIR filters use only input samples, are always stable and can have a perfectly even delay. IIR filters also use past outputs, so they need fewer calculations, but they can become unstable if designed badly. Design methods include windowing for FIR and converting analog designs for IIR.

Real life example 1: A phone call from a noisy bus stop in Farmgate. Step 1: the mic samples your voice and the honking traffic together.
