Step 2: the phone's DSP chip uses FFT to see which frequencies are voice and which are noise. Step 3: a second mic on the phone records mostly noise, and the chip subtracts it. Step 4: filters cut what's left of the hum and hiss. Step 5: the clean voice is compressed and sent. Your friend hears you, not the horns.

Real life example 2: Making an MP3. Step 1: the song is sampled at 44,100 times per second with 16 bits. Step 2: FFT-like transforms split it into frequency bands. Step 3: a model of human hearing throws away sounds your ears can't notice, like a quiet sound right next to a loud one. Step 4: what remains is packed tightly. A 50 MB song becomes about 5 MB, and most people can't hear the difference.

Where people get confused and what comes in exams: Students often mix up sampling frequency and signal frequency, forget the 'twice' in Nyquist, or confuse DFT (the math) with FFT (the fast method to compute it). Many think IIR is always better because it's cheaper, forgetting stability. Common exam questions: find the minimum sampling rate, compute a short convolution, find the Z-transform of a sequence, check stability from poles, compute a 4-point DFT, and compare FIR and IIR filters.

After this course you can design simple filters, analyse frequencies with FFT, avoid aliasing and understand how phones, audio apps and medical sensors clean their data. Next: Digital Image Processing and Computer Vision, where you do DSP on pictures.
key_points: DSP uses computers to process signals stored as numbers.
Sample at least twice the highest frequency, or you get aliasing.
More bits per sample means less quantization noise.
The Z-transform turns difference equations into algebra; poles inside the unit circle mean stable.
The FFT computes the DFT in about N log N steps instead of N².
FIR filters are always stable; IIR filters are cheaper but can go unstable.
lessons.tip: Try every filter in a free tool like Audacity or Python. Hearing the result makes the theory stick far better than reading.
lessons.task: Record a 10-second voice note near a noisy fan or road, then one in a quiet room. Listen to both. Write down what a filter would need to remove from the first one.

quiz.q: What happens if you sample a signal too slowly?
options: The signal turns into an image
quiz.explain: Sampling below twice the highest frequency causes aliasing, where high frequencies pretend to be low ones.

quiz.q: A low-pass filter...
options: Keeps low frequencies and cuts high ones like hiss
quiz.explain: Low-pass lets slow, low-frequency parts through and blocks high-frequency noise.

quiz.q: What is the FFT?
options: A fast way to compute the frequencies in a signal
quiz.explain: The Fast Fourier Transform computes the DFT very quickly, so it's used everywhere in DSP.

lessons.title: Software Testing & Quality Assurance
lessons.content:
What is it? Software testing means checking that a program does what it should, and catching the places where it doesn't, before real users find them. Quality Assurance, or QA, is the bigger idea: setting up the whole way a team works so fewer bugs get made in the first place. Think of a school exam. Checking your answer sheet before you hand it in is testing. Practising every day so you make fewer mistakes is QA.

Why learn it? Bugs cost money and trust. Imagine a payment app that sends 1000 taka when you typed 100. People would delete it the same day. Fixing a bug while you are still coding is cheap. Fixing it after a million people installed the app is very expensive. That's why companies hire QA engineers and SDETs (developers who write test code), and why every good developer tests their own code. This course also helps a lot in Software Engineering, Software Project Management and your final year project.

What's in the course? A typical syllabus covers: the basics of errors, faults and failures, levels of testing, black-box test design, white-box testing and code coverage, test automation and regression testing, non-functional testing like performance and security, and finally QA processes, standards and reviews. Let's go through them one by one.

Error, fault and failure: these three sound the same but aren't. An error is the human mistake, like typing > instead of >=. That mistake sits in the code as a fault, also called a bug. When the program runs and gives a wrong result because of it, that's a failure. Example: the rule is "age 18 or more can vote", but the code says if age > 18. The error was the typo, the fault is the wrong line, and the failure is an 18 year old being told "you can't vote".

Levels of testing: unit testing checks one small piece on its own, like one function add(2, 3) should give 5. Integration testing checks that pieces work together, like the login screen talking to the database. System testing checks the whole app from start to end. Acceptance testing checks that it's what the customer actually wanted. Small and many at the bottom, big and few at the top. People draw this as a testing pyramid.

Black-box testing: you don't look at the code at all, only inputs and outputs, like a normal user. Two key tricks. Equivalence partitioning groups inputs that behave the same, so you test one from each group. Boundary value analysis tests the edges, because bugs love edges. If a form accepts ages 18 to 60, you test 17, 18, 60 and 61. That one trick would have caught our voting bug instantly.

White-box testing: now you open the box and read the code. You design tests so every line runs at least once (statement coverage), and every if goes both the true and the false way (branch coverage). Example: if (balance >= amount) send() else showError(). You need at least two tests: one with enough balance and one without. Coverage tools tell you which lines your tests never touched.

Automation and regression testing: running tests by hand every day is slow and boring. So we write test code that the computer runs in seconds, for example assert add(2, 3) == 5. Every time someone changes the code, all old tests run again to make sure nothing broke. That's regression testing. In CI (Continuous Integration), this happens automatically on every push to GitHub.

Non-functional testing: does the app work well, not just correctly? Performance testing checks speed. Load testing checks what happens when 10,000 people use it at once. Security testing tries to break in, for example by typing weird code into a login box. Usability testing watches real people use the app and notes where they get confused.

QA process and reviews: QA is about stopping bugs early. Teams do code reviews, where a teammate reads your code before it's merged. They follow standards like ISO 9001 or models like CMMI, keep a test plan, and track every bug in a bug tracker with steps to reproduce it, expected result and actual result. A good bug report is half the fix.

Real life example 1: think of a bKash style send money screen. A tester writes cases step by step. Send 100 taka with enough balance: should work. Send 100 with only 50 in the account: should show an error. Send 0 taka: should be blocked. Send -100: must be blocked, or someone could steal money. Type the PIN wrong 3 times: account should lock. Each case has an input and an expected result, and every one runs again after each new app update.

Real life example 2: a cricket bat factory. Before a bat goes to the shop, someone checks the wood, the grip and how the ball bounces off it. That's testing. If the factory also trains workers, picks good wood and follows the same steps every time so bad bats rarely happen, that's QA. Both are needed: checking catches today's bad bat, the process stops tomorrow's.

Where students get confused: many mix up verification ("are we building the product right?", meaning does it match the design) and validation ("are we building the right product?", meaning does the customer want it). Many also think testing can prove there are no bugs. It can't: testing only shows bugs are present, never that they're absent. Common exam questions: design boundary value test cases for a given range, draw a control flow graph and count paths, differentiate black-box and white-box testing, and explain the testing levels with examples.

After this course you can write proper test cases, think like someone trying to break your app, and set up automated tests that guard your code forever. Next, look at Software Project Management to see where testing fits into a full project, and try a testing tool like JUnit, pytest or Flutter's test package on your own project.
key_points: Testing finds bugs before users do; QA improves the process so fewer bugs happen.
Error is the human mistake, fault is the bug in code, failure is the wrong result.
Levels: unit, integration, system and acceptance testing, like a pyramid.
Black-box tests inputs and outputs; boundary values catch the most bugs.
White-box testing aims for statement and branch coverage.
Automated regression tests rerun after every change so nothing old breaks.
lessons.tip: When you test, stop being the proud author of the code. Become the naughty user who presses every wrong button.
lessons.task: Open any sign up form on your phone. Write 5 weird inputs to try, like an empty name or a 50 digit phone number, and note what the app does with each.

quiz.q: Checking one single function on its own is called...
quiz.explain: Unit testing checks the smallest piece, like one function, on its own.

quiz.q: In black-box testing, the tester...
options: Only looks at inputs and outputs, not the code inside
Reads every line of the code
quiz.explain: Black-box testing treats the program like a closed box: give input, check output.

quiz.q: Running old tests again after changing the code, to make sure nothing broke, is called...
quiz.explain: Regression testing makes sure a new change didn't break something that used to work.

lessons.title: Multimedia Systems
lessons.content:
What is it? Multimedia means mixing different kinds of media: text, pictures, sound, video and animation. A multimedia system is the hardware and software that captures, stores, compresses, sends and plays all of that. YouTube, Spotify, video calls, and even a PowerPoint with a video inside are multimedia systems. Think of it like a tiffin box with rice, curry and dessert in separate parts: different things packed together and delivered as one meal.

Why learn it? Most of the internet today is video and pictures. Raw video is huge: one minute of uncompressed HD video can be several gigabytes. Without clever tricks, you couldn't watch a single YouTube video on mobile data. This course shows how computers make media small and fast while still looking and sounding good. It helps if you want to work on streaming apps, video calling, social media, e-learning platforms or game development, and it leads into Digital Image Processing and Computer Vision.

What's in the course? A typical syllabus covers: how media becomes digital (sampling and quantization), images and colour models, digital audio, compression basics, image and audio compression standards like JPEG and MP3, video compression like MPEG and H.264, and multimedia networking and streaming.

Digitization, sampling and quantization: computers only understand numbers, so real world sound and light must become numbers. Sampling means measuring the signal many times a second. Quantization means rounding each measurement to a fixed set of levels. CD audio takes 44,100 samples per second, each stored as a 16 bit number. More samples and more bits mean better quality but bigger files. The Nyquist rule says you must sample at least twice as fast as the highest frequency you want to keep.

Images and colour models: a picture is a grid of tiny dots called pixels. Each pixel usually stores red, green and blue (RGB) values from 0 to 255. Pure red is (255, 0, 0) and white is (255, 255, 255). A 1920x1080 photo has about 2 million pixels, and at 3 bytes each that's about 6 MB raw. Printers use a different model called CMYK (cyan, magenta, yellow, black), and video often uses YCbCr, which separates brightness from colour.

Digital audio: sound is air vibrating. A microphone turns it into an electric wave, and the computer samples it. File size = sample rate x bits per sample x channels x seconds. So 1 minute of CD quality stereo is 44,100 x 16 x 2 x 60 bits, about 10 MB. That's why we need compression for music apps. MIDI is different: it doesn't store the sound, only the notes, like sheet music, so the files are tiny.

Compression basics: lossless compression keeps every detail, so you get back exactly the original. Run length encoding turns AAAAABBB into 5A3B. Huffman coding gives short codes to common symbols and long codes to rare ones, like how we say "ok" a lot so it's short. ZIP and PNG are lossless. Lossy compression throws away details your eyes and ears barely notice, so files get much smaller. Compression ratio = original size / compressed size.

JPEG and MP3: JPEG splits the image into 8x8 blocks, converts each block into frequencies with the DCT (Discrete Cosine Transform), then throws away most of the fine high frequency details our eyes don't care about. That's why a heavily compressed JPEG looks blocky. MP3 uses a psychoacoustic model: if a loud sound hides a quiet one, the quiet one is simply dropped because you wouldn't hear it anyway.

Video compression: a video is many pictures per second, usually 25 to 60. Neighbouring frames are mostly the same, so instead of storing every full frame, MPEG and H.264 store an I-frame (a full picture) now and then, and in between store P-frames and B-frames that only describe what moved. This trick, called motion compensation, can make video 100 times smaller.

Streaming and multimedia networking: streaming sends media in small chunks so playback starts before the whole file arrives. A buffer keeps a few seconds ready in case the network hiccups. Adaptive bitrate streaming, used by YouTube and Netflix, keeps several quality versions and switches between them depending on your internet speed. Live video calls use protocols like RTP, and prefer speed over perfection: a lost packet is skipped rather than resent.

Real life example 1: you watch a Bangladesh vs India match live on your phone. The camera's raw video goes to an encoder that compresses it with H.264. The green field stays the same, so mostly only the players and the ball are updated. The stream is cut into 2 to 6 second chunks in several qualities. Your app downloads chunks one by one. When you step into a lift and the signal drops, it switches to 360p, so the picture gets blurry but doesn't stop. Back outside, it climbs back to 1080p.

Real life example 2: sending a photo on WhatsApp or Messenger. Your phone's 4 MB photo becomes around 200 KB before it's sent. The app resizes it and saves it as a stronger JPEG. On a small screen it looks almost the same, but zoom in a lot and you'll see blurrier details. That's lossy compression trading a little quality for much faster sending and less data cost.

Where students get confused: many think lossless means "no compression". It doesn't, it means compressed with no information lost. Another mix up is resolution versus file size: two images with the same resolution can have very different sizes depending on compression. Common exam questions: calculate the size of an uncompressed image or audio file, encode a string with Huffman or RLE, explain I, P and B frames, and compare lossy with lossless compression.

After this course you'll understand how images, audio and video are stored, compressed and streamed, and you can pick the right format and quality settings for any app. Next, look at Digital Image Processing and Computer Vision to go deeper into pictures, or Computer Networks to understand the delivery side better.
key_points: Multimedia mixes text, images, audio, video and animation.
Sampling and quantization turn real sound and light into numbers.
Images are pixel grids, usually stored as RGB values from 0 to 255.
Lossless compression (Huffman, RLE, PNG) keeps everything; lossy (JPEG, MP3) drops what we barely notice.
Video saves space with I, P and B frames, storing only what changes.
Adaptive streaming switches quality to match your internet speed.
lessons.tip: Keep a few media files on your computer and check their sizes as you study each format. Seeing the numbers makes compression click.
lessons.task: Take the same photo and save it once as PNG and once as JPEG (any phone editor or Paint works). Compare the file sizes and zoom in to see which one lost details.

quiz.q: Which of these is a lossy format?
quiz.explain: MP3 throws away sound details we barely hear to make the file small. PNG and ZIP are lossless.

quiz.q: Why can video compression skip storing every full frame?
options: Because phones can't show full frames
Because the internet only carries text
Because most of the picture stays the same between frames
quiz.explain: Neighbouring frames are mostly the same, so storing only the changes saves a lot of space.

quiz.q: When your internet slows down and the video gets blurry but keeps playing, that's...
quiz.explain: Adaptive streaming switches to a lower quality so playback doesn't stop.

lessons.title: Game Development
lessons.content:
What is it? Game development is making video games: designing the fun, writing the code, making the art and sound, and putting it all together. It mixes almost everything in CSE: programming, math, physics, graphics, AI, and networking for online games. Think of it like making a film where the audience gets to control the hero, so everything has to react instantly to what they do.

Why learn it? Games are a huge industry, bigger than movies and music combined. Even if you never make games for a living, game projects teach real engineering: making things run fast, handling many objects at once, and keeping users hooked. Many students learn programming best by making a small game. The skills carry over to Computer Graphics, AI, simulations, AR/VR and even app animations. Bangladeshi studios also build mobile games for global players.

What's in the course? A typical syllabus covers: game design basics, the game loop, 2D and 3D math for games (vectors and transforms), physics and collision detection, game AI, game engines and assets, and finally multiplayer and publishing.

Game design: before coding, decide what makes the game fun. Every game has a core loop of actions you repeat, like jump, collect coin, avoid enemy. It has rules, a goal, challenges and rewards. Difficulty should rise slowly so players feel in flow, not bored and not frustrated. Designers write this down in a GDD (Game Design Document) and test early versions on paper or with simple shapes before making nice art.

The game loop: every game runs the same loop again and again, about 60 times a second. while (running) { readInput(); update(dt); render(); }. dt is the time since the last frame. Moving things by speed x dt means the game runs at the same speed on a slow phone and a fast PC. If one frame takes too long, the game feels laggy, so the whole loop must finish in about 16 milliseconds.

Vectors and transforms: positions and speeds are vectors, like (x, y). If a ball is at (100, 200) with velocity (5, -3), next frame it's at (105, 197). To move, rotate or scale an object we apply transforms, usually with matrices. 3D games add a z axis, and a camera transform turns the 3D world into the 2D picture on your screen.

Physics and collision detection: simple physics adds gravity to velocity each frame: vy = vy + g * dt. Collision detection checks if two objects overlap. The easiest way is AABB, axis aligned bounding boxes: two rectangles collide if they overlap on both the x axis and the y axis. Circles collide if the distance between centres is less than the sum of their radii. After detecting a hit, collision response decides what happens: bounce, stop, or lose a life.

Game AI: enemies need to look smart without being too hard. A finite state machine is the classic tool: an enemy has states like Patrol, Chase and Attack, and rules to switch, for example if the player is within 5 metres, go from Patrol to Chase. For finding a way around walls, games use pathfinding algorithms like A* (A-star) on a grid. Bigger games use behaviour trees to organise more complex decisions.

Game engines and assets: most people don't build all of this from scratch. Engines like Unity (C#), Unreal (C++) and Godot (GDScript) give you rendering, physics, sound, input and an editor. You add assets: sprites (2D pictures), 3D models, animations, sound effects and music. Engines use a scene made of game objects with components, like a player object with a sprite, a collider and a movement script.

Multiplayer and publishing: online games send player actions over the network. Usually a server is the boss and decides what really happened, so cheaters can't lie about their score. Lag is handled with tricks like client side prediction, where your phone guesses the result before the server replies. Finally you test the game, optimise it for slow phones, and publish it to Google Play, the App Store or Steam.

Real life example 1: Ludo King on your phone. The game loop waits for your tap. Then it rolls the dice with a random number from 1 to 6, moves your piece step by step with a small animation, checks whether it landed on an opponent's piece (a collision on the board grid) and sends that piece home, then checks the win rule. In an online match, your move is sent to a server, which checks it's legal and forwards it to your friend's phone.

Real life example 2: a Flappy Bird style game. Every frame, gravity pulls the bird down a little. A tap sets its upward speed. Pipes move left at a fixed speed, and new ones are created off screen. An AABB check between the bird and each pipe decides game over. The score goes up when the bird passes a pipe. That's a complete game built from a loop, a few vectors and one collision check.

Where students get confused: many tie movement to frames instead of time, so the game runs faster on faster phones. Always multiply by dt. Others think a game engine does everything. You still need design, logic and math. Common exam questions: write pseudo-code for a game loop, check whether two rectangles collide, draw a state machine for an enemy, and explain what a game engine provides.

After this course you can build a small 2D game, understand how a game engine works inside, and use the game loop idea in any real time app. Start by finishing a tiny clone like Pong or Snake. Next, look at Computer Graphics for better visuals and Artificial Intelligence for smarter enemies.
key_points: A game runs a loop: read input, update the world, render the screen, about 60 times a second.
Multiply movement by dt so the game runs at the same speed on every device.
Positions and speeds are vectors; transforms move, rotate and scale objects.
AABB and circle checks detect collisions; gravity is added to velocity each frame.
State machines and A* pathfinding make enemies look smart.
Engines like Unity, Unreal and Godot give you physics, graphics and sound ready-made.
lessons.tip: Start tiny. A finished Pong or Flappy Bird clone teaches you more than a half built open world game.
lessons.task: Pick a simple game you know, like Snake. On paper, write what happens in one turn of its game loop: what input it reads, what it updates and what it draws.

quiz.q: What are the three main steps of a game loop?
options: Read input, update the world, draw the screen
quiz.explain: The game loop keeps reading input, updating the game world and drawing it, many times a second.

quiz.q: Checking whether a bullet touched an enemy is called...
quiz.explain: Collision detection checks if two objects overlap, like a bullet and an enemy.

quiz.q: Unity, Unreal and Godot are examples of...
quiz.explain: Game engines come with physics, graphics, sound and tools so you don't build everything from scratch.

lessons.title: Machine Learning
lessons.content:
What is it? Machine Learning, or ML, is teaching a computer to learn from examples instead of giving it every rule by hand. Think of how a child learns what a cat is. Nobody gives the child a rulebook like "four legs, whiskers, pointy ears". They just see many cats and someone says "cat". Soon they can spot a cat they have never seen before. ML does the same with data.

Why learn it? ML is behind Facebook's news feed, YouTube suggestions, Google Translate, spam filters, face unlock, fraud detection in banks and price suggestions on Daraz. It is one of the most wanted skills in the job market. This course uses your Linear Algebra, Probability & Statistics and programming, and it leads to Deep Learning, NLP, Computer Vision and Data Mining.

What's in the course? The main topics are types of learning, the data and features, regression, classification, model training and loss, overfitting and underfitting, evaluating a model, and unsupervised learning like clustering. Usually you also learn algorithms like linear regression, logistic regression, decision trees, k-nearest neighbours, support vector machines and k-means.

Types of learning: In supervised learning, the training data has labels, meaning the correct answers. Example: 10,000 emails, each marked spam or not spam. The model learns the pattern. In unsupervised learning there are no labels; the model finds groups or patterns by itself, like grouping customers by shopping habits. In reinforcement learning, an agent learns by trial and error with rewards, like a game player getting points.

Data and features: A feature is one piece of information about each example. For a flat, features could be size in square feet, number of rooms, area name and floor number. Choosing good features matters a lot. Data is split into a training set to learn from and a test set to check the model later, often 80 percent and 20 percent. Data must be cleaned first: missing values, wrong entries and duplicates cause bad models.

Regression: Predicting a number. Predicting a flat's price is regression. The simplest version is linear regression, which draws the best straight line through the data: price = w x size + b. The model learns w and b. If w = 8,000 and b = 500,000, a 1,000 square foot flat gives 8,000 x 1,000 + 500,000 = 85 lakh taka.

Classification: Predicting a category, like spam or not spam, cat or dog, or which digit is in a picture. Logistic regression gives a probability, like 0.92 chance of spam. A decision tree asks yes/no questions: does the email contain "lottery"? Is the sender unknown? k-nearest neighbours looks at the k most similar examples and takes a vote.

Training and loss: The model starts with random guesses. A loss function measures how wrong it is, for example the average of (prediction minus real answer) squared. Gradient descent then nudges the weights a little bit in the direction that lowers the loss, again and again, like walking downhill in fog one step at a time until you reach the bottom.

Overfitting and underfitting: A model that does great on training data but badly on new data is overfitting. It memorised the answers instead of learning the pattern, like a student who memorises last year's questions and fails when the questions change. Underfitting is the opposite: the model is too simple to even fit the training data. Fixes for overfitting include more data, simpler models, regularisation and cross-validation.

Evaluation and clustering: Accuracy is the percentage of correct answers, but it can lie. If 99 percent of transactions are normal, a model that always says normal gets 99 percent accuracy and catches zero fraud. So we also use precision, recall and the confusion matrix. For unsupervised learning, k-means clustering puts data into k groups by repeatedly moving each group's centre to the middle of its points.

Real life example 1: A Gmail spam filter. Step 1, collect millions of emails that users marked as spam or not spam. Step 2, turn each email into features: which words appear, the sender, links. Step 3, train a classifier. Step 4, test it on emails it has never seen. Step 5, when a new email arrives, the model gives a spam probability, and above a threshold it goes to the spam folder. When you click "not spam", you create a new label and the model keeps learning.

Real life example 2: A ride app predicting your fare and arrival time. It uses regression with features like distance, time of day, rain and traffic. It learned from millions of past rides. That is why at 6 pm on a rainy weekday in Dhaka the estimated time is higher.

Where people get confused / exam questions: Many mix up regression and classification. Ask: is the answer a number (regression) or a category (classification)? People also think high training accuracy means a good model; only test accuracy on new data tells the truth. Common exam questions: supervised vs unsupervised, define overfitting and how to fix it, calculate accuracy, precision and recall from a confusion matrix, run one step of k-means or k-NN by hand, and explain gradient descent.

After this course you can take a dataset, pick a suitable algorithm, train a model and check honestly if it works. Try Python with scikit-learn on a small dataset from Kaggle. Next, go to Deep Learning, Pattern Recognition and Data Mining.
key_points: Machine learning lets computers learn patterns from examples instead of hand-written rules.
Supervised learning uses labels (correct answers); unsupervised learning finds patterns without labels.
Regression predicts a number; classification predicts a category.
Training lowers a loss function step by step using gradient descent.
Overfitting means great on training data but bad on new data.
Judge a model on test data, using accuracy, precision and recall.
lessons.tip: Spend most of your time understanding the data. A simple model on clean data beats a fancy model on messy data.
lessons.task: Write down the last 7 days: hours you slept and how fresh you felt (1 to 5). Look for a pattern. Can you predict tomorrow's freshness from sleep? That is a tiny ML model in your head.

quiz.q: In supervised learning, the training data has...
quiz.explain: Supervised learning learns from examples where the right answer is already given.

quiz.q: A model that does great on training data but badly on new data is...
quiz.explain: Overfitting means it memorized the training examples instead of learning the general pattern.

quiz.q: Predicting a flat's price (a number) is an example of...
quiz.explain: Regression predicts a number. Classification predicts a category.

lessons.title: Computer Security & Cryptography
lessons.content:
What is it? Computer Security is about protecting computers, data and people from attackers. Cryptography is the maths of secret writing that makes much of that protection possible. Think of your house: locks on the door, a guard at the gate, and a safe for valuables. Security is all of those, but for data. Cryptography is the special lock that even a smart thief cannot open without the key.

Why learn it? Every day we send passwords, bank details, OTPs and private messages over the internet. Hackers steal money, data and even shut down hospitals with ransomware. Banks, mobile financial services like bKash and Nagad, government offices and every tech company need security people. It is one of the fastest growing jobs, and it connects with Networks, Operating Systems and later Advanced Cyber Security.

What's in the course? Main topics are the CIA triad, common attacks, symmetric encryption, public-key cryptography, hashing, digital signatures and certificates, authentication, and network and web security like firewalls and HTTPS.

CIA triad: The three goals of security. Confidentiality: only the right people can read the data. Integrity: no one can change the data without being caught. Availability: the system works when you need it. A leaked password breaks confidentiality, a changed bank amount breaks integrity, and a website taken down by a flood of traffic breaks availability.

Common attacks: Malware is bad software like viruses, worms and ransomware, which locks your files and asks for money. Phishing is when someone pretends to be trusted, like a fake bank call or SMS asking for your OTP. A DoS or DDoS attack floods a server so real users cannot get in. SQL injection is typing database commands into a login box to trick a badly written website. Man-in-the-middle means someone secretly sitting between you and the server, reading or changing messages.

Symmetric encryption: The same key locks and unlocks. A very old example is the Caesar cipher: shift every letter by 3, so HELLO becomes KHOOR. Modern ciphers like AES are far stronger and are used everywhere, from WiFi to your phone storage. The problem: how do two people who have never met share the secret key safely?

Public-key cryptography: Each person has two keys. The public key can be given to everyone; the private key must be kept secret. Something locked with your public key can only be opened with your private key. Think of a post box with a slot: anyone can drop a letter in, but only you have the key to open it. RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography are famous examples. They solve the key sharing problem.

Hashing: A hash function turns any data into a short fixed-size fingerprint, like SHA-256. The same input always gives the same hash, but you cannot go backwards from the hash to the input, and a tiny change gives a totally different hash. Websites store the hash of your password, not the password itself. When you log in, they hash what you typed and compare. Adding a random salt to each password stops attackers from using precomputed tables.

Signatures, certificates and authentication: A digital signature is made with a private key; anyone can check it with the public key, proving who sent the message and that it was not changed. Certificates are like an ID card for websites, issued by trusted authorities, so your browser knows it really is your bank's website. Authentication is proving who you are: something you know (password), something you have (phone for OTP), something you are (fingerprint). Using two of them is two-factor authentication.

Real life example 1: Opening your bank's website. Step 1, your browser connects using HTTPS. Step 2, the server sends its certificate, and your browser checks it is signed by a trusted authority. Step 3, using public-key cryptography, they agree on a fresh secret key. Step 4, all data after that is encrypted with fast symmetric encryption like AES. Step 5, you log in with a password plus an OTP. The little lock icon in the address bar means all of this worked.

Real life example 2: Someone calls pretending to be from your bank: "Your account will be blocked, tell us the OTP". That is phishing, a social engineering attack. No encryption can save you if you hand over the key yourself. Real banks never ask for your PIN or OTP. Security is about people as much as maths.

Where people get confused / exam questions: Encryption and hashing are different: encryption can be reversed with a key, hashing cannot. In public-key systems, you keep the private key secret, never the other way round. Encoding like Base64 is not encryption at all. Typical exam questions: explain the CIA triad, encrypt a word with Caesar or a simple cipher, symmetric vs asymmetric, how RSA works with small numbers, what is a hash and why salt, and how HTTPS protects you.

After this course you can spot common attacks, choose the right crypto tool for a job and build systems that keep data safe. Practise with free capture-the-flag (CTF) challenges. Next, go to Advanced Cyber Security, Blockchain and Network Security.
key_points: Security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability (the CIA triad).
Phishing tricks people into giving secrets like OTPs; banks never ask for them.
Symmetric encryption uses one shared key; AES is the common modern choice.
In public-key cryptography, you share the public key and keep the private key secret.
A hash is a one-way fingerprint of data, used for storing passwords safely.
HTTPS combines certificates, public-key and symmetric encryption to protect your browsing.
lessons.tip: Think like an attacker. For any system you build, ask "How would I break this?" before someone else does.
lessons.task: Make a simple Caesar cipher: shift each letter 3 forward (A becomes D). Encrypt your name, give it to a friend with the rule, and let them decrypt it.

quiz.q: In public-key cryptography, which key must you keep secret?
quiz.explain: The public key can be shared with everyone. The private key must stay only with you.

quiz.q: Someone calls pretending to be from your bank and asks for your OTP. This is...
quiz.explain: Phishing tricks people into giving away secrets by pretending to be someone trusted.

quiz.q: What is a hash mainly used for?
options: Making a fingerprint of data, like for storing passwords
quiz.explain: A hash turns data into a fixed fingerprint. Websites store password hashes, not the passwords.

lessons.title: Distributed Systems
lessons.content:
What is it? A distributed system is many computers working together over a network so that, to the user, they look like one single system. When you open Facebook, you do not talk to one computer. You talk to thousands of machines in data centres around the world, but it feels like one website. Think of a big wedding kitchen: many cooks, each doing part of the work, but the guests just see one big feast.

Why learn it? One computer cannot handle a billion users, and one computer can break. Google Search, YouTube, bKash, Daraz during an 11.11 sale, online banking and cloud services are all distributed systems. Big companies pay very well for engineers who understand this. This course builds on Operating Systems and Networks and leads to Cloud Computing, Big Data and Blockchain.

What's in the course? Main topics: why distribute, communication between machines, time and clocks, replication, consistency, consensus, fault tolerance, and scaling with load balancers and partitioning.

Why distribute and the problems it brings: We distribute for scale (more users), speed (servers closer to users) and reliability (if one dies, others continue). But new problems appear: messages can be slow or lost, machines crash at random times, and there is no single shared clock. The famous saying: a distributed system is one where a computer you did not even know existed can break your work.

Communication: Machines talk by sending messages over the network. A common style is RPC (Remote Procedure Call), where calling a function on another machine looks like calling a normal function. Others use message queues, where a sender drops a message in a queue and the receiver picks it up later, like leaving a note on the fridge. Since messages can get lost, systems use timeouts and retries.

Time and clocks: Every machine's clock drifts a little, so you cannot fully trust timestamps to know what happened first. Lamport clocks solve this with a counter: every event adds 1, and every message carries the counter, so the receiver sets its own counter higher. This gives a consistent order of events without a perfect clock.

Replication: We keep copies of data on many machines so data survives when a machine fails and so more people can read at the same time. If a server in one data centre burns down, the copy in another still has your photos. The hard part is keeping all copies the same when data changes.

Consistency and the CAP theorem: Strong consistency means every read sees the latest write, like a bank balance. Eventual consistency means copies may differ for a short time but will match soon, like a like-count on a post that shows 99 on one phone and 100 on another for a second. The CAP theorem says when the network splits, you must choose between consistency and availability; you cannot have both perfectly.

Consensus: Sometimes machines must agree on one value, like who is the leader or which order transactions happen in, even if some machines crash. Raft and Paxos are algorithms for helping machines agree. In Raft, servers vote for a leader; the leader receives every update and copies it to followers; once a majority confirms, the update is final. With 5 servers, the system keeps working even if 2 crash.

Scaling and fault tolerance: A load balancer spreads users across many servers, like a ticket counter manager sending each new person to the shortest queue. Partitioning or sharding splits the data, for example users A to M on one database and N to Z on another. Health checks remove dead servers automatically, and the system keeps running even when parts fail.

Real life example 1: Daraz on 11.11. Step 1, millions of people open the app at midnight. Step 2, a load balancer sends each request to one of hundreds of web servers. Step 3, product data is replicated so many servers can read it at once. Step 4, the stock count uses strong consistency so two people cannot buy the last phone. Step 5, if a server crashes, health checks remove it and users go to others, mostly without noticing.

Real life example 2: WhatsApp group messages. Your message goes to a server, gets stored in replicated storage, and is delivered to each member's phone. If someone is offline, the message waits in a queue. The order is kept the same for everyone. The one tick, two ticks and blue ticks show steps of this distributed process.

Where people get confused / exam questions: People think more machines always means faster; coordination adds overhead, so not always. Many confuse replication (copies of the same data) with partitioning (splitting different data). Also, eventual consistency does not mean data is wrong forever. Exam favourites: advantages and challenges of distributed systems, Lamport clock example, explain CAP theorem, how Raft elects a leader, replication vs partitioning, and the role of a load balancer.

After this course you will understand how giant apps stay alive with millions of users and broken machines. Try running a small app with two servers behind a load balancer using Docker. Next, go to Cloud Computing, Big Data and Blockchain.
key_points: A distributed system is many computers working together that look like one system.
We distribute for scale, speed and reliability, but must handle lost messages and crashes.
Replication keeps copies so data survives when a machine fails.
The CAP theorem: during a network split, choose consistency or availability.
Raft and Paxos help machines agree on a value, like who is the leader.
A load balancer spreads users across many servers.
lessons.tip: In distributed systems, always ask "What if this message is lost or this machine dies right now?" That one question finds most bugs.
lessons.task: With 3 friends, each write a number on paper without talking. Now agree on one number by only passing notes. Notice how slow and tricky agreement is. That is consensus.

quiz.q: Why keep copies of data on many machines?
options: So data survives when a machine fails
quiz.explain: Replication makes the system survive failures.

quiz.q: Raft and Paxos are used for...
options: Helping machines agree on a value
quiz.explain: They are consensus algorithms that let many machines agree even if some fail.

quiz.q: A load balancer...
quiz.explain: It sends each request to a server that can handle it, so no one server is overloaded.

lessons.title: Digital Image Processing
lessons.content:
What is it? Digital Image Processing is about using a computer to change, improve and understand pictures. To a computer, a picture is just a big grid of numbers. Each tiny square is a pixel, and its number says how bright it is. Think of a picture made of graph paper where each box is coloured with a shade. Image processing is doing maths on those boxes.

Why learn it? Every phone camera uses it to make photos sharp and bright. Instagram filters, the beauty mode in selfie cameras, scanning documents with your phone, number plate reading at toll plazas, X-ray and MRI enhancement in hospitals, satellite images for flood maps in Bangladesh: all of these are image processing. It also is the foundation for Computer Vision and Deep Learning on images.

What's in the course? Main topics: how images are stored, point operations like brightness and contrast, histograms, filtering for blur and sharpening, noise removal, edge detection, segmentation, colour models, the frequency domain, and compression like JPEG.

Pixels and representation: In an 8-bit gray image each pixel holds a value from 0 to 255. A pixel value of 0 means black and 255 means white; 128 is middle gray. A 1000 x 1000 image has one million pixels. A colour image usually stores three numbers per pixel: red, green and blue (RGB). So pure red is (255, 0, 0) and yellow is (255, 255, 0). Resolution is the number of pixels; more pixels means more detail.

Point operations and histograms: A point operation changes each pixel on its own. Add 50 to every pixel to make the image brighter. Use 255 minus the value to make a negative. A histogram is a bar chart that counts how many pixels have each brightness. A dark photo has bars crowded on the left. Histogram equalisation spreads them out, which improves contrast and makes hidden details visible.

Filtering: Here each new pixel depends on its neighbours. We slide a small window, like 3 x 3, over the image; this is called convolution. An average (mean) filter replaces each pixel with the average of the 9 around it, so it blurs and reduces noise. A sharpening filter does the opposite and makes edges crisp. A median filter takes the middle value instead of the average and is excellent for removing salt-and-pepper noise, those random white and black dots.

Edge detection: An edge is where brightness changes suddenly, like the border between a black shirt and a white wall. Operators like Sobel and Prewitt measure how fast the brightness changes from one pixel to the next. The Canny edge detector is a famous multi-step method that gives thin, clean edges. Edges help find the borders of objects, which is the first step to recognising shapes.

Segmentation: Splitting an image into meaningful parts, like separating a person from the background. The simplest method is thresholding: every pixel brighter than 100 becomes white, the rest black. This works well for scanning a page, where text is dark and paper is bright. Other methods grow regions from a seed pixel or group pixels with similar colour.

Colour, frequency and compression: Besides RGB, the HSV model separates colour (hue) from brightness, which makes it easier to find, for example, all green leaves. The Fourier transform shows an image as a mix of slow changes (low frequency) and fast changes (high frequency, like fine details and noise). JPEG compression throws away high-frequency details your eyes hardly notice, which is why a 10 MB photo can become 1 MB.

Real life example 1: Scanning a document with CamScanner. Step 1, the app finds the four edges of the paper using edge detection. Step 2, it straightens the page with a geometric transform so it looks flat. Step 3, it converts to gray and uses thresholding so text becomes black and the paper pure white. Step 4, a filter removes noise and shadows. Step 5, it compresses the result into a small PDF.

Real life example 2: A doctor's X-ray looks too dark. Histogram equalisation stretches the contrast so a small crack in a bone becomes visible. A median filter removes speckle noise without blurring the bone edges. Image processing literally helps doctors see more.

Where people get confused / exam questions: Students forget that 0 is black and 255 is white in an 8-bit image. Many think blurring removes noise for free; it also blurs edges, which is why the median filter is often better. Also, image processing changes images, while computer vision tries to understand them. Typical exam questions: apply a 3 x 3 mean or median filter on a small matrix by hand, draw and equalise a histogram, apply Sobel to find edges, threshold an image, and explain RGB vs HSV.

After this course you can write programs that brighten, clean, sharpen and cut up images. Try Python with OpenCV and play with blur, edges and threshold on your own photo. Next, go to Computer Vision, Pattern Recognition and Deep Learning.
key_points: A digital image is a grid of pixels; in 8-bit gray, 0 is black and 255 is white.
Colour images store red, green and blue values for each pixel.
A histogram counts brightness levels; equalisation improves contrast.
A mean filter blurs and reduces noise; a median filter removes salt-and-pepper noise.
Edge detection (Sobel, Canny) finds borders of objects.
Thresholding and segmentation split an image into meaningful parts.
lessons.tip: Use OpenCV in Python and see results instantly. Seeing the output picture makes each formula click.
lessons.task: Open any photo editor on your phone. Change brightness, then contrast, then blur. For each one, write in one line what you think happens to the pixel numbers.

quiz.q: In an 8-bit gray image, a pixel value of 0 means...
quiz.explain: 0 is black and 255 is white in a usual 8-bit grayscale image.

quiz.q: An average (mean) filter is mainly used to...
quiz.explain: Averaging nearby pixels smooths out random noise, but also blurs details.

quiz.q: Which operation helps find the borders of objects?
quiz.explain: Edge detectors like Sobel find places where brightness changes sharply, which are object borders.

lessons.title: Simulation & Modeling
lessons.content:
What is it? Simulation and Modeling means building a pretend version of a real system on a computer and then running it to see what happens. A model is a simplified description of the real thing, and a simulation is running that model over time. Think of how pilots train in a flight simulator. They can crash a hundred times without anyone getting hurt. Simulation lets us crash ideas safely.

Why learn it? Companies simulate before doing things in real life to test ideas safely and cheaply. Building a new flyover to check if traffic gets better costs crores of taka; simulating it costs a laptop and a few days. Weather forecasts, hospital planning, factory lines, airport queues, epidemic spread during COVID and video game physics all use simulation. It uses your Probability & Statistics and programming, and connects to Operations Research and Machine Learning.

What's in the course? Main topics: systems and models, types of simulation, random numbers, Monte Carlo simulation, discrete-event simulation, queuing theory, building and validating a model, and analysing the output.

Systems and models: A system is the real thing you care about, like a bank branch. Its parts are entities (customers), resources (tellers), events (arrival, service finished) and state (how many people are waiting). A model keeps the important parts and drops the rest; we do not care about the colour of the tellers' shirts. Models can be physical (a small model of a bridge), mathematical (equations) or computer simulations.

Types of simulation: Static simulation has no time, like estimating a probability. Dynamic simulation changes over time. Deterministic models have no randomness, so the same input always gives the same output. Stochastic models include randomness, like random customer arrivals. Continuous simulation changes smoothly, like water level in a tank, while discrete simulation jumps from event to event, like customers arriving one by one.

Random numbers: Real life is random, so simulations need random numbers. Computers make pseudo-random numbers using formulas, for example the linear congruential generator: next = (a x current + c) mod m. They look random but are repeatable if you use the same starting seed, which is great for checking results. Then we shape them to match real data, like making arrival gaps follow an exponential distribution.

Monte Carlo simulation: A simulation that uses random numbers many times to estimate a result is called Monte Carlo, named after a famous casino. Example: to estimate pi, throw random dots into a square with a circle inside. The fraction landing in the circle is about pi/4. With 1,000,000 dots you get close to 3.14. Banks use the same idea to estimate risk across thousands of possible futures.

Discrete-event simulation: The computer keeps an event list sorted by time and a clock. It takes the next event, jumps the clock to that time, updates the state and may schedule new events. Customer arrives at 10:02, teller free, so service starts and a finish event is set for 10:07. Next arrival at 10:04 sees a busy teller and joins the queue. It skips empty time, so even a whole year can be simulated in seconds.

Queuing theory: Queuing theory is mostly about lines and waiting times. Key values are arrival rate (lambda, how many come per hour) and service rate (mu, how many one server can handle per hour). If lambda = 10 and mu = 12, the server is busy 10/12, about 83 percent of the time. If lambda goes above mu, the line grows forever. Notation like M/M/1 means random arrivals, random service times and one server.

Building, validating and analysing: Steps: define the problem, collect real data, build the model, verify (is the code doing what we meant?) and validate (does the model behave like the real system?). Then run many times, because one random run can mislead, and report averages with confidence intervals. Finally compare options, like 3 tellers vs 4 tellers.

Real life example 1: A hospital emergency room in Dhaka. Step 1, collect data: about 20 patients per hour, a doctor takes 15 minutes per patient on average. Step 2, build a discrete-event model with patients, doctors and beds. Step 3, simulate a whole month in seconds. Step 4, try 4 doctors vs 6 doctors at night. Step 5, see waiting time drop from 90 minutes to 20, so management knows exactly how many to hire.

Real life example 2: A traffic signal at a busy intersection. Engineers simulate cars arriving from four roads with random gaps, try different green-light timings, and measure average waiting time. Instead of testing on real roads and causing jams, they find the best timing on a computer first.

Where people get confused / exam questions: Students confuse verification (did we build the model right?) with validation (did we build the right model?). Many trust a single run; you need many runs. Also, a model is always a simplification, not the real thing. Common exam questions: define system, model and simulation; advantages and disadvantages of simulation; generate numbers with a linear congruential generator; hand-simulate a single-server queue for 5 customers in a table; calculate utilisation; and explain Monte Carlo with an example.

After this course you can turn a messy real-world question into a model, run it with random inputs and make data-based decisions. Try simulating a tea stall queue in a spreadsheet or Python. Next, explore Operations Research and Parallel Computing for bigger simulations.
key_points: A model is a simplified version of a real system; a simulation runs it over time.
Simulation tests ideas safely and cheaply before doing them for real.
Monte Carlo uses random numbers many times to estimate a result.
Discrete-event simulation jumps from event to event using an event list and clock.
Queuing theory studies lines and waiting times using arrival and service rates.
Verify the code, validate against reality, and run many times before trusting results.
lessons.tip: Start with the simplest model that could work. Add details only when the results look wrong.
lessons.task: Roll a dice 20 times and write each number. Pretend each number is how many minutes a customer takes at a shop. Add them up to estimate how long one cashier needs for 20 customers.

quiz.q: Why do companies simulate before doing things in real life?
options: To test ideas safely and cheaply
quiz.explain: Simulation saves money and risk by testing ideas in a computer first.

quiz.q: A simulation that uses random numbers many times to estimate a result is called...
quiz.explain: Monte Carlo simulation repeats random trials to estimate an answer.

quiz.q: Queuing theory is mostly about...
quiz.explain: Queuing theory studies how lines form and how long people wait.

lessons.title: Professional Ethics & Cyber Law
lessons.content:
What is it? Professional Ethics & Cyber Law is the course about doing the right thing with your computer skills, and knowing what the law says about it. Think of it like the rules of cricket. You can be the best batsman in the world, but if you tamper with the ball, you are out. Being a great programmer is not enough. You also have to play fair.

Why learn it? Software now touches everyone: money in bKash, health records in hospitals, marks in your university portal. One careless or greedy engineer can hurt millions of people. Companies want engineers they can trust, and courts can punish people who break cyber laws. This course helps you stay out of trouble and helps you build things people can safely depend on.

What's in the course: what ethics means for engineers, professional codes of conduct (like the ACM and IEEE codes), intellectual property (copyright, patents, licences), privacy and data protection, computer crime and cyber law (including Bangladesh's laws), and the social impact of technology like AI bias and automation.

Ethics and codes of conduct: Ethics is simply asking "Is this right?" before you act. Professional bodies like ACM and IEEE have written codes for engineers. The big ideas are short: avoid harm, be honest, respect privacy, do work you are actually qualified to do, and speak up if something you build could hurt people. Example: if your boss asks you to hide a known bug in a medical app, the code says your duty to the public comes first. Real codes also talk about competence: if a client asks you to build a payment system and you've never touched security, the honest move is to say so, learn, or bring in someone who knows. Pretending can cost people their money.

Plagiarism and honesty: Copying someone's code, report or idea and submitting it as your own is plagiarism. In university it can fail you; in a job it can get you fired. Using open source or someone's help is fine, as long as you give credit and follow the licence. A simple rule: if it isn't yours, say where it came from.

Intellectual property: This is the law about ownership of ideas. Copyright protects an original work, like a book, a song or a piece of software, from being copied without permission. It applies automatically when you create the work. A patent protects a new invention or method, but you must apply for it. A trademark protects a brand name or logo, like the bKash logo. Software licences (MIT, GPL and so on) say what others may do with your code. Open source licences differ a lot. MIT lets almost anyone reuse your code, even in paid products, as long as they keep your name in it. GPL says that if someone shares a modified version, they must share their source code too. Always read the licence before you copy a library into a company project.

Privacy and data protection: Apps collect huge amounts of personal data: phone numbers, locations, photos, NID numbers. The golden rule is: collect only what you need and protect it. Store passwords hashed, encrypt sensitive data, ask for consent, and delete what you no longer need. Europe's GDPR is a famous privacy law, and many countries, including Bangladesh, are making their own.

Computer crime and cyber law: Hacking into systems without permission, spreading malware, stealing data, online fraud and cyberbullying are crimes. In Bangladesh, cyber crimes are handled under laws like the ICT Act and the newer Cyber Security Act. You also learn about digital evidence, how police trace crimes, and why "I was just testing" is not an excuse without written permission. Ethical hacking is the legal version: companies hire security testers and give written permission, a clear scope and a time window. Same skills, but with a signed agreement, so it's a job instead of a crime.

Social impact of technology: Technology is never neutral. A loan app's AI might reject people from poor areas unfairly because of biased training data. Automation can replace jobs. Social media can spread fake news fast. As an engineer, you are expected to think about these side effects before you ship, not after.

Real life example 1: Imagine you build a food delivery app for Dhaka. The marketing team wants to secretly read users' contact lists to send invitations. Step 1: ask, is this necessary for food delivery? No. Step 2: did users clearly agree? No. Step 3: could it harm them? Yes, their friends' numbers get leaked. So the ethical answer is to refuse or ask for clear permission. That one decision protects thousands of people.

Real life example 2: A student downloads a cracked copy of paid software to finish a project. It feels harmless, but it breaks copyright law and cracked software often carries malware. The ethical and safer choice is to use the free student licence or an open source alternative. Same project, no risk.

Where people get confused and what comes in exams: Students mix up copyright, patent and trademark. Remember: copyright for creative works and code, patent for inventions, trademark for brand names and logos. Another confusion is thinking "if it's online, it's free to use". Not true. Exams often ask you to define plagiarism, explain the ACM code, compare IP types, discuss a case study and name relevant cyber laws.

Wrap-up: After this course you will know how to handle tricky situations at work, protect user data, respect other people's work, and stay on the right side of the law. Next, Computer Security & Cryptography will show you the technical side of protecting people.
key_points: Ethics means asking "is this right?" before acting; codes like ACM and IEEE guide engineers.
Submitting someone else's work as yours is plagiarism; always give credit.
Copyright protects original works like software; patents protect inventions; trademarks protect brands.
Collect only the user data you need, and protect it.
Hacking, fraud and data theft are crimes under cyber laws, including Bangladesh's.
Think about the social impact of what you build before you ship it.
lessons.tip: When unsure, ask: "Would I be okay if this decision appeared on the front page of a newspaper?" If not, don't do it.
lessons.task: Open the privacy settings of one app you use. Write down what data it collects (location, contacts, photos). Decide if each one is really needed.

quiz.q: Copying someone's code and submitting it as yours is...
quiz.explain: Using others' work without credit and calling it yours is plagiarism.

quiz.q: A good rule for user data is...
options: Collect only what you need and protect it
quiz.explain: Collect the minimum data and keep it safe. That protects users and you.

quiz.q: Which one protects an original software or book from being copied?
quiz.explain: Copyright gives creators legal rights over their original work.

lessons.title: Technical Writing
lessons.content:
What is it? Technical writing means explaining technical things in writing so clearly that the reader gets it on the first read. Reports, user manuals, project proposals, README files, emails to your team and research papers are all technical writing. It's like giving directions to your house: if you are clear, your guest arrives; if you are vague, they end up lost in Mirpur.

Why learn it? Engineers write a lot more than people think. Your code might be brilliant, but if nobody understands your report, your proposal gets rejected and your thesis gets marks cut. In jobs, the person who explains clearly gets trusted with bigger work. And your final year thesis is basically one big piece of technical writing.

What's in the course: knowing your audience, planning structure, writing clear sentences, reports and proposals, documentation and manuals, using figures and tables, citing sources and avoiding plagiarism, and editing and revising.

Know your reader: Before writing a single word, ask who will read this and what they need. A teacher wants to see you understand the method. A customer wants to know which button to press. Another programmer wants the exact API details. Same topic, three different documents. Writing for the wrong reader is the most common mistake. A quick test: write one sentence saying who your reader is and what they should be able to do after reading. If you can't, you're not ready to write yet. For a mixed audience, put a simple summary first and the deep details later.

Structure: Plan the skeleton first. A typical report has a title, abstract (a short summary of everything), introduction (the problem), method (what you did), results (what you found), conclusion (what it means) and references. A user manual has steps in order. A good structure lets readers jump straight to the part they need. An abstract deserves special care because many readers read only that. In 150 to 250 words it should say the problem, what you did, the main result with a number, and why it matters. Write it last, after everything else is done, so it truly matches the report.

Clear sentences: Use short sentences and simple words. One paragraph should carry one idea. Prefer active voice: "The program saves the file" is clearer than "The file is saved by the program". Cut words that add nothing: "due to the fact that" can simply be "because". Be precise with numbers and terms too. "The app is very fast" tells the reader nothing; "the app loads in 1.2 seconds on a 4G phone" tells them everything. And once you call something "user", don't switch to "client" and "customer" for the same thing later, or readers will think they are different people.

Figures, tables and steps: A good diagram can replace a page of text. Put numbers in tables so readers can compare them quickly. Write instructions as numbered steps, one action per step. Always label figures and tables ("Figure 1: System architecture") and refer to them in the text. For code documentation, write comments that explain why, not what: "retry 3 times because the payment server sometimes times out" is useful; "add 1 to i" is not. API documentation should show each function's inputs, outputs, errors and one small example call.

Citing sources and plagiarism: Whenever you use someone else's idea, data, figure or words, you must cite the source. Using someone else's words or results without giving credit is plagiarism, and universities treat it very seriously. Common citation styles are IEEE (numbered, like [1]) and APA (author and year). Tools like Zotero or Mendeley keep your references organised.

Editing and revising: The first draft is never the final one. Read it again after a break, cut extra words, fix spelling and check that every claim is supported. Reading it out loud is a great trick: wherever you stumble, the sentence needs fixing. Ask a friend to read it, too. A useful checklist before you submit: Is the title clear? Does every figure have a caption? Is every reference cited in the text? Are there any sentences longer than about 25 words? Did you spell-check? Five minutes with a checklist can save marks and embarrassment.

Real life example 1: Think of the instruction on a bKash app screen: "Enter your PIN to confirm". It is short, clear and impossible to misread. Now imagine it said "Kindly proceed to furnish your personal identification number for the purpose of transaction verification". Same meaning, but much harder to follow. Technical writing is choosing the first version every time. In the same way, "Click Save to keep your changes" beats any long, formal version.

Real life example 2: Your team project on GitHub needs a README. A good one says: what the project does (one line), how to install it (numbered steps), how to run it (one command), and who to contact. A new teammate can start in five minutes instead of messaging you ten times. That's technical writing saving real time.

Where people get confused and what comes in exams: Many students think big words sound smarter. In technical writing, simple wins. Another mistake is writing everything as one huge paragraph. Exams often ask you to write a short report or proposal, improve a badly written paragraph, explain the parts of a report, or show proper citations.

Wrap-up: After this course you can write lab reports, project documentation, proposals and your thesis without fear, and people will actually enjoy reading them. Start practising with your next lab report, and later check Research Methodology for the MSc side of writing.
key_points: Technical writing explains technical things so the reader gets it on the first read.
Know your reader before you write.
Plan the structure first: title, abstract, introduction, method, results, conclusion, references.
Short sentences, simple words, active voice, one idea per paragraph.
Using others' words or results without credit is plagiarism; always cite.
Revise: read it again, read it out loud, cut extra words.
lessons.tip: After writing, read it out loud. Wherever you run out of breath or stumble, the sentence is too long or unclear.
lessons.task: Write the steps to send money with bKash in 6 numbered lines or fewer, for someone who has never used it. Give it to a family member and see if they can follow it without asking you anything.

quiz.q: What should you think about first before writing a technical document?
options: Using as many big words as possible
Making it as long as possible
Who the reader is and what they need
quiz.explain: Knowing your reader decides your words, your detail level and your structure.

quiz.q: Using someone else's words or results without giving credit is called...
quiz.explain: Plagiarism means using others' work without credit. Citing your sources avoids it.

quiz.q: Which sentence is better technical writing?
options: Click Save to keep your changes.
It is hereby requested that the user kindly proceed to click upon the Save button.
Saving may or may not be required, depending.
Changes, if desired to be kept, require saving activity.
quiz.explain: Short, direct and clear wins. The reader knows exactly what to do.

lessons.title: VLSI Design
lessons.content:
What is it? VLSI means Very Large Scale Integration: putting millions or even billions of tiny transistors on one small chip. The processor in your phone, the memory in your laptop and the chip in your smartwatch are all VLSI chips. This course teaches how such chips are designed, from one transistor up to a full circuit. Think of it like building a huge city out of tiny bricks, where every brick is a switch.

Why learn it? Every gadget, from a calculator to a supercomputer, runs on chips. Chip design is one of the most important and best-paid industries in the world. Intel, AMD, Apple, Nvidia, Qualcomm and TSMC all need VLSI engineers, and Bangladesh now has chip design companies too. Even software engineers benefit, because knowing how hardware works helps you write faster code. It also connects to Computer Architecture, Embedded Systems and AI hardware.

What's in the course? A typical VLSI syllabus covers: MOS transistors and CMOS technology, CMOS logic gates, the chip fabrication process, layout and design rules, delay and power, combinational and sequential circuit design, hardware description languages (Verilog/VHDL), the design flow from idea to chip, FPGAs, and testing.

MOS transistors and CMOS: A MOSFET is a tiny switch controlled by voltage. An nMOS transistor turns on when its gate is high (1); a pMOS turns on when its gate is low (0). CMOS uses both together so that in a steady state almost no current flows, which saves a lot of power. That's why nearly every modern chip is CMOS. The simplest CMOS circuit is the inverter: one pMOS on top, one nMOS below. Input 1 gives output 0, input 0 gives output 1.

CMOS logic gates: From transistors we build gates. A CMOS NAND gate uses 4 transistors: two pMOS in parallel on top and two nMOS in series below. A NOR gate flips that arrangement. NAND and NOR are called universal gates because any logic can be built from them alone. Bigger blocks like adders, multiplexers and flip-flops are made by combining gates. A 1-bit full adder takes about 28 transistors in standard CMOS.

Fabrication and layout: Chips are made on thin slices of silicon called wafers, using light to print patterns (photolithography), then adding and removing layers again and again. Designers draw a layout: the exact shape and position of every transistor and wire on each layer. Design rules say how small and how close things can be, like 'wires must be at least this far apart'. Breaking a rule can short circuit the chip, so tools check the layout automatically (DRC).

Delay and power: Every gate takes a little time to switch, called propagation delay. The longest chain of delays, the critical path, sets the chip's top speed. If the critical path is 1 ns, the clock can run at about 1 GHz. Power comes in two kinds: dynamic power, used when switching, roughly P = C × V² × f, and static power, from small leaks. Lowering the voltage V cuts power a lot, which is why phone chips run at low voltage.

Verilog and the design flow: Nobody draws billions of transistors by hand. Engineers describe the circuit in a hardware description language. In Verilog, a 1-bit adder can be as short as: assign sum = a ^ b; assign carry = a & b. The flow is: specification, writing RTL code, simulation to test it, synthesis to turn it into gates, placement and routing to make the layout, then checks for timing, rules and power, and finally sending it to the factory (tape-out).

FPGAs and testing: An FPGA is a chip full of programmable logic blocks and wires that you can reconfigure in seconds. Designers load their Verilog onto an FPGA to test it on real hardware before spending millions on a real chip. After manufacturing, chips are tested for defects, for example a wire stuck at 0. Design-for-test tricks like scan chains add special paths that make testing easier.

Real life example 1: Think of building a planned city. Step 1: transistors are bricks. Step 2: gates are houses built from bricks. Step 3: adders and memory are neighbourhoods. Step 4: the processor is the whole city. Step 5: the layout is the city map, showing every road (wire) and building. One mistake in the map can cause a traffic jam everywhere, and you can't rebuild the city cheaply. That's why chip designers simulate and test again and again before the factory builds anything.

Real life example 2: Your phone battery lasting all day. Step 1: chip designers know that power ≈ C × V² × f. Step 2: they lower the voltage when you're just reading messages. Step 3: they turn off parts of the chip you're not using, like the camera processor (power gating). Step 4: they lower the clock speed when the phone is idle. These VLSI tricks are why a modern phone can do so much on a small battery.

Where people get confused and what comes in exams: Students often mix up which transistor (nMOS or pMOS) goes in series or parallel for NAND and NOR. Many forget that static CMOS uses almost no power when idle. Others think Verilog runs line by line like C, but hardware runs in parallel. Common exam questions: draw a CMOS NAND/NOR or a complex gate, explain the fabrication steps, calculate dynamic power, find the critical path delay, write a small Verilog module, and explain the VLSI design flow.

After this course you can design CMOS gates, write and simulate Verilog, understand how a chip goes from code to silicon, and try your designs on an FPGA. Next: Embedded Systems, advanced computer architecture or a hardware-focused thesis.
key_points: VLSI means putting millions or billions of transistors on one chip.
CMOS uses nMOS and pMOS together to save power.
Transistors form gates, gates form adders, memory and processors.
The critical path sets the top speed; dynamic power ≈ C × V² × f.
Chips are written in Verilog or VHDL and go through simulation, synthesis and layout.
FPGAs let you test a design before making a real chip.
lessons.tip: Simulate everything. Write a tiny Verilog module, like a 4-bit adder, and test it in a free online simulator before learning the next topic.
lessons.task: Search your phone's settings or online for the name of its processor chip and how many transistors it has (or roughly). Write that number down and compare it with how many people live in Bangladesh.

quiz.q: What does VLSI stand for?
quiz.explain: VLSI means Very Large Scale Integration, putting a huge number of transistors on one chip.

quiz.q: Which language is used to describe chip hardware?
quiz.explain: Verilog (and VHDL) are hardware description languages used to describe digital circuits.

quiz.q: Why use an FPGA during chip design?
options: To test the design on reprogrammable hardware before making the real chip
quiz.explain: An FPGA can be reprogrammed, so engineers try their design on it before paying to manufacture a real chip.

lessons.title: Operations Research
lessons.content:
What is it? Operations Research, or OR, is using math to find the best way to do something when you have limits: limited money, time, trucks or people. OR helps you answer, "what is the cheapest, fastest or most profitable plan?" Think of planning your Eid shopping with fixed money: you want the most happiness without going over budget. OR does that, but with equations.

Why learn it? Every business and government makes these choices every day. Which route should the delivery van take? How many of each product should a factory make? How many counters should a bank open at lunch time? Guessing wastes money. OR gives the best answer, or one very close to it. Airlines, delivery companies, supply chains and ride sharing apps all run on OR. It also builds on Linear Algebra and connects to Algorithms, Simulation & Modeling and Machine Learning, where optimisation is everywhere.

What's in the course? A typical syllabus covers: building a model, linear programming and the graphical method, the Simplex method, duality and sensitivity analysis, transportation and assignment problems, network models like shortest path and CPM/PERT, queuing theory, and game theory.

Building a model: first turn the real problem into math. Decision variables are what you choose, like x = number of shirts. The objective is what you maximise or minimise, like profit = 200x + 300y. Constraints are your limits, like 2x + 3y <= 120 hours of sewing. Plus non-negativity: x, y >= 0, because you can't make minus 5 shirts.

Linear Programming and the graphical method: if the objective and constraints are straight line relationships, it's a linear program. With two variables you can solve it by drawing. Each constraint is a line, and the area that satisfies all of them is the feasible region, usually a polygon. The best answer is always at one of its corner points. Calculate the objective at every corner and pick the best one.

The Simplex method: with many variables, you can't draw. The Simplex method, invented by George Dantzig, walks from one corner of the feasible region to a neighbouring corner that improves the objective, again and again, until no neighbour is better. It's done with a table called a tableau, choosing a pivot column and pivot row each step. Slack variables turn <= constraints into equations, like 2x + 3y + s = 120.
