Duality and sensitivity: every LP has a twin problem called its dual. If the original maximises profit from limited resources, the dual tells you how much each resource is worth, its shadow price. Sensitivity analysis asks what happens if a number changes, like cloth getting 10% more expensive: does the best plan change, and by how much?

Transportation and assignment: the transportation problem sends goods from several warehouses to several shops at minimum total cost. You start with a method like Northwest Corner or Vogel's Approximation, then improve it. The assignment problem gives n jobs to n workers, one each, at minimum cost or time. The Hungarian method solves it by subtracting row and column minimums until a zero in every row and column lets you assign.

Network models, queuing and game theory: network models find shortest paths and plan projects. CPM and PERT find the critical path of a project. Queuing theory studies waiting lines. In the simple M/M/1 model, with arrival rate λ and service rate μ, the server is busy ρ = λ/μ of the time, and the line explodes if λ gets close to μ. Game theory studies decisions when two sides compete, like two shops setting prices, and finds a saddle point or mixed strategy.

Real life example 1: a garments factory in Gazipur makes shirts and trousers. A shirt gives 200 taka profit and a trouser 300. A shirt needs 2 hours of sewing and a trouser 3, with only 120 sewing hours a day. Cloth allows at most 50 pieces a day. Model: maximise 200x + 300y with 2x + 3y <= 120, x + y <= 50, x, y >= 0. The corner points are (0,0), (50,0), (30,20) and (0,40). The profits there are 0, 10,000, 12,000 and 12,000. Making 30 shirts and 20 trousers, or just 40 trousers, both earn the most, 12,000 taka.

Real life example 2: a bank branch in Motijheel at lunch time. Customers arrive at about 30 per hour, and one counter serves 20 per hour. With one counter, λ > μ, so the line grows forever and people get angry. With two counters, each handles about 15 an hour out of a capacity of 20, so they're busy 75% of the time and the line stays short. Queuing theory tells the manager to open the second counter at lunch only, which saves staff time in the quiet hours.

Where students get confused: many forget the non-negativity constraints, or flip >= and <= while drawing. Some think the best point can be in the middle of the feasible region, but for LP it's always on a corner. In the transportation problem, if supply and demand aren't equal, you must add a dummy row or column first. Common exam questions: formulate an LP from a word problem, solve it graphically, do 2 or 3 Simplex iterations, solve an assignment problem with the Hungarian method, and find the critical path of a project.

After this course you can turn messy real decisions into math models and solve them to find the best plan. Next, look at Simulation & Modeling for problems too random to solve exactly, and Advanced Algorithms for optimisation on huge inputs. Try Excel Solver or Python's PuLP library to solve your own LPs.
key_points: OR uses math to find the best plan when resources are limited.
A model has decision variables, an objective, and constraints.
In linear programming the best answer is always at a corner of the feasible region.
The Simplex method walks from corner to corner until no better corner is left.
The Hungarian method solves assignment; Vogel's method gives a good start for transportation.
Queuing theory: if arrivals λ get close to service rate μ, the line explodes.
lessons.tip: Don't jump into formulas. First write the problem in plain words: what do I want, and what stops me? The math almost writes itself after that.
lessons.task: You have 500 taka for a trip and want to visit as many places as possible. Write your objective and at least 3 constraints, like money, time and transport, in plain words.

quiz.q: In an OR model, the thing you want to maximise or minimise is called the...
quiz.explain: The objective is the goal, like maximum profit or minimum cost.

quiz.q: Which method is commonly used to solve Linear Programming problems?
quiz.explain: The Simplex method is the classic way to solve Linear Programming problems.

quiz.q: Deciding how many bank counters to open so people don't wait too long is studied in...
quiz.explain: Queuing theory studies waiting lines and how to serve people with less waiting.

lessons.title: Software Project Management
lessons.content:
What is it? Software Project Management is planning and running a software project so it gets finished on time, within budget, and actually does what the customer wanted. Writing code is one part. Deciding who does what, when, how much it will cost, and what to do when things go wrong is the other part. Think of a cricket team captain: they may not bowl every ball, but they plan the field, change bowlers and react when the match changes.

Why learn it? Lots of software projects fail, not because people can't code, but because of bad planning. Deadlines slip, the budget runs out, the client keeps changing their mind, and the team burns out. Knowing project management makes you a better teammate now and a team lead or project manager later. It also makes your final year project much less stressful. It builds on Software Engineering and connects to Testing and System Analysis & Design.

What's in the course? A typical syllabus covers: project planning and scope, work breakdown and estimation, scheduling with Gantt charts and the critical path, risk management, process models like Waterfall and Agile/Scrum, team management and communication, and finally monitoring, quality and configuration management.

Project planning and scope: first answer what's being built, for whom, by when and with what money. The scope says what's in and what's out. The triple constraint says scope, time and cost are tied together: if the client adds features, either time or cost must grow, or quality suffers. Uncontrolled extra features are called scope creep, the number one project killer. A project charter writes all of this down and gets everyone to agree.

Work breakdown and estimation: break the project into smaller and smaller pieces until each task is small enough to estimate. That tree is the WBS (Work Breakdown Structure). Then estimate effort. Expert judgement asks experienced people. Function points count features like screens and reports. COCOMO estimates effort from size, for example Effort = a x (KLOC)^b person-months. Three point estimation uses (Optimistic + 4 x Most likely + Pessimistic) / 6.

Scheduling, Gantt chart and critical path: a Gantt chart shows each task as a bar on a timeline. Tasks have dependencies: you can't test before you build. In CPM (Critical Path Method), you draw tasks as a network and find the longest path from start to finish. That's the critical path, and its length is the shortest possible project time. Tasks on it have zero slack. Others can slip a bit without hurting the deadline. PERT does the same with uncertain three point estimates.

Risk management: a risk is something that might go wrong. List risks early, like the main developer leaving, a third party API changing, or the client's server being slow. For each, estimate probability and impact, and risk exposure = probability x cost. Then plan a response: avoid it, reduce it, transfer it (for example insurance or outsourcing), or accept it with a backup plan ready.

Process models, Waterfall and Agile: Waterfall goes step by step: requirements, design, code, test, deploy. It's good when requirements are clear and fixed. Agile works in short cycles and welcomes change. In Scrum, the Product Owner keeps a prioritised product backlog. The team picks items for a 1 to 4 week sprint, meets for a 15 minute daily stand-up, and at the end shows working software in a sprint review, then improves its process in a retrospective. Kanban uses a board with To Do, Doing and Done columns.

Team, monitoring and configuration management: people matter most. A manager builds the team, assigns roles, keeps communication clear and protects the team from burnout. To monitor progress, Earned Value Management compares planned work, completed work and money spent: if CPI = earned value / actual cost is below 1, you're over budget. Configuration management keeps track of versions with tools like Git, so everyone knows which code is in which release.

Real life example 1: planning a wedding. There's a date that can't move, a budget, and a long task list: venue, catering, decoration, cards, photographer. Some tasks run in parallel, but the cards can't be printed before the venue is fixed, and decoration needs the venue too. Venue to cards to sending is the critical path. If the caterer cancels a week before, a backup caterer you found earlier saves the day. That's risk management. Software projects work exactly like this, just with features instead of biryani.

Real life example 2: a team of 5 students building a food delivery app for their final year project, in 12 weeks. They write a WBS: login, menu, cart, payment, rider tracking. They estimate each, and use Trello with 2 week sprints. Week 6 review: payment integration is late, and it's on the critical path. They cut the "rate your rider" feature (scope control) and move a teammate from UI to payment. They finish on time with the core features working, instead of a half built app with everything.

Where students get confused: many think the critical path is the shortest path. It's the longest, because it decides the minimum time to finish. Others think Agile means no planning. It means planning in small, frequent pieces. Common exam questions: draw a network diagram and find the critical path and slack, calculate a PERT estimate, compute earned value numbers, compare Waterfall and Scrum, and explain risk exposure with an example.

After this course you can plan a project, estimate time and cost, track progress, and handle surprises without panic. Use it right away on your final year project. Next, try leading a small team project, explore tools like Jira or GitHub Projects, and if you love this side of work, look into certifications like Scrum Master or PMP later in your career.
key_points: Project management is about finishing on time, within budget and with the right features.
Scope, time and cost are tied together, and scope creep is the number one killer.
Break the work into a WBS and estimate with COCOMO, function points or three point estimates.
The critical path is the longest chain of tasks and sets the earliest finish date.
Plan risks early: risk exposure = probability x impact.
Waterfall goes step by step; Scrum works in short sprints with a backlog, stand-ups and reviews.
lessons.tip: Whatever you estimate, things usually take longer. Add some buffer time and you'll look like a genius when you finish on time.
lessons.task: Plan your next class assignment like a project: list 5 tasks, estimate hours for each, and mark which ones must happen before others.

quiz.q: The chain of tasks that, if delayed, delays the whole project is called the...
quiz.explain: The critical path has no spare time, so any delay there pushes the finish date.

quiz.q: In Scrum, work is done in short cycles called...
quiz.explain: Scrum uses sprints of 1 to 4 weeks, each ending with working software.

quiz.q: A chart that shows tasks as bars on a timeline is a...
quiz.explain: A Gantt chart shows when each task starts and ends on a timeline.

lessons.title: Pattern Recognition
lessons.content:
What is it? Pattern recognition is teaching a computer to notice patterns in data and put each thing into the right group. Is this photo a cat or a dog? Is this handwritten digit a 7 or a 1? Is this email spam or a real message from your teacher? Your brain does this all day without trying. You see a friend from far away and know it is them just from the way they walk. This course shows how to give a computer that same skill, using math instead of eyes.

Why learn it? Almost every smart feature you touch is pattern recognition: face unlock on your phone, fingerprint scanners at the office gate, voice assistants that understand "call Ammu", bank fraud alerts, and the cameras on the Dhaka-Mawa expressway that read car number plates. It sits right between statistics and machine learning, so once you get this course, Machine Learning, Computer Vision and Deep Learning become much easier. Jobs in data science, biometrics, medical imaging and security all use it daily.

What is in the course? A typical syllabus covers: what a pattern and a class are, feature extraction and selection, Bayesian decision theory, the nearest neighbour family of classifiers, linear classifiers and Support Vector Machines, clustering without labels (like k-means), reducing many features to a few (like PCA), and finally how to evaluate a classifier with accuracy and a confusion matrix.

Features: a computer cannot look at a mango and "feel" it. So first we turn every object into a list of numbers called a feature vector. A mango might become (weight 250, colour 0.8 yellow, softness 0.6). Good features make the job easy, bad ones make it impossible. If you try to tell oranges from apples using only weight, you will struggle, but add colour and suddenly it is simple. Choosing which features to keep is called feature selection, and it is often more important than the fancy classifier you use later.

Bayesian decision theory: this is the "most likely" rule. Using probability, we ask: given these features, which class has the highest chance? Bayes' rule says P(class | features) is proportional to P(features | class) times P(class). Example: 90% of emails you get are normal, 10% are spam. An email has the word "lottery". If 60% of spam has "lottery" but only 1% of normal emails do, then spam score = 0.6 x 0.1 = 0.06 and normal score = 0.01 x 0.9 = 0.009. Spam wins, so it goes to the spam folder.

Nearest neighbour (k-NN): the laziest classifier, and it works surprisingly well. Keep all your labelled examples. When a new item comes, find the k examples closest to it (usually using straight-line distance) and take a vote. With k = 3, if the 3 closest fruits are mango, mango, guava, the new fruit is a mango. Small k is jumpy and gets fooled by one odd example, big k is smoother but can blur the borders between classes. There is no training at all, but every prediction has to search through the data, so it gets slow with millions of examples.

Linear classifiers and SVM: instead of remembering everything, draw a line (in 2D) or a flat surface (in more dimensions) that separates the classes. The rule looks like: if w1*x1 + w2*x2 + b > 0 then class A, else class B. A Support Vector Machine picks the line with the widest possible gap, the margin, between the two classes, because a wide gap handles new data better. When the classes cannot be split by a straight line, the kernel trick lifts the data into a higher dimension where a straight cut becomes possible.

Clustering: sometimes nobody gives you labels. You just have a pile of data. Clustering finds natural groups by itself. In k-means, you pick k (say 3), place 3 centre points randomly, assign every item to its nearest centre, move each centre to the average of its items, and repeat until nothing changes. Shops use it to group customers into "weekly big buyers", "monthly small buyers" and so on, without anyone labelling them first.

Dimensionality reduction (PCA): sometimes you have too many features, like 10,000 pixels in a small photo. Many of them repeat the same information. Principal Component Analysis finds a few new directions that keep most of the variety in the data, so 10,000 numbers might shrink to 50 without losing much. Fewer features means faster training, less noise and pictures you can actually plot on a graph.

Evaluation: a classifier that scores 100% on the data it learned from might still fail on new data, like a student who memorised last year's answers. So we split data into training and test sets, or use cross-validation. Accuracy is the share of correct guesses, but a confusion matrix tells more: how many spam emails were wrongly let in (false negatives) and how many real emails were wrongly blocked (false positives). In medicine, missing a sick patient can be far worse than a false alarm.

Real life example 1, the mango seller: walk into Karwan Bazar and watch a mango seller sort a basket. Step 1, they pick up a mango and check colour, smell and softness, those are the features. Step 2, they compare it in their head with thousands of mangoes they have handled before, that is like k-NN. Step 3, they say "ripe, sell today" or "two more days", that is the class. A fruit factory does exactly this with a camera, a scale and a classifier, sorting thousands of mangoes an hour.

Real life example 2, handwritten postcodes: post offices around the world read handwritten postcodes on envelopes automatically. A scanner turns each digit into a grid of pixels, PCA squeezes those pixels into a smaller feature vector, and a classifier decides which digit it is, 0 to 9. The famous MNIST dataset of 70,000 handwritten digits came from this kind of problem, and almost every pattern recognition student practises on it.

Where students get confused: many mix up classification (labels are known, you predict them) with clustering (no labels, you discover groups). Another common mistake is testing on the training data and bragging about 100% accuracy. Typical exam questions: compute a Bayes decision with given probabilities, run k-NN by hand on 6 points, do 2 rounds of k-means, explain what the SVM margin is, and read a confusion matrix to find precision and recall.

Wrap-up: after this course you can turn real objects into features, choose a sensible classifier, find groups in unlabelled data and honestly measure how good your model is. That is the core of every AI system. Next, Machine Learning gives you more powerful models, and Computer Vision applies these ideas to images and video.
key_points: Pattern recognition puts things into the right group by looking at their features.
Features turn real objects into numbers; good features matter more than fancy classifiers.
Bayes picks the most probable class; k-NN votes among the closest examples.
SVM draws the separating line with the widest margin.
Clustering like k-means finds groups without labels; PCA shrinks many features into few.
Always test on unseen data and read the confusion matrix, not just accuracy.
lessons.tip: For every algorithm, try it by hand on 5 or 6 tiny examples on paper. Once you can do k-NN with a pencil, the formulas stop looking scary.
lessons.task: Pick 3 fruits at home. Write 3 features for each (weight guess, colour, shape). Then hide one fruit, give a friend only its features, and see if they can guess which one it is.

quiz.q: In pattern recognition, what are features?
options: The colours of the computer screen
Numbers that describe an object, like weight or colour
The final group an object belongs to
quiz.explain: Features turn a real object into numbers the computer can compare, like weight, colour or shape.

quiz.q: k-nearest neighbours decides the group of a new item by...
options: Looking at the most similar known examples and taking a vote
Counting the letters in its name
quiz.explain: k-NN finds the k most similar examples it already knows and goes with the majority group.

quiz.q: You have a big pile of data with no labels and want to find natural groups. What do you use?
quiz.explain: Clustering finds groups by itself when there are no labels. k-means is the most common example.

lessons.title: System Design
lessons.content:
What is it? System Design is the art of planning how a really big app works behind the screen, so it stays fast and doesn't crash when millions of people use it at once. Think of the difference between a tea stall and a wedding with 5,000 guests. One person can make tea for ten customers. But for 5,000 guests you need many cooks, many serving tables, a store room, a plan for when the gas runs out, and someone checking that everything is going fine. System Design is that wedding plan, but for software.

Why learn it? Every app you love, like Facebook, YouTube, bKash or Daraz, is used by millions of people at the same time. Writing code that works for one user is the easy part. Making it work for ten million users, without losing anyone's money or data, is the hard part. That's why big tech companies ask System Design questions in almost every senior job interview. The name sounds like System Analysis & Design, but they are different courses. System Analysis & Design is about understanding what a business needs: talking to users, drawing DFDs and use cases, and deciding which features to build. System Design starts after that. It is the engine room: how many servers, which database, where the cache goes, what happens when a machine dies. One asks "what should we build?", the other asks "how will it survive a huge crowd?"

What's in the course? A typical System Design course covers requirements and estimation, client-server architecture and APIs, scaling and load balancing, caching and CDNs, databases (SQL vs NoSQL), replication and sharding, the CAP theorem and consistency, message queues, monolith vs microservices, rate limiting and monitoring. At the end you practise by designing famous systems like a URL shortener, a chat app or a news feed.

Requirements and estimation: Before drawing anything, you write two lists. Functional requirements are what the system does, like "a user can send money". Non-functional requirements are how well it does it, like "reply within 200 milliseconds" or "never lose a transaction". Then you do quick math on paper, called back-of-the-envelope estimation. Say 10 million users each make 5 requests a day. That's 50 million requests. A day has 86,400 seconds, so about 580 requests per second on average. Busy hours can be 5 times that, so plan for about 3,000 per second. Now you know how big the system must be.

Client-server, APIs and load balancing: Your phone is the client. It sends a request, like "give me my balance", to a server through an API, which is just an agreed menu of requests the server understands. When one server is not enough, you have two choices. Vertical scaling means buying a bigger, more powerful machine, but there's always a limit. Horizontal scaling means adding more normal machines side by side. Then a load balancer sits in front, like a traffic police officer at a busy junction, sending each request to a server that isn't busy. A simple rule is round robin: server 1, server 2, server 3, then back to server 1. If a server dies, the load balancer stops sending it work.

Caching and CDN: Reading from a database is slow compared to reading from memory. A cache, like Redis, keeps popular answers in fast memory. When a request comes, the server checks the cache first. If the answer is there, that's a cache hit and it's super fast. If not, it's a cache miss, so the server reads the database and saves a copy in the cache for next time, often with a TTL (time to live) like 60 seconds, so old data doesn't stay forever. A CDN (Content Delivery Network) does the same for images and videos: copies are kept on servers near users, so someone in Dhaka gets a Daraz product photo from a nearby server, not from one across the ocean.

Databases, replication and sharding: SQL databases like MySQL and PostgreSQL store data in neat tables with strict rules, great for money and orders. NoSQL databases like MongoDB or Cassandra are more flexible and easier to spread over many machines, good for things like chat messages or activity logs. Replication means keeping copies: one primary database takes all the writes, and several replicas copy it and handle the reads. If the primary dies, a replica can take over. Sharding means splitting the data across machines. For example, with 4 shards a user goes to shard number user_id % 4, so user 10 lands on shard 2. Each machine holds only a quarter of the data.

CAP theorem and consistency: When data lives on many machines, sometimes the network between them breaks. That's called a partition. The CAP theorem says that during a partition you must choose: Consistency (everyone sees the same correct data, even if some requests have to wait or fail) or Availability (every request gets an answer, even if the data might be a bit old). A bank balance needs consistency, because showing a wrong balance is dangerous. A Facebook like count can be eventually consistent: if it shows 1,203 instead of 1,205 for a few seconds, nobody gets hurt.

Message queues: Some work doesn't need to happen right now. When you place an order, the important part is saving the order. Sending the SMS, the email and making the invoice can happen a few seconds later. So the server drops these jobs into a message queue, like Kafka or RabbitMQ, and replies "order placed" right away. Worker programs pick jobs from the queue one by one. If 100,000 orders arrive in one minute, the queue simply gets longer instead of the whole system falling over, and the workers catch up.

Monolith vs microservices: A monolith is one big program that does everything, like one giant shop selling food, clothes and medicine under one roof. It's easy to start with. Microservices split the system into small services, each with one job, like payments, users, search and notifications, talking to each other through APIs. Now each team can update its own service, and you can add machines only for the busy part, like search during a sale. The cost is complexity: more network calls, more things that can fail, and harder debugging. Many companies start as a monolith and split later, and that's often the smart choice.

Rate limiting and monitoring: Rate limiting protects the system from too many requests, whether they come from a bug, a bot or an attacker. A popular method is the token bucket: each user gets a bucket of, say, 10 tokens that refills at 1 token per second. Every request uses one token, and when the bucket is empty the request is rejected with an error like "too many requests". Monitoring is how you see what's happening inside: metrics (requests per second, error rate, response time), logs (what happened, in detail) and alerts (wake up the engineer when errors jump). You can't fix what you can't see.

Real life example 1, bKash on Eid: The night before Eid, millions of people send salami and pay shopping bills at the same time, so traffic can jump to many times the normal level. Step by step: estimation tells engineers how many requests per second to expect, so they add servers before Eid. Load balancers spread the requests across them. Balances live in a strongly consistent database with replicas, because money can't be "a little bit wrong". Notifications and SMS go through a queue, so a slow SMS gateway never blocks payments. Rate limits stop bots from flooding the system, and monitoring dashboards let the team spot trouble within seconds.

Real life example 2, Pathao ride matching: Every driver's phone sends its location every few seconds. That's a huge stream of small writes, so the latest locations are kept in a fast in-memory store instead of a slow database. The city is split into small map areas, a kind of sharding by location, so when you ask for a ride in Dhanmondi, the matching service only looks at drivers in Dhanmondi and nearby areas, not the whole of Bangladesh. Once a driver accepts, the trip is saved permanently in the database, and receipts and ratings are handled later through a queue.

Where people go wrong and what exams ask: The biggest mistake is jumping straight into boxes and arrows without asking for the requirements or doing the estimation. Another is stuffing a cache, microservices and sharding into a small app that doesn't need them, because building more than you need is also a mistake. People also forget failure, so always ask "what if this server dies?". Exams and interviews usually ask you to design a URL shortener, a chat app or a news feed, to compare SQL and NoSQL, to explain vertical vs horizontal scaling or the CAP theorem, or to show how a cache or load balancer works. There is rarely one correct answer; they want to hear your trade-offs.

After this course you'll be able to look at any big app and guess how it works behind the screen, and you'll be ready for System Design interview rounds. To go deeper, take Distributed Systems, Cloud Computing and Advanced Database Systems & Big Data next. A great way to practise is to pick an app you use every day and design it on paper.
key_points: System Design plans how a big app keeps working fast and safely when millions use it at once.
System Analysis & Design decides what to build; System Design decides how it survives huge traffic.
Start with requirements and quick estimation before drawing any boxes.
Load balancers, caches, CDNs, replicas and shards spread the work across many machines.
CAP theorem: during a network split, choose consistency or availability.
Queues, rate limiting and monitoring keep the system calm under sudden spikes.
lessons.tip: For every design, ask three questions out loud: how many users, what happens when a machine dies, and which data must never be wrong.
lessons.task: Pick an app you use daily, like bKash or Facebook. On paper, draw boxes for client, load balancer, servers, cache, database and queue, and write one line on what each does in that app.

quiz.q: What is the main focus of System Design compared to System Analysis & Design?
options: Only interviewing users to collect requirements
Making a big system handle huge numbers of users reliably with servers, caches, databases and queues
Choosing the colours of the buttons
quiz.explain: System Analysis & Design figures out what to build. System Design plans the engine room so it survives huge traffic.

quiz.q: A bank balance must never be wrong. During a network partition, which side of CAP should it choose?
options: Availability: always answer, even with old data
Consistency: show correct data, or wait or fail
quiz.explain: Money needs consistency. It is better to make a request wait or fail than to show a wrong balance.

quiz.q: Why do shops put SMS, email and invoice jobs into a message queue when an order is placed?
options: It turns the database into SQL
Slow jobs run later, so the customer doesn't wait and spikes don't crash the system
quiz.explain: The order is saved and confirmed right away. Workers handle the slower jobs from the queue, and a spike just makes the queue longer.

lessons.title: Data Science
lessons.content:
What is it? Data Science is the art of asking questions and answering them with data. Imagine a huge pile of numbers: every ball bowled in a cricket season, every click on a shopping app, every patient who came to a hospital. On its own the pile says nothing. A data scientist cleans it, looks at it from many angles, finds patterns and then tells people something useful, like "this batter struggles against left-arm spin" or "dengue cases will jump in two weeks". Think of a detective, but the clues are numbers.

Why learn it? Almost every company now collects data, but very few know what to do with it. Banks, hospitals, telecom companies, e-commerce shops and even the government need people who can turn data into decisions. That is why data scientist is one of the most wanted jobs in the world. It also helps you to know how it differs from its cousins. Machine Learning is one tool inside Data Science: it builds models that learn from data. Data Mining is about digging patterns out of large databases. Data Science is the whole journey, from asking the right question, to collecting and cleaning data, to analysis, models and finally explaining the result to humans.

What's in the course? A typical Data Science course covers data collection and cleaning, exploratory data analysis and visualization, the statistics you need, Python tools like pandas and Jupyter notebooks, feature engineering, building and evaluating machine learning models, telling a story with data, and the ethics of using people's data. You usually finish with a project on a real dataset.

Data collection and cleaning: Data comes from forms, sensors, websites, apps and spreadsheets, and it is almost always messy. Some ages are missing, someone typed "Dhaka" as "dhaka" or "Dhk", a price is written as 5000 in one row and "5,000 tk" in another, and some rows appear twice. Cleaning means fixing all that: filling or removing missing values, making formats match, deleting duplicates and catching impossible values like a 250 year old customer. Data scientists joke that 80 percent of the job is cleaning, and honestly it is not a big exaggeration.

Exploratory analysis and visualization: Before building anything, you look at the data like a curious kid. What is the average? What is the biggest and smallest value? How do two things move together? You draw charts: a histogram shows how values are spread, a bar chart compares groups, a line chart shows change over time and a scatter plot shows if two things are related. One good chart can show in two seconds what a table of 10,000 rows hides.

Statistics for Data Science: Statistics gives you the tools to not fool yourself. Mean, median and mode tell you the center of the data. Standard deviation tells you how spread out it is. Correlation tells you if two things rise and fall together, but remember the golden rule: correlation is not causation. Ice cream sales and drowning both go up in summer, but ice cream does not cause drowning. Hypothesis testing and p-values help you check if a difference is real or just luck, and sampling helps you learn about millions of people by studying a few thousand.

Python, pandas and notebooks: Most data scientists work in Python. The pandas library lets you load a spreadsheet into a table called a DataFrame and then filter, group and summarize it in one line, like df.groupby("city")["sales"].sum() to get total sales per city. NumPy handles fast number crunching, Matplotlib and Seaborn draw charts, and scikit-learn gives you ready-made ML models. Jupyter notebooks let you write code, see the output and write notes all on one page, which is perfect for exploring step by step.

Feature engineering: A feature is a piece of information you give a model. Raw data often needs to be turned into better features. From a date you can make "day of the week" or "is it Eid week?". From a customer's purchase history you can make "how many days since last order". Text like "Male" and "Female" must become numbers. Good features often matter more than a fancy model, because the model can only learn from what you show it.

Models and evaluation: Next you train a model, for example linear regression to predict a number like house rent, or a decision tree to predict a yes or no, like "will this customer leave?". The key trick is to split data into a training set and a test set. The model learns from the training part, and you check it on the test part it has never seen. You measure accuracy, precision, recall or error. If it does great on training data but badly on test data, it has memorized instead of learned. That is called overfitting.

Storytelling with data: The best analysis is useless if nobody understands it. A data scientist must explain results to managers who do not know statistics. That means one clear message, a simple chart, and a recommendation: "Sales drop every Tuesday, so let's run a Tuesday discount." Dashboards in tools like Power BI or Tableau help people see the numbers every day.

Ethics and bias: Data is about real people, so you must be careful. Protect privacy, never share personal details, and ask for permission. Also watch for bias. If a loan model learns only from past approvals, and past approvals were unfair to some group, the model will copy that unfairness. A responsible data scientist checks who might be hurt by a model before using it.

Real life example 1, cricket: Bangladesh's team analysts collect data on every ball: the line, length, speed and where the batter hit it. They clean it, then plot each opposing batter's scoring areas on a pitch map. They notice one batter scores few runs from short balls outside off stump. The bowling plan for the next match is built around that. Add recommendation engines like Daraz showing you "customers who bought this phone also bought this cover" and you see data science working every day.

Real life example 2, dengue in Dhaka: Health officials collect daily dengue cases by area, along with rainfall and temperature. After cleaning the data, a scientist notices cases rise about two to three weeks after heavy rain, because standing water helps mosquitoes breed. A simple model uses rainfall to forecast cases, and a clear map shows which wards are at risk. City workers can then clean drains and hospitals can prepare beds before the wave hits.

Where people go wrong and what exams ask: Students often skip cleaning, confuse correlation with causation, test the model on the same data it trained on, or report only accuracy on unbalanced data (if 95 percent of emails are not spam, a model that always says "not spam" gets 95 percent accuracy and is useless). Exams ask you to explain the data science life cycle, compare mean and median, read a chart, explain overfitting and train/test split, and say how Data Science differs from Data Mining and Machine Learning.

After this course you can take a messy dataset, clean it, explore it, build a simple model and explain what it means. Next, go deeper with Machine Learning, Data Mining and Data Engineering, and practise on free datasets from Kaggle or the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics.
key_points: Data Science is the whole journey: question, data, cleaning, analysis, model and explaining the result.
Machine Learning is one tool inside Data Science; Data Mining digs patterns out of large databases.
Most of the work is cleaning messy data and exploring it with charts.
Correlation is not causation; statistics stops you from fooling yourself.
Always test a model on data it has never seen, or you can't spot overfitting.
Data is about real people: protect privacy and check models for bias.
lessons.tip: Learn by doing: pick one small dataset you care about, like your favourite team's scores, and ask it one question a week.
lessons.task: Write down how much you spend each day for one week in a table. Then find your average daily spend, the biggest day and draw a simple bar chart on paper. What one message would you tell your family from it?

quiz.q: What is the best description of Data Science?
options: Only storing data in big databases
The whole journey from a question and raw data to an answer people can use
quiz.explain: Data Science covers collecting, cleaning, analysing, modelling and explaining. Machine Learning is just one tool inside it.

quiz.q: Ice cream sales and drowning both rise in summer. What should a data scientist conclude?
options: Correlation is not causation; something else (hot weather) drives both
Drowning causes people to buy ice cream
quiz.explain: Two things moving together doesn't mean one causes the other. Here summer heat causes both.

quiz.q: A model scores 99% on training data but 60% on new test data. What is happening?
options: The test data is too small to matter
Overfitting: the model memorized the training data instead of learning
quiz.explain: Doing great on seen data but badly on unseen data is overfitting. That's why we keep a separate test set.

lessons.title: Final Year Project / Thesis
lessons.content:
What is it? The final year project or thesis is the big finale of your BSc. Instead of studying one topic from a teacher, you pick a problem yourself, work on it for months under a supervisor, and show what you built or discovered. It's like the final match of a tournament: everything you practised over four years now gets used for real.

Why do it? It proves you can work independently on something big. Employers love asking about final year projects in interviews, and a good thesis can turn into a published paper that helps with higher studies abroad. It also teaches you skills no exam can: planning, research, solving unexpected problems and presenting your work.

What's in it: choosing a topic and supervisor, writing a proposal, the literature review, designing the method or system, implementation and experiments, analysing results, writing the report, and the final presentation or defence.

Project vs thesis: A project is mostly about building something useful: an app, a system, a device. A thesis is usually more about a research question and experiments: "Does method A detect fake news better than method B?" Many universities let you choose. Both need planning, documentation and a final presentation.

Choosing a topic: Pick something you genuinely find interesting, small enough to finish in the time you have, and where you have the data or equipment. "Make an AI that solves everything" is too big. "Detect rotten mangoes from photos using a small CNN" is clear and doable. Talk with your supervisor early and often. A good trick is to write your topic as one question: "Can a phone camera detect rotten mangoes with at least 90% accuracy?" If you can't write it as one clear question, the topic is probably still too vague. Also check if your supervisor actually works in that area, their guidance will be much better.

Proposal: A short document explaining the problem, why it matters, what you plan to do, how you'll test it, and a timeline. It is your map for the whole year. A clear proposal saves months of wandering.

Literature review: Before building anything, study what others have already done on your topic. Read papers, note their methods and results, and find the gap: what hasn't been solved yet, or what could be done better? This stops you from reinventing the wheel and shows your examiners you know the field. Use Google Scholar to find papers, start with recent survey papers because they summarise a whole area, then follow their references. Keep a simple table: paper, method, dataset, result, weakness. After 20 to 30 papers, the gap usually becomes clear on its own.

Method and implementation: Now you design your system or experiment and build it. Keep your code in Git, write notes every week and test small pieces as you go. Expect things to break. Finding and fixing problems is a normal part of research, not a sign of failure. Break the work into milestones: data ready by month 2, first working version by month 4, experiments by month 6, writing by month 8. Show your supervisor something every two weeks, even if it's small. Regular small progress beats one huge push at the end.

Results and honesty: You measure how well your work performs, usually with clear numbers, tables and graphs. If your results are worse than expected, report them honestly and explain why. Faking or hiding results is serious misconduct. A well-explained negative result is still valuable science. Always compare against a baseline, a simple existing method, so the numbers mean something. "Our model got 85%" means little alone; "the old method got 70%, ours got 85% on the same data" shows real progress. Also explain where your system fails, that's often the most interesting part.

Writing and defence: Finally you write the thesis book (introduction, related work, method, results, conclusion, references) and present it before a board. They will ask questions to check that you really understand your work. Practice your presentation with friends and prepare for "why did you choose this method?" questions. Keep your slides simple: one idea per slide, big figures, few words. Start with the problem, show your method as a diagram, then your key results, and end with limitations and future work. Finish within the given time, examiners notice.

Real life example 1: A team wants to help farmers in Rajshahi. Step 1: problem: farmers can't easily detect leaf diseases. Step 2: literature review shows image-based detection works but most datasets are from other countries. Step 3: they collect 2,000 local leaf photos. Step 4: train a model and test it. Step 5: build a simple Bangla app. Step 6: write the thesis and present. One clear problem, solved step by step.

Real life example 2: Another student builds a bus tracking system for their university. They didn't invent new science, but they designed the system, built the app and server, tested it with real buses and documented everything. That's a solid project that shows real engineering skills to employers.

Where people get confused and what's checked: Students often start coding before the literature review and later discover their idea already exists. Others leave writing until the last week. Examiners check: is the problem clear, is the method sound, are results honest and well analysed, and do you understand your own work?

Wrap-up: After your final year project you'll have planned, built, tested and defended something real, a huge confidence boost. Next comes either a job, where you'll do this daily, or an MSc, where Research Methodology and the MSc thesis take it further.
key_points: A project focuses on building something; a thesis focuses on a research question and experiments.
Choose a topic that's interesting, small enough and doable.
A literature review means studying what others have already done on your topic.
Keep code in Git, take weekly notes, test small pieces as you go.
Report results honestly, even when they're worse than expected.
Write early and practise your defence.
lessons.tip: Pick a problem you truly care about. You will live with it for many months, and passion keeps you going when bugs pile up.
lessons.task: Write 3 problems you have seen around you that tech could help with. For each one, write one sentence about what you might build.

quiz.q: What is a literature review?
options: Studying what others have already done on your topic
quiz.explain: A literature review shows what exists, so your work adds something new.

quiz.q: Which is usually more about a research question and experiments?
quiz.explain: A thesis focuses on research; a project focuses more on building a system.

quiz.q: If your results are worse than expected, you should...
options: Report them honestly and explain why
quiz.explain: Honest reporting is the heart of good engineering and research.

lessons.title: Advanced Algorithms
lessons.content:
What is it? Advanced Algorithms is the MSc course for problems that are too hard, too big or too messy for the normal algorithms you learned in BSc. Think of it as moving from solving puzzles in a school book to solving puzzles where the book says "nobody knows a fast answer". You learn clever tricks to still get a good answer.

Why learn it? Real companies face hard problems every day: Pathao routing thousands of riders, Daraz packing delivery trucks, Google indexing billions of pages. Many of these problems have no known fast exact solution. This course shows you how researchers and top engineers still solve them well enough, fast enough. It is also the base for research in almost every CS area.

What's in the course: NP-completeness and NP-hard problems, approximation algorithms, randomized algorithms, network flow and linear programming, amortized analysis, streaming and big-data algorithms, and sometimes online algorithms and parameterized algorithms.

NP-hard problems: Some problems seem to need checking almost every possibility. The Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP) is the classic example: find the shortest route visiting every city once and returning home. With 10 cities you can try all routes; with 100 cities there are more routes than atoms in the universe. TSP is an NP-hard problem, meaning no one knows a fast (polynomial-time) algorithm for it, and finding one would solve the famous P vs NP question.

Approximation algorithms: If the perfect answer is too slow, take a guaranteed good answer quickly. An approximation algorithm finds an answer that is provably close to the best. For example, there is a simple TSP method (for maps where direct roads are always shortest) that guarantees a route at most 2 times the best one, and Christofides' algorithm guarantees at most 1.5 times. "Provably close" is the key: it's not just a guess. To prove a new problem is NP-hard, you use a reduction: show that if you could solve your problem fast, you could also solve a known NP-hard problem fast. It's like saying "if you can lift this truck, you can surely lift this car".

Randomized algorithms: Sometimes flipping coins makes an algorithm faster or simpler. Randomized quicksort picks a random pivot so no input can consistently make it slow. Some algorithms might be wrong with a tiny probability, like 1 in a billion, but they're much faster. Testing whether a huge number is prime uses this idea, and so does your phone's security.

Network flow and linear programming: Imagine water flowing through pipes of different sizes: how much can reach the end per second? Max-flow algorithms answer this, and the same idea solves matching problems like assigning students to projects. Linear programming optimises a goal (like profit) under limits (like budget and stock), and it's used everywhere from airlines to factories. There are two flavours: Las Vegas algorithms are always correct but their running time is random (randomized quicksort), while Monte Carlo algorithms are always fast but may be wrong with a small, controllable probability (the Miller-Rabin prime test). Running a Monte Carlo test several times shrinks the error almost to zero.

Amortized analysis: Some operations are occasionally expensive but usually cheap. A dynamic array (like a Python list) sometimes has to copy everything into a bigger space, but on average each append still costs O(1). Amortized analysis gives a fair average cost over a long sequence of operations. A beautiful fact here is max-flow min-cut: the most water you can push through equals the capacity of the narrowest set of pipes you'd need to cut to separate start from end. Find the bottleneck and you've found the maximum flow.

Streaming algorithms: Sometimes data is too big to store, like every click on Facebook. Streaming algorithms read the data once and keep only a small summary. For example, you can estimate how many different users visited a site using only a few kilobytes of memory (the HyperLogLog idea). You give up a tiny bit of accuracy for huge savings.

Real life example 1: A delivery company in Dhaka has 50 stops for one van. Step 1: exact TSP is too slow to run every morning. Step 2: use an approximation algorithm to get a route quickly. Step 3: improve it with small swaps (local search). Step 4: the van finishes 20% earlier than with a random order. The route may not be perfect, but it's very good and it's ready in seconds.

Real life example 2: A cricket streaming site wants to know how many unique viewers watched a Bangladesh vs India match. Storing every viewer ID would need a lot of memory. A streaming algorithm counts approximately with a tiny memory and answers "about 12.4 million" in real time. Close enough for the business, and much cheaper.

Where people get confused and what comes in exams: Students confuse NP and NP-hard. NP means a solution can be checked quickly; NP-hard means the problem is at least as hard as every NP problem. Another confusion: approximation algorithms are not random guesses; they come with a proven bound. Exams ask you to prove a problem is NP-complete via reduction, analyse an approximation ratio, do amortized analysis or run a max-flow algorithm by hand.

Wrap-up: After this course, when someone says "this problem is impossible to solve fast", you'll know how to answer: approximate it, randomize it, stream it or model it as flow or linear programming. Next, Parallel Computing and Data Mining use these ideas on real big data.
key_points: NP-hard problems, like the Travelling Salesman Problem, have no known fast exact algorithm.
Approximation algorithms find an answer that is provably close to the best, quickly.
Randomized algorithms use randomness to be faster or simpler.
Network flow and linear programming model many real optimisation problems.
Amortized analysis gives the average cost over many operations.
Streaming algorithms read data once and keep a small summary when data is too big to store.
lessons.tip: For every new algorithm, ask two questions: how fast is it, and how close to the best answer is it? Write both on your note card.
lessons.task: Pick 5 places in your area. On paper, try to find the shortest round trip visiting all 5. Count how many different orders exist (hint: it grows very fast) and see why computers need shortcuts.

quiz.q: What does an approximation algorithm do?
options: Always finds the exact best answer
Finds an answer that is provably close to the best, quickly
quiz.explain: Approximation algorithms trade a little accuracy for a lot of speed, with a promise about how far from the best answer they can be.

quiz.q: The Travelling Salesman Problem is an example of...
options: A problem solved instantly by sorting
quiz.explain: Finding the shortest tour through all cities is NP-hard: no known method solves big cases exactly and fast.

quiz.q: Streaming algorithms are useful when...
options: You need a nice user interface
The data is too big to store, so you read it once and keep a small summary
quiz.explain: Streaming algorithms look at each item once and keep only a tiny summary, perfect for huge flows of data.

lessons.title: Advanced Database Systems & Big Data
lessons.content:
What is it? Advanced Database Systems & Big Data is about storing and processing data that is way too large or too fast for one ordinary database on one computer. In BSc you learned to keep a neat notebook. Now imagine a library with billions of pages arriving every hour. You need many shelves, many librarians and a clever system to keep it all working.

Why learn it? Facebook, Google, bKash and Daraz all handle huge amounts of data. Every tap, payment and search becomes data. Companies need engineers who can store it safely, query it fast and turn it into useful insights. Data engineering and big data jobs are some of the best-paid in tech.

What's in the course: query processing and optimisation, transactions and concurrency at scale, distributed databases (replication and sharding), the CAP theorem, NoSQL databases, MapReduce, Hadoop and Spark, and data warehouses and data lakes.

Query optimisation: When you write an SQL query, the database decides how to run it: which index to use, which table to join first. A good plan can be 1000 times faster than a bad one. The optimiser estimates costs using statistics about the data, like a GPS choosing the fastest route. You can peek at the plan yourself with the EXPLAIN command in SQL. If you see the database scanning a whole table of 10 million rows to find one phone number, adding an index on that column can turn seconds into milliseconds.

Replication and sharding: Replication means keeping copies of the same data on several machines, so if one dies, others still answer. Sharding means splitting data into pieces stored on different machines. For example, users with IDs 1 to 1 million on server A, the next million on server B. Sharding lets you grow beyond the limits of one computer. Choosing the shard key is the hardest part. If you shard by city and half your users live in Dhaka, one server gets half the load, a "hot shard". A good key, like a hash of the user ID, spreads data evenly.

CAP theorem: In a distributed database, when the network breaks between machines (a partition), you must choose: Consistency (everyone sees the same latest data) or Availability (every request still gets an answer). You can't fully have both during a partition. A bank usually chooses consistency; a social media like counter usually chooses availability. Systems that choose consistency are often called CP (like HBase), and systems that choose availability are called AP (like Cassandra). Many modern databases even let you choose per query: strong consistency for a payment, weaker but faster reads for a news feed.

NoSQL databases: Not all data fits nicely into tables. NoSQL databases offer other shapes: key-value stores (Redis) for super fast lookups, document stores (MongoDB) for JSON-like data, column stores (Cassandra) for huge write-heavy data, and graph databases (Neo4j) for relationships like friends of friends. Pick by the shape of your questions: if you always look things up by one ID, key-value is perfect; if you need complex joins and strict transactions, a normal SQL database is still the best choice.

MapReduce, Hadoop and Spark: MapReduce is a way to process huge data on many machines. In the map step, each worker processes its own chunk and produces partial results. In the reduce step, those partial results from all workers are combined into the final answer. Example: counting words in a billion pages: each machine counts its pages (map), then the counts are added together (reduce). Hadoop popularised this; Spark does it faster by keeping data in memory. Spark also lets you write these jobs in Python or SQL, and it can process streaming data that arrives every second, not just old files. That's why most companies now choose Spark for new big data work.

Data warehouses and data lakes: A data warehouse stores cleaned, organised data for reports and business analysis, like a well-arranged supermarket. A data lake stores raw data of every kind cheaply, like a big storeroom, so it can be processed later. Many companies now use both.

Real life example 1: Daraz during an 11.11 sale. Step 1: millions of users browse at once, so product data is replicated across many servers. Step 2: orders are sharded by user ID so no single server gets overloaded. Step 3: payments use a consistent database so no order is charged twice. Step 4: at night, Spark jobs process the day's clicks to find which products to recommend. Different tools for different jobs.

Real life example 2: A mobile operator in Bangladesh wants to know which areas have the most dropped calls. They have billions of call records. A MapReduce job maps each record to its tower area, then reduces by adding up the drops per area. By morning, engineers know exactly which towers to fix.

Where people get confused and what comes in exams: Students mix up replication (copies) and sharding (splitting). Also, CAP is only about what happens during a network partition, not all the time. NoSQL doesn't mean "no SQL ever"; it means "not only SQL". Exams ask you to explain CAP with examples, design a sharding scheme, write a MapReduce for word count, or compare SQL and NoSQL.

Another important idea: in big systems many databases use eventual consistency: copies may differ for a short time but become the same soon. That's why sometimes a like count on a post shows a slightly different number on two phones for a few seconds.

Wrap-up: After this course you can design data systems that keep working when data grows from thousands to billions of records. Next, Data Mining and Cloud Computing show you how to analyse this data and run these systems cheaply.
key_points: Query optimisers choose the fastest way to run a query.
Replication keeps copies; sharding splits data into pieces on different machines.
CAP theorem: during a network partition, choose consistency or availability.
NoSQL offers key-value, document, column and graph databases.
MapReduce: map processes chunks in parallel, reduce combines the partial results.
Data warehouses hold cleaned data; data lakes hold raw data.
lessons.tip: Don't memorize tools first. Understand the ideas: split the data, copy the data, process in parallel. Every big data tool is built on these.
lessons.task: Take a page of a book. Count the word 'the' alone and time yourself. Then split the page with 2 friends, each counts their part, and add up. That's MapReduce on paper.

quiz.q: What is sharding?
options: Splitting data into pieces stored on different machines
quiz.explain: Sharding splits a big dataset into smaller parts so each machine stores and handles only a piece.

quiz.q: In MapReduce, what does the reduce step do?
options: Combines the partial results from all workers
quiz.explain: Map lets each worker process its own piece; reduce gathers and combines those partial results into the final answer.

quiz.q: The CAP theorem is about the trade-off between...
options: Consistency and availability when the network is partitioned
quiz.explain: CAP says that during a network partition, a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability.

lessons.title: Cloud Computing
lessons.content:
What is it? Cloud computing means using computers, storage and software over the internet instead of owning them yourself. It's like electricity: you don't build a power plant at home, you just plug in and pay for what you use. Companies like Amazon (AWS), Microsoft (Azure) and Google (GCP) own huge data centres and rent them out.

Why learn it? Almost every modern app runs on the cloud. Startups in Bangladesh can launch globally without buying a single server. Companies need cloud engineers, DevOps engineers and architects, and cloud skills are some of the most in-demand in the job market.

What's in the course: the service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS), deployment models (public, private, hybrid), virtualization, containers and Kubernetes, scalability and auto-scaling, storage and networking in the cloud, serverless computing, and cost and security.

Service models: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) gives you raw virtual machines; you manage everything on them, like renting an empty flat. PaaS (Platform as a Service) gives you a ready platform to run your code, like a furnished flat. SaaS (Software as a Service) gives you finished software you just use, like staying in a hotel. Gmail, for its users, is SaaS: you don't install or manage anything. There are also deployment models. A public cloud is shared by many customers (AWS, Azure). A private cloud is used by only one organisation, often a bank or government that wants full control. A hybrid cloud mixes both: sensitive data stays private, everything else uses the public cloud.

Virtualization: This is the magic underneath the cloud. A program called a hypervisor splits one powerful physical machine into many virtual machines. Each VM thinks it is a full computer with its own operating system. So one big server can safely host dozens of customers at once, which makes cloud cheap. There are two kinds of hypervisor. Type 1 runs directly on the hardware, which is what cloud data centres use because it's fast. Type 2 runs on top of a normal OS, like VirtualBox on your laptop, handy for trying Linux without deleting Windows.

Containers and Kubernetes: A container packages your app with everything it needs, so it runs the same on any machine. Docker is the popular tool. Containers are lighter than VMs because they share the host OS. Kubernetes manages thousands of containers: starting them, restarting crashed ones and spreading them across machines. A container image is built once and runs the same on your laptop, your friend's laptop and the cloud, so the old excuse "but it works on my machine" disappears. Kubernetes also does rolling updates: it replaces old containers with new ones a few at a time, so users never see the app go down.

Scalability and auto-scaling: Scaling up means getting a bigger machine; scaling out means adding more machines. Auto-scaling helps when traffic suddenly rises or falls: the cloud adds servers when traffic rises and removes them when it drops, so you only pay for what you need. A load balancer spreads users across the servers. Auto-scaling works with rules you set, like "if average CPU stays above 70% for 5 minutes, add 2 servers; if it drops below 20%, remove one". Choosing these numbers well is part of the job: too slow and users wait, too eager and you waste money.

Storage and serverless: Cloud storage like Amazon S3 keeps files safely with multiple copies. Managed databases handle backups for you. In serverless computing (like AWS Lambda), you just write a function; the cloud runs it only when it's called and charges per request. No servers to think about at all. Serverless is perfect for small jobs that run now and then, like resizing a photo whenever a user uploads one. But for a busy app running all day, a normal server can be cheaper, and the first call after a quiet period can be slow, called a "cold start".

Cost and security: Cloud is pay-as-you-go, which is cheap if you manage it well and very expensive if you forget to switch things off. Security is a shared responsibility: the provider protects the data centre, but you must protect your passwords, data and settings. Many data leaks come from storage buckets left public by mistake. Smart teams set budget alerts, delete unused resources, and use cheaper "spot" machines for jobs that can be paused. On security, turn on two-factor login, give each person only the permissions they need, and never put secret keys inside code you push to GitHub.

Real life example 1: A Bangladeshi ticketing startup sells Eid bus tickets. Step 1: normal days need 2 servers. Step 2: the day before Eid, traffic jumps 20 times. Step 3: auto-scaling adds 40 servers within minutes. Step 4: after the rush, it goes back to 2. If they had bought physical servers for the peak, most would sit idle all year.

Real life example 2: When you write a document in Google Docs, your file is stored in Google's cloud, so you can open it from your phone, laptop or a cyber cafe. If your laptop breaks, nothing is lost. That's SaaS plus cloud storage in your daily life.

Where people get confused and what comes in exams: Students mix up IaaS, PaaS and SaaS; remember the flat analogy (empty, furnished, hotel). Also VMs vs containers: VMs include a full OS, containers share the host OS. Exams ask you to compare service and deployment models, explain virtualization, describe auto-scaling, or give pros and cons of cloud.

Wrap-up: After this course you can deploy apps that serve millions without owning a single server, and keep costs under control. Next, Distributed Systems and Big Data help you understand what's happening inside these massive cloud platforms.
key_points: Cloud computing means renting computing over the internet and paying for what you use.
IaaS gives machines, PaaS gives a platform, SaaS gives finished software like Gmail.
Virtualization splits one physical machine into many virtual machines.
Containers package apps; Kubernetes manages many containers.
Auto-scaling adds or removes servers when traffic rises or falls.
Security in the cloud is a shared responsibility.
lessons.tip: Most cloud providers have a free tier. Learning by deploying a tiny real app teaches more than reading ten chapters.
lessons.task: List 5 apps on your phone. For each, guess whether it's SaaS for you (you just use it) and whether it likely runs on a cloud like AWS or Google Cloud. Look up one to check.

quiz.q: Gmail is an example of which cloud model for its users?
quiz.explain: With SaaS you just use finished software through the internet. You don't manage any servers or code.

quiz.q: What does virtualization do?
options: Splits one physical machine into many virtual machines
quiz.explain: Virtualization lets one powerful server run many isolated virtual machines, each acting like its own computer.

quiz.q: Auto-scaling helps when...
options: You want to write less code
quiz.explain: Auto-scaling automatically adds machines during traffic spikes and removes them when traffic drops, saving money.

lessons.title: Advanced Computer Networks & Wireless Networks
lessons.content:
What is it? Advanced Computer Networks & Wireless Networks goes deeper into how data travels across the internet and through the air. In BSc you learned the basic layers. Now you learn how the internet stays fast when billions of people use it, and how your phone stays connected while you move around on a bus.

Why learn it? Every app depends on the network: video calls, online games, mobile banking. Telecom companies like Grameenphone and Robi, cloud providers and big tech firms need network engineers who understand performance, mobility and new ideas like 5G and SDN. It is also a rich research area for MSc theses.

What's in the course: TCP congestion control, quality of service (QoS), routing at internet scale (BGP), wireless basics and Wi-Fi, cellular networks (4G and 5G) and handover, mobile ad hoc and sensor networks, and software-defined networking (SDN) and network virtualization.

TCP congestion control: If everyone sends data as fast as possible, routers overflow and packets are lost, like a traffic jam at Farmgate. TCP congestion control slows sending when the network is crowded and speeds up when it's clear. It grows the sending window step by step, and cuts it when packets get lost. This rule is why the internet doesn't collapse at peak hours. In numbers: TCP starts with slow start, doubling the window every round trip (1, 2, 4, 8 packets), then switches to congestion avoidance, adding just one packet per round trip. When a loss happens, it cuts the window roughly in half. This "add a little, cut a lot" pattern is called AIMD.

Quality of service: Not all traffic is equal. A video call needs low delay; a file download just needs to finish eventually. QoS techniques give priority to time-sensitive traffic, like an ambulance lane on the road. Delay, jitter (variation in delay), bandwidth and packet loss are the key measurements. A common QoS tool is the priority queue: routers keep separate lines for voice, video and normal data, and always serve the voice line first. Mobile operators also use QoS to guarantee speed for packages people pay more for.

Internet-scale routing: The internet is made of thousands of separate networks (autonomous systems) owned by different companies. BGP is the protocol they use to tell each other which addresses they can reach. It's based on business agreements as much as distance. A mistake in BGP can make a country's internet go down for hours.

Wireless and Wi-Fi: Radio signals get weaker with distance, bounce off walls and interfere with each other. Wi-Fi uses tricks like checking whether the channel is free before sending (CSMA/CA) to avoid collisions. Newer Wi-Fi versions use multiple antennas (MIMO) to send more data at once.

Cellular networks and handover: Mobile networks divide the area into cells, each served by a tower. Handover is your connection moving from one cell tower to another as you travel, without dropping your call. 4G gave fast mobile internet; 5G adds very high speed, very low delay, and support for huge numbers of devices like sensors. Handover is decided by measuring signal strength all the time. When the new tower's signal is stronger than the current one by a margin for a short while, the network switches. The margin prevents "ping-pong", jumping back and forth between two towers when you're standing right between them.

SDN and network virtualization: In traditional networks, every switch makes its own decisions. In software-defined networking (SDN), a central program controls how many switches forward traffic. It's like one traffic police control room managing all the signals in the city, instead of each signal working alone. This makes networks easier to manage and change by writing software. In SDN the switches become simple: they just follow forwarding rules. The controller, a program, sees the whole network and installs those rules. Want to block a hacker's traffic or send video over a less busy path? Change a few lines in the controller, and every switch updates in seconds.

Real life example 1: You're on a video call while riding a bus from Mohakhali to Gulshan. Step 1: your phone is connected to tower A. Step 2: as you move, tower B's signal gets stronger. Step 3: the network performs a handover to tower B in a fraction of a second. Step 4: QoS gives your call priority so your voice doesn't break. You never notice any of it.

Real life example 2: At 9pm, half of Dhaka starts streaming a cricket match. Routers get busy and some packets drop. TCP congestion control on every viewer's connection slows down slightly, so the network isn't overwhelmed. The video player switches to a lower quality for a moment instead of freezing. The whole internet shares fairly.

Where people get confused and what comes in exams: Students confuse flow control (protecting the receiver) with congestion control (protecting the network). Also handover vs roaming: handover is moving between towers; roaming is using another operator's network. Exams ask you to explain TCP's slow start and congestion avoidance, describe handover, compare traditional networking with SDN, or explain how BGP works.

Another key idea is mobile ad hoc networks, where devices talk to each other directly without any tower, useful after floods or disasters when infrastructure is down. Sensor networks are a special case, covered more in Wireless Sensor Networks.

Wrap-up: After this course you'll understand why your internet is fast or slow, how mobile networks keep you connected, and how modern networks are built with software. Next, explore IoT and Wireless Sensor Networks, or research topics like 5G and network security.
key_points: TCP congestion control slows sending when the network is crowded and speeds up when it's clear.
QoS gives priority to time-sensitive traffic like video calls.
BGP connects the thousands of networks that make up the internet.
Handover moves your connection between cell towers as you travel.
5G brings higher speed, lower delay and support for many devices.
In SDN, a central program controls how many switches forward traffic.
lessons.tip: Draw diagrams for every protocol: who sends what, to whom, and when. Networks make sense when you can see the arrows.
lessons.task: Walk around your home with your phone's WiFi on. Notice where the signal bars drop. Guess why: walls, distance or interference from other devices.

quiz.q: What is handover in mobile networks?
options: Your connection moving from one cell tower to another as you travel
Giving your phone to a friend
quiz.explain: Handover lets your call or data continue as your phone switches between towers while you move.

quiz.q: What does TCP congestion control do?
options: Slows sending when the network is crowded and speeds up when it's clear
quiz.explain: Congestion control adjusts the sending speed so the network doesn't get overloaded.

quiz.q: In software-defined networking (SDN)...
options: A central program controls how many switches forward traffic
Data is stored in paper files
quiz.explain: SDN separates the control logic from the switches, so one central controller can manage the network.

lessons.title: Parallel & High Performance Computing
lessons.content:
What is it? Parallel computing means doing many parts of a job at the same time, instead of one after another. High Performance Computing, or HPC, is about using huge numbers of processors together, like the supercomputers in big labs, to solve giant problems. Think of it like this: one person painting a long wall takes a whole day, but ten people with ten brushes can finish before lunch.

Why learn it? Single processors stopped getting much faster around the mid-2000s, because they got too hot. So chip makers started putting more cores on one chip instead. Today your phone has 8 cores and a graphics card can have thousands. If your program uses only one core, it wastes most of the machine. Weather forecasting, training AI, simulating medicines, physics, banking risk checks and even video games need parallel power. Jobs in AI engineering, scientific computing, game engines and cloud systems all expect you to know this.

What's in the course: the course usually covers why parallelism matters and how fast you can go (speedup and Amdahl's law), parallel hardware (multi-core CPUs, GPUs, clusters), shared memory programming with threads and OpenMP, message passing with MPI, GPU programming basics with CUDA, and the classic dangers: race conditions, deadlocks and load balancing.

Speedup and Amdahl's law: speedup is how many times faster the parallel version is. If one core takes 100 seconds and 4 cores take 25 seconds, speedup is 100 / 25 = 4. But almost every job has a part that can't be split. Amdahl's law says that part decides your limit. If 10% of the job must run alone, then even with a million cores the best speedup is 1 / 0.1 = 10 times. So before adding more cores, shrink the part that can't be split.

Parallel hardware: a multi-core CPU has a few strong cores, each smart enough to do different jobs. A GPU has thousands of small, simple cores that are great at doing the same thing to lots of data, like changing the color of every pixel or multiplying big tables of numbers. A cluster is many separate computers joined by a fast network, and a supercomputer is basically a giant, well-tuned cluster. Each kind needs a slightly different style of programming.

Shared memory and threads (OpenMP): on one machine, all cores can see the same memory. You split the work into threads, and each thread handles part of it. With OpenMP in C, you can write one line like "#pragma omp parallel for" above a loop, and the loop's rounds get shared among the cores. It's the easiest way to start, but because everyone shares memory, you must be careful who changes what.

Message passing (MPI): when the work runs on many separate computers, they don't share memory. Each process has its own data and they talk by sending messages, like "MPI_Send" and "MPI_Recv". For example, to add up a billion numbers, each of 100 computers adds its own 10 million, then they send their partial sums to one leader who adds the 100 results. This is how most supercomputer programs work.

Race conditions: a race condition happens when two workers change the same data at the same time and the result depends on who was faster. Say a counter is 5 and two threads both read 5, both add 1 and both write 6. You expected 7 but got 6. The fix is a lock (a mutex) or an atomic operation, so only one thread can update at a time.

Deadlocks and load balancing: a deadlock is when workers wait for each other forever. Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2, while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Nobody moves. A simple rule fixes most deadlocks: always take locks in the same order. Load balancing means keeping every worker equally busy. If one worker gets the hard half of the job and the others finish early and sit idle, your speedup drops.

GPU programming basics (CUDA): with CUDA you write a small function called a kernel, and the GPU runs it on thousands of threads at once, each working on a different piece of data. For example, to add two lists of a million numbers, each thread adds just one pair. The tricky parts are copying data between CPU memory and GPU memory, which is slow, and keeping all those threads busy.

Real life example 1: think of making pitha for a big family event. One person making 500 pithas takes all day. Ten people working together, each shaping 50, finish much faster. But if there's only one stove for frying, everyone waits at the stove. That stove is the part that can't be parallelized, and Amdahl's law says it decides how fast you can ever finish. Buy a second stove, and suddenly everything speeds up.
