Real life example 2: the Bangladesh Meteorological Department and weather services around the world forecast cyclones by splitting the map into a huge grid. Each processor handles a few squares of the grid, calculates wind, pressure and rain there, and shares the edges with its neighbours using MPI. A forecast that would take weeks on one computer finishes in hours, fast enough to warn coastal people before the cyclone hits.

Where people get confused: students often think doubling the cores always doubles the speed. It doesn't, because of Amdahl's law and communication cost. Another confusion is mixing up concurrency and parallelism: concurrency means handling many tasks by switching between them, parallelism means truly running them at the same moment. Common exam questions: calculate speedup and efficiency, apply Amdahl's law, explain a race condition with an example, explain deadlock conditions, and compare shared memory with message passing (MPI).

After this course you can make programs use all the cores of a machine, run jobs on clusters and GPUs, and spot what's slowing things down. You'll also write safer code that doesn't break when many things happen at once. Next steps include deeper CUDA programming, distributed training for AI, and scientific computing.
key_points: Parallel computing means doing many parts of a job at the same time.
Speedup = time on one core ÷ time on many cores.
Amdahl's law: the part of a job that can't be parallelized limits the total speedup.
OpenMP uses threads on shared memory; MPI uses message passing between separate processes or computers.
A race condition is two workers changing the same data at once; locks or atomic operations fix it.
Deadlock means waiting for each other forever; load balancing keeps every worker equally busy.
lessons.tip: Before writing parallel code, ask: which parts are independent? Those are the parts you can split. The rest stays in a line.
lessons.task: Pick a home chore like cleaning a room with siblings. Write which steps can happen at the same time and which must wait. Find the bottleneck.

quiz.q: What is a race condition?
options: Two workers changing the same data at the same time, causing wrong results
quiz.explain: A race condition happens when the result depends on which thread gets there first, often giving wrong data.

quiz.q: Amdahl's law tells us that...
options: More cores always means unlimited speed
The part of a job that can't be parallelized limits the total speedup
quiz.explain: Even with infinite workers, the sequential part of a job still takes the same time, capping the speedup.

quiz.q: MPI is mainly used for...
options: Message passing between separate processes or computers
quiz.explain: MPI (Message Passing Interface) lets separate processes, often on different machines, work together by sending messages.

lessons.title: Data Mining
lessons.content:
What is it? Data mining means digging through huge piles of data to find useful patterns hiding inside. Just like miners dig through rock and mud to find gold, data miners dig through millions of records to find knowledge. The data is the rock, the pattern is the gold.

Why learn it? Shops, banks, hospitals, telecom companies and apps collect tons of data every single day. Raw data is useless until someone finds the meaning in it. Data mining helps businesses predict what customers want, catch fraud, recommend products, and make smarter decisions. Data analyst, data scientist and business intelligence jobs are built on these skills, and it connects directly to machine learning and databases.

What's in the course: most data mining courses cover the knowledge discovery process (KDD), data preprocessing (cleaning and preparing data), association rule mining with algorithms like Apriori, classification (decision trees, Naive Bayes, k-nearest neighbours), clustering (K-means, hierarchical clustering), outlier detection, and how to evaluate whether patterns are real and useful.

The KDD process: data mining is one step in a bigger journey called Knowledge Discovery in Databases. First you select the data you need, then clean it, then transform it into a useful shape, then mine it for patterns, and finally interpret and evaluate what you found. Skipping the early steps is like cooking with unwashed rice: the final dish won't be good.

Data preprocessing: real data is messy. Some ages are missing, some are typed as 250, some names are spelled three ways, some records appear twice. Preprocessing means filling or removing missing values, fixing errors, removing duplicates, and putting numbers on a similar scale (normalization), for example squeezing all values between 0 and 1. People say 60 to 80 percent of a data miner's time goes here, and it's true.

Association rules: these find things that happen together. A rule looks like {bread} → {butter}. Support tells how often the items appear together in all receipts, for example 5 percent of all receipts have both. Confidence tells how often butter is bought when bread is bought, for example 70 percent. The Apriori algorithm finds such rules smartly: if a small item set is rare, any bigger set containing it must also be rare, so it skips those.

Classification: this sorts things into known groups, using examples where the answer is already known. Spam or not spam, loan approved or rejected, sick or healthy. A decision tree asks yes/no questions like "Is income above 30,000?" then "Has old loans?" until it reaches an answer. Naive Bayes uses probability, and k-nearest neighbours looks at the closest known examples and follows the majority. You test the classifier on data it hasn't seen and measure accuracy.

Clustering: this groups similar things together without any labels. Nobody tells the computer what the groups are. K-means is the classic: choose K, say 3, place 3 centres randomly, put each point with its nearest centre, move each centre to the middle of its group, and repeat until nothing changes. Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of groups instead, merging the closest groups step by step.

Outlier detection: an outlier is a record that looks very different from the rest. Sometimes it's a typing mistake, sometimes it's the most important thing in the data, like fraud or a machine about to break. Simple methods flag values far from the average (for example more than 3 standard deviations away), smarter ones look at how lonely a point is compared to its neighbours.

Evaluating patterns: a pattern found by luck is worse than no pattern, because people will act on it. So you check: is the support big enough to matter, is the confidence high, does the classifier work on new data, and does the pattern make real-world sense? Measures like accuracy, precision, recall and lift help here. A rule like "people who buy rice also buy rice" is true but useless.

Real life example 1: a superstore like Shwapno looks at millions of receipts and discovers that people who buy chal and dal often also buy oil. So they place oil nearby and give a combo offer. They also cluster customers: one group buys in bulk once a month, another buys small amounts daily. Each group gets different offers on their phone.

Real life example 2: mobile banking services like bKash use outlier detection. If your account normally sends 500 taka to your family once a week and suddenly sends lots of money at 3 AM to a strange number, the system flags it as possible fraud. Telecom companies like Grameenphone also use classification to predict which customers are about to switch to another operator, and offer them a deal before they leave.

Where people get confused: students mix up classification and clustering. Classification needs labelled examples and puts things into known groups; clustering has no labels and discovers groups by itself. Another confusion is support vs confidence. Common exam questions: run Apriori on a small table of transactions, calculate support and confidence, do a few rounds of K-means by hand, build a small decision tree, and explain the steps of KDD and why preprocessing matters.

After this course you can take a big messy dataset, clean it and pull out patterns that help people decide better. You can explain those patterns to non-technical people too. Next you can go deeper into machine learning, big data tools and data science.
key_points: Data mining finds useful, hidden patterns in large amounts of data.
Preprocessing (cleaning, fixing missing values, normalizing) takes most of the effort.
Association rules find items that happen together, measured by support and confidence.
Classification uses labelled examples; clustering groups similar things without labels.
Outlier detection finds unusual records, like fraud.
Always check that a pattern is real and useful, not just luck.
lessons.tip: Always look at the data with your own eyes first. Plot it, count it, find weird values. Half of data mining is cleaning.
lessons.task: Collect 10 of your family's shopping lists or receipts. Find two items that often appear together. You just found an association rule.

quiz.q: Grouping customers by similar behavior without any labels is called...
quiz.explain: Clustering groups similar items together when no predefined labels are given, like K-means.

quiz.q: Finding that people who buy bread often buy butter is an example of...
quiz.explain: Association rules discover items that frequently occur together in transactions.

quiz.q: Which technique helps catch unusual transactions like fraud?
quiz.explain: Outlier detection finds records that look very different from normal behavior, such as fraud.

lessons.title: Research Methodology
lessons.content:
What is it? Research Methodology teaches you how to do proper research: how to ask a good question, find what others already did, test your idea fairly and write it up so others can trust it. In an MSc, this is the course that turns you from a learner into a discoverer. Think of it as the rulebook detectives follow so their case holds up in court.

Why learn it? Your MSc thesis needs real research. Without a method, you might spend months on an idea that was already solved, or make claims that don't hold up when someone checks. Good research also helps in jobs: companies test new features with experiments, and they want people who decide with evidence instead of guessing. If you want a PhD, a research job or a scholarship abroad, this course is your foundation.

What's in the course: you typically learn the types of research, how to do a literature review, how to find a research gap and write a research question and hypothesis, how to design experiments (datasets, baselines, metrics), basic statistics for checking results, academic writing and citing, plagiarism, research ethics, and how to publish and present your work.

Types of research: quantitative research works with numbers, like measuring accuracy or speed. Qualitative research works with words and opinions, like interviewing doctors about a hospital app. Some research builds something new (a system or an algorithm), some compares existing methods, and some surveys a whole field. Knowing which type you're doing tells you what proof you need.

Literature review: before doing anything new, you read what's already known. You search Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore and ACM Digital Library, read abstracts first, then fully read the most relevant papers. You note what each paper did, how well it worked and what it couldn't do. The empty spot nobody has filled yet is called the research gap, and your work should aim at it.

Research question and hypothesis: a good research question is clear and specific. "Can AI help farmers?" is too wide. "Can a phone-based CNN detect rice blast disease from leaf photos with over 90 percent accuracy?" is much better. A hypothesis is a testable educated guess, like "our model will be more accurate than the current best method on the same dataset". If you can't test it, it's not a hypothesis.

Experiment design: you decide what data to use, what to compare against and how to measure. The baseline is the existing method you compare with; without it, "95 percent accuracy" means nothing, because maybe the old method already got 97. You choose metrics like accuracy, precision, recall or running time, split data fairly into training and testing parts, and keep everything the same except the one thing you're testing.

Basic statistics: if your method gets 91 percent and the baseline gets 90 percent, is yours really better, or was it luck? You run experiments several times, report averages and spread (standard deviation), and use tests like the t-test to check if the difference is significant. A p-value below 0.05 is the common rule of thumb for "probably not just luck".

Academic writing and citing: a research paper usually has an abstract, introduction, related work, method, experiments, results, discussion, conclusion and references. Every idea or result you take from someone else must be cited, using styles like IEEE or APA. Tools like Zotero or Mendeley keep your references organised. Copying text or ideas without credit is plagiarism, and universities check with software like Turnitin.

Research ethics: if your study involves people, you need their informed consent, you must protect their private data, and often you need approval from an ethics committee. You never fake or change data to look better. You report failures honestly. Research is built on trust; one faked result can end a career.

Real life example 1: say you think your new rice-disease detection app is better than the old one. Just saying "mine is better" is not research. You read papers to see what methods exist, test both apps on the same 1000 leaf photos, compare their accuracy, run it a few times, check that the difference isn't luck, and write it all down so another student can repeat it. Now it's research.

Real life example 2: a team wants to know if Bangla voice commands help elderly people use mobile banking. They interview 30 elderly users (qualitative), then measure how many tasks each user completes with and without voice (quantitative). They get consent, hide names, compare results, and publish. Banks can now make decisions based on evidence, not guesses.

Where people get confused: students often think a literature review is just a summary of papers; it should actually compare them and point to the gap. Many confuse a research question with a topic, and a hypothesis with a hope. Others forget the baseline. Common exam questions: define research gap and hypothesis, write a research question for a given topic, explain qualitative vs quantitative research, list the parts of a research paper, and explain plagiarism and research ethics.

After this course you can plan a thesis, read papers smartly and write your own. You'll know how to prove things, not just believe them. Next, pick a topic you love, read ten recent papers on it, and you're already on your way to the MSc thesis.
key_points: A literature review finds what is already known and where the research gap is.
A good research question is clear and specific; a hypothesis is a testable educated guess.
Compare against a baseline to show if your method is really better.
Use statistics to check that results aren't just luck.
Cite every source; copying without credit is plagiarism.
Research ethics: consent, privacy and honest reporting.
lessons.tip: Keep a research diary. Every day write what you tried, what happened and what you'll try next. Your future self will thank you.
lessons.task: Pick a simple question, like 'Do I study better with music or without?'. Write a hypothesis, how you'd test it fairly for a week, and what you'd measure.

quiz.q: What is a literature review for?
options: Finding what is already known and where the research gap is
quiz.explain: A literature review surveys existing work so you don't repeat it and can find an open problem.

quiz.q: A hypothesis is...
quiz.explain: A hypothesis is a clear prediction that your experiments can support or reject.

quiz.q: Why do we compare against a baseline?
options: To show if our method is really better than an existing one
quiz.explain: A baseline gives a fair point of comparison, showing whether the new method actually improves things.

lessons.title: Neural Networks & Fuzzy Systems
lessons.content:
What is it? This course has two halves that both deal with messy, real-world problems. Neural networks are computer models loosely inspired by the brain: lots of tiny units called neurons, connected in layers, that learn from examples instead of following hand-written rules. Fuzzy systems deal with ideas that are not simply true or false, like "a bit hot", "quite fast" or "very tired". Together they are called soft computing, because they are flexible and forgiving, like a person, rather than rigid like a calculator.

Why learn it? Normal logic says a room is either hot (1) or not hot (0), but real life is full of in-between. Fuzzy logic lets machines think in shades, which is why it runs washing machines, air conditioners, rice cookers, camera autofocus and even metro train brakes. Neural networks are the foundation of deep learning, the engine behind ChatGPT, face filters and Google Translate. This course shows how they work from the ground up, and it leads straight into Deep Learning, Computer Vision and control engineering jobs.

What is in the course? A typical syllabus covers: the biological neuron and the artificial neuron (perceptron), activation functions, multilayer networks and backpropagation, other network types like Hopfield and Kohonen self-organising maps, fuzzy sets and membership functions, fuzzy operations and IF-THEN rules, fuzzy inference and defuzzification, and finally neuro-fuzzy systems that combine both.

Perceptron: the simplest artificial neuron. It takes inputs, multiplies each by a weight, adds them up with a bias, and fires if the total crosses a threshold. Output = 1 if (w1*x1 + w2*x2 + b) > 0, else 0. With w1 = 1, w2 = 1 and b = -1.5, it fires only when both inputs are 1, so it acts like an AND gate. A single perceptron can only draw one straight line, so it famously cannot learn XOR, which needs two lines. That limitation is exactly why we stack neurons into layers.

Activation functions: after adding up the inputs, a neuron passes the sum through an activation function that decides how strongly it fires. A step function gives only 0 or 1. Sigmoid squeezes any number into a smooth value between 0 and 1. ReLU simply outputs max(0, x), so negatives become 0 and positives pass straight through. Smooth, non-linear functions matter because without them, a hundred layers would behave like one single straight line.

Backpropagation: this is how a multilayer network learns. Step 1, forward pass: feed an input through and get a guess. Step 2, measure the error, for example (guess - correct)². Step 3, backward pass: using the chain rule from calculus, work out how much each weight contributed to that error. Step 4, nudge every weight a little in the direction that reduces the error: new w = old w - learning rate x gradient. Repeat over thousands of examples. A learning rate that is too big makes it jump around wildly, one that is too small makes it crawl.

Other networks: a Hopfield network acts as memory. Show it a damaged pattern and it settles back to the closest stored pattern, like recognising a song from a few notes. A Kohonen self-organising map arranges data on a grid so similar items sit next to each other, which is great for visualising customer types without labels. These are less popular today, but they still show up in exams and help you understand how networks can store and organise information.

Fuzzy sets and membership: in a normal set, 32°C is either in "hot" or not. In a fuzzy set, it has a membership degree between 0 and 1. Maybe 32°C is 0.7 hot and 0.3 warm. We draw membership functions, often simple triangles or trapezoids, to define words like cold, warm and hot. Fuzzy operations are easy: AND takes the minimum, OR takes the maximum, NOT is 1 minus the value. So "hot AND crowded" with 0.7 and 0.4 gives 0.4.

Fuzzy inference and defuzzification: a fuzzy controller follows a few human-style rules, like "IF temperature is hot AND humidity is high THEN fan speed is fast". Step 1, fuzzify: convert real sensor readings into membership degrees. Step 2, apply all the rules, each firing partly. Step 3, combine the results into one fuzzy shape. Step 4, defuzzify: turn that shape back into one crisp number, usually with the centroid method, which takes the balance point of the shape. The result might be "fan speed 68%".

Neuro-fuzzy systems: fuzzy rules are easy for humans to read, but tuning the triangles by hand is boring. Neural networks learn automatically but are hard to explain. A neuro-fuzzy system like ANFIS uses fuzzy rules as its structure and adjusts the membership functions with neural-style learning. You get a controller that both learns from data and can be explained in plain words.

Real life example 1, the fuzzy washing machine: you throw in a half load of school uniforms covered in mud. Step 1, a sensor measures how cloudy the water gets, say 0.8 dirty. Step 2, a load sensor says 0.5 heavy. Step 3, rules fire: "IF very dirty AND medium load THEN long wash", "IF medium load THEN medium water". Step 4, defuzzification gives something like 47 minutes and 60% water. A plain machine would only offer "short" or "long". The fuzzy one saves water and electricity and still gets the mud out.

Real life example 2, fraud detection: mobile money services watch every transaction. A neural network is trained on millions of old transactions, each labelled normal or fraud, using features like amount, time of day, new device and location. After training, if a midnight transfer of 25,000 taka suddenly comes from a new phone in another district, the network outputs a high fraud score and the system asks for extra verification, all within a fraction of a second.

Where students get confused: fuzzy logic is not the same as probability. A probability of 0.7 means "it might happen", while a membership of 0.7 means "it is partly true right now". Students also forget that a single perceptron cannot solve XOR. Typical exam questions: compute one perceptron update by hand, do one backpropagation step on a tiny network, draw triangular membership functions, apply min and max for fuzzy AND and OR, and defuzzify with the centroid method.

Wrap-up: after this course you can build and train a small neural network, explain backpropagation without fear, and design a fuzzy controller for a real machine. Next, Deep Learning takes neural networks to huge sizes, and Reinforcement Learning and Robotics use these ideas to control things in the real world.
key_points: Neural networks are layers of simple neurons that learn from examples.
A single perceptron draws one line and cannot learn XOR; layers fix that.
Backpropagation measures the error and nudges every weight to reduce it.
Fuzzy logic uses membership degrees from 0 to 1; AND is min, OR is max.
Fuzzy controllers fuzzify, apply IF-THEN rules, then defuzzify to one number.
Neuro-fuzzy systems combine readable rules with automatic learning.
lessons.tip: Do one full backpropagation step by hand with a 2-input, 1-neuron network. One page of calculation will teach you more than ten pages of reading.
lessons.task: Write 3 fuzzy rules for a ceiling fan, like "IF room is very hot THEN speed is high". Use words like a bit, quite, very. Then decide what speed your rules give for a warm, crowded room.

quiz.q: How does a neural network mainly learn?
options: By someone typing every rule by hand
By adjusting its weights to reduce error, using backpropagation
By copying files from the internet
quiz.explain: Backpropagation measures how wrong the guess was and nudges each weight to make the next guess better.

quiz.q: In fuzzy logic, a temperature can be...
options: Partly hot and partly warm at the same time, like 0.7 and 0.3
quiz.explain: Fuzzy logic gives membership degrees between 0 and 1, so one value can belong to several groups partly.

quiz.q: Which everyday machine often uses fuzzy logic?
options: A washing machine that picks wash time by dirt and load
quiz.explain: Fuzzy washing machines blend rules about dirt and load to choose a smooth wash setting.

lessons.title: Information Retrieval
lessons.content:
What is it? Information retrieval (IR) is the science of finding the right documents from a huge pile, fast. When you type something into Google and the best pages show up in half a second, that is IR at work. It is about search engines: how they store text, understand what you are asking for and decide which result goes first. Think of a librarian who has read every book and can point to the right shelf instantly.

Why learn it? There are billions of web pages, products, emails and videos. Without good search, all of it is useless noise. Every app with a search bar, from Daraz to Facebook to your email inbox, needs IR. Modern AI assistants also first search for relevant information and then write their answer, which is called retrieval-augmented generation. Search engineers, data engineers and recommendation system developers all build on this course.

What is in the course? A typical syllabus covers: text processing (tokens, stop words, stemming), the inverted index, the Boolean retrieval model, term weighting with TF-IDF, the vector space model and cosine similarity, link analysis with PageRank, evaluation with precision and recall, and web crawling. Many courses also touch on query expansion and recommendation systems.

Text processing: before a computer can search text, it cleans it up. Tokenisation splits a sentence into words. Everything becomes lowercase so "Cricket" and "cricket" match. Stop words like "the", "is" and "of" are removed because they appear everywhere and tell us nothing. Stemming cuts words to their root, so "playing", "played" and "plays" all become "play". The sentence "The boys are playing cricket" ends up as [boy, play, cricket].

Inverted index: reading every document for every search would take forever. So the search engine prepares an inverted index in advance, exactly like the index at the back of a textbook. For each word, it keeps a list of documents that contain it. If doc1 = "red saree", doc2 = "blue saree", doc3 = "red bucket", then the index is red → [1, 3], saree → [1, 2], blue → [2], bucket → [3]. Searching "red saree" just means intersecting [1, 3] and [1, 2], which gives [1]. That takes microseconds even with millions of documents.

Boolean retrieval: the oldest model. You search using AND, OR and NOT. "cricket AND bangladesh NOT football" returns only documents with both cricket and bangladesh but no football. It is exact and predictable, which is why lawyers and librarians still love it. The problem is that a document either matches or it does not. There is no ranking, so you might get 5,000 results in random order.

TF-IDF weighting: to rank results, we need to know how important each word is in each document. TF (term frequency) counts how often the word appears in this document. IDF (inverse document frequency) is high for rare words and low for common ones: idf = log(N / df), where N is the number of documents and df is how many contain the word. Weight = tf x idf. In 1,000 cricket articles, "cricket" appears everywhere, so its IDF is tiny, but "Shakib" appears in only 20, so it gets a big weight and helps find the right article.

Vector space model: picture every document and every query as an arrow in a space with one direction for each word. A document about cricket and Shakib points one way, a document about rice prices points somewhere else. To rank, we measure the angle between the query arrow and each document arrow using cosine similarity: cos = (A · B) / (|A| x |B|). A cosine near 1 means very similar, near 0 means unrelated. The documents are then sorted from highest cosine to lowest.

PageRank: on the web, links matter too. Google's original idea was that a page linked by many important pages is probably important itself, like a student recommended by many good teachers. Each page shares its score among the pages it links to, and this repeats until the scores settle. A random surfer clicking links forever would visit high-PageRank pages more often. Final ranking mixes text match (like TF-IDF) with link importance.

Evaluation: how do we know a search engine is good? Precision = relevant results shown / total results shown. Recall = relevant results shown / all relevant documents that exist. If you show 10 results and 6 are useful, precision is 0.6. If there were 12 useful documents in total, recall is 6/12 = 0.5. Showing more results usually raises recall but lowers precision, so there is always a trade-off. The F1 score combines the two into one number.

Real life example 1, shopping search: you type "red saree" on Daraz. Step 1, the query is cleaned: [red, saree]. Step 2, the inverted index returns every product with both words. Step 3, each product gets a text score like TF-IDF, so a product titled "Red Jamdani Saree" beats one that mentions red only in a long description. Step 4, business signals are mixed in: sales, ratings, delivery speed. Step 5, the top 20 show up. A good system shows the right saree first, not a red bucket.

Real life example 2, a library catalogue: a university library has 200,000 books. A student searches "database design". The catalogue uses Boolean and TF-IDF retrieval on titles, authors and subjects, so books with "database design" in the title come first, followed by books where the words appear only in the subject list. Precision matters here because nobody wants to scroll through 300 unrelated books.

Where students get confused: precision and recall get mixed up all the time. Remember that precision asks "of what I showed, how much was good?" and recall asks "of all the good stuff, how much did I find?". People also forget that IDF uses a log and that very common words get almost zero weight. Typical exam questions: build an inverted index from 4 short documents, answer a Boolean query, compute TF-IDF for a small table, calculate cosine similarity, and work out precision and recall from a result list.

Wrap-up: after this course you can build a small search engine, explain how indexing and ranking work, and measure search quality honestly. You will also understand what happens behind every search bar you use. Next, Natural Language Processing helps search understand meaning, not just matching words, and Data Mining helps you find patterns in all that text.
key_points: Information retrieval finds the most relevant documents from a huge collection, fast.
Text is cleaned first: tokens, lowercase, stop word removal, stemming.
An inverted index maps each word to the documents that contain it.
TF-IDF weights words; cosine similarity ranks documents in the vector space model.
PageRank says a page linked by important pages is important.
Precision checks what you showed; recall checks what you found.
lessons.tip: Build a tiny inverted index by hand from 4 or 5 short sentences. Seeing how a search answers instantly from the index makes the whole course click.
lessons.task: Write 4 short sentences about your favourite foods. Make an inverted index: list each important word and which sentence numbers contain it. Then 'search' for two words and see which sentences come back.

quiz.q: What does an inverted index store?
options: For each word, the list of documents containing it
quiz.explain: Like the index at the back of a book, it tells you instantly where each word appears.

quiz.q: TF-IDF gives a word high weight in a document when it...
options: Appears often in this document but rarely in others
quiz.explain: Words that are common here but rare elsewhere best describe what this document is about.

quiz.q: Precision in search means...
options: How many of the returned results were actually useful
How many words the query has
How colourful the results page is
quiz.explain: Precision checks the results you showed: what share of them were relevant. Recall checks how many relevant ones you found.

lessons.title: Fault Tolerant Systems
lessons.content:
What is it? A fault tolerant system keeps working even when some part of it breaks. A hard disk fails, a server crashes, a cable gets cut, a bit in memory flips, and the system still runs, maybe a bit slower, but it does not collapse. Think of a four-engine airplane that can still fly safely with one engine off. This course teaches you how to design computers and software that survive failures instead of hoping failures never happen.

Why learn it? Everything breaks eventually: hard disks wear out, power cuts happen, cosmic rays can even flip bits in memory. If a hospital system, an airplane's flight computer or a bank's server stops for a few minutes, people can get hurt or lose money. Big services promise to be up 99.99% of the time, which means less than one hour of downtime per year. That is only possible with fault tolerance. Cloud engineers, site reliability engineers and embedded system designers use these ideas every day.

What is in the course? A typical syllabus covers: the difference between faults, errors and failures, reliability and availability math (MTBF, MTTR), hardware redundancy (duplication, TMR, RAID), information redundancy (parity, Hamming codes, checksums), time redundancy (retry, re-execution), software fault tolerance (checkpointing, N-version programming, recovery blocks), and fault tolerance in distributed systems (replication and consensus).

Fault, error and failure: these three words sound similar but mean different things. A fault is the root cause, like a broken wire or a bug in the code. An error is the wrong internal state the fault creates, like a wrong value stored in memory. A failure is when the user actually sees wrong behaviour, like the ATM giving the wrong amount. Fault tolerance tries to stop faults from ever becoming failures, by catching errors in between.

Reliability and availability: reliability is the chance the system keeps working for a given time without failing. MTBF (mean time between failures) is the average time it runs before something breaks. MTTR (mean time to repair) is how long the fix takes. Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). If a server runs 999 hours on average and takes 1 hour to fix, availability = 999/1000 = 99.9%. You can raise availability by failing less often or by fixing faster.

Hardware redundancy: keep spare hardware. Duplication with comparison runs two copies and raises an alarm if they disagree, which detects errors but cannot tell which copy is right. Triple Modular Redundancy (TMR) runs three copies and a voter takes the majority: if outputs are 5, 5 and 7, the answer is 5, and the faulty one is outvoted. RAID 1 mirrors data on two disks, so if one dies the other still has everything. Spacecraft and airplanes use TMR for their most critical computers.

Information redundancy: add extra bits to detect or fix errors in data. A parity bit makes the number of 1s even: data 1011 has three 1s, so we add 1 to get 10111. If one bit flips during transfer, the count becomes odd and we know something went wrong. Hamming codes add several check bits in clever positions so that a single flipped bit can be both found and corrected. Checksums and CRCs protect files and network packets the same way.

Time redundancy: if something fails, try again. Many faults are temporary, like a glitch caused by electrical noise or a network packet lost once. Simply retrying the operation, or running the calculation twice and comparing, catches these cheaply without extra hardware. The cost is time. Systems usually retry a few times with a growing wait between tries, so they do not hammer an already overloaded server.

Software fault tolerance: bugs are faults too. Checkpointing saves the program's state regularly, so after a crash it restarts from the last checkpoint instead of from zero, like saving your game before a boss fight. N-version programming gives the same specification to different teams who write separate programs, then a voter compares their outputs. Recovery blocks run a primary routine, check its result with an acceptance test, and switch to a simpler backup routine if the test fails.

Distributed fault tolerance: in big systems, data is replicated on several machines, often in different cities. The tricky part is keeping copies in agreement when machines crash or messages get lost. Consensus algorithms like Paxos and Raft let a group of servers agree on one value as long as a majority are alive. With 5 servers, the system survives 2 crashes. Removing single points of failure, any part that brings everything down when it breaks, is the main design goal.

Real life example 1, mobile money during a flood: a mobile money company keeps your account data in two data centres in different places. Step 1, every transaction is written to both. Step 2, one data centre floods during the monsoon and loses power. Step 3, health checks notice it stopped answering within seconds. Step 4, traffic automatically switches to the second data centre. Step 5, you send money to your cousin and never even notice. When the first site comes back, it catches up from the second.

Real life example 2, a cricket tour: a cricket team never travels with only 11 players. They carry extra batsmen, bowlers and a backup wicketkeeper. If the fast bowler gets injured in practice, a replacement steps in and the match goes ahead. The squad has no single point of failure. A good fault tolerant computer system is built the same way: every critical role has a backup ready to take over.

Where students get confused: many use fault, error and failure as if they mean the same thing, but exams test the difference. Students also think redundancy alone is enough, but two copies can only detect a problem, you need three to vote and correct. Typical exam questions: calculate availability from MTBF and MTTR, add a parity bit or a Hamming code to some data, show TMR voting, compute the reliability of series and parallel systems, and explain checkpointing.

Wrap-up: after this course you can find weak points in any system, calculate how reliable it is and add the right kind of redundancy to protect it. Next, Distributed Systems and Cloud Computing put these ideas into practice at huge scale, and Embedded Systems uses them in cars, planes and medical devices.
key_points: A fault tolerant system keeps working when some parts fail.
Fault → error → failure: stop faults before users see failures.
Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR).
Hardware, information, time and software redundancy are the main tools.
TMR uses three copies and a majority vote; parity and Hamming codes catch bit errors.
Remove single points of failure; replication and consensus protect distributed systems.
lessons.tip: For every topic, ask "what happens if this one part dies?" If the answer is "everything stops", you have found a single point of failure.
lessons.task: Think about your home internet. List every part it depends on (router, electricity, cable, ISP). Mark which ones are single points of failure, and write one backup idea for each.

quiz.q: What is the main idea behind fault tolerance?
options: Redundancy: keeping extra copies so one failure doesn't stop everything
quiz.explain: Extra hardware, extra data bits, retries and replicas let the system survive when one part fails.

quiz.q: Triple Modular Redundancy handles a faulty module by...
options: Taking a majority vote among three copies
Asking the user which answer is right
quiz.explain: With three copies voting, one wrong answer is outvoted by the two correct ones.

quiz.q: A single point of failure is...
options: One part whose failure brings the whole system down
The fastest part of the system
quiz.explain: Good fault tolerant design finds these parts and adds backups for them.

lessons.title: Data Engineering
lessons.content:
What is it? Data Engineering is about building the pipes that carry data from where it is born to where it is used. Think of a city's water system. Water comes from rivers, gets cleaned at a treatment plant, is stored in tanks and flows through pipes to every house. Data engineers do the same with data: they collect it from apps, databases and sensors, clean it, store it in the right place and deliver it so analysts and data scientists can open the tap and use it.

Why learn it? A data scientist cannot analyze data that never arrives, arrives broken or arrives a week late. Companies say that for every data scientist they need two or three data engineers. The difference is simple. Data Science asks questions and finds answers in data. Data Engineering makes sure the data is there, correct and on time. Big Data is about the size problem itself, the volume, speed and variety of data and the tools for it. Data Engineering uses Big Data tools when data is huge, but it is also needed for small and medium data, which is most companies.

What's in the course? You learn data pipelines, ETL and ELT, batch versus streaming processing, data warehouses, data lakes and lakehouses, data modeling with the star schema, workflow orchestration with tools like Apache Airflow, processing engines like Spark and Kafka, data quality and governance, and how cloud data platforms work.

Data pipelines: A pipeline is a series of steps that moves data automatically. For example: every night, copy yesterday's orders from the shop's database, remove test orders, convert all prices to taka, join them with customer details and save the result in a reporting table. Each step takes the output of the step before it, like a factory line. A good pipeline runs by itself, shouts when it fails, and can be rerun safely without creating duplicate data.

ETL and ELT: ETL means Extract, Transform, Load. You extract data from sources, transform it (clean, join, calculate) on a separate server, then load the finished result into the warehouse. ELT flips the last two steps: you load raw data first into a powerful warehouse and transform it there using SQL. ELT became popular because modern cloud warehouses are fast and cheap enough to do the heavy work, and keeping the raw data lets you redo transformations later if you made a mistake.

Batch versus streaming: Batch processing handles data in chunks at set times, like processing all of today's sales at 2 AM. It is simple and efficient when you can wait. Streaming processes each event the moment it happens, within seconds, like detecting a suspicious transaction while it is still happening. Streaming is harder to build, so you use it only when you really need answers right now.

Warehouses, lakes and lakehouses: A data warehouse stores clean, structured tables made for fast reports, like a well organized library. A data lake stores everything in its raw form, including logs, images and JSON files, cheaply, like a big storeroom where you throw things to sort later. A lakehouse tries to give both: cheap storage like a lake with the tables and reliability of a warehouse. On the cloud, services like Amazon Redshift, Google BigQuery, Snowflake and Databricks give you these without buying servers.

Data modeling and the star schema: How you arrange tables decides how easy reports are. The star schema puts one fact table in the middle, holding events with numbers, like each sale with its amount. Around it sit dimension tables that describe the who, what, where and when: customer, product, store and date. Draw it and it looks like a star. A question like "total sales of rice in Chattogram in Ramadan" becomes one simple query joining the fact table to a few dimensions.

Orchestration with Airflow: A company may have hundreds of pipelines, and many depend on each other: the sales report must wait for the orders pipeline to finish. An orchestrator like Apache Airflow lets you describe these tasks and their order as a graph called a DAG (directed acyclic graph), schedule them, retry failed ones and send alerts. It is like a cricket captain deciding who bowls when, so the team works in the right order.

Spark and Kafka: When data is too big for one computer, Apache Spark splits the work across many machines and runs it in parallel, so a job that would take a day on a laptop finishes in minutes. Apache Kafka is a system for streaming. Apps write events, like "ride requested", into Kafka topics, and many other systems read them in real time. Kafka acts like a super fast, never-forgetting post office for events.

Data quality and governance: Bad data spreads like a rumor. If a pipeline silently doubles every order, every report and every model downstream becomes wrong. So data engineers add checks: no empty customer IDs, no negative prices, today's row count close to yesterday's. Governance means knowing who owns each dataset, who may see sensitive data like phone numbers, how long data is kept, and where each number came from, which is called data lineage.

Real life example 1, bKash daily reports: Millions of transactions happen every day. A batch pipeline runs after midnight. It extracts the day's transactions from the main database, removes failed ones, groups them by type (send money, cash out, payment) and by district, and loads the summary into a warehouse. By morning, managers open a dashboard showing how much money moved and where. Quality checks flag it if the total suddenly drops by half, which usually means a broken pipeline, not a real crash.

Real life example 2, Pathao trip streaming: Every few seconds, each rider's phone sends its location. These events flow into Kafka. A streaming job reads them, works out where demand is high right now, and updates the surge map and the estimated arrival times within seconds. The same events are also saved into the data lake, so later a batch job can study which areas need more riders during rain.

Where people go wrong and what exams ask: Students mix up ETL and ELT, think streaming is always better than batch, or confuse a warehouse with a lake. Many forget that pipelines must be safe to rerun. Exams ask you to draw a star schema for a shop, explain ETL versus ELT, compare batch and streaming with examples, explain what a DAG is in Airflow, and say how Data Engineering differs from Data Science and Big Data.

After this course you can design a pipeline that moves data reliably from apps into a warehouse, model it for easy reporting and choose between batch and streaming. Practise by building a small pipeline with Python and SQL on your own computer, then learn a cloud platform. Next, look at Cloud Computing and Distributed Systems.
key_points: Data Engineering builds pipelines that move data from sources to where it's used, clean and on time.
Data Science finds answers in data; Data Engineering makes sure the data is there and correct.
ETL transforms before loading; ELT loads raw data first and transforms inside the warehouse.
Batch processes data in chunks on a schedule; streaming handles each event within seconds.
Warehouses hold clean tables, lakes hold raw everything, lakehouses mix both; the star schema makes reporting easy.
Airflow orchestrates pipelines as DAGs; Spark processes big data in parallel; Kafka streams events.
lessons.tip: Draw every pipeline as boxes and arrows before writing any code. If you can't draw where data comes from and goes, you can't build it.
lessons.task: Pick a small shop near you. Draw a star schema for its sales: one fact table in the middle and at least four dimension tables around it, with 3 columns each.

quiz.q: How is ELT different from ETL?
options: ELT loads raw data into the warehouse first and transforms it there
quiz.explain: ETL transforms on a separate server before loading. ELT loads raw data first and uses the powerful warehouse to transform it.

quiz.q: Which job needs streaming instead of batch processing?
options: Flagging a suspicious transaction while it is happening
quiz.explain: Streaming is for answers within seconds. Reports that can wait are simpler and cheaper as batch jobs.

quiz.q: In a star schema, what sits in the middle?
options: A fact table holding events with numbers, like each sale
quiz.explain: The fact table holds measurable events. Dimension tables like customer, product, store and date surround it.

lessons.title: Deep Learning
lessons.content:
What is it? Deep learning is a kind of machine learning that uses artificial neural networks with many layers. Each layer learns a little more, step by step, from simple patterns to complex ideas. It's loosely inspired by how neurons in the brain connect. "Deep" just means there are many layers stacked one after another.

Why learn it? Deep learning powers face unlock on your phone, Google Translate, voice assistants, self-driving research, medical scan analysis and chatbots like the ones you talk to today. Whenever there's lots of data like pictures, sound or text, deep learning often beats older methods by a big margin. It's one of the hottest areas in CS, and almost every AI job asks for it.

What's in the course: the course usually covers the artificial neuron and activation functions, multi-layer networks, loss functions, gradient descent and backpropagation, overfitting and regularization (like dropout), convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for images, recurrent networks (RNNs, LSTMs) for sequences, Transformers and attention, and practical training with tools like PyTorch or TensorFlow.

The neuron and activation: an artificial neuron takes some inputs, multiplies each by a weight, adds them up with a bias, and passes the result through an activation function. For example, inputs 2 and 3 with weights 0.5 and 1 give 2×0.5 + 3×1 = 4. The activation decides what goes out; ReLU, the most popular one, simply keeps positive numbers and turns negatives into 0. Without activations, stacking layers would be no smarter than one layer.

Layers and depth: neurons are arranged in layers: an input layer, several hidden layers and an output layer. Early layers learn simple things, later layers combine them into bigger ideas. In a face photo, the first layers notice edges, the middle ones notice eyes and noses, and the last ones recognize whose face it is. More layers can learn more complex patterns, but need more data and computing power.

Loss function: to learn, the network needs to know how wrong it is. The loss function gives a number for that mistake. If the network says "80 percent cat" for a dog photo, the loss is high; if it says "5 percent cat", the loss is low. For yes/no or category answers we use cross-entropy loss, for number answers we use mean squared error. Training means making this number as small as possible.

Gradient descent and backpropagation: imagine standing on a foggy hill and wanting to reach the bottom. You feel which way the ground slopes and take a small step downhill. That's gradient descent. Backpropagation is the clever trick that calculates, for every single weight, which direction and how much it should change to reduce the error, going backwards from the output to the input. The step size is called the learning rate: too big and you jump around, too small and you take forever.

Overfitting and regularization: overfitting means the model memorizes the training data instead of learning the real pattern, like a student who memorizes past exam answers and fails when the questions change. You spot it when training accuracy is high but test accuracy is low. Fixes include more data, data augmentation (flipping or rotating images), dropout (randomly switching off some neurons during training), and stopping training early.

CNNs for images: a convolutional neural network slides small filters, like 3×3 windows, across an image to find patterns such as edges, corners and textures. Pooling layers shrink the image while keeping the important parts. Because the same filter is used everywhere, a CNN can find a cat whether it's in the corner or the middle. CNNs are the most famous network type for images.

RNNs and Transformers for sequences: text, speech and time data come in order, so the network needs memory. RNNs and LSTMs read one item at a time and carry a memory forward, but they struggle with long sequences. Transformers use attention instead: they look at all the words at once and decide which ones matter for each word. Transformers power modern translation and large language models.

Real life example 1: think of teaching a small child to recognize a cat. You show many cat pictures and say "cat". At first they make mistakes, you correct them, and slowly they get it. That correction is the loss and backpropagation. The first layers learn edges and lines, middle layers learn ears and whiskers, and the last layers say "cat". That's exactly how a deep network learns from lots of photos.

Real life example 2: when you speak into your phone in Bangla and it types the words, a deep network turns the sound wave into small slices, recognizes sounds in each slice, and uses context to choose the right words. It learned this from thousands of hours of recorded speech. The same idea helps doctors: a CNN trained on chest X-rays can flag possible tuberculosis so a doctor checks those first.

Where people get confused: students mix up deep learning with machine learning; deep learning is one part of machine learning, the part with many-layered neural networks. Many think backpropagation is a separate learning algorithm, but it's the way to calculate gradients, while gradient descent uses them to update weights. Common exam questions: compute a neuron's output by hand, explain backpropagation and the learning rate, define overfitting and how to reduce it, explain how a CNN works, and compare RNNs and Transformers.

Tools and practice: in real work you don't write backpropagation by hand. Libraries like PyTorch and TensorFlow do it automatically. You define layers, pick a loss and an optimizer like Adam, feed data in batches for several epochs (full passes over the data), and watch the training and validation loss. GPUs make training many times faster. Free tools like Google Colab let you try this without buying anything.

After this course you can build and train neural networks for images, text and sound, and understand why they work or fail. Next you can specialize in NLP, computer vision or generative AI.
key_points: Deep learning uses neural networks with many layers, from simple to complex patterns.
A neuron multiplies inputs by weights, adds a bias and applies an activation like ReLU.
The loss function measures how wrong the network is.
Backpropagation calculates how each weight should change; gradient descent makes the change.
Overfitting means memorizing the training data; dropout and more data help.
CNNs are best known for images; Transformers with attention for text and sequences.
lessons.tip: Start with a tiny network on a tiny dataset and watch the loss go down. Seeing it learn makes all the math click.
lessons.task: Open your phone gallery and search 'food' or 'car'. Your phone found them using a deep learning model. Notice which ones it got wrong and guess why.

quiz.q: What does backpropagation do?
options: Calculates how each weight should change to reduce the error
quiz.explain: Backpropagation computes gradients that tell each weight which direction to move to reduce the loss.

quiz.q: Which network type is most famous for images?
quiz.explain: CNNs use filters that slide over images, making them great at finding visual patterns.

quiz.q: Overfitting means the model...
options: Memorizes the training data and does badly on new data
quiz.explain: An overfitted model learns the training examples too exactly and fails to generalize to new data.

lessons.title: Natural Language Processing
lessons.content:
What is it? Natural Language Processing, or NLP, is about teaching computers to understand and produce human language, like Bangla and English. Computers love numbers, but we talk in words full of jokes, slang, spelling mistakes and double meanings. NLP is the bridge between the two.

Why learn it? Google Translate, spell checkers, voice typing, spam filters, chatbots, search engines and AI assistants are all NLP. Companies use it to read thousands of customer reviews in seconds. For a language like Bangla, spoken by over 250 million people but with far fewer tools than English, there's a huge need for NLP engineers and researchers. It's also the field behind today's large language models.

What's in the course: you usually learn text preprocessing and tokenization, language models (from n-grams to neural ones), word embeddings, text classification and sentiment analysis, sequence labelling like part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition, machine translation, question answering, Transformers with attention, and large language models, plus how to evaluate NLP systems.

Text preprocessing and tokenization: first, text is broken into small pieces called tokens. "Ami bhat khai" becomes three tokens: "Ami", "bhat", "khai". Modern systems often split rare words into smaller sub-word pieces, so "unhappiness" might become "un", "happi", "ness". Preprocessing may also lowercase text, remove extra symbols and handle different spellings of the same word.

Language models: a language model guesses the next word. An n-gram model counts how often word groups appear; if "bhat" is often followed by "khai", it predicts "khai" after "bhat". Neural language models learn far richer patterns. Large language models are giant Transformers trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token, and that simple job, done at a massive scale, lets them write, answer and translate.

Word embeddings: computers need numbers, so each word becomes a list of numbers called an embedding. Words with similar meanings sit close together: "king" near "queen", "Dhaka" near "Chittagong". Methods like Word2Vec learn these from how words appear in sentences: words used in similar places get similar numbers. Famous example: king − man + woman ≈ queen.

Text classification and sentiment analysis: text classification puts a whole text into a category, like spam or not spam, sports or politics news. Sentiment analysis is a special case: is this review positive, negative or neutral? "Delivery khub fast chilo" is positive, "product ta faltu" is negative. Businesses use this to understand thousands of comments without reading each one.

Sequence labelling and NER: here, every word gets a label. Part-of-speech tagging marks each word as noun, verb and so on. Named entity recognition (NER) finds names of people, places, organisations and dates. In "Sakib played for Bangladesh in Dhaka", NER marks Sakib as a person, Bangladesh as a country (team) and Dhaka as a place.

Transformers and attention: the attention mechanism lets the model look at every word in a sentence and decide which ones matter most for understanding each word. In "The ball hit the window and it broke", attention helps figure out that "it" means the window. Transformers are built from layers of attention, and they made translation, summarization and chatbots dramatically better.

Translation, question answering and evaluation: machine translation turns text from one language to another, question answering finds or writes an answer to a question, and summarization makes long text short. To measure quality, we use scores like accuracy and F1 for classification, and BLEU for translation, which checks how much the machine's output overlaps with a human translation. Human checking is still important.

Real life example 1: you write a Facebook comment in Banglish: "khub bhalo laglo vai". An NLP system has to figure out this is Bangla written in English letters, convert or understand it, and decide the feeling is positive. A company like Daraz can run this on lakhs of product reviews to find which sellers make customers angry.

Real life example 2: when you type on Gboard and it suggests the next word, a language model is guessing what you'll say next. When you ask Google Translate to change an English notice into Bangla, a Transformer reads the whole sentence, uses attention to line up the meaning, and writes it in Bangla word by word.

Where people get confused: students mix up text classification (one label for the whole text) and sequence labelling (one label per word). Many think embeddings are just word IDs, but IDs carry no meaning while embeddings place similar words close together. Common exam questions: tokenize a sentence, compute n-gram probabilities from a small text, explain word embeddings, explain attention, do NER on a sentence, and explain why Bangla NLP is harder (less data, mixed scripts, rich word forms).

After this course you can build text classifiers, chatbots and translation tools, and maybe help Bangla get better AI tools. Speech processing and large language models are great next steps.
key_points: NLP teaches computers to understand and produce human language.
Tokenization breaks text into small pieces called tokens.
Word embeddings are numbers for words, with similar words close together.
Sentiment analysis finds if a text is positive, negative or neutral.
Attention lets a Transformer focus on the most relevant words in a sentence.
Language models predict the next word; large language models are giant Transformers.
lessons.tip: Work with a language you know well, like Bangla. You'll spot errors that a non-speaker would miss.
lessons.task: Type a Bangla sentence into Google Translate and translate it to English and back. See what changed. Where did the machine get confused?

quiz.q: What is sentiment analysis?
options: Finding if a text is positive, negative or neutral
quiz.explain: Sentiment analysis detects the emotion or opinion in a piece of text.

quiz.q: What are word embeddings?
options: Numbers that represent words, with similar words close together
quiz.explain: Embeddings turn words into vectors so meaning can be measured as distance.

quiz.q: The attention mechanism in Transformers helps the model...
options: Focus on the most relevant words in a sentence
quiz.explain: Attention lets each word look at all other words and weigh which ones matter most for meaning.

lessons.title: Computer Vision
lessons.content:
What is it? Computer vision is about teaching computers to see and understand pictures and videos. For a computer, a photo is just a big grid of numbers, one for each pixel. Computer vision turns those numbers into meaning: that's a face, that's a bus, that's a cricket ball flying towards the stumps.

Why learn it? Face unlock, Google Lens, medical scans, self-driving cars, factory quality checks, sports replays and crop disease detection all use computer vision. Cameras are everywhere, in phones, roads, shops and hospitals, so the need to understand images is everywhere too. Jobs in AI, robotics, healthcare tech and security look for these skills.

What's in the course: usually you learn image basics (pixels, color, filters), edge and feature detection, image classification, object detection, segmentation, deep learning for vision (CNNs and vision Transformers), video and object tracking, and 3D vision with cameras and depth.

Image basics: a grayscale image is a grid where each pixel is a number from 0 (black) to 255 (white). A color image has three grids, one each for red, green and blue. A 1000×1000 color photo is three million numbers. Filters are small grids of numbers slid over the image; a blur filter averages neighbours, and an edge filter highlights places where brightness changes suddenly.

Edges and features: edges are where objects begin and end, so finding them is an early step. The Sobel and Canny methods are classic edge detectors. Features are special, easy-to-find spots like corners. Methods like SIFT and ORB find these spots in two photos and match them, which is how your phone stitches several photos into one panorama.

Image classification: this says what's in the picture as a whole: "cat", "dog" or "rickshaw". Modern classifiers are deep CNNs trained on millions of labelled images like ImageNet. Instead of training from zero, people often use transfer learning: take a network already trained on a big dataset and fine-tune it on a small new dataset, like 2000 photos of rice leaves.

Object detection: detection finds every object and draws a box around each, with a label. In a street photo, it might draw 5 boxes for people, 3 for cars and 2 for rickshaws. Models like YOLO ("You Only Look Once") look at the whole image once and predict all boxes quickly enough for live video. We judge boxes using IoU (intersection over union): how much the predicted box overlaps the true box.

Segmentation: segmentation colors every pixel by what it belongs to. Semantic segmentation says "these pixels are road, these are sky". Instance segmentation also separates individual objects: "this is person 1, this is person 2". It's used in medical images to outline a tumour exactly, and in self-driving cars to know exactly where the road ends.

Video and tracking: a video is many images per second, often 30. Tracking follows the same object across frames and gives it an ID, so the system knows car number 7 in this frame is the same car 7 in the next. Optical flow measures how pixels move between frames. This is how cricket ball-tracking for LBW decisions follows the ball's path.

3D vision: our two eyes see slightly different views, and the brain uses the difference to judge distance. Stereo vision does the same with two cameras. Depth sensors and LiDAR measure distance directly. 3D vision lets robots grab objects, drones avoid trees and AR apps place a virtual sofa on your real floor.

Real life example 1: think of Dhaka traffic cameras. A computer vision system can detect and count how many buses, cars and rickshaws pass each minute, track each vehicle across frames, spot one breaking the signal, and read its number plate using text recognition (OCR). Traffic police could then plan signal timing using real numbers.

Real life example 2: a farmer takes a photo of a rice leaf with a cheap phone. An app with a CNN, fine-tuned on thousands of diseased and healthy leaf photos, classifies it as blast disease in a second and suggests what to do. Similarly, in garment factories, cameras check fabric for holes and stains faster than a person can.

Where people get confused: students mix up classification (one label for the whole image), detection (boxes around each object) and segmentation (a label for every pixel). Many think a computer "sees" like us, but it only sees numbers. Common exam questions: apply a 3×3 filter to a small grid by hand, explain edge detection, compare classification, detection and segmentation, calculate IoU for two boxes, and explain how a CNN learns features.

After this course you can build apps that recognize, detect and track things in images and video. Next steps include robotics, medical imaging and augmented reality.
key_points: For a computer, an image is a grid of numbers representing pixels.
Filters slide over images to blur, sharpen or find edges.
Classification labels the whole image; object detection draws boxes around each object.
Segmentation labels every pixel with what it belongs to.
Tracking follows objects across video frames; 3D vision estimates depth.
Modern vision uses deep learning: CNNs, vision Transformers and transfer learning.
lessons.tip: Always visualize your model's outputs on real images. Boxes in the wrong place teach you more than any accuracy number.
lessons.task: Use Google Lens on 5 objects around you. Note which ones it recognizes correctly and which it fails on. Think about lighting and angle.

quiz.q: For a computer, an image is basically...
options: A grid of numbers representing pixels
quiz.explain: Every image is stored as numbers for each pixel's brightness or color.

quiz.q: Which task draws boxes around each object in a picture?
quiz.explain: Object detection finds where objects are and draws bounding boxes around them, like YOLO does.

quiz.q: Segmentation means...
options: Labeling every pixel with what it belongs to
quiz.explain: Segmentation classifies each pixel, so you get the exact shape of every object.

lessons.title: Reinforcement Learning
lessons.content:
What is it? Reinforcement learning, or RL, is learning by trial and error. An agent tries actions in an environment, gets rewards for good moves and penalties for bad ones, and slowly figures out the best way to behave. Nobody gives it the right answers; it learns from experience, just like you learned which teachers don't like late homework.

Why learn it? RL taught computers to beat world champions at Go and chess and play video games better than humans. It's used in robotics, recommending content, controlling traffic lights, managing power in data centers and fine-tuning chatbots with human feedback (RLHF). Any problem where you make a series of decisions and only find out later if they were good is an RL problem.

What's in the course: you usually learn the agent-environment loop, Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), rewards and discounting, policies and value functions, the Bellman equation, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo and temporal difference learning, Q-learning, exploration vs exploitation, and deep RL like Deep Q-Networks and policy gradient methods.

The agent-environment loop: the agent sees the current state, picks an action, and the environment replies with a reward and a new state. Then it repeats. In a Ludo game, the state is where all the pieces are, the action is which piece to move, and the reward could be +1 for winning and −1 for losing. One full game from start to end is called an episode.

Markov Decision Process: an MDP is the math description of an RL problem: a set of states, a set of actions, rules for how actions change states (sometimes with chance), and rewards. "Markov" means the future depends only on the current state, not the full history. In chess, the current board tells you everything; it doesn't matter how you got there.

Rewards and discounting: the agent wants to collect the most total reward, not just the next reward. But a reward now is usually worth more than the same reward much later, so we multiply future rewards by a discount factor γ (gamma), like 0.9. A reward of 10 two steps later is worth 10 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 8.1 now. This also stops the total from growing to infinity.

Policy and value function: a policy is the agent's rulebook: in each state, which action to take. A value function estimates how much total future reward a state is worth if you follow the policy. A Q-value goes one step further: how good it is to take a specific action in a specific state. If you know good Q-values, the best policy is simple: always pick the action with the highest Q-value.

The Bellman equation: this is the key idea that links values together. It says: the value of a state = the reward you get now + the discounted value of where you land next. It's like saying how good your current position in a cricket chase is depends on the runs you score this ball plus how good the position after this ball is. Dynamic programming uses this to calculate values when the full rules are known.

Q-learning: when the agent doesn't know the rules, it learns Q-values from experience. After each step it updates: new Q = old Q + learning rate × (reward + γ × best Q of next state − old Q). Little by little, the Q-table gets accurate. It's a temporal difference method, because it learns from the difference between what it expected and what actually happened, step by step, without waiting for the episode to end.

Exploration vs exploitation: should the agent try something new to learn more (explore), or use the best action it already knows (exploit)? Only exploiting means it might miss a much better path; only exploring means it never uses what it learned. A simple rule is ε-greedy: with probability ε, like 10 percent, pick a random action; otherwise pick the best one. Deep RL, like Deep Q-Networks, replaces the Q-table with a neural network so it can handle huge state spaces like video game screens.

Real life example 1: think of learning to ride a bicycle. Nobody can give you an exact formula. You try, you wobble, you fall, which is a penalty. You balance a bit longer, which feels great, a reward. After many tries, your brain learns the policy. Or think of training a pet: give it a treat when it sits, and soon it sits on command.

Real life example 2: imagine an RL agent controlling a traffic signal at a busy Dhaka intersection. The state is how many vehicles are waiting on each road, the actions are which road gets green and for how long, and the reward is minus the total waiting time. By trying different timings in a simulator thousands of times, it learns a policy that cuts waiting time compared to fixed timers.

Where people get confused: students mix up RL with supervised learning. In supervised learning, every example comes with the right answer; in RL there's only a reward signal, often delayed. Many confuse the policy (what to do) with the value function (how good a state is). Common exam questions: define the parts of an MDP, calculate a discounted return, write and explain the Bellman equation, do one Q-learning update by hand, and explain exploration vs exploitation and ε-greedy.

After this course you can build agents that learn to make decisions over time, in games, simulations and robots. Next you can explore robotics, game AI and multi-agent systems.
key_points: In RL, an agent learns mainly from rewards and penalties from its actions.
An MDP describes the problem: states, actions, transitions and rewards.
A policy is a rule for which action to take in each state.
A value function estimates total future reward; the Bellman equation links them.
Q-learning learns action values from experience, step by step.
Exploration vs exploitation: try new actions vs use the best known one.
lessons.tip: Start with tiny grid-world problems you can draw on paper. Once you can follow the agent by hand, bigger problems feel natural.
lessons.task: Think of a game you got better at, like Ludo or a phone game. Write down what the 'rewards' and 'penalties' were and how your strategy changed over time.

quiz.q: In reinforcement learning, the agent learns mainly from...
options: A teacher giving the correct answer each time
Rewards and penalties from its actions
quiz.explain: RL agents improve by trying actions and getting reward signals, not labelled correct answers.

quiz.q: What is a policy in RL?
options: A rule for which action to take in each state
quiz.explain: A policy maps each situation (state) to an action. Learning a good policy is the goal of RL.

quiz.q: The exploration vs exploitation trade-off is about...
options: Trying new actions vs using the best known action
quiz.explain: The agent must balance learning more by exploring and earning reward by exploiting what it already knows.

lessons.title: Robotics
lessons.content:
What is it? Robotics is the study of building machines that can sense the world, decide what to do and then move to do it. A robot is like a body plus a brain made of a computer. Think of a robot vacuum cleaner: it feels the walls, decides where to go next and drives there, all by itself.

Why learn it? Robots already pack boxes in Daraz-style warehouses, weld cars in factories, help doctors in surgery and explore Mars. Robotics mixes almost everything in CSE: programming, math, electronics, AI and control. If you like seeing your code actually move something in the real world, this course is pure fun. Jobs in automation, drones, self-driving cars and smart factories all need it.

What is in the course? Usually you learn the sense-think-act loop, sensors and actuators, kinematics (how arms and wheels move), control systems like PID, localization and mapping (SLAM), path planning, and a bit of robot software like ROS (Robot Operating System).

Sense, think, act: Every robot runs this loop again and again, many times a second. Sense means reading the sensors. Think means deciding what to do with that data. Act means sending commands to the motors. A line-following robot senses the black line with light sensors, thinks "the line is drifting left" and acts by turning a little left. Then it repeats.

Sensors and actuators: Sensors are the robot's eyes, ears and skin: cameras, ultrasonic distance sensors, LiDAR (laser distance scanners), IMUs (they feel tilt and turning) and wheel encoders (they count wheel turns). Actuators are the muscles: DC motors, servo motors that turn to an exact angle, and stepper motors that move in tiny exact steps. Sensors are never perfect, so robots often combine several of them, a trick called sensor fusion. For example, wheel encoders drift slowly over time while GPS jumps around a bit, but mixed together with a Kalman filter they give a much better guess of the true position than either alone.

Kinematics: This is the math of movement. Forward kinematics answers "if I turn each joint of the arm by these angles, where does the hand end up?". Inverse kinematics is the harder opposite: "I want the hand at this cup, what angles do I need?". For a simple 2-joint arm you use a bit of trigonometry, sin and cos, to get the answer. There is also the idea of degrees of freedom: each joint that can move independently adds one. Your own arm from shoulder to wrist has about seven, which is why you can touch your nose in many different ways. Industrial robot arms usually have six, enough to reach any point from any angle in their workspace.

Control and PID: Telling a motor "go to 90 degrees" is not enough, because it may overshoot, shake or stop short. A PID controller fixes this. P (proportional) pushes harder when the error is big. I (integral) fixes small errors that stay for a long time. D (derivative) slows things down when the error is shrinking fast, so the robot does not overshoot. Together they keep the movement smooth and on target, like a good driver pressing the brake gently before a speed breaker.

Localization and SLAM: A robot must know where it is. Localization means figuring out your position on a map. But what if there is no map yet? SLAM, Simultaneous Localization and Mapping, builds the map and finds the robot's place on it at the same time. A robot vacuum going into a new house uses SLAM: as it moves, it draws the room and keeps track of where it is in that drawing.

Path planning: Once the robot knows the map and its position, it needs a route. Algorithms like A* (A-star) search the map for the shortest safe path, just like Google Maps finds a route around a traffic jam. Then the robot follows that path and replans if someone suddenly walks in front of it. Robots also need local planning: while the global path says "go down this corridor", a local planner reacts every fraction of a second to things the map never showed, like a bucket left on the floor.

Real life example 1: Imagine a delivery robot in a big hospital in Dhaka carrying medicine from the pharmacy to Ward 5. It senses with LiDAR and cameras, uses SLAM to know which corridor it is in, plans a path with A*, and uses PID to drive straight and stop exactly at the door. If a patient's trolley blocks the corridor, it senses the obstacle, thinks of a new path and acts by turning. Sense, think, act, all day long.

Real life example 2: A drone spraying pesticide over a rice field in Bogura.
