Its IMU senses tilt from the wind, a PID controller adjusts each propeller many times a second so it stays level, GPS gives its position, and a planned zigzag path makes sure every part of the field gets sprayed once. A farmer finishes in one hour what used to take a whole day.

Where people get confused / exam stuff: Many mix up forward and inverse kinematics; remember forward goes from angles to position, inverse from position to angles. Another common mistake is thinking a robot is just a program; real sensors are noisy, so robots must handle wrong readings. Exam questions often ask: draw the sense-think-act loop, explain what P, I and D each do, write the full form of SLAM, or compare sensors like ultrasonic vs LiDAR.

After this course you can explain how a robot moves, tune a simple controller and plan a path on a map. A great next step is building a small line-follower or obstacle-avoiding car with an Arduino, then learning ROS, Computer Vision and Reinforcement Learning to make your robots smarter.
key_points: A robot runs a sense, think, act loop many times a second.
Sensors (camera, LiDAR, IMU, encoders) read the world; actuators (motors, servos) move the robot.
Forward kinematics: angles to position; inverse kinematics: position to angles.
A PID controller keeps movement smooth and on target.
SLAM means Simultaneous Localization and Mapping: build the map and find yourself on it together.
Path planning algorithms like A* find a safe, short route.
lessons.tip: Real sensors are noisy. Always test in the real world early, because what works in simulation often surprises you outside it.
lessons.task: Blindfold yourself (safely!) and try to walk from your bed to the door by counting steps. Notice how small errors add up. Robots face the same problem, and that's why localization matters.

quiz.q: What is the basic loop every robot runs?
quiz.explain: Robots sense the world, decide what to do and then act, again and again.

quiz.q: SLAM stands for...
quiz.explain: SLAM lets a robot build a map of an unknown place while figuring out where it is inside that map.

quiz.q: A PID controller is used to...
options: Keep a robot's movement smooth and on target
quiz.explain: PID control constantly corrects errors so motors reach and hold the desired position or speed.

levels.title: MSc: The future and your thesis

lessons.title: Internet of Things (IoT)
lessons.content:
What is it? The Internet of Things, or IoT, means everyday things connected to the internet so they can send data and take commands. A light bulb, a fan, a water tank, a cow's collar, even a dustbin can become "smart" when you give it a tiny chip, a sensor and a network connection.

Why learn it? Billions of IoT devices already exist: smart meters, fitness bands, CCTV cameras, smart farms and factory machines. IoT joins hardware, networking, cloud and data together, so it is a perfect MSc topic. Companies need people who can build devices, connect them safely and make sense of the huge stream of data they produce.

What is in the course? Usually: IoT architecture (layers), sensors and actuators, microcontrollers like Arduino and ESP32, communication technologies (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, LoRa, cellular), IoT protocols like MQTT and CoAP, cloud and edge computing, data analytics and IoT security.

IoT architecture: Think of it in layers. The perception layer has sensors and actuators that touch the real world. The network layer carries the data. The processing layer, in the cloud or at the edge, stores and analyses it. The application layer is the app or dashboard you see on your phone. Every IoT system, small or big, fits into these layers. Many real systems add a gateway between the devices and the internet. A gateway collects data from dozens of small sensors that speak Zigbee or LoRa, translates it, and forwards it over Wi-Fi or 4G, so each tiny sensor does not need its own expensive internet connection.

Devices: An IoT device usually needs three things: a sensor or actuator, a small chip (microcontroller) and a network connection. For example, an ESP32 board costs a few hundred taka, has Wi-Fi built in and can read a temperature sensor. A sensor measures (temperature, humidity, motion); an actuator does something (turns on a pump, opens a lock). Power is a huge deal for IoT devices. A sensor in a field may run on two AA batteries for years, so it sleeps most of the time, wakes up for a fraction of a second to measure and send, and then sleeps again. Choosing a chip and radio that sip power is often more important than raw speed.

Connectivity: Different jobs need different radios. Wi-Fi is fast but uses a lot of power. Bluetooth Low Energy is good for short distances like a fitness band and phone. Zigbee makes small mesh networks in smart homes. LoRa sends tiny messages kilometres away using very little power, great for farms. Cellular (4G, NB-IoT) works almost anywhere there is a mobile network.

Protocols, MQTT: Devices are small and networks can be weak, so they need light ways to talk. MQTT is the most popular. It uses a publish/subscribe idea: a sensor publishes a message like "tank/level = 80" to a broker (a middleman server), and any app subscribed to "tank/level" gets it. Messages are tiny, so MQTT works even on slow connections. CoAP is another light protocol, similar to a mini version of HTTP. MQTT also has Quality of Service levels: QoS 0 sends a message once and does not check, QoS 1 makes sure it arrives at least once, and QoS 2 makes sure it arrives exactly once. A temperature reading every minute can use QoS 0, but a command to unlock a door should use a higher level.

Edge vs cloud computing: Sending every single reading to a far away cloud is slow and costs data. Edge computing means processing data close to the device, on the device itself or a nearby gateway. A smart camera can detect "a person is here" on the spot and send only that alert, not hours of video. The cloud is still used for long-term storage and big analysis. There is also fog computing, a middle layer between edge and cloud, like a local server in a factory that handles data from all machines on that floor.

IoT security: Many IoT devices ship with weak default passwords like "admin", and attackers have hijacked millions of them to build botnets (Mirai is a famous one). Good IoT design means changing default passwords, encrypting data, updating firmware and keeping devices on a separate network.

Real life example 1: A smart irrigation system on a farm in Rajshahi. Soil moisture sensors in the field send readings over LoRa to a gateway. The gateway checks: "soil is dry and no rain is forecast", and turns on the water pump (actuator). The farmer gets an MQTT-powered notification on their phone and sees a chart of soil moisture. Water is saved, and the crop gets exactly what it needs.

Real life example 2: Prepaid smart electricity meters in Dhaka homes. The meter measures your usage, sends data to the power company, and cuts the line when your balance is finished, then reconnects when you recharge through bKash. That is IoT: a sensor, a chip, a network and an action, all working without a meter reader visiting your house.

Where people get confused / exam stuff: Students often think IoT just means "internet"; the key part is physical things sensing and acting. Another confusion is edge vs cloud: edge is near the device, cloud is far away. Exam questions often ask: draw the IoT layered architecture, explain MQTT publish/subscribe with a broker, compare Wi-Fi, BLE, Zigbee and LoRa, or list IoT security problems.

After this course you can design a full IoT system from sensor to dashboard. Try building one with an ESP32, a sensor and a free MQTT broker. Next, look at Wireless Sensor Networks, Embedded Systems, Cloud Computing and Advanced Cyber Security to go deeper.
key_points: IoT means everyday things connected to the internet to sense, send data and act.
An IoT device needs a sensor or actuator, a small chip and a network connection.
IoT layers: perception, network, processing, application.
MQTT is a lightweight publish/subscribe protocol using a broker.
Edge computing processes data close to the device instead of sending everything to the cloud.
Weak default passwords make IoT devices easy targets, so security matters.
lessons.tip: IoT clicks fastest when you build something tiny. A cheap ESP32 board and one sensor will teach you more than ten slides.
lessons.task: Walk around your home and list 5 things that could become IoT devices. For each one, write what sensor it needs, what data it would send, and what action it could take.

quiz.q: What does an IoT device usually need?
options: Only a big screen and a keyboard
A sensor or actuator, a small chip and a network connection
A full desktop computer inside it
quiz.explain: An IoT device senses or acts on the world, has a small processor like a microcontroller, and connects to a network to share data.

quiz.q: What is MQTT commonly used for in IoT?
options: Sending small messages between devices and servers in a lightweight way
quiz.explain: MQTT is a light publish and subscribe messaging protocol, great for small devices with weak networks and little power.

quiz.q: What does edge computing mean?
options: Processing data close to the device instead of sending everything to a far away cloud
Putting computers on the edge of a table
Only using the cloud for everything
quiz.explain: Edge computing does some of the thinking near the device, which cuts delay, saves bandwidth and can keep data more private.

lessons.title: Blockchain
lessons.content:
What is it? A blockchain is a shared digital notebook (ledger) that many computers keep a copy of. New records are added in groups called blocks, and each block is locked to the one before it, making a chain. Once something is written and accepted, it is almost impossible to secretly change it.

Why learn it? Blockchain powers cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum, but it is also used for supply chain tracking, digital certificates, land records and cross-border payments. It mixes cryptography, distributed systems and economics. Understanding it helps you tell real uses from hype, which is a valuable skill.

What is in the course? Usually: hash functions and digital signatures, the structure of blocks and chains, distributed ledgers and peer-to-peer networks, consensus mechanisms (Proof of Work, Proof of Stake), smart contracts, public vs private blockchains, and the limits of blockchain like speed and energy use.

Hash functions: A hash function takes any data and gives a fixed-size fingerprint, like a 64-character code for SHA-256. Change even one letter of the input and the fingerprint changes completely. You cannot go backwards from the hash to the data. This fingerprint is the glue of the chain. Hashes also make blocks compact to check: instead of comparing two huge files letter by letter, two computers can just compare their 64-character fingerprints. If the fingerprints match, the data is the same.

Blocks and the chain: Each block holds some transactions, a timestamp and the hash of the previous block. So block 5 contains the fingerprint of block 4. If someone secretly changes a transaction in block 4, its hash changes, block 5 no longer matches, and the whole chain after it breaks. On top of that, thousands of other computers have the correct copy, so they all disagree with the cheater. That is why old blocks are so hard to tamper with.

Digital signatures and wallets: Your wallet has a private key (secret, like a PIN) and a public key (like your account number). When you send coins, you sign the transaction with your private key, and anyone can check it with your public key. Lose the private key and the coins are gone forever; no bank can reset it. Your public address is made from your public key, so you can share it freely, like giving someone your bKash number to receive money. But you never share the private key or the recovery words, the same way you never share your PIN.

Consensus mechanisms: With no boss in charge, how do all computers (nodes) agree on which block gets added next? A consensus mechanism decides. In Proof of Work (Bitcoin), miners race to solve a hard math puzzle; the winner adds the block. It is secure but uses huge electricity. In Proof of Stake (Ethereum now), validators lock up coins as a deposit, and one is chosen to add the block; cheating means losing the deposit. It uses far less energy. Proof of Work also protects against a cheater rewriting history: to change an old block, they would have to redo the puzzle for that block and every block after it, faster than the rest of the world combined. That would need more than half of all mining power, a so-called 51% attack, which is extremely expensive on a big network like Bitcoin.

Smart contracts: A smart contract is a program stored on the blockchain that runs automatically when its conditions are met. For example: "if the buyer pays 1 ETH, send them the digital ticket". No middleman is needed, and everyone can see the rules. But bugs in a smart contract are dangerous, because once deployed they are hard to fix, and attackers have stolen millions this way.

Public vs private blockchains: Public ones like Bitcoin let anyone join and read. Private or permissioned ones (like Hyperledger Fabric) let only approved members in, which suits banks or companies that want shared records but not full openness. There are also limits to remember: Bitcoin handles only a few transactions per second, while a card network like Visa handles thousands. Engineers are building faster "layer 2" systems on top to fix this.

Real life example 1: Suppose a garment buyer in Europe wants proof that a shirt from a Gazipur factory used certified cotton. Each step, the cotton farm, the spinning mill, the factory and the shipping company, adds a record to a shared blockchain. Nobody can later change "uncertified" to "certified" without the chain and other copies exposing it. The buyer scans a QR code and sees the whole history.

Real life example 2: Think of a university issuing degree certificates on a blockchain. When you apply for a job abroad, the employer checks the certificate's hash on the chain instead of emailing the registrar and waiting weeks. Fake certificates fail the check immediately.

Where people get confused / exam stuff: Blockchain is not the same as Bitcoin; Bitcoin is just one use. Blockchain is not magic either: if wrong data is entered in the first place, the chain keeps the wrong data forever (garbage in, garbage out). It is also slower than a normal database. Exam questions often ask: explain why changing an old block is hard, compare Proof of Work and Proof of Stake, define a smart contract, or draw a chain of blocks with previous hashes.

After this course you can explain how a blockchain stays tamper-proof, write a tiny smart contract and judge when a blockchain is actually useful and when a normal database is better. Next, explore Advanced Cyber Security, Distributed Systems and cryptography in more depth.
key_points: A blockchain is a shared ledger copied across many computers, built from linked blocks.
Each block stores the previous block's hash, so changing an old block breaks the chain.
Private keys sign transactions; public keys let anyone verify them.
Consensus (Proof of Work, Proof of Stake) lets all nodes agree on the next block.
A smart contract is a program on the blockchain that runs automatically when conditions are met.
Blockchain is not always the right tool; a normal database is often faster and simpler.
lessons.tip: Always ask: do we really need a blockchain here, or would a normal database do? Being able to answer that makes you sound like a real expert.
lessons.task: On paper, make 4 blocks. In each, write a small transaction and a made-up fingerprint built from the previous block's fingerprint plus its own text. Now change block 2 and see how blocks 3 and 4 no longer match.

quiz.q: Why is it hard to secretly change an old block?
options: Because blocks are written in pen
Because blocks are deleted after one day
Because each block holds the previous block's hash, so changing one breaks the chain and the other copies disagree
quiz.explain: Hashes link the blocks. A change alters the fingerprint, breaks every link after it, and doesn't match the copies held by other nodes.

quiz.q: What is a smart contract?
options: A paper contract signed by a lawyer
A program stored on the blockchain that runs automatically when its conditions are met
quiz.explain: Smart contracts are code on the chain. Like a vending machine, they act automatically once the rules are satisfied.

quiz.q: What does a consensus mechanism do?
options: Helps all nodes agree on which block gets added next
Chooses the color of the coin
quiz.explain: Consensus rules like Proof of Work or Proof of Stake let many independent computers agree on one shared history.

lessons.title: Quantum Computing
lessons.content:
What is it? Quantum computing is a new kind of computing that uses the strange rules of tiny particles, quantum physics, to process information. Normal computers use bits that are either 0 or 1. Quantum computers use qubits, which can be in a mix of 0 and 1 at the same time until you look at them.

Why learn it? For some special problems, like simulating molecules for new medicines, optimising huge delivery routes or breaking certain kinds of encryption, a big quantum computer could be far faster than any normal supercomputer. Companies like IBM and Google already let you run programs on real quantum chips over the internet. It is a frontier where new researchers are badly needed.

What is in the course? Usually: qubits and superposition, measurement, entanglement, quantum gates and circuits, famous algorithms like Grover's and Shor's, quantum cryptography, and the real-world problem of noise and error correction. A little linear algebra (vectors and matrices) is the main math you need.

Qubits and superposition: A normal bit is like a coin lying on a table: heads (1) or tails (0). A qubit is like a coin spinning in the air: it is in a superposition, a mix of both, with some chance of each. When you measure it, the spinning stops and you get just 0 or 1. Two qubits can hold a mix of 4 states at once, 3 qubits 8 states, and n qubits 2 to the power n states. Mathematically, a qubit's state is written as a mix like a|0> + b|1>, where a and b are numbers called amplitudes. The chance of getting 0 is a squared and the chance of 1 is b squared, and these chances always add up to 1, that is 100%.

Measurement: Here is the tricky part. You cannot read all those states at once. Measuring gives just one answer, randomly, based on the chances. So quantum algorithms are clever recipes that make the wrong answers cancel out and the right answer become very likely before you measure.

Entanglement: Two qubits can be linked so that their results are connected, even when far apart. Measure one and you instantly know something about the other. Einstein called it "spooky action at a distance". Entanglement is a key ingredient that gives quantum computers their extra power.

Quantum gates and circuits: Just like normal computers have AND, OR and NOT gates, quantum computers have gates like X (a quantum NOT), H (Hadamard, which puts a qubit into superposition) and CNOT (which can entangle two qubits). A quantum program is a circuit: qubits flow left to right through gates, and at the end you measure. For example, start a qubit at 0 and apply H: now it is 50% 0 and 50% 1. Apply H again and it goes back to 0 for sure, because the two paths interfere and cancel. This interference, waves adding up or cancelling, is the real secret behind quantum speedups.

Famous algorithms: Grover's algorithm searches an unsorted list of N items in about square root of N steps instead of N, so a million items need about a thousand steps. Shor's algorithm can factor huge numbers very quickly. That matters because RSA encryption, which protects online banking, relies on factoring being extremely hard. So a big enough quantum computer running Shor's algorithm could break RSA style encryption. This is why security experts are already building post-quantum cryptography.

Noise and error correction: Today's quantum computers are small (hundreds to a few thousand qubits) and noisy. Heat, vibration or tiny disturbances knock qubits out of their state, a problem called decoherence, so errors are a major challenge. Quantum error correction uses many physical qubits to make one reliable logical qubit, but it needs lots of qubits, which is why big useful machines are still being built. Different companies build qubits in different ways: superconducting circuits cooled colder than outer space, trapped ions held by lasers, or particles of light. Each has trade-offs in speed, error rate and how easily it can grow bigger.

Real life example 1: A medicine company wants a new drug molecule. Simulating how electrons behave in a big molecule is so hard that normal computers must use rough guesses. A quantum computer is naturally made of quantum stuff, so it can simulate molecules more directly. This could speed up discovery of medicines and better fertiliser, which matters a lot for a farming country like Bangladesh.

Real life example 2: Think about your bKash or bank app. It uses encryption like RSA to keep your PIN and money safe. Hackers could record encrypted data today and decrypt it years later when quantum computers are strong enough, an attack called "harvest now, decrypt later". That is why banks and governments are slowly switching to new quantum-safe encryption standards.

Where people get confused / exam stuff: A quantum computer is not just a faster normal computer; it is only faster for certain problems, and it will not replace your laptop. Superposition does not mean you read all answers at once. Exam questions often ask: difference between a bit and a qubit, what superposition and entanglement mean, what the Hadamard gate does, why Shor's algorithm threatens RSA, and why noise is a problem today.

After this course you can read simple quantum circuits, explain Grover's and Shor's algorithms at a high level and understand the security impact. Try a free tool like IBM Quantum or Qiskit to run a tiny circuit online. Next, strengthen your linear algebra and look into post-quantum cryptography.
key_points: A qubit can be in a superposition of 0 and 1 until it is measured.
Measuring gives one answer; algorithms make the right answer most likely.
Entanglement links qubits so their results are connected.
Quantum gates (X, H, CNOT) build circuits, like logic gates in normal computers.
Shor's algorithm could break RSA style encryption on a big enough quantum computer.
Today's quantum computers are small and noisy, so errors are a major challenge.
lessons.tip: Don't fight the weirdness with everyday intuition. Treat qubits as vectors and gates as matrices, and the math will guide you.
lessons.task: Flip a coin 20 times and write down the results. Think of the coin in the air as a superposition and the landed coin as a measurement. Then write 3 lines on why you only ever see heads or tails, never both.

quiz.q: What makes a qubit different from a normal bit?
options: It can only store the number 2
It can be in a superposition of 0 and 1 until measured
quiz.explain: A classical bit is 0 or 1. A qubit can hold a mix of both until measurement makes it pick one.

quiz.q: Why does quantum computing worry security experts?
options: Shor's algorithm could break RSA style encryption on a big enough quantum computer
quiz.explain: Shor's algorithm factors big numbers efficiently, which would break RSA. That's why post-quantum cryptography is being adopted.

quiz.q: What is a big problem with quantum computers today?
options: They are noisy and small, so errors are a major challenge
They cannot be programmed at all
quiz.explain: Current machines have few, error-prone qubits. Quantum error correction is a key research area.

lessons.title: Bioinformatics
lessons.content:
What is it? Bioinformatics is where biology meets computer science. Living things store their instructions in DNA, which is basically a very long text written with four letters. Bioinformatics uses programming, algorithms and statistics to read, compare and understand this biological data.

Why learn it? Machines can now read a human's whole DNA in a day, producing billions of letters. No human can read that by hand; computers must. Bioinformatics helps find disease genes, design medicines, track viruses and improve crops. Bangladeshi scientists even decoded the jute genome. If you like both coding and biology, this is a high-impact field.

What is in the course? Usually: basic molecular biology (DNA, RNA, proteins), biological databases, sequence alignment (pairwise and multiple), tools like BLAST, phylogenetic trees, genome assembly, protein structure prediction and a bit of machine learning on biological data.

DNA, RNA and proteins: DNA is made of four letters: A, C, G and T. A gene is a section of DNA that holds the recipe for a protein. The cell copies the gene into RNA (where T becomes U), then reads RNA three letters at a time, called a codon, to build a protein chain. Proteins do the actual work in your body. This flow, DNA to RNA to protein, is called the central dogma. DNA letters also pair up: A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G. That is why DNA has two strands that fit together like a zip, and why, if you know one strand, say ACGT, you can write the other one, TGCA. Programs use this rule all the time to find genes on either strand.

Biological databases: Scientists around the world store sequences in huge free databases like GenBank (DNA) and UniProt (proteins), and structures in PDB. Bioinformaticians search these the way you search Google, but with sequences as the query. Files have special formats too. The simplest is FASTA: one line starting with > gives the name, and the next lines hold the letters. Learning to read and write these formats with a bit of Python is often the very first lab of the course.

Sequence alignment: Sequence alignment lines up two biological sequences to measure how similar they are. For example, ACGTTGA and ACGTCGA match in every position except one. Algorithms add points for matches and subtract for mismatches and gaps. Needleman-Wunsch aligns whole sequences and Smith-Waterman finds the best matching part; both use dynamic programming, the same idea from your Algorithms course. A tiny scoring example: give +1 for a match, -1 for a mismatch and -2 for a gap. Aligning ACGTTGA with ACGTCGA gives six matches and one mismatch, so the score is 6 - 1 = 5. The algorithm fills a table cell by cell, each cell picking the best of three moves, so it never has to try every possible alignment.

BLAST: Comparing against millions of sequences with full dynamic programming is too slow. BLAST is a fast tool that first finds short exact matching "seeds" and then extends them. You paste an unknown sequence, and BLAST tells you which known genes or organisms it looks like. BLAST also gives an E-value for each hit, which tells you how likely such a match would appear just by chance. A very small E-value, like 0.0000001, means the match is almost surely real.

Phylogenetic trees: By comparing sequences from many species or virus samples, you can draw a family tree showing who is closely related and who split off earlier. The more two sequences differ, the further apart they sit on the tree. Trees are built with methods like neighbour-joining, which repeatedly joins the two closest sequences into one branch, or maximum likelihood, which picks the tree that best explains the mutations seen.

Genome assembly and protein structure: Sequencing machines read DNA in small broken pieces. Genome assembly puts these pieces back together, like solving a giant jigsaw puzzle using overlapping ends. Protein structure prediction guesses the 3D shape a protein folds into; AI tools like AlphaFold made huge progress here, which helps in designing medicines. Assembly is hard because genomes have repeated regions, like the same sentence printed many times in a book. Short pieces from these regions fit in many places, so longer reads from newer machines help a lot.

Real life example 1: During COVID-19, labs around the world, including in Bangladesh, sequenced virus samples from patients. Bioinformatics tools compared these virus sequences, found mutations, and built phylogenetic trees to track which variants, like Delta or Omicron, were spreading where. This helped governments decide about lockdowns and vaccines.

Real life example 2: A farmer's rice crop keeps dying in salty soil in the coastal south. Scientists compare DNA of salt-tolerant rice with normal rice using alignment tools, find the genes that help survive salt, and breeders develop new salt-tolerant varieties. Computer science ends up helping food reach your plate.

Where people get confused / exam stuff: Students forget that RNA uses U instead of T. Many think alignment just counts equal letters, but gaps matter too. Exam questions often ask: name the four DNA bases, explain the central dogma, do a small alignment with a scoring table, explain how BLAST is faster than full dynamic programming, or interpret a phylogenetic tree.

After this course you can search biological databases, align sequences and explain how computers help in medicine and agriculture. Try BLAST on the NCBI website with any short sequence. Next, look at Data Mining, Machine Learning and Deep Learning, which are now used heavily in biology.
key_points: Bioinformatics uses computing to read, compare and understand biological data.
DNA is written with four letters: A, C, G, T; DNA to RNA to protein is the central dogma.
Sequence alignment lines up two sequences to measure how similar they are.
BLAST quickly finds known sequences similar to an unknown one.
Phylogenetic trees show how species or virus variants are related.
During COVID-19, comparing virus sequences helped track spreading variants.
lessons.tip: You don't need to be a biology expert to start. Treat DNA as text and learn the biology bit by bit as each problem needs it.
lessons.task: Write two short DNA strings, like ACGTTGCA and ACGATGCA. Line them up and count how many positions match. That match count is a very simple alignment score.

quiz.q: Which four letters make up DNA?
quiz.explain: DNA is built from four bases: adenine, cytosine, guanine and thymine, written A, C, G and T.

quiz.q: What does sequence alignment do?
options: Lines up two biological sequences to measure how similar they are
quiz.explain: Alignment lines up sequences, allowing matches, mismatches and gaps, to find similarity and shared ancestry.

quiz.q: How did bioinformatics help during COVID-19?
options: It compared virus sequences to track which variants were spreading
quiz.explain: Sequencing and comparing virus genomes let scientists identify variants like Delta and Omicron and follow how they spread.

lessons.title: Advanced Cyber Security
lessons.content:
What is it? Advanced Cyber Security is about protecting big, real systems, companies, banks, governments, from serious attackers. In the BSc you learned the basics like encryption and passwords. Here you learn how real attacks happen step by step and how professionals defend, detect and respond.

Why learn it? Every digital service, from bKash to hospital records, is attacked every day. Bangladesh Bank lost 81 million dollars in a famous 2016 cyber heist. Security experts are in huge demand worldwide, and the work is like being a digital detective and a guard at the same time.

What is in the course? Usually: threat modelling, network security (firewalls, IDS/IPS), zero trust architecture, web application attacks, malware analysis, social engineering and phishing, penetration testing, digital forensics and incident response, and security standards and policies.

Threat modelling: Before defending, ask: what do we need to protect, who might attack, and how? You list your assets (customer data, money), the threats (insider, hacker, ransomware gang) and the weak points. A simple method is STRIDE, which reminds you of spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege.

Network defence: Firewalls decide which traffic is allowed in or out. An IDS (Intrusion Detection System) watches traffic and raises an alarm on suspicious patterns; an IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) also blocks them. A SIEM collects logs from everywhere so a security team can see the whole picture on one screen. Networks are also split into segments, so the public website, the staff computers and the database servers sit in separate zones. If the website is hacked, a firewall between zones stops the attacker from walking straight to the database.

Zero trust: The old idea was a castle: everything inside the office network is trusted. Zero trust says never trust any user or device automatically, always verify. Every request must prove who it is (strong login, often with multi-factor authentication), and users only get the minimum access they need. So even if an attacker gets inside, they cannot freely move around.

Web attacks: Many breaches start from websites. SQL injection means an attacker types database commands into a form field, like ' OR 1=1 --, to dump data. Cross-site scripting (XSS) sneaks malicious JavaScript into a page others will view. The fix: never trust user input, use parameterised queries and escape output. The OWASP Top 10 list ranks the most common web risks. Here is how SQL injection works: a login page may build the query "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + input + "'". If the input is ' OR 1=1 --, the condition becomes always true and the rest is commented out, so the attacker logs in without a password. A parameterised query sends the input as plain data, never as code, so the trick fails.

Malware and ransomware: Malware is bad software: viruses, worms, trojans, spyware. Ransomware encrypts your files and demands money to unlock them. Analysts study malware safely inside sandboxes (isolated computers) to learn how it works. The best protection is regular backups, updates and careful email habits. Good backups follow the 3-2-1 rule: three copies of your data, on two different kinds of storage, with one copy kept offline or in another place, so ransomware cannot reach it.

Social engineering and phishing: Often the easiest way in is tricking a human. Phishing messages pretend to be from a bank or company and ask for passwords, PINs or OTPs. An SMS saying "Your wallet is blocked, send your PIN and OTP to unlock" is classic phishing and social engineering. No real company ever asks for your PIN or OTP.

Penetration testing, forensics and incident response: Penetration testing means attacking a system with permission to find its weaknesses before real attackers do; ethical hackers write a report so the holes get fixed. When an attack does happen, incident response follows steps: prepare, detect, contain, remove the threat, recover and learn lessons. Digital forensics collects evidence, like logs and disk images, carefully so it can be used in court. A pen test usually follows phases: planning and permission, reconnaissance (collecting public information), scanning for open doors, trying to exploit them, and finally reporting with clear steps to fix each problem, ranked by risk.

Real life example 1: A bank's SIEM shows a staff computer suddenly logging in at 3 am and copying huge amounts of data. The incident response team isolates that computer from the network (contain), finds a phishing email that installed malware, removes it, resets passwords, restores from clean backups and then trains staff to spot such emails. Quick response turns a disaster into a small story.

Real life example 2: Before launching a new e-commerce site, a company hires a penetration tester. The tester finds that the search box is open to SQL injection and could reveal all customer phone numbers. Developers fix it with parameterised queries before launch, so real attackers never get the chance.

Where people get confused / exam stuff: IDS only detects, IPS also blocks. Zero trust does not mean "trust nobody so block everything"; it means verify every request. Penetration testing is legal only with written permission. Exam questions often ask: explain zero trust, define phishing with an example, describe SQL injection and its fix, list the incident response steps, or compare IDS and IPS.

After this course you can think like an attacker to defend like a pro, plan an incident response and explain modern security models. Practise legally on platforms like TryHackMe or Hack The Box. Next, explore digital forensics, cryptography and security certifications like Security+ or CEH.
key_points: Zero trust: never trust any user or device automatically, always verify.
Penetration testing attacks a system with permission to find weaknesses first.
Phishing and social engineering trick people into giving PINs, OTPs or passwords.
SQL injection and XSS come from trusting user input; fix with parameterised queries and escaping.
IDS detects attacks, IPS also blocks them; SIEM collects logs in one place.
Incident response: prepare, detect, contain, remove, recover, learn.
lessons.tip: Learn to think like an attacker, but act like a guardian. Always get written permission before testing any system.
lessons.task: Pick an app you use every day. Write down 3 ways someone might try to break into your account and one layer of defense for each, like a strong password, two factor login or not sharing an OTP.

quiz.q: What does zero trust mean?
options: Trust everyone inside the office network
Never trust any user or device automatically, always verify
quiz.explain: Zero trust assumes no user or device is safe by default, so every access request must be checked.

quiz.q: What is penetration testing?
options: Testing how strong a pen is
Breaking into any system you like
Attacking a system with permission to find its weaknesses before real attackers do
quiz.explain: Pen testing is ethical, authorized hacking whose goal is to discover and fix holes.

quiz.q: An SMS asking for your wallet PIN and OTP is an example of...
quiz.explain: It tricks a person into giving away secrets. Real services never ask for your PIN or OTP like that.

lessons.title: Wireless Sensor Networks
lessons.content:
What is it? A wireless sensor network (WSN) is a group of tiny, cheap devices called sensor nodes, spread over an area, that measure things like temperature, moisture, light, sound or movement and send the data wirelessly to a central point. Each node is like a small spy with four parts: a sensor to feel the world, a tiny processor to think, a radio to talk and a battery to stay alive. Hundreds of them working together can watch a whole forest or factory.

Why learn it? WSNs let us watch places that are hard, dangerous or expensive to watch by hand: farms, forests, rivers, bridges, volcanoes, factories and even patients' bodies. They are the eyes and ears of the Internet of Things. Designing them is a real challenge because the nodes are small, run on batteries and are often left alone for months or years. IoT engineers, embedded developers and smart agriculture and environment researchers use this knowledge every day.

What is in the course? A typical syllabus covers: node hardware and architecture, network topologies and deployment, energy saving and MAC protocols, routing protocols, clustering (like LEACH), localization (finding where nodes are), time synchronization, data aggregation, coverage and connectivity, and security for sensor networks.

Node architecture: every sensor node has a sensing unit (like a temperature or moisture sensor), a processing unit (a small microcontroller with a little memory), a radio transceiver for communication, and a power unit, usually AA batteries or a coin cell, sometimes with a small solar panel. The radio uses by far the most energy. Sending one bit can cost as much battery as running thousands of processor instructions, so it is smarter to process data on the node and send less.

Topology and multi-hop: radios on sensor nodes are weak and reach only tens of metres. So data travels hop by hop: node A sends to its neighbour B, B to C, and so on until it reaches the sink, also called the base station, which connects to the internet. It is like passing a message along a line of friends. Nodes near the sink carry everyone else's messages too, so they drain faster, a problem called the energy hole.

Energy-saving MAC protocols: the MAC (medium access control) layer decides when each node uses the radio. Keeping the radio on to listen is surprisingly expensive, even when nothing arrives. Protocols like S-MAC make nodes follow a sleep schedule: for example, awake for 10% of the time and asleep for 90%. Neighbours agree on a shared schedule so they wake up together. The duty cycle is the share of time a node is awake. A 1% duty cycle can stretch battery life from days to years.

Routing: routing decides which path data takes to the sink. The shortest path is not always best, because it may run through a node with almost no battery left. Energy-aware routing picks paths that balance remaining battery. Flooding, where every node forwards everything to everyone, is simple but wastes energy. Directed diffusion lets the sink send out an "interest", like "I want temperature from the north side", and only the matching nodes answer along reinforced paths.

Clustering and LEACH: instead of every node talking to the sink, nodes form groups. Each group has a cluster head that collects data from its members, combines it, and sends one summary to the sink. LEACH (Low Energy Adaptive Clustering Hierarchy) rotates the cluster head role randomly every round, because being cluster head is the hardest job, so rotating spreads the battery drain fairly. Data aggregation helps too: if 10 nodes report 30, 31, 30, 29..., the cluster head sends only the average, 30.

Localization and time sync: a temperature reading is useless if you do not know where it came from. GPS on every node is too expensive and power hungry, so only a few anchor nodes have known positions. Other nodes estimate their location by measuring distance to anchors (from signal strength or timing) and using trilateration: if you know your distance to 3 known points, there is only one place you can be. Nodes also need synchronised clocks so events can be ordered correctly, using protocols that exchange timestamps.

Coverage, connectivity and security: coverage means every spot in the area is watched by at least one sensor. Connectivity means every node can still reach the sink. Both need enough nodes placed well, plus a few extras in case some die. Security is hard because nodes are cheap and can be stolen, and there is little power for heavy encryption. Lightweight encryption and checking that messages really come from trusted nodes protect against fake data being injected.

Real life example 1, a tea garden in Sylhet: step 1, sensor nodes are buried at different spots across the hills, each measuring soil moisture every hour. Step 2, each node wakes up, takes a reading, sends it to its cluster head and goes back to sleep. Step 3, cluster heads average their group's readings and pass them hop by hop to a gateway near the office. Step 4, the gateway uploads data to a server. Step 5, when one section drops below 20% moisture, the manager gets a phone alert and waters only that part. Water is saved and nobody walks the whole hill every day.

Real life example 2, flood warning on a river: water level sensors on poles along a river measure height every 10 minutes. Nodes far from town pass readings downstream node to node to a base station in the town. If the level rises faster than a set limit, the base station sends SMS alerts to people living nearby, giving them hours to move family and cattle to safety. Small, cheap nodes can do a job that once needed people standing by the river all night.

Where students get confused: many think the processor uses the most energy, but the radio is the real battery killer. Students also confuse coverage (every place is sensed) with connectivity (every node can reach the sink). Typical exam questions: explain why multi-hop saves energy, describe how LEACH works and why the cluster head rotates, compute battery lifetime from a duty cycle, explain trilateration with a diagram, and compare flooding with directed diffusion.

Wrap-up: after this course you can design a sensor network, pick protocols that make batteries last for years, and think clearly about coverage, location and security. It connects directly with the Internet of Things and Embedded Systems. Next, try building a tiny network yourself with a couple of cheap microcontroller boards and sensors.
key_points: A WSN is many small battery powered sensor nodes sending data wirelessly to a sink.
The radio uses the most energy, so process locally and send less.
Data travels hop by hop; sleep schedules and low duty cycles save battery.
LEACH rotates the cluster head role so no node dies early; aggregation sends summaries.
Localization uses anchor nodes and trilateration; clocks must be synchronised.
Coverage, connectivity and lightweight security are key design goals.
lessons.tip: Whenever you read a protocol, ask one question: how does this save battery? That single question explains most design choices in WSN.
lessons.task: Draw a map of your school or neighbourhood. Mark where you would place 6 sensor nodes to measure air quality, and draw arrows showing how the data could hop to one base station.

quiz.q: What is usually the biggest limit of a sensor node?
options: Number of colours it can show
quiz.explain: Nodes run on small batteries for months, so almost every WSN design is about saving energy.

quiz.q: Where does the data from sensor nodes finally go?
options: It stays in each node forever
To the sink, or base station
quiz.explain: Nodes pass data hop by hop until it reaches the sink, which connects to the outside world.

quiz.q: Why does LEACH rotate the cluster head role?
options: To make the network look colourful
So one node doesn't drain its battery early
quiz.explain: The cluster head works hardest, so rotating the role spreads the energy cost across nodes.

lessons.title: MSc Thesis
lessons.content:
What is it? An MSc thesis is your own research project, where you pick a real unanswered question, try to answer it with experiments or analysis, and write it all down in a long, careful document. It is like the final boss of your MSc: everything you learned comes together here.

Why do it? A thesis proves you can do independent research, not just learn what others found. It is very important if you want a PhD, a research job, or a university teaching post. Even in industry, the skills, finding a problem, testing ideas honestly and explaining results clearly, make you stand out.

What is in the process? Usually: choosing a topic and supervisor, literature review, finding the research gap and question, methodology, experiments and data collection, analysis of results, writing the thesis chapters, citations and avoiding plagiarism, and finally the defence presentation.

Choosing a topic and supervisor: Pick something you actually enjoy, because you will live with it for a year. Talk to a supervisor whose research matches your interest. A good topic is narrow, doable with your time and resources, and useful. "Improve AI" is too big; "detect sentiment in Bangla and Banglish mixed text" is just right.

Literature review: Before doing anything new, you read what others have already done. You collect papers from Google Scholar, IEEE and ACM, read their abstracts, and note methods, datasets and results. The point of a literature review is learning what others have already done so you can find the gap your work fills. Keep a table: paper, method, dataset, result, weakness. Read smart, not hard: first read only the title and abstract, then the conclusion and figures, and only read the full paper if it is really close to your topic. Thirty well-summarised papers are worth more than a hundred half-read ones.

Research gap and research question: The gap is what is still missing, for example, "existing sentiment tools work in pure Bangla but fail on mixed Bangla-Banglish Facebook comments". Then you write a clear, testable question: "Can a model trained on mixed Bangla and Banglish text detect sentiment better than existing tools?". A good question is specific and can be answered with evidence.

Methodology: This is your plan for answering the question. What data will you use, how will you collect and clean it, what model or method will you build, what will you compare against (baselines), and how will you measure success (accuracy, F1 score, time)? A clear methodology lets another researcher repeat your work. Also think about ethics in your method. If you use people's data, like Facebook comments or GPS traces, remove names and personal details, and get approval or consent where it is needed.

Experiments and results: Now you actually run things. Keep a log of every experiment, setting and result, because you will forget. Report results honestly, including the ones that did not work. Use tables and graphs, and check whether improvements are real or just luck, using repeated runs or statistical tests. Split your data properly: train on one part, tune on a validation part and report final numbers on a test part the model never saw. Testing on training data gives fake, too-good results, and examiners catch it fast.

Writing and citations: A typical thesis has chapters: Introduction, Literature Review, Methodology, Results and Discussion, Conclusion and Future Work, plus References. Write a bit every week instead of all at the end. Always cite every source you use; copying text or ideas without credit is plagiarism and can cancel your degree. Tools like Zotero or Mendeley manage references for you. A simple weekly plan helps a lot: month 1 to 2 reading, month 3 to 4 method and data, month 5 to 8 experiments, month 9 to 10 writing, and the last two months for revision and defence practice. Share drafts with your supervisor early, not on the last day.

Defence: At the end, you present your work to a board of teachers who ask questions. Prepare clear slides: problem, gap, method, results, limitations. Practise answering "why did you choose this?" and "what are the weaknesses?". Honest answers about limitations impress examiners more than pretending your work is perfect.

Real life example 1: Rafi wants to help farmers. He reads 30 papers on plant disease detection and finds that most datasets use foreign crops, not Bangladeshi rice. His gap: no good dataset for local rice leaf diseases. He collects 5,000 photos from fields in Mymensingh, trains a deep learning model, compares it with existing models and shows his works better on local images. He publishes a paper and later builds a mobile app.

Real life example 2: Nusrat studies traffic in Dhaka. Her question: "Can GPS data from ride-sharing apps predict traffic jams 15 minutes ahead?". She gets anonymised data, builds a model, and honestly reports that it works well on main roads but poorly on small lanes. That limitation becomes the "future work" section, and the next student picks it up.

Where people get confused / exam stuff: Many students choose a topic that is too big, start writing too late or skip the literature review. Some hide failed experiments, but honest reporting is required. Copy-pasting from papers, even with small changes, counts as plagiarism. Supervisors and examiners often ask: what is your research gap, why this method, how did you evaluate it, what are the limitations and what is the contribution?

After your thesis you will know how to do real research from start to finish: ask a sharp question, test it fairly and explain it clearly. Try to publish your work at a conference or journal. If you enjoyed it, a PhD or research job could be your next step.
key_points: A literature review shows what others have done so you can find the gap your work fills.
A good research question is specific, testable and answerable with evidence.
Methodology explains data, method, baselines and how success is measured.
Report results honestly, including what did not work.
Always cite every source; copying without credit is plagiarism.
In the defence, clearly explain the gap, method, results and limitations.
lessons.tip: Start small and specific. A sharp question you can actually finish beats a giant question you can only start.
lessons.task: Write down 3 problems you've noticed around you that technology could help with. For each, turn it into a one line research question that starts with: Can we... or How well does...

quiz.q: What is a literature review for?
options: Learning what others have already done so you can find the gap your work fills
quiz.explain: Reviewing existing research shows what's known and where the open question is, so your work adds something new.

quiz.q: Which is the better thesis question?
options: Can a model trained on mixed Bangla and Banglish text detect sentiment better than existing tools?
How do we solve all of AI?
quiz.explain: A good research question is specific, testable and doable in the time you have.

quiz.q: What must you always do in a thesis?
options: Copy text from papers without citing
Report results honestly and cite every source you use
quiz.explain: Research integrity is the foundation. Honest results and proper citations keep your work trustworthy.
